News.title: Word of the year 2026 is named — after massive boom in popularity
News.content:
Word of the year 2026 is named — after massive boom in popularity

'Maxxing' has been named word of the year for 2026 by one of the internet's most visited dictionary websites after use of the youth slang term soared by over 1,000%

View 3 Images A top online dictionary has named 'maxxing' its word of the year (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

One of the world's most visited dictionary websites has named 'maxxing' as the word of the year.

‌



‌



The internet slang phrase — which means to do more of something — emerged as Dictionary.com's top word for 2026 after being chosen by lexicographers.

‌



It is typically used as a suffix — such as in 'tokenmaxxing', which involves using AI to make workplace tasks easier, the more self-explanatory 'sleepmaxxing', and 'cosymaxxing', making your home a more relaxing environment.

‌



The term has also been linked to more harmful trends, such as 'looksmaxxing', in which young men carry out extreme DIY cosmetic procedures in a bid to enhance their physical appearance.

View 3 Images Use of the term 'maxxing' increased by over 1000% this year (Image: Dictionary.com)

London residents call for further change after Oxford Street transforms READ MORE :

DWP to ban 4 benefits including state pension for certain crimes - list READ MORE :

Dictionary.com bosses said 'maxxing' was chosen because of its boom in popularity — with web searches and overall usage for the term increasing by 1,000% this year — as well as its versatility, having been widely used for a variety of contexts.

‌



Steve Johnson, the director of lexicography for Dictionary Media Group, told US media: "Maxxing really stood out this year because not only was it everywhere, in all types of articles, but it crossed a lot of different domains."

Other terms on the websites Word of the Year Shortlist included 'affordability', reflecting pressures on consumers across the world, and 'data centre', the fiercely-debated facilities used for AI servers.

‌



Another word on the runners-up list was 'unc', a slang term with origins in African American vernacular used to described someone as old, or out-of-touch.

View 3 Images 'Data centre' was a runner-up owing to the fierce debate over the large AI facilities (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Previous winners of Word of the Year

Last year's Dictionary.com word of the year was in fact a number - '67', the viral dance trend which spread across the world after becoming popular among US sports fans.

News.title: Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, who led Epstein prosecution, judge rules
News.content:
Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, who led Epstein prosecution, judge rules

Maurene Comey is the daughter of former FBI boss James Comey - someone who Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy

View 2 Images A judge has found the Trump administration illegally fire Maurene Comey (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

The Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, who led the Epstein prosecution, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge has ruled.

‌



‌



Maurene Comey, who was an assistant US attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation's highest-profile cases - also including the Sean 'Diddy' Combs prosecution - and consistently receiving "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found.

‌



After her firing, Comey sued the Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.

‌



View 2 Images Maurene Comey was a federal prosecutor in New York (Image: AP)

She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.

Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" powers.

‌



He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."

Furman added: "Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system."

‌



The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled.

The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through December 20 to "make her whole" and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the "unlawful termination."

‌



Comey's lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.

"This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," they said in a statement. "As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power `would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system.' This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."

‌



The Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration's agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.

‌



The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father's longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.

The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican's successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.

Article continues below

An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

News.title: Man, 38, 'murdered by gang with weapons' as police swarm Leeds streets
News.content:
Man, 38, 'murdered by gang with weapons' as police swarm Leeds streets

A huge cordon is in place in the New Wortley area of Leeds after a man was the victim of a 'targeted' attack thought to be carried out by four people

Cordon erected in New Wortley area of Leeds as murder investigation launched

A man has died after he was "attacked with weapons" in Leeds with police launching a murder investigation.

‌



‌



A huge cordon remains in place in the New Wortley area of Leeds after the attack was reported to police on Saturday just before 10.30pm. West Yorkshire Police said the report concerned a man being attacked with weapons outside a property on Hedley Chase.

‌



Despite treatment by paramedics, the 38-year-old victim was pronounced dead a short time later. Yorkshire Live reports that a large police presence remains in the area, including at an open space between Holforth Gardens and Oak Road.

‌



View Image Police pictured at the scene in New Wortley (Image: Leeds Live/MEN MEDIA)

Body of woman found on Rhyl beach as police probe 'unexpected' death READ MORE :

A footpath there has been closed off with several police officers guarding the scene. It is thought four people were involved in the "targeted" attack but no one has yet been identified by the police.

‌



Detective Chief Inspector Dan Bates said: "A man has tragically lost his life, and we are supporting his family at this tragic time. From initial reports, we understand that four people who were armed with weapons, carried out a sustained attack on the victim.

"We are working extremely hard to identify those individuals. We have significant resources working to get answers for his family and ensure that those responsible face justice for their actions.

Article continues below

"This was a targeted and isolated attack; we are appealing for any information to who may have been involved to come forward and provide details to us."

News.title: Nigel Farage and Robert Jenrick face rows of empty seats as big speech falls flat
News.content:
Nigel Farage and Robert Jenrick face rows of empty seats as big speech falls flat

Nigel Farage and Robert Jenrick were forced to face rows of empty seats as they set out a limp package of rehashed plans ahead of John Healey's Budget

View 2 Images Nigel Farage and Robert Jenrick were forced to face rows of empty seats (Image: Stefan Rousseau/Press Association)

Nigel Farage and Robert Jenrick were forced to face rows of empty seats as they set out a limp package of rehashed plans ahead of the Budget.

‌



‌



The Reform UK leader was seen pacing around a balcony and appearing to sigh as he watched Mr Jenrick, his Shadow Chancellor, deliver Reform’s so-called economic rescue plan on the floor below. He was filmed failing to laugh as his Reform colleague joked that he might watch former BBC show Cash in the Attic instead of Chancellor John Healey's Budget on Wednesday.

‌



Ahead of the speech, guests who had attended were moved to seats behind the podium to make it appear the hall was full behind Mr Farage and Mr Jenrick when they appeared on TV. The miserable turnout marked another sign of Reform’s sliding popularity, after a poll by Ipsos this weekend put Labour on 32%, the Tories on 24% and Reform on 20%.

‌



Asked about the poor attendance in the grand Lindley Hall in Westminster, Mr Farage blamed “staff incompetence” and admitted business leaders were probably too busy to attend. He told reporters: “As for this hall, well, staff incompetence. It's all well and good advertising to businesses, but on Mondays, people who run businesses tend to be rather busy.

"For those who are here, it's going to have cost them a very great deal of money to have driven up here today to come visit us here in London. As you know, our party conferences etc, we get crowds like no other British political party has done in modern times."

Reform 'newspaper' sent to millions features councillor who called for mosque ban and praised Tommy Robinson READ MORE :

View 2 Images Farage admitted business leaders were probably too busy to attend (Image: Stefan Rousseau/Press Association)

‌



After a clip online showed Mr Farage pacing around during Mr Jenrick's speech, a Labour source said: "We can only hope the crickets in the room enjoyed it as much as Nigel clearly did." And a party spokesman added: “No wonder Reform’s press conference was full of empty seats - nobody is going to listen to them until they start to deal with the sleaze and scandal engulfing their party." A Conservative Party spokesman added: “It must be cringingly embarrassing for Farage and Jenrick to be forced to address a half-empty room."

Ahead of John Healey’s Budget on Wednesday, Mr Farage’s party is scrambling to set out eye-catching and controversial announcements as it battles sinking poll ratings. Among proposals, Reform wants to reverse a ban on new drilling for oil and gas, prohibit consideration of carbon emissions in individual planning applications and abolish the energy profits levy.

‌



They also want to scrap the Renters' Rights Act and revoke the future homes standard, which requires new homes to be low-carbon and energy efficient to help reach Net Zero but also to stop Brits freezing in poorly insulated homes.

Simon Francis, coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, branded the package a "wish list" for fossil fuel campaigners. He told The Mirror: "This isn't a serious set of policies to bring down energy bills. Rather it is a wish list dreamt up by fossil fuel lobbyists. This is the industry that has made more than £125billion in UK profits since 2020 as households have seen their bills rise.

‌



"Scrapping the Energy Profits Levy will just hand oil and gas giants a tax cut while approving more oil and gas fields won’t take a penny off bills when the gas is sold at global prices. What is more, axing energy efficiency rules for rented homes, the Future Homes Standard and the Renters’ Rights Act means more families will be trapped in cold, damp homes for decades to come."

Elsewhere during the press conference, Mr Farage - whose party received a record £72million in two £36m sums from crypto billionaires last month - defended Reform's policy to slash capital gains tax on cryptocurrency assets from 24% to 10%.

Article continues below

Asked if it was still Reform's policy, the Reform leader insisted he wanted to bring crypto under regulatory control, but added: "I want a tax rate that makes people declare what their income is."

News.title: Meghan Markle's dad brands sex offender allegations 'sick lies' as police reveal new details
News.content:
Meghan Markle's dad brands sex offender allegations 'sick lies' as police reveal new details

Thomas Markle Sr's son has accused his father of possessing child abuse material, which he said he has passed onto Philippine investigators - who have launched a probe

View 6 Images Thomas Markle Sr has been accused of possessing child abuse material (Image: Channel 5)

A minister in the nation where Meghan Markle's dad is being investigated over alleged child abuse images says that pending forensic analysis "the signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind."

‌



‌



Thomas Markle Sr, the 82-year-old dad of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was allegedly in possession of child sex images, according to his son, Thomas Markle Jr. The images were left in storage boxes and uncovered when he moved out of a property in Cebu, the Philippines, Markle Jr claimed. He said he reported his dad to the police when he found the material earlier this year. Markle Sr has denied the claims, dubbing them "sick lies", but local officials are now investigating the dad, the country's interior minister has said early signs point to him being a "possible sex offender".

‌



View 6 Images Markle Sr is the father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex (Image: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP)

‌



Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine interior minister, said authorities would be considering "all the angles" but revealed his early impression. He told the Guardian: "In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles. "Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week."

Remulla's comments came as it was alleged a letter sent to the Metropolitan Police in 2019 contained similar claims.

View 6 Images Markle has denied all the claims against him (Image: ITV)

‌



While he has denied ever abusing any children aged under 18, the former Hollywood lighting director admitted to paying for sex with prostitutes while he lived in the Philippines. Thomas Jr, who said he packed four boxes of material to take to investigators, insisted his dad is "still in denial".

View 6 Images Mr Markle Jr said he packed boxes of evidence to bring to the police (Image: Channel 5)

‌



It is thought that, among the inventory were surrendered computers, DVDs, mobile phones, books, pictures, data cards, film negatives and video tapes, The Sun claimed. The inventory is said to include around 80 separate item listings, among them computer files and document evidence, which has been signed over to police. Both Mr Markle Jr and his sister, the Duchess of Sussex, have ended contact with their father, with his royal daughter reportedly ceasing contact with her father last year. Sources close to the duchess said Meghan had warned Markle Sr in a letter that he would never meet his two grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet. The letter was sent to her dad as he recovered in a Philippine hospital after having his leg amputated.

View 6 Images Mr Markle Jr has also broken contact with his father (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The duchess, who has been estranged from her father since 2018, is said to have been told by UK police about claims of abuse against him in 2019. She has since said, via a statement issued by her husband, Prince Harry, that she was left "deeply distressed" by the allegations against her father. She said last week: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

View 6 Images The Duchess of Sussex cut contact with her father in 2018

Article continues below

"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. "It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated." It is understood that the Metropolitan Police is not currently investigating Markle Sr, and has not done so in the past.

News.title: 'I'm a doctor and doing 1 thing for 30 seconds will dramatically reduce risk of falling'
News.content:
'I'm a doctor and doing 1 thing for 30 seconds will dramatically reduce risk of falling'

Falls can be a serious risk for older people, potential leading to serious injury, and even a trip to hospital. One doctor has explained an easy exercise you can do which will help reduce your risk

View 2 Images Falls can be extremely serious for older people (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

A part of getting older is having to be more conscious of your health. And one thing we have to be especially aware of as we reach our later years is falls.

‌



‌



While children and young people can quite happily bounce right back up again after a fall, for older folk it can cause serious issues, and even injury. So it's important that, as we get older, we make sure to keep ourselves upright and balanced. Now one TV doctor has explained how you can do just that.

‌



Dr Amir Khan, who is a familiar face on programmes such as ITV's Lorraine and Good Morning Britain, recently posted a video on TikTok explaining five essential health tips for people aged older than 35. Among them is to train your balance every day - and Dr Khan explained a simple way you can do that.

‌



How to train your balance daily

"We need to all be doing this," he said. "Train your balance daily. Balance relies on your cerebellum, inner ear, and tiny sensors in your muscles called proprioceptors. These systems decline after 35 unless you challenge them.

"Thirty seconds standing on one leg while brushing your teeth is a really good way to train it, and train your core coordination and brain-body signalling. It dramatically reduces future fall and injury risk. So tonight, when you're brushing your teeth, do it on one leg."

View 2 Images Dr Amir Khan is often seen on ITV's Lorraine and Good Morning Britain (file image) (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

‌



Dr Khan also outlined four other tips, saying each would "genuinely can change how you age".

Getting some light in the morning

"After 35, your circadian rhythm becomes a little less responsive," he said. "So five minutes of outdoor morning light hits receptors in the back of your eyes and it sends signals to your brain's master clock. That resets cortisol timing, boosts energy, improve sleep pressure at night, and even stabilises appetite hormones. It's the most powerful free tool we have."

‌



The circadian rhythm is your internal clock which signals to your body when to sleep and when to wake up. It also governs processes such as digestion and hormones. Cortisol regulates stress hormones.

Boost the amount of oxygen you can take in

The maximum rate of oxygen your body can take in is known as VO2 max. It can be used as a measure of fitness - the more oxygen you can absorb during exercise, the better, and Dr Khan called it "one of the strongest predictors of our health". "As we age, our heart becomes slightly less efficient at pumping blood and our mitochondria become less efficient at using oxygen," he said.

‌



"So, short bursts of intensity, such as 20 to 40 seconds of fast stairs, a brisk uphill walk, or a quick cycle sprint, forces your muscles to demand more oxygen than usual, and that stimulates new mitochondria and improves oxygen extraction." Dr Khan added: "So you don't need HIIT (high-intensity interval training) classes every day, just a moment each day where your heart genuinely rises."

‌



Check your blood pressure at home

Continuing, Dr Khan said: "Blood pressure creeps up quietly as your arteries stiffen with age. Checking it, say, once a month at rest gives you a baseline. If it's higher than 135 over 85 at home, do daily readings for a week and work out the average. If that's high, speak to your doctor. That average is what predicts your stroke and heart attack risk, not one random reading. And catching it early can make all the difference."

Blood pressure readings are displayed as two numbers - the first is the pressure in your arteries when your heart contracts and pumps blood, the second is the pressure when your heart rests between beats. Home blood pressure monitors are available from pharmacies or online.

‌



Build muscles and bones

For his final tip, Dr Khan said: "From your mid-30s onwards, you slowly lose muscle fibres and bone density. Strength and impact exercises send mechanical signals through your muscles and bones, what we call mechanotransduction.

"Your body responds by building them back stronger. This protects metabolism, joint stability, glucose control and long term fracture risk. So get them in twice a week."

News.title: 'I moved 6,000 miles to country with 30C November temperatures - and found incredible bonus'
News.content:
'I moved 6,000 miles to country with 30C November temperatures - and found incredible bonus'

Retiree Luis swapped Spain for Thailand, where he enjoys warm weather, low household bills and a relaxed pace of life after building a home for £16,700 on his Thai wife's land

View 3 Images Luis says he built a house for less than £17,000 (Image: Sergio Castillo/YouTube)

Warm weather, affordable living and a slower pace of life have made moving from Europe to a country 6,000 miles away a rewarding choice for one pensioner. Luis, 68, left Spain to spend his retirement in Thailand, a country some 6,000 miles away where November temperatures reach 30C.

‌



‌



He says he built his home for just 20,000 euros (£16,700) on land belonging to his Thai wife. He told YouTuber Sergio Castillo Calderon: "With 20,000 euros (£16,700), you can build yourself a house and live a peaceful life."

‌



Luis lives in Isan, in the north-east of the country, away from tourist hotspots such as Bangkok, Phuket and Ko Samui, reports the Express.

‌



The savings extend beyond the cost of building his home. His monthly electricity bill comes to roughly 60 euros, or about £50, helping keep his day-to-day expenses down.

Ensure our latest world news headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings

But for Luis, the appeal of his new life goes well beyond money. He values the local sense of community and enjoys a gentler routine, without the urgency he felt back in Europe.

‌



View 3 Images Luis moved to the less touristy region of Isan (Image: Getty Images)

His day can begin as early as 3.30am or 4am, when he makes coffee and sits on the porch. He then takes his dogs for a walk and decides how to spend his time.

‌



There is no alarm clock, and no traffic updates or urgent phone notifications interrupting his peace. He has even chosen to do without a television.

He said: "You realise that many things weren't as important as you once thought. I don't even have a TV. It's more relaxing this way.

‌



"Here, no one honks their horn, no one shoves you. If something doesn't go as planned, it's no big deal."

View 3 Images Luis is loving life in Thailand (Image: Sergio Castillo/YouTube)

‌



The warm climate is another draw. Thailand enjoys warm temperatures throughout the year, with average monthly highs ranging from 29C in December to 37C in April. However, anyone considering a move should also bear in mind the rainy season, which typically runs from May to October and peaks in September and October.

There are other practical considerations, too. Luis built his house on his wife's land, and foreigners face restrictions on land ownership in Thailand. Understanding the local rules is essential before making plans to relocate.

Article continues below

His move has also brought a healthcare hurdle: he admits he has struggled to secure private medical insurance because of his medical history.

Luis acknowledges, however, that his move to Thailand hasn't been entirely plain sailing. The retiree admits he has struggled to secure private medical insurance owing to his medical history.

News.title: Donald Trump is facing a humiliating Midterms defeat and the stakes for the UK are serious
News.content:
Donald Trump is facing a humiliating Midterms defeat and the stakes for the UK are serious

But this isn't just a local - or even a national election. The choices American voters make in this election will have repercussions around the world for global security, trade and the future of America's relationship with the world

View Image Trump's Republicans are in for a shoeing - here's why you should care (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

A croaky-sounding Donald Trump, 80, is on the road, holding rallies across America in a vain bid to swerve his most humiliating defeat since 2020.

‌



‌



Trump's approval rating is historically poor - hitting an all time low of 36% last week. Partly as a result of his being deeply, deeply unpopular, his Republican Party is likely to suffer crushing losses in both the House of Representatives and Senate - with Democrats expected to take control of one or both houses of Congress.

‌



All 435 House seats - the equivalent of the House of Commons - as well as 35 senate seats - their upper chamber, like an elected, more powerful House of Lords - are up for grabs on Tuesday.

‌



But this isn't just a local - or even a national election. The choices American voters make in this election will have repercussions around the world for global security, trade and the future of America's relationship with the world.

Losing control of both houses would theoretically limit Trump's power, leaving him open to more targeted scrutiny, investigations and even impeachment.

For more of our coverage of Trump's America: Subscribe to The Trump Desk on YouTube

Subscribe to the US Dispatch - our weekly newsletter exclusively for Mirror+ readers - following all the gossip and intrigue from Trump's DC swamp

- following all the gossip and intrigue from Trump's DC swamp Follow Mikey Smith on Twitter, TikTok, Bluesky or Facebook.

‌



Congress controls the purse strings of government - with most large budget spending approved by them - and trade agreements and tariffs subject to their scrutiny. Trump was able to introduce his maniacal tariff plan because the Republican-controlled Congress didn't stop him.

Any chink in Trump's armour, any limit on his ability to do whatever he wants, puts Andy Burnham in a better negotiating position. It's much easier to negotiate with a tiger if it's lost a few of its teeth. Still dangerous, but a little less of a hopeless case.

‌



Similarly, losing control of America's money could limit what Trump can do militarily. Congress is currently deadlocked on approving a $1.5 trillion military budget in 2027, a 40% increase on this year - and it's unlikely to get any closer to approval with fewer Senators on his side.

Is Congress going to be able to insist Trump back away from siding with Russia over Ukraine? No. Can it order him to withdraw from Iran and leave Cuba alone? Again no.

‌



Congress can't make Trump change his international obsessions. But it can make pursuing some of those obsessions more difficult.

All of that being said, Trump has never been one for following the rules if he can get away with it - and there are growing fears he'll increasingly ignore Congress if it tries to stand in the way of what he wants.

‌



He's already tried to do this during his second term. His tariff plan was imposed through executive order, as was his bid to scrap birthright citizenship - the guarantee of citizenship to any child born in the United States.

Both were challenged or stuck down by the Supreme Court - but neither should have got anywhere near that far.

‌



He overstepped his authority by clawing back funds from approved projects he doesn't like, by firing officials without good reason and by trying to deploy National Guard troops to states like Tennessee, Illinois and California over the objection of Governors.

And many Democrats are deeply uncomfortable with trusting a Trump-appointee-stuffed Supreme Court to defend American democracy.

‌



Trump's authoritarian shenanigans will almost certainly start on election night. He's already laid the groundwork to challenge and undermine the result and cry foul if Republicans suffer the heavy losses the polls predict.

Donald Trump likes power, and strongly dislikes others having power over him. Moreover, he hates to look like a loser.

Article continues below

And we only have to look back to January 6th, 2021 to see what happens when Donald Trump loses.

News.title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder.

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

News.title: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
News.content:
In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.

By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.

Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.

A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.

For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.

The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.

And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

News.title: Drivers who killed mum and girl while racing jailed
News.content:
Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.

Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023.

At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years.

Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind.

Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him.

The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash.

Prosecutors said Riyat's BMW reached speeds of up to 89mph in the 40mph zone before Bhachu lost control of his Audi, mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter.

News.title: Storm Boelo leaves 22,000 without power as Met Office issues new wind warning
News.content:
A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties are still without power as of Monday afternoon.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.

The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

News.title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around
News.content:
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.

Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.

Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."

By contrast, Holzhacker argues that FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.

Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.

"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."

In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.

"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.

She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."

Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.

In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.

"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

News.title: What is walking down the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street like?
News.content:
Almost a kilometre of London's Oxford Street, a famous shopping area in the heart of the capital, is now pedestrian-only.

The first phase of the major overhaul is expected to be finished by spring 2027.

London Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan said the move marked the "end of decline" for the street.

"We will have a great lead up to Christmas, safe and spacious, and next year you'll be seeing more trees and seats and public squares", the mayor said.

BBC reporter Graham Satchell went to Oxford Street's pedestrian-only section for a stroll.

News.title: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
News.content:
The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.

More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.

The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.

Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.

The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.

Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".

The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.

Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

News.title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
News.content:
Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.

Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".

But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.

He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."

"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.

"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."

She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

News.title: Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears
News.content:
A former personal assistant of Russell Brand has told a court she was instructed to get phone numbers for the entertainer from female fans when she first started working with him.

Helen Berger, who worked closely with Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, said the request "felt uncomfortable" and, after seeking advice, she told the TV personality that she would not do that anymore.

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

Brand had an "insane sexual appetite", Berger told Southwark Crown Court in a written statement on Monday.

Berger left her job with Brand after she became "sick of him", she said. She added that he had sex with numerous women during the time she was his assistant.

She described a work environment where Brand would ask her if he could "go and have sex now" when frustrated with a particular task.

Berger added that she never "witnessed anything against the law" but that "everyone normalised and dismissed his behaviour" so it "made me think it was accepted."

She told the court that "peacock" Brand found random women online to satisfy his "insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night", but sex often made him depressed.

She told the court Brand used MySpace to find women for sex, and said: "At his house, women often came over and it was clear they were there for sex."

She recalled once finding a female celebrity asleep in Brand's bed while he was wandering around the house half-dressed, and said of the comedian: "He was like a peacock, women would always approach him."

Russell Brand's defence team says any sexual activity was consensual and accounts have been twisted in the light of a defamatory TV documentary in 2023 which made allegations of sexual abuse against the entertainer.

The prosecution is due to finish on Tuesday morning.

News.title: Army officer killed by reversing Warrior with faulty alarm - inquest
News.content:
The armoured vehicle was stationary for between 38 and 43 seconds after the collision, the inquest heard, as soldiers shouted "wait" and horns sounded.

A stop call was sent at 10:25, which halted the exercise.

A built-in alarm system, which would have sounded a noise and shown a light to indicate the rear doors were open, did not work as a wire was broken, the inquest was told.

Col Watson said: "The built-in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped."

Alarms had been installed on Warriors after two fatal incidents in the 1990s.

Col Watson said several faults with the armoured vehicles were known about, but he told the inquest that these had not meant the vehicle should have been taken out of service.

The inquest also heard the FV-511model involved in the incident was not ordinarily used for disembarking troops and close combat.

"The student commander had done the majority of his training on the FV-510, which is the platoon variant of the vehicle," Col Watson said.

"In general, the crew and service personnel within 5 Rifles were not that familiar with the FV-511 and its differences with the FV-510."

News.title: Daughter wins £127k claim for caring for mum at home
News.content:
A woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid Â£127k from her mother's estate for caring for her in her final years.

Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which led to her facing criminal charges.

Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.

The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern Â£127,500 for care provided.

News.title: Consultant doctors in England to strike next month
News.content:
Consultant doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and working conditions.

The walkout will begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only.

This is known as Christmas Day cover and is likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services.

The announcement comes after talks had been taking place with the government over the past month, following the vote in favour of strike action by British Medical Association members in July.

Consultants â the most senior doctors in hospitals â were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.

But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account.

The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken.

News.title: Knighting Sinfield 'easiest decision anyone's had to make,' says Prince William
News.content:
The Prince of Wales has said awarding a knighthood to rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield "was probably the easiest decision anyone's ever had to make".

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Prince William spoke about his personal admiration for Sir Kevin, who recently completed seven ultra marathons in seven days.

It was his latest endurance challenge to raise money for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities following the death of his friend and former team-mate, Rob Burrow, from the condition in 2024.

"I think frankly he should have been Sir Kevin years ago," said Prince William.

"What Kevin does, is he can bind and glue communities together by being that leader. The more Kevs we have in this country the better."

The Prince and Princess of Wales were in Wakefield in West Yorkshire last month to see for themselves just how gruelling the seven ultramarathon challenge was.

William and Catherine surprised Sir Kevin as he completed the third of the marathons.

"I don't know how he keeps going, I'm worried about his knees, I'm worried about his hips. The guy is just a machine," Prince William told the BBC.

News.title: 'The storm didn't ruin our wedding, it made it'
News.content:
A couple whose wedding day coincided with Storm Boelo said last-minute changes caused by the weather did not ruin their day, "it made it".

Leigh and Paul Hutchinson had planned to surprise their wedding guests with a glass of fizz at the top of Blackpool Tower, but high winds forced the venue to close the area.

Instead, staff arranged a private bar on the upper balcony of the Tower Ballroom and later cleared the dance floor so the newlyweds could share their first dance there.

"They did something really special for us," Leigh said. "It made the day so much more than we could have ever imagined."

The couple met 10 years ago and decided they wanted a low-key wedding at the chapel next door to The Beach House where they met.

Leigh said: "It was just going to be us. A quick wedding and a meal with family afterwards. So it spiralled to say the least."

News.title: Photos show potholes days before fatal crash
News.content:
Newly released photographs show a road riddled with potholes just days before a speeding car struck one and plunged into a river, killing two teenagers.

A VW Polo driven by Declan Berry was travelling at about 90mph (145km/h) moments before it entered the River Nene on North Brink, near Wisbech, Cambridgeshire, on 17 March, killing him and one of his passengers.

Four days earlier, Cambridgeshire County Council had ordered repairs to 98 potholes along the road, with the work scheduled to start on 3 April.

The authority said repairs to that section of North Brink had been "scheduled in line with our normal maintenance processes and response times".

News.title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
News.content:
Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.

Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a Â£442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.

Ahead of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further Â£432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.

Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.

The government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will either be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas or will have been offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.

Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to Â£874m.

Burnham told ITV's Good Morning Britain he was confident it could be done, saying: "I have this strong feeling about putting the right standards at the heart of the country again and we can't get to a position where we just become used to walking past people sleeping rough: it's about care for people."

He added: "In the end, actually, it's cheaper to do that than to leave people sleeping rough going in and out of A&E, that's not good for anybody."

News.title: How Joe Marchant is relishing his ‘surreal’ England return
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The old wooden walls and somewhat dated soft furnishings of England’s 19th-century Surrey training base may be unchanged but Joe Marchant could not shake a surreal feeling when he strolled back in to Pennyhill Park on Sunday. When the centre last left the hotel in August of 2023, he was embarking on twin French adventures: first to a World Cup where he emerged as one of England’s most reliable and important performers; then to a three-season stint with Stade Francais in the Top 14 after leaving Harlequins.

“I think surreal is a good word for it,” Marchant smiles after earning a first recall to the England squad following his summer move to Sale. “I’ve had loads of good memories here, loads of times where I have been in camp just fighting to get my place.

open image in gallery Joe Marchant made his return to English rugby with Sale Sharks this summer ( Getty )

“A lot has changed, especially the faces. That’s the big one walking into camp, there are a lot of lads that I’ve only seen on TV. I didn’t even play a game in England while I was in France. I’ve enjoyed getting to know all the lads.”

One would forgive Marchant ruing what might have been across his three years out of the England rugby picture. Few had foreseen him taking on quite such prominence during the tailend of the last World Cup cycle – not least Eddie Jones, who had all but told Marchant that he did not see him in his plans for that tournament. It was after that conversation that a player in his prime elected for a move to Paris, only to become a favourite after Steve Borthwick’s elevation.

open image in gallery Joe Marchant started all of England’s knockout games at the last World Cup ( Getty )

But Marchant, to borrow a phrase, regrette rien. “I've never really had that mindset with a lot of the decisions I've made throughout my career. Even when I went and played Super Rugby [with the Blues in Auckland] in 2020, a lot of people said the same thing. They were like 'Oh, do you wish you'd made different decisions?' And for me, it was a massive learning experience, and I came back a better player. So hopefully this experience in France has made me come back a better player.

“It was a good opportunity to come back. I spoke to Al [Sanderson] at Sale and a lot of the messages were all similar, where he thought I was at. I said I wanted to be back in the England mix, all those kind of things, and I wanted to be back playing in the Prem. It was a hope that I would be back in here today, now I am, but this is not the concrete squad for the autumn but hopefully I can be here in a week's time.”

Courtney Lawes – overlooked for a Test return, at least initially – made the same switch as Marchant from across the Channel to the outskirts of Manchester, and recently voiced his opinion that England should reverse their long-standing policy to not pick players based overseas. His new club colleague does not take such a strident view. “We all know the rules,” Marchant explains. I made my decision to go over there at a time when I was told that I wasn't really going to play for England again, and lots of stuff going on salary cap-wise with Quins. I had this opportunity to go over and I thought it was really good at the time.

open image in gallery Courtney Lawes believes England should pick players based overseas ( Getty )

“Then, Steve came in, and I played a lot of rugby for England. At the end of the World Cup, I had had a really good experience but I was going on to something else and I knew I would not be eligible. I just hoped maybe one day that I could get back in the mixer. The whole time I was there, I watched all the games. When I was a kid, I wanted to play for England; that's not changed.”

The language barrier was an initial hurdle after Marchant’s switch three years ago, and has proved so again having returned home. “There was one, for a high ball you'd say 'J'ai'. I just styled it out with ‘Joe’s’,” he chuckles. “I styled that out okay and no one said anything, so I'm happy with that. Just little things like that.” But the 30-year-old feels his time in the Top 14 has helped him hugely, too. Ever versatile, Stade Francais used Marchant everywhere from No 12 to full-back, even if a more capricious and chaotic play style was not always to his liking.

Still, though, opportunity may knock this November with England’s centres still an area of concern. Seb Atkinson is expected to be fit for their opener against Australia and may even feature for Gloucester this weekend, and would therefore be likely to retain the No 12 shirt. Could Marchant wear 13 alongside him? For now, his first focus is simply settling back in.

open image in gallery Joe Marchant is enjoying being back in England camp ( Getty )

“You've just got to get your head around it. I've come in from Sale now and I'm sat in my room going through all my homework of trying to get all the lingo right. In terms of that stuff and getting your connections, it's always going to be tough. That's what I was doing last night – trying to get all my lingo up and hopefully I can make the right calls when it comes to being on the field. literally just trying to listen to everything that has been going on. It seems like the boys know the direction they want to go. And I feel like, especially even in training today, you can feel yourself slotting into it in a way of being like, OK, this is where the opportunity is. You never know what can happen.”

News.title: England match at U15 World Cup abandoned after allegation of racism
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An England match at Fifa’s new Under-15 World Cup has been abandoned after their players walked off the field following an allegation of racism.

Footage on social media appears to show England coach Matt Thorpe beckoning his players off the field after a confrontation between one of their players and an Irish opponent.

As he signalled his players towards the touchline, Thorpe could be heard saying: “It’s not happening.”

Words continued appeared to be exchanged between the two coaching teams, and the game at the tournament in Azerbaijan was stopped with the Republic of Ireland leading 4-1.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Fifa is aware of an incident at the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland.

“The match was abandoned by the referee following England’s refusal to continue.

“The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent disciplinary committee who will decide in due course.”

The Football Association is aware of the incident and understood to be awaiting more information, with England due to be back in action against Zimbabwe on Monday evening.

The tournament features 189 ⁠countries with teams comprised of ​eight players and matches ‌played over two ​20-minute halves.

PA

News.title: British man set for hero's welcome in Hull after epic 28-year walk from South America
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A homecoming celebration is planned in Hull for a walker who has spent 28 years covering 50,000km on foot from South America.

Karl Bushby, now 57, set off from the southern end of Chile in 1998, when he was 28, vowing at the time to walk all the way home without using any form of motorised transport.

The journey brought years of dangerous escapades, including crossing the notorious Darien Gap in Central America, while he also traversed the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on the frozen sea.

Mr Bushby arrived back in England earlier this month, and announced upon his return that he had swum the Channel.

Karl Bushby is expected to make his final stop at Queen Victoria Square, in the centre of the city, on Monday November 2, before returning to his mother's house.

open image in gallery Bushby arrived back in the UK earlier this month ( tiktok.com/@karlcbushby )

The Lord Mayor of Kingston upon Hull and Admiral of the Humber Maria Coward said on Monday that residents and visitors are being encouraged to come out and welcome him home.

Ms Coward said: “So many people have followed Karl on his epic journey.

“We have all felt inspired by his spirit, tenacity and dogged determination to carry on in challenges faced by the most fearless of explorers. We all share pride in his incredible achievement.

“We also know what it’s like to come home to Hull, that feeling as your car or train, or feet in Karl’s case, crosses or goes under the Humber Bridge and over the city boundary.

“As the world’s media and documentary crews gather in our city we can show them how proud we are of Karl’s achievement and how proud we are to be from Hull.”

Following his arrival back in the UK earlier this month, Mr Bushby reflected on his epic journey spanning almost three decades.

"[It] feels good to have UK soil under my feet after all these years,” he told ITV news.

"It hasn’t been easy, and that’s part of the point - proving I’m more capable than I give myself credit for. All of us can accomplish more than we will ever imagine,” he added.

News.title: Nicki Minaj flirting with Trump’s third-term fantasy is no joke
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump is an ass man, and he still doesn’t care about the Constitution. These are the two main things we learned at a rally over the weekend.

Onstage in Michigan, the rapper promised to support Trump “forever and ever.” Minaj told the crowd that it was an “honor to stand with” Trump, adding: “If you run again, I will support you again.” Trump, who is constitutionally barred from being elected to a third presidential term, presumably has other things to worry about right now than the prospect of a future campaign endorsement. But the enthusiasm with which Minaj delivered her pledge was striking. “I love him so much,” she said.

In return, the president told the crowd that Minaj has “one hell of a beautiful ass” that’s “hard to miss.” He even asked her to show off her rear end to the crowd.

Possibly the weirdest thing about this exchange is that it started with Trump explaining why he’d fixated on a man’s ass at an earlier rally in Ohio. A few days prior, he’d praised Sen. Jon Husted’s “ass” and the rest of his athletic body.

Of course, Trump is no stranger to ogling people’s bodies — I’ve seen him make remarks about young men and women’s bodies in every iteration, from more PG but strangely admiring comments during graduation ceremonies and executive order signings in the Oval Office to outright lechery in more casual contexts, right back to the infamous Hollywood Access tape — but a laser-focus on the butt has become a central part of his midterms commentary that few people saw coming.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump spent nearly two hours of his Sunday afternoon talking about rapper Nicki Minaj’s “beautiful” rear, his indifference to Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and owning Greenland ( Getty )

There is something quite obviously unsettling about watching the president of the United States talk about a female celebrity's backside at a campaign rally while that celebrity stands beside him, pledging everlasting political devotion. But misogyny and disregard for normal democratic process are both central themes of the increasingly radical core of MAGA. So are we that surprised that Trump is flying the singer of ‘Anaconda’ around on Air Force One, so he can talk about her ass about five seconds after calling the Democratic candidate for the local Senate seat a “jihadist”? Well, how could we be?

Minaj has not always been MAGA: she openly criticized Trump’s immigration policies during his first term. In 2018, she tweeted about coming to the U.S. as “an illegal immigrant” from Trinidad at 5 years old and added that she was horrified by family separation policies that would’ve impacted her if they had been enacted at the time. It’s hard to square that Minaj with the one who declared that she loved Trump so much she wished he could flout the Constitution on Sunday, while in the background Ilhan Omar — the Democratic congresswoman who, like Minaj, came to the US with her family as a child — spoke about a recent federal raid on her house. Arresting and/or deporting Omar has become another rally-talk obsession with Trump lately.

Never mind, though, because if they come for Omar then I’m sure they won’t come for anyone else! On the flight to Michigan, Minaj praised Trump's current foreign policy and described him as a man who had “won three elections,” echoing his false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election. White House communications director Steven Cheung subsequently floated her as a potential press secretary, a joke that the official Trump War Room account enthusiastically amplified.

It is tempting to dismiss this whole thing as another episode of Trumpian absurdity, a celebrity cameo designed to generate headlines in the final stretch before the midterms, with a nice bit of weird ass banter to rile everything up. Yet the spectacle is revealing. Republican politics has increasingly become a form of personal loyalty theater, in which allegiance to Trump is demonstrated through extravagant praise, public displays of affection and performances of devotion.

Trump’s inner circle are looking and sounding nervous these days, opening almost all their speeches with effusive thanks to the president and closing them with toadying little phrases about how so-and-so policy could only ever have been achieved by this, the best president of all time, the cleverest and most handsome and most incredible man who ever lived.

Anything that could even be interpreted as a criticism — or an insufficient display of gratitude and praise — is now potentially career-ending. If you’re a politician who hasn’t paid your dues, prepare to be cut loose. If your press conference didn’t go well, you’re out the job after less than a week. If you’re a reporter in the White House who asked more than a softball question, prepare to be barred from future events. So dance to the tune of Trump the savior, and dance prettily, and make it quick!

open image in gallery Trump appears to be taking it all in as Minaj speaks during the rally in support of Mike Rogers in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday ( Reuters )

Minaj openly stating that she has no respect for the 22nd Amendment and that she would back Trump “forever” is just the logical endpoint of these sycophantic displays. She is saying what is meant to be heard, even if the administration officials are better at saying it without saying it.

We have no reason to be surprised: Trump has flirted with these ideas for a long time. A lot of it is ragebait and trolling (see: the “Trump 2028” merch that’s been on sale on the official Trump website for months, with the tagline “Rewrite the rules with the Trump 2028 high crown hat”) but it’s never not had a kernel of truth. It was 2016 when he confidently claimed at a rally that he could shoot someone in broad daylight on Fifth Avenue and not lose the backing of his supporters, and look where we are now.

Indeed, Trump has always sought to inspire this Bonnie-and-Clyde, us-against-the-world kind of worship among a dedicated fanbase, rather than seeking to elevate policies (I mean, policies are hard work!) He clearly much prefers “I love you” to “I respect you,” and his idea of a lasting legacy is more ‘big gold arch’ than ‘economic stability’.

If what you really, really want is simply a fierce, romantic, star-crossed, illogical devotion, then why not add in a little admiration for the ass, too? After all, every successful love story has a bit of sexual tension. And if that turns your stomach, then maybe you’re in the wrong room — because here in MAGA HQ in 2026, we smile and we nod, and we leer and we grab, and of course we want your body but we also, increasingly, demand your mind.

Or, as Minaj herself put it in her iconic verse in Monster, “First things first, I’ll eat your brains.”

News.title: Microsoft offers a quarter of its global workforce voluntary buyouts as AI spending accelerates
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence.

Chief People Officer Amy Coleman said in a blog post Monday that the company's voluntary exit offer was available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman wrote. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”

The company, which releases its quarterly financial performance Wednesday, had approximately 223,000 full-time employees at the end of June.

Shares of Microsoft Corp., based in Redmond, Washington, hit an all-time high this month.

In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2.1% of its global workforce, including a large number of workers at its Xbox video game business.

News.title: Tottenham outcast Richarlison convicted of running red light in £60k sportscar
News.content:
