Justice Mojisola Dada admitted the documents in a bench ruling, holding that they were relevant to the proceedings and duly certified in line with Section 104 of the Evidence Act, 2011.

The documents were tendered by counsel to the second defendant, Mr Uyi Giwa-Osagie, to counter the claim by the fourth prosecution witness, Bawa Usman Kaltungo, that Kuru had unilaterally authorised the receivership.

Kaltungo, head of the AMCON desk at the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, and leader of its investigating team, had maintained during cross-examination that Kuru, as AMCON’s managing director and chief executive officer, had unfettered powers and personally sanctioned the receivership.

However, Giwa-Osagie tendered the certified board resolutions to establish that the decision was approved by AMCON’s board as a corporate body.

The prosecution counsel, Dr Wahab Shittu, SAN, objected to the admissibility of the documents, arguing that they were too remote and irrelevant to the charges.

But Giwa-Osagie argued that his client was not standing trial over the propriety of appointing a receiver but over other allegations contained in the charge sheet.

He maintained that the documents went to the root of the case and were capable of establishing his client’s innocence. He also argued that they were public documents duly certified and tendered from the Bar.

In her ruling, Justice Dada upheld their admissibility, noting that the resolutions emanated from AMCON’s board as a corporate body and had been certified in accordance with the law.

The EFCC had arraigned Kuru; Kamilu Omokide, former receiver-manager of Arik Air; Captain Roy Ilegbodu, the airline’s chief executive officer; Union Bank Limited; and Super Bravo Limited over allegations arising from the airline’s receivership.

The prosecution followed a petition by Mr Femi Falana, SAN, on behalf of Arik Air’s promoters and shareholders.

The court adjourned the case until October 27, 2026, for continuation of trial.

World.title: 2027 Polls: Don’t let politicians manipulate the law, CJN warns judges
World.content:
Chief Justice of Nigeria, CJN, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun

By Ilechukwu Nnochiri, Abuja

In anticipation of litigation that could arise from the 2027 general elections, the Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, on Monday warned judges across the country against allowing politicians to manipulate the legal system to gain undeserved advantage.

The CJN particularly urged heads of courts to remain vigilant against practices capable of undermining the integrity of judicial proceedings.

She identified such practices as including forum shopping, concealment of related proceedings and attempts to obtain conflicting orders from courts of coordinate jurisdiction.

Speaking during the opening session of the 2026 roundtable for heads of courts, organised by the National Judicial Institute (NJI) in Abuja, the CJN said the issues called for particular attention as the nation heads towards another election season.

While acknowledging that election-related disputes usually attract intense public interest and considerable pressure on the courts, the CJN said the judiciary must be prepared to discharge its constitutional responsibilities with impartiality, courage and fidelity to the law.

“Political sensitivity, public sentiment or the urgency with which a matter is presented must never displace the careful application of the Constitution, the Electoral Act and the applicable rules of court.

“I urge your lordships to ensure that appropriate administrative arrangements are in place to facilitate the timely and orderly handling of election-related matters.

“Judicial officers must be reminded of the need to scrutinise applications carefully, insist on full and frank disclosure of relevant facts, pay due regard to related proceedings and resist any attempt to use urgent applications or ex-parte orders to secure an improper advantage.

“The integrity of judicial proceedings must not be compromised by competing political interests or pressure from any quarter.

“Forum shopping is particularly damaging because it undermines consistency, encourages abuse of process and exposes the Judiciary to avoidable public controversy.

“Your lordships must therefore ensure that existing procedural safeguards are observed and that appropriate steps are taken whenever attempts to circumvent established judicial processes come to light.

“No litigant should be permitted to manipulate the judicial system in search of a favourable decision. Public confidence in the judiciary will be tested during this period,” she added.

Moreover, Justice Kekere-Ekun reminded the heads of courts that they are expected to provide the leadership necessary to ensure that election-related cases are handled competently, expeditiously and strictly in accordance with the law.

She said the objective is to ensure that the courts remain impartial arbiters of disputes, free from political influence and guided solely by the facts, the applicable law and the demands of justice.

The CJN equally spoke about the need for judges to always ensure prompt determination of cases, noting that the timely determination of cases remains one of the most pressing challenges confronting the judiciary.

She said delay imposes financial and emotional burdens on litigants, diminishes the practical value of judicial remedies and weakens public confidence in the justice system.

“While some causes of delay arise from inadequate funding, infrastructure and judicial manpower, others can be addressed through effective administration.

“Inefficient docket management, repeated adjournments, poor scheduling and failure to monitor inactive cases can prolong proceedings unnecessarily.

“Every head of court should have a clear understanding of the condition of the court’s docket, including the number of pending cases, their age, the categories experiencing the greatest delays and the reasons for their continued pendency.

“This information should inform realistic strategies for reducing backlog, improving the allocation of hearing dates and ensuring that concluded matters are promptly removed from the active docket.

“Efficiency, however, must not be measured solely by the number of cases disposed of. It requires cases to be determined fairly, competently and within a reasonable time, with the right to fair hearing fully protected,” the CJN stated.

Stressing the need to preserve the integrity of judicial appointments through a fair, transparent and merit-based selection process, the CJN maintained that heads of courts must “strongly and courageously resist pressure from external interests and ensure that appointments are guided by objective criteria, competence, character and suitability for judicial office.”

She said, “Public confidence in the judiciary depends, in part, on the assurance that those entrusted with judicial office have emerged through rigorous and credible processes.

“Your lordships also have an important role in promoting professional standards, supporting the development of judicial officers and fostering an institutional culture that upholds impartiality and accountability.”

She directed the heads of courts to put in place mechanisms to ensure judges sit on time, notify litigants and lawyers promptly when sittings are cancelled, and treat court users with dignity.

Heads of courts, she said, must communicate clear sitting times, monitor compliance and deal with persistent or unjustified lateness through established supervisory and disciplinary channels.

The CJN described as unacceptable the situation where counsel and parties travel long distances at great expense, only to learn on arrival that the court will not sit.

In courtroom conduct, she said judicial authority is best exercised with “fairness, composure and respect”.

“Every litigant, regardless of social status, financial means or education, deserves dignity, while lawyers are entitled to courteous treatment. Firmness and courtesy are entirely compatible. A judge can control proceedings without humiliating counsel or a litigant,” she added.

Earlier in his remarks, the Administrator of the NJI, Justice Babatunde Adejumo, said the Judiciary, as custodian of justice and guardian of the rule of law, is under constant public scrutiny, placing a heavy responsibility on those steering its affairs to safeguard its image and shape positive public perceptions.

He said the annual roundtable provides a platform for candid exchange, identifying cross-cutting challenges and collectively developing solutions.

He added that the programme was deliberately designed with minimal external intervention so that the heads of courts would direct discussions and determine outcomes.

Justice Adejumo lauded the CJN for the many reforms she has introduced, which he said have entrenched judicial independence and enhanced integrity across all rungs of the judiciary.

World.title: ‘Atiku majored in hygiene, cannot rule Nigeria’s modern economy’ — Shettima
World.content:
VP Shettima

By Enitan Abdultawab

Vice President Kashim Shettima has criticised former vice president Atiku Abubakar over his proposal to restore fuel subsidy, questioning his ability to govern Nigeria’s modern economy.

Shettima said Atiku’s proposal would push the country back into poverty, accusing the former vice president of supporting the return of subsidy for political reasons.

Speaking at the Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja on Monday, Shettima said, “One of the leading presidential candidates is advocating for the return of the subsidy scheme. He wants us to backslide into penury for political convenience.”

He also questioned Atiku’s professional background, referring to his training at the Kano School of Hygiene as he challenged his capacity to manage the country’s economy.

“I dare to put forward that his skill set — he was trained in sanitation at the Kano School of Hygiene — so he doesn’t have the skill set to govern a modern economy. That’s the painful truth,” Shettima said.

Shettima further questioned Atiku’s knowledge of environmental sanitation, using the difference between flu and Ebola to make his point.

“Even his decisions in environmental sanitation, I do not think he can make a distinction between flu and even Ebola,” he said.

Shettima urged Nigerians to assess the proposals and qualifications of political leaders before making decisions, warning against ignoring the implications of their choices.

“Nigerians must have to decide and those of you here cannot afford to play the ostrich,” he added.

Atiku has advocated the restoration of fuel subsidy as part of his proposed approach to managing the economy.

The issue remains a major point of disagreement between the opposition and the administration of President Bola Tinubu, which removed the subsidy in May 2023.

While the government has defended the removal as necessary to reduce the financial burden on public finances, the policy has been accompanied by higher fuel prices and increased living costs for many Nigerians.

World.title: The Shadow In The Twilight: An Ode to Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti (1926–2026)
World.content:
By Marindoti Oludare

There are men whose lives are measured in years, others whose lives are measured in accomplishments, and a rare few whose lives are measured by the generations they have inspired. Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti belonged to that rare breed of men whose very existence became a moral compass for society. He lived for a century, but the measure of his life was never in the number of years he lived. It was in the principles he upheld, the lives he touched, the institutions he built, and the causes for which he never ceased to fight.

For as long as I can remember, Baba Fasoranti has been one of the men I looked up to. He represented everything I believed public service ought to be: integrity without compromise, leadership without arrogance, political conviction without blind loyalty, and an abiding belief that the welfare of the people must always be the supreme purpose of government.

It was this admiration that, in the lead-up to the 2023 presidential election, made his endorsement of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu one of the most consequential influences on my decision to join the campaign for his presidency. I believed that a man who had spent his life advocating true federalism, restructuring, state police, and public accountability would not lend his moral authority lightly. If Baba believed that Tinubu could advance these causes, I believed there was good reason to join that effort.

Today, as we mourn his passing, I find myself reflecting not only on the extraordinary life he lived but also on the promises we owe his memory, some of which remain painfully unfulfilled.

Baba was born on May 11, 1926, into a Nigeria still under British colonial rule, long before independence, long before the First Republic, and before many of the political institutions we now take for granted had been conceived. To say that he participated in Nigerian politics for almost as long as modern Nigerian politics has existed is hardly an exaggeration. His life traversed colonialism, nationalism, independence, civilian administrations, military dictatorships, and the return to democracy.

Yet his journey began not in the corridors of power but in the humble pursuit of knowledge.

As a young man, he dreamed of becoming a medical doctor. But the educational limitations of his time stood between him and that ambition. At Ondo Boys’ High School, where he received his secondary education, the absence of adequate science teaching denied him the opportunity to pursue the subjects needed for medicine.

For many young men, such a disappointment might have ended in bitterness or resignation. For Baba, it became the foundation of a lifelong mission. He would dedicate himself to ensuring that the generations coming after him did not have their ambitions determined by the limitations of the schools they attended.

He went on to study at Yaba Higher College and University College, Ibadan, before pursuing advanced studies in education in Britain and Australia. He became a teacher, an administrator, and subsequently a principal. In 1957, he became the founding principal of Anglican Grammar School, Iju-Itaogbolu, which began with only 30 students. He would later help establish Omolere Nursery and Primary School, Akure High School, and St. Frances’ Academy, named in memory of his beloved wife.

The young man who could not study medicine because his school could not adequately teach the sciences devoted his life to building schools where other people’s children could pursue their dreams.

What greater testimony to selfless leadership could there be?

Baba’s political life was equally remarkable. He was an admirer and disciple of Chief Obafemi Awolowo, whose philosophy of progressive governance, education, social welfare, and federalism resonated deeply with his own convictions. But Baba was no political sycophant. His loyalty was to principles, not personalities.

Perhaps no episode demonstrates this better than his extraordinary encounter with the political establishment of the Action Group in Akure.

When Awolowo’s political machinery supported a candidate for the chairmanship of the Akure Local Council whom Baba and his associates believed did not represent the wishes of their people, he refused to surrender his convictions to party authority.

Instead, he and his supporters established the Alarm Clock Party, challenged the established political order, and defeated the Action Group candidate at the polls.

Imagine the audacity of that young man! A committed disciple of Awolowo, standing against the candidate preferred by the very political leader he revered, not out of personal animosity but because he believed that the people of Akure deserved the right to determine who represented them.

And perhaps even more remarkable was what followed. Having made his point and secured the mandate of his people, Baba returned to the Action Group. He had not abandoned his political philosophy; he had merely refused to abandon the people for the sake of party convenience.

There lies a lesson for today’s political class: loyalty to a political party must never become disloyalty to the people. A party is merely the vehicle through which the people exercise their democratic rights. It must never become an instrument for suppressing those rights.

The story of Baba’s service in the Akure Local Council also provides an enduring lesson in public morality. While serving as council chairman and simultaneously working as a school principal, he refused to draw two salaries. He considered his income as a principal sufficient and chose to offer his political service without collecting remuneration from the council.

At a time when public office has become, for too many, an invitation to personal enrichment, such a disposition almost sounds unbelievable. But Baba belonged to a generation that regarded leadership as a duty to be discharged, not a privilege to be exploited.

His years in local government are also remembered in Akure’s history of early public infrastructure, including local recollections of pioneering road development around Arakale. For him, the measure of political authority was not the prestige of occupying an office but the visible improvement in the lives of those who elected him.

This philosophy followed him into the Second Republic when he served as Commissioner for Finance under the administration of Chief Michael Adekunle Ajasin between 1979 and 1983.

Together, Ajasin and Fasoranti represented a tradition of public probity that has become distressingly scarce in contemporary Nigerian politics. The resources of the state were held in trust for the people, and public officials were expected to account for their stewardship.

Their reputation for integrity was tested when the military overthrew the civilian government in December 1983.

The succeeding military administration subjected members of that government to imprisonment, investigation, and prosecution. Chief Ajasin was famously tried twice and acquitted twice, yet remained in detention. Baba Fasoranti also endured imprisonment and prosecution in the aftermath of the coup.

It was an era in which allegations against the political class became a convenient justification for military intervention, and men who had devoted their lives to public service could find themselves deprived of liberty by those who claimed to be rescuing the nation.

Baba emerged from these ordeals without abandoning his principles. He would go on to participate in the struggle against military dictatorship, lending his voice to the campaign for the restoration of democratic government.

The same man who had challenged his own party over the wishes of the Akure electorate would later stand against military rule in defence of the sovereignty of the Nigerian people.

His was not a convenient democracy that mattered only when his preferred candidates won. It was a conviction that the people’s mandate must remain sacred.

And so I wonder what Baba would make of the political developments in our country today, where party nominations are sometimes determined not by the wishes of the electorate but by the influence of powerful individuals far removed from the communities whose futures they seek to control.

What would he say to political imposition, the manipulation of electoral processes, and the growing belief that power belongs to those who can control the machinery of a party rather than those who can win the confidence of its members?

I believe his life has already answered these questions.

A man who once challenged Awolowo’s preferred candidate to defend the democratic rights of Akure people would hardly have wanted future generations to surrender those same rights without resistance.

Baba’s life was not without profound personal tragedy. He lost his beloved wife, Frances, in 1991. He endured the death of a daughter while he was in military detention. Then, in July 2019, another daughter, Funke Olakunrin, was brutally murdered by gunmen along the Benin-Ore highway.

For any father, the loss of a child is an unbearable burden. To lose a daughter to the same insecurity against which one has spent years warning one’s country is a cruelty beyond words.

Yet Baba did not allow his personal grief to diminish his concern for the suffering of others. If anything, the tragedy reinforced the urgency of his lifelong advocacy for the protection of lives and property.

This brings me to one of the most poignant images of Baba’s final years: the frail, elderly statesman, confined to a wheelchair, who nevertheless found the strength to travel to Abuja and appeal directly to President Tinubu for the restructuring of Nigeria and the establishment of state police.

Dr. Marindoti Oludare, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, and Marindoti’s dad, Dr Patrick Oludare, at the home of Papa in Akure, on July 6, 2023

On April 17, 2024, Baba led an Afenifere delegation to the Presidential Villa. At an age when most men would have withdrawn completely from the affairs of the world, he was still pleading for a country where its citizens could live without fear.

He was not asking for a contract. He was not seeking a political appointment. He was not requesting a favour for his children or grandchildren.

He was asking for a safer Nigeria.

There is something profoundly moving about a man nearing a hundred years of age, who has already lost a daughter to violence, continuing to spend what little strength remains in his body demanding the security of other people’s children.

That, to me, is the essence of Baba Fasoranti.

And it is here that my admiration must coexist with my disappointment.

President Tinubu has taken steps toward the establishment of state police, including supporting constitutional changes and legislative proposals. These developments deserve acknowledgment. But I remain deeply saddened that the reform did not become a functioning reality while Baba was alive to witness it.

Indeed, the irony of history could hardly be more painful. On October 23, 2026, just three days after Baba’s death, the Presidency announced that the proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police had secured the support of 24 state Houses of Assembly, crossing the constitutional threshold necessary for the reform to advance.

Three days after he departed.

Baba had lived a hundred years. He had waited through colonialism, military dictatorship, and successive civilian administrations for the emergence of a truly federal Nigeria. Yet he departed before seeing one of his most enduring aspirations become reality.

I wish President Tinubu had moved with greater urgency, not merely for Baba’s sake but for the countless Nigerians whose lives remain vulnerable to insecurity. Baba deserved to witness more than promises and proposals. He deserved to see the machinery of a restructured security system take shape in his lifetime.

Nevertheless, this disappointment must not become an excuse to abandon the struggle. Rather, it must strengthen our resolve to complete it.

We who remain must now take up the mantle.

We must insist on state policing that is genuinely accountable to the communities it serves, with proper safeguards against political abuse, independent oversight, and a firm commitment to protecting every Nigerian, regardless of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or social standing.

We must continue the struggle against corruption, that malignant disease which robs our schools of classrooms, our hospitals of medicines, our roads of durability, and our security institutions of the resources required to protect the people.

We must resist the manipulation of elections and the imposition of candidates, for a society that permits its people’s votes to be stolen cannot credibly claim to honour the memory of a man who once defied his own political leader to defend the right of his people to choose.

We must remember that political leadership is not measured by the number of convoys surrounding an officeholder, the size of the allowances he collects, or the fortunes accumulated by his associates. It is measured by the opportunities created for the next generation and by the dignity with which the ordinary citizen is treated.

Above all, we must restore integrity to public life.

For me, Baba Fasoranti will remain a North Star, a constant moral reference by which to judge not only those who seek to govern us but also our own conduct as citizens.

At a hundred years of age, he had nothing more to prove. He could have spent his final years in the comfort of his family, receiving tributes and enjoying the gratitude of a society he had already served beyond measure. Instead, he continued to concern himself with the unfinished business of Nigeria.

Therein lies the final lesson of his remarkable existence: a life of service never truly retires, and a conviction worth holding is a conviction worth defending until one’s final breath.

Now Baba has entered the twilight of eternity.

The sun that illuminated a century of Nigerian history has finally dipped below the horizon. The voice that once rose in defence of the people of Akure, that challenged political imposition, that upheld probity in the management of public resources, that resisted military tyranny, and that pleaded for the security of our country has fallen silent.

But there is something about the twilight that we must remember.

As the sun descends, the shadows of great things stretch farther across the earth.

And so it shall be with Baba Fasoranti.

Though he has sailed beyond the horizon into the quiet embrace of the night, his shadow remains cast upon our nation. It will stretch across our political institutions, across the schools he founded, across the roads of Akure, and across the conscience of every Nigerian who still believes that public office should be an instrument of service rather than self-enrichment.

His body may have surrendered to the passage of time, but his ideals have not. His voice may have fallen silent, but his example still speaks. His eyes may have closed to the troubles of our nation, but the light of his convictions must continue to illuminate our path.

And when the darkness of corruption, electoral manipulation, insecurity, and political expediency threatens to overwhelm our country, may we look toward the North Star of his example and find the courage to do what is right.

Let us not merely mourn Baba. Let us become worthy of him.

Let us complete the work he could not finish.

Let us build the Nigeria he believed in.

For Baba Fasoranti may have departed into the twilight, but his shadow will remain with us long after the night has fallen.

And so long as we keep his ideals alive, the darkness shall never claim his light.

Rest peacefully, Baba.

Your struggle is now ours. Your mantle has fallen into our hands. And we must not let it fall to the ground.

World.title: Shoga: City Boy Movt’s Efforts Contributed To Success Of APC’s Kaduna Rally
World.content:
.Says inauguration of Abuja–Kaduna highway opens economic platform for N’West

Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

Director-General of the City Boy Movement (CBM), Hon. Oluwatosin Shoga, has attributed the large turnout of youth at Saturday’s flag-off of the All Progressives Congress (APC) re-election campaign of President Bola Tinubu in Kaduna as an affirmation of the Movement’s sustained grassroots enlightenment and mobilisation efforts in support of the President.

According to him, the impressive youth participation at the rally demonstrated growing interest among young Nigerians in the Tinubu’s development programme and their determination to participate actively in determining Nigeria’s political and economic future.

In a reflection titled, “Beyond the Road: Unlocking Opportunities, Empowering Young Nigerians, and Building a Prosperous Future,” released in Abuja, the CBM boss attributed the enthusiasm witnessed at the Kaduna rally partly to sustained grassroots engagements, including the Movement’s mobilisation activities and street walk in Kano.

His words: “The City Boy Movement was proudly on the ground, engaging with young Nigerians and grassroots supporters who came out to demonstrate their commitment to the future of our country.

“The enthusiasm witnessed in Kaduna, alongside our grassroots engagement and street walk in Kano, reinforces our conviction that young Nigerians want to be part of a national conversation about development, opportunity, and a more prosperous Nigeria.”

Shoga stressed that the Movement’s activities extended beyond mobilising electoral support for Tinubu, adding that its central mission was to educate and empower young people to understand government policies and take advantage of emerging economic opportunities.

He referenced the inauguration of an 81-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna highway during the campaign flag-off, describing the development as a demonstration of the Tinubu administration’s commitment to improving infrastructure and stimulating economic activities in the North-West.

According to him, the strategic road corridor linking Abuja, Kaduna, Zaria and Kano offers opportunities for agricultural transformation, industrial expansion, regional trade, private investment and employment generation.

He noted that improved connectivity could benefit farmers, traders, transport operators and young entrepreneurs by facilitating access to markets, reducing transportation difficulties and encouraging investments in logistics, manufacturing, food processing and related businesses.

“The objective is not simply to build infrastructure. It is to create the conditions in which people can build businesses, earn sustainable incomes, create jobs, and improve their standard of living”.

Shoga, however, emphasised that infrastructure development must be complemented by sustained security operations, effective intelligence gathering, reliable electricity and investment-friendly policies to unlock the region’s full economic potential.

“A good road connects destinations. A secure road connects people to opportunity. Together, infrastructure and security can help unlock the economic potential of an entire region”, he further said.

World.title: DGI Consult, UNICEF Strengthen Primary Healthcare Management in Adamawa, Kwara, Sokoto
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Development Governance International (DGI) Consult, through the UNICEF-supported Enhancing Leadership, Governance and Management Capacities (ELGMC) project, has trained local government health managers and frontline health workers in Adamawa, Kwara and Sokoto States to strengthen primary healthcare delivery and improve maternal and child health outcomes.

The training focused on equipping health teams with practical leadership, management and problem-solving skills to improve the implementation of Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH+N) and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) programmes.

Held in selected local government areas (LGAs) across the three states, the workshops addressed gaps identified through earlier facility assessments, with participants developing practical strategies to improve service organisation, resource management, accountability and decision-making.

Speaking at the opening of the training in Song LGA of Adamawa State, the Executive Chairman of the Adamawa State Primary Health Care Development Agency (ADSPHCDA), Dr Sulaiman Saidu Bashir, underscored the importance of strengthening leadership and management at the local government and facility levels.

He stressed the collective responsibility of health-sector stakeholders to ensure effective programme implementation and prevent avoidable deaths among women, newborns, children and adolescents.

The Chief Executive Officer of DGI Consult, Dr Gafar Alawode, said the intervention was designed to strengthen the capacity of health facility and LGA teams to identify and address challenges affecting service delivery.

“This is not only in Adamawa State but across health systems. The central purpose of the training is to strengthen the ability of facility and LGA teams to identify and solve problems encountered while delivering health services,” he stated.

Alawode added that the intervention would not only help participating facilities develop solutions to their immediate challenges but also generate practical approaches that could contribute to wider improvements across health facilities in the states.

During the workshops, participants examined challenges affecting service delivery and identified actions within their areas of responsibility to address them.

They also explored how programme data and results frameworks could be used to establish priorities, monitor performance and support evidence-based decisions.

Through group exercises and discussions, the health workers translated identified priorities into action plans with defined responsibilities, expected results and timelines.

The workshops also introduced participants to the whole–part–rest approach to problem-solving, which encourages teams to examine challenges comprehensively, identify actions within their control, determine the support required from other stakeholders and mobilise relevant partners to implement solutions.

An example of the approach was demonstrated at Primary Health Centre Yallabe in Wamakko LGA of Sokoto state, where collaboration with local health stakeholders helped address service delivery challenges.

Engagement with the nutrition focal person led to the facility being designated as a distribution point for ready-to-use therapeutic food, reportedly increasing patient turnout.

In addition, an official of the Sokoto State Primary Health Care Development Agency with health training from the community agreed to support the facility during busy immunisation and antenatal care sessions.

Speaking during the engagement in Gwadabawa LGA of Sokoto State, the Director of Health, Alhaji Usman Aliyu Shehu, urged participants to apply the lessons from the training in their daily work and remain focused on measurable results.

He said the training should be regarded as part of an ongoing improvement process rather than a stand-alone activity.

Participants, he added, should routinely review progress, identify emerging challenges and take corrective action to ensure that agreed priorities translate into tangible improvements at the facility level.

In Kwara State, the Director of Primary Health Care Services at the Kwara State Primary Health Care Development Agency (KWSPHCDA), Dr. Oguntoye, expressed confidence that the intervention would strengthen health workers’ capacity to deliver quality services and improve health outcomes across the state.

He emphasised the importance of translating improved leadership and management into effective programme implementation, with facility teams better equipped to plan, coordinate and improve healthcare services.

World.title: Court Orders El-Rufai to Enter Defence on Alleged Wiretapping Trial
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja

Justice Joyce Abdulmalik of a Federal High Court, Abuja, on Monday ordered a former Governor of Kaduna State, Nasir El-Rufai, to enter his defence if he so desires in his ongoing trial on bugging the telephone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu.

Justice Abdulmalik made the order shortly after dismissing the no-case submission filed by El-Rufai, in response to the prosecution’s case.

In her ruling on the no-case submission, the judge held that there is sufficient evidence by the prosecution to warrant the court to call on the defendant to enter his defence if he so desires.

She subsequently adjourned till November 25 for the former governor to open his defence.

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) chieftain is standing trial on a five-count criminal charge brought against him by the Department of State Services (DSS).

At the no-case submission hearing on September 22, the prosecution, represented by Oluwole Aladedoye (SAN), objected to the submission and urged the court to dismiss it and order the defendant to enter his defence.

According to Aladedoye, the defendant failed to address Exhibit “B”, which the prosecution claimed contains El-Rufai’s admission in relation to the tapping of Ribadu’s phone.

He contended that since the prosecution has effectively established a prima facie case against El-Rufai, through its two witnesses, the defendant is required by law to enter a defence.

Defence lawyer, Akinyemi Aremu, while adopting his client’s no-case submission, argued that the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case against the ex-governor to require him to be called upon to enter a defence.

Aremu urged the court to uphold the no-case submission and discharge his client.

El-Rufai opted for a no-case submission after the prosecution closed its case upon calling two witnesses — an operative of the DSS and a lawyer, Deji Adeyanju.

Adeyanju, who testified as a subpoenaed witness, told the court that the ex-governor admitted during a television interview that he wiretapped the NSA’s phone lines.

World.title: Osinbajo, Traditional Rulers Seek End to Polarisation in N’ central
World.content:
Yemi Kosoko in Jos

Former Vice-President, Prof. Yemi Osinbajo, traditional rulers, religious leaders and policy experts have called for urgent action to counter growing polarisation and rebuild civic cohesion in North-central Nigeria, warning that injustice, impunity and divisive narratives continue to fuel conflict across the region.

The leaders spoke at a national dialogue organised by the Justice Research Institute (JRI) in partnership with the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS) under the theme, ‘Countering Polarisation and Rebuilding Civic Cohesion in North Central Nigeria: Beyond Tribe and Faith, Reclaiming Our Shared Stories.’

Osinbajo stressed that lasting peace cannot be achieved without justice, accountability and intentional reconciliation, drawing lessons from South Africa and Rwanda.

He said communities affected by violence and displacement must be helped to heal through truth-telling, restitution and institutional reforms that restore confidence in the justice system.

He warned that impunity undermines social stability, insisting that justice must include restitution and restoration.

“People cannot simply be told to forget. Where land has been taken unjustly, it must be returned. Where people have suffered losses, appropriate compensation and justice are necessary for healing,” he said.

Speaking at the event, NIPSS Director-General, Prof. Ayo Omotayo, described storytelling as a powerful tool for national reconciliation, noting that societies are held together not only by laws and institutions but also by the stories citizens tell about one another.

He warned that distorted narratives, misinformation and inherited prejudices can deepen divisions and undermine national development.

Also addressing participants, the Emir of Lafia, Justice Sidi Bage (rtd), said conflict begins when justice, identity and belonging are denied.

He urged Nigerians to reject collective blame, ethnic profiling and religious stereotyping, emphasizing that dialogue, active listening and mutual respect are essential for peaceful coexistence.

Similarly, the Secretary-General of Jama’atu Nasril Islam (JNI), Prof. Khalid Abubakar Aliyu, warned against exploiting ethnic and religious differences for political or social gain.

He called for stronger accountability, responsible communication and greater investment in youth employment, arguing that widespread poverty and joblessness remain major drivers of insecurity.

Participants agreed that no community can achieve lasting peace by promoting the insecurity of another and called for inclusive governance, stronger conflict-resolution mechanisms, support for displaced persons and greater involvement of women and young people in peacebuilding efforts.

The dialogue ended with a renewed commitment to promote justice, truth, responsible leadership and shared citizenship as foundations for peace, unity and development in North-central Nigeria and beyond.

World.title: Tunji Olowolafe Foundation, OAU Partner to Expand Digital Research, Postgraduate Access
World.content:
The Founder of the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation (TOF), Dr. Tunji Olowolafe, has called on Nigerian universities to open research to more people, test long-held beliefs with scientific rigour and carry discoveries out of the laboratory and into the economy.

Speaking at the Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife 65th anniversary celebration, on the theme, ‘Promoting Research Excellence and Innovation in Postgraduate Studies: Charting the Future,’ Dr. Olowolafe reframed research as the disciplined habit of correcting a nation’s course based on evidence.

He described the postgraduate college as the intellectual engine room of a nation, where society sends its sharpest minds to challenge conventional wisdom and demand honest, data-driven answers.

His first strategy called for the opening of the gates of research earlier, wider and more flexibly.

He urged OAU to make its staff schools benchmarks for Africa, with science, technology and artificial intelligence at the core of the curriculum.

He pointed to the Foundation’s Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial Community Secondary School in Are Ekiti, which opened in September 2025 with 100 students and now has more than 170, alongside an ICT centre teaching artificial intelligence (AI), coding, graphic design and Mandarin, with instructors teaching live from Beijing through a Starlink connection.

“The postgraduate researchers of 2040 are sitting in primary classrooms today,” he said.

He also questioned whether every road to postgraduate research must run through a four-year degree, inviting universities to recognize prior learning and demonstrated expertise without lowering standards.

With only about one million of the two million UTME candidates admitted in 2025, he argued that flexible, digital study must become the standard model, since a digital campus needs no physical acreage. This builds on the Foundation’s Project Digi-Teach, which is training academic staff at Ekiti State University (EKSU) for digital proficiency.

His second strategy urged researchers to test what society believes. Rather than dismissing indigenous knowledge without investigation or defending it without validation, he called for rigorous testing, citing Chinese scientist Tu Youyou, whose study of a centuries-old herbal remedy produced the malaria treatment artemisinin and a Nobel Prize.

He extended the same principle to national history, including sensitive chapters such as the Civil War.

“She neither rejected tradition nor accepted it. She tested it,” he said.

The third strategy, according to him, focused on pushing research out of the laboratory and directly into the economy.

Olowolafe advocated university promotion structures that reward patents, commercial products and solved industrial problems alongside traditional journal publications.

“Research is complete only when it leaves the laboratory and improves lives,” he said.

Pointing to OAU’s exceptional tech pedigree, including Flutterwave and Moniepoint founded by its graduates, he challenged the global alumni community to scale up their financial, institutional and mentorship support for research tenfold.

To support this vision, the Foundation will install a solar power system for the Postgraduate College, provide a virtual learning and oral defence facility and modernize the college boardroom.

TOF will also fund pilot studies on a case-by-case basis and sponsor training in grant writing and donor compliance, working with OAU’s Central Office of Research and Advancement Office.

“Our ambition must go beyond providing infrastructure to building institutions that can generate knowledge and attract global research funding. By strengthening the capacity of our universities, we can expand opportunities for our people and position Nigeria to compete more effectively in the global knowledge economy,” he noted.

Through these ideas and commitments, the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation continues to advance its broader ambition of strengthening the institutions, skills and opportunities that support Nigeria’s long-term development.

Its work across education, digital learning and research capacity reflects a sustained commitment to equipping institutions and the next generation with the tools to compete and thrive in an increasingly knowledge-driven world.

World.title: NDC Unveils Campaign Council As Dickson, Obi, Kwankwaso Take Charge
World.content:
* OK Movement mocks late preparations, says rivals may seek its grassroots structure

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has unveiled its National Campaign Council for the 2027 general election, appointing its National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, as chairman, with its presidential candidate, Mr Peter Obi, and vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, occupying key positions in the campaign hierarchy.

The announcement has, however, drawn criticism from the OK Movement, whose National Director-General, Hon. John Ozyl Ughulu, questioned the preparedness of political organisations still putting their campaign machinery together, warning that prominent names on a campaign council do not necessarily translate into electoral strength.

Ughulu argued that political ambition without a functional grassroots structure could prove inadequate in a nationwide election, predicting that some political actors who had criticised the movement might eventually seek its organisational networks and mobilisation capacity.

“The funny part of this list is that 90 per cent of the people on it will still come knocking on the doors of the OK Movement to beg for the very structure they have failed to build themselves,” he said.

“The irony is unbelievable! With less than three months to the general election, they are only just announcing their presidential campaign council. What exactly have they been doing all this time? Where is the structure? Where is the strategy? Where is the machinery required to prosecute a serious national election?”

The NDC’s campaign council, according to the announcement, will have the party’s National Chairman, Senator Cleopas Moses Zuwoghe, as vice-chairman, while its National Secretary, Ikenna Morgan Enekweizu, will serve as council secretary. Mallam Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim has been appointed Director-General.

The composition brings the party’s principal political figures into a central campaign structure expected to coordinate its electoral strategy, nationwide mobilisation and communication of its policy agenda ahead of the January 2027 general election.

Dickson’s appointment as chairman, with Obi serving as co-chairman and Kwankwaso as co-vice-chairman, places the party’s leading figures at the centre of the campaign organisation as it seeks to translate its political platform into a nationwide electoral operation.

The council is expected to coordinate campaign activities across the states, local government areas, wards and polling units, while aligning the party’s leadership, grassroots organisation and policy messaging around a common strategy.

The NDC said its campaign would be people-centred and issue-based, anchored on its vision of a new, just and prosperous Nigeria. It also called on members, supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to remain united and focused as preparations for the election intensify.

But Ughulu insisted that the announcement of a campaign council, irrespective of the political stature of its members, should not be mistaken for evidence of adequate electoral preparation.

“Elections are not won by titles, press releases, political noise, or the number of big names on a campaign council,” he said.

“Elections are won through grassroots mobilisation, effective coordination, strategic planning, committed people, and a well-established structure that reaches every polling unit.”

He maintained that effective electioneering required sustained groundwork, an established network of committed supporters and the ability to coordinate political activities beyond announcements and public appearances.

According to him, political organisations that delay building their operational structures until the election approaches could find it difficult to convert public enthusiasm and political prominence into votes.

The OK Movement director-general said his organisation had deliberately prioritised grassroots mobilisation and organisational development, arguing that the distinction between political ambition and the capacity to execute it would become clearer as the election drew nearer.

He said: “This is where the OK Movement stands apart. While others are still trying to figure out how to build their structures, the OK Movement has been doing the hard work. We have demonstrated foresight, organisational capacity, strategic thinking, and leadership when it matters most.

“We did not wait for the election to approach before recognising the importance of grassroots organisation. We understood from the beginning that a presidential ambition without a functional grassroots structure is nothing more than a political wish!”

Ughulu also predicted that the pressure of electioneering could compel some political organisations to seek assistance from established mobilisation networks, including those of the OK Movement.

“Let the truth be told: when the pressure mounts and the reality of electioneering sets in, many of those who look down on the OK Movement today may be the same people who will come seeking our coordinators, our networks, our mobilisation capacity, and our organisational expertise,” he said.

He, however, questioned whether such political actors would respect the movement’s independence if they eventually needed its organisational resources.

“But the question is: Will they respect the structure they are now coming to depend on?” he asked.

The NDC’s unveiling of its campaign council and the OK Movement’s criticism highlight the importance of organisation, coordination and grassroots reach in the unfolding contest for the presidency.

For the NDC, the immediate challenge will be to translate the experience and political standing of its campaign leadership into an effective nationwide structure capable of sustaining voter engagement and communicating its policy proposals.

The OK Movement, on its part, is seeking to establish grassroots capacity as a central measure of electoral preparedness, insisting that political organisations must demonstrate their ability to organise and mobilise rather than rely solely on prominent personalities.

Ughulu stressed that the movement was neither a temporary platform for political endorsements nor an organisation established merely to applaud political leaders.

“The OK Movement is not a political decoration, a temporary support group, or an organisation that exists merely to applaud political leaders. We are a movement built on principles, driven by purpose, and determined to demonstrate what serious political organisation should look like,” he said.

He added that leadership should be judged by the quality of preparation and the ability to deliver results, rather than the volume of political rhetoric.

“Leadership is not about who makes the loudest noise. Leadership is about who prepares, who organises, who builds, and who delivers when it matters most,” he said.

Reaffirming the movement’s readiness for the electoral contest, Ughulu challenged other political organisations to demonstrate that they had undertaken the necessary groundwork to compete effectively.

“We have demonstrated our capacity. We have shown our commitment. We have done the necessary groundwork,” he said.

He urged political actors still assembling their campaign machinery to recognise the difference between aspiring to political office and possessing the organisational capacity to pursue that ambition.

“Let those who are only just waking up to the realities of election preparation learn from the difference between having political ambition and possessing the capacity to execute it,” he said.

Ughulu concluded with a challenge to political rivals: “The OK Movement is ready. The question is: Are they?”

World.title: Tinubu Felicitates Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, On Re-Election For Record Fourth Term
World.content:
Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu has felicitated his friend and President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, on his reelection for a record fourth term.

The president also reiterated Nigeria-Brazil multilareral cooperation and historical ties.

Tinubu, in a six-paragraph release issued on Monday stated inter alia: “I congratulate my friend, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, on his re-election for a record fourth term.

“Your renewed mandate offers an opportunity to strengthen the longstanding friendship and historical ties between Nigeria and Brazil.

“As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order.

“I look forward to expanding cooperation in trade and investment, agriculture and food security, energy, oil and gas, manufacturing, science and technology, education, aviation, and cultural exchange.

“I affirm Nigeria’s continued commitment to working with Brazil to strengthen multilateral cooperation and advance shared priorities in Africa, South America, and across the Global South.

“On behalf of the people of Nigeria, I wish you a successful new term in office.”

World.title: Wicknell Chivayo’s unpaid car bills: Uebert Angel steps in
World.content:
Zimbabwean self-proclaimed prophet Uebert Angel has pledged to pay up to US$2 million (R33.2 million) towards verified debts left by businessman Wicknell Chivayo, following reports that three car dealerships are owed millions of dollars for vehicles supplied to the late businessman.

Angel made the announcement while addressing his congregation on Sunday, 25 October, saying he was prepared to help settle legitimate claims because his family had also benefited from Chivayo’s generosity.

According to reports by Tuko and My Zimbabwe News, Angel’s offer is subject to strict conditions, with claimants required to provide documentary evidence proving that Chivayo owed them money.



Angel sets conditions for paying Chivayo’s debts

Angel reportedly said he would consider claims from a limited number of creditors, with his commitment capped at US$2 million.

He urged those seeking assistance to provide proof of their claims, indicating that he would not simply pay every person who alleged that Chivayo owed them money.

The self-proclaimed prophet also reportedly said he had arranged meetings with people seeking payment and that the businessman’s estate still needed to be assessed to establish its overall financial position.



Angel’s offer comes as questions emerge over the outstanding obligations of Chivayo’s estate following the businessman’s death in a helicopter crash near Marondera on 30 September 2026.

Chivayo died alongside his wife, Lucy Muteke, and four other people.

Car dealerships reportedly owed US$5.1 million

Reports have linked three Harare dealerships to outstanding payments totalling approximately US$5.1 million for vehicles supplied to Chivayo.



Enterprise Car Sales has reportedly been linked to a claim of US$1.3 million (R21.58 million), while Exquisite Cars and Faramatsi Motors have been associated with reported balances of US$1.4 million (R23.24 million) and US$2.4 million (R39.84 million), respectively.

However, the claims have not all been accepted by the businesses involved.

Reports indicate that the circumstances and amounts surrounding some transactions remain disputed.



The reported debts have drawn attention because Chivayo was widely known for gifting luxury vehicles to musicians, footballers, religious leaders and other public figures.

Some of the vehicles were reportedly supplied under arrangements that allowed payment at a later date, leaving questions about outstanding balances after his death.

Angel’s family benefited from Chivayo’s generosity

Angel’s pledge also comes against the backdrop of his close relationship with Chivayo, who reportedly gifted the preacher’s family luxury items, including a Rolls-Royce Ghost.



The prophet has described Chivayo as a close friend and family member following his death.

His offer has prompted mixed reactions on social media, with some users questioning why the announcement was made publicly during a church service rather than handled privately.

It remains to be seen how many claims will meet Angel’s requirements and whether the proposed US$2 million will be used to settle any of the reported dealership debts.



The administration of Chivayo’s estate will also be central to determining his outstanding liabilities and how legitimate claims are ultimately resolve

World.title: New report: Kaizer Chiefs in talks with top local coach
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs are said to be exploring the idea of appointing Manqoba Mngqithi. Amakhosi previously made contact with the 55-year-old before deciding to hire Fernando Da Cruz in July.

According to the leading Amakhosi insider Innocent Mkhabela on X, talks are underway with Mngqithi resisting the idea of working with the current techincal team at Naturena.

KAIZER CHIEFS TALKS WITH MANQOBA MNGQITHI

“Amakhosi are back to MANQOBA MNQITHI. Based on what im hearing now is that talks are already taking place behind the scenes but Manqoba doesn’t want current technical team,” Mkhabela said on X.



These developments follow after Kaizer Chiefs crashed out of the CAF Confederation Cup at the hands of Red Arrows last weekend.

Coach Da Cruz is yet to taste defeat in the league. But the Glamour Boys’ performances under the Frenchman have left him with an uncertain future.

Meanwhile, Mngqtihi is currently a free agent after parting with Tanzanian giants Young Africans last weekend. The Umzimkhulu-born coach previously confirmed he held advanced talks with Amakhosi before the start of the season.



MOVE TO AMAKHOSI WAS BLOCKED

“Kaizer Chiefs did have interest in me. But someone blocked the move and I know who it is,” said Mngqithi.

“I have had very cordial talks with Chiefs, even with Kaizer Motaung Sn. It is not a lie. But it never reached any fruition because there are people who block these moves.” “I’m fortunate to know that the person who blocked it I am not even worried about. But it’s true there was interest recently,” he continued.  “Kaizer Chiefs even wanted me before I joined Sundowns. I’ve had very cordial talks with senior Kaizer Motaung. I know they have always shown interest in me. But for whatever reason it never happened.”

World.title: ‘Attitude is there’: Siya Kolisi’s sister dances with Rachel, fans react
World.content:
Liphelo Madlingozi, the half-sister of Springboks captain Siya Kolisi, shared a video dancing with his ex-wife Rachel Kolisi via TikTok on Monday 26 October.

SIYA KOLISI’S SISTER AND RACHEL DANCE TOGETHER

Liphelo and Siya Kolisi’s ex-wife, Rachel Kolisi, often share videos together on social media. Liphelo also often gets Rachel to try dance challenges with her. In a recent video, the pair were dancing to Too Cool by Uncle Waffles. Take a look…







RACHEL AND SIYA KOLISI LEGALLY ADOPTED HIS SIBLINGS

Siya has two half-siblings Liyema and Liphelo. The siblings were reportedly left bouncing from orphanages to foster homes after their mother and father passed away. Siya and Rachel officially adopted his siblings in 2014, when they were financially stable enough to do so.

Siya reportedly found his siblings in foster care in Zwide – a township in Gqeberha. Siya explained that when he went to see his siblings, his sister didn’t know him.

“My little sister didn’t know me. She had been crawling when I last saw her. I told the woman taking care of them that I was going to take them for December holidays that year, which I did. But afterwards I said I can’t send them back,” he said according to reports.



“I had to go through a legal process, which I started after that holiday. It took about 18 months, but I finally legally adopted them,” he continued.

It’s been 12 years since Rachel and Siya adopted Liyema and Liphelo. Back in 2024, Rachel reflected on it being 10 years with the brother and sister duo.

“While celebrating Liphelo’s birthday last week, and having all 4 kids home for the weekend, we reflected on the fact that almost to the day, 10 years ago, Liphelo and Liyema came to spend a week with us in Cape Town to see that they were comfortable to make the move and come stay with us forever,” she wrote.



“I was 24 years old Nic was 3 months old, Liphelo had just turned 7 and Liyema 12. 10 years, of the greatest gift God could have ever given me,” she continued.

World.title: Khoza bought Rele Mofokeng a house after losing R200k bet
World.content:
Royal Union Saint-Gilloise attacker Relebohile Mofokeng reportedly made a bold bet with Orlando Pirates chairman Dr Irvin Khoza ahead of last season’s league campaign.

The 22-year-old spent four years with the Buccaneers before moving to Belgium in July. During his time at Pirates, Mofokeng won seven trophies, including the league title.

According to his father, Sechaba Mofokeng, the talented winger made a R200,000 bet with Khoza over whether Pirates would end their 14-year wait for a league championship.



Speaking to Soccer Laduma, Sechaba revealed that the agreement was that Mofokeng would pay the Pirates chairman R200,000 if the team failed to win the league. However, if the Buccaneers lifted the title, Khoza would buy the winger a house of his choice.

“So they made a bet, if they didn’t win the league, he [Mofokeng] would give the Chairman R200,000. He said, if I win the league, the Chairman would buy him any house of his choice,” Sechaba said.

He added that the exchange left his son speechless.



As it turned out, Pirates ended their 14-year league drought by winning the championship last season, with Mofokeng playing an instrumental role in helping the Soweto giants secure the title.

Sechaba also opened up about his son’s relationship with Khoza, explaining that the Pirates chairman had played a significant role in Mofokeng’s life.

“He did so much for me in my life and he taught me a lot about life. I think he deserved to get something back,” Sechaba said.



He further confirmed that Khoza honoured his side of the agreement by buying Mofokeng a house.

“The house is there, he delivered,” Sechaba added.

Mofokeng left Pirates having scored 29 goals in over 120 matches and has already impressed in Belgium in just four months.



How good has Rele been in 2026?

World.title: Springbok stars undergo scans after injury scares
World.content:
The latest round of the URC competition came at a heavy cost as the likes of Andre Esterhuizen, Handre Pollard and Deon Fourie all suffered what looked to be serious injuries.

According to the Bulls, Pollard has now undergone a scan on a hamstring complaint, and there are understandable concerns that it is an injury that could rule him out of the end-of-year tour.

Meanwhile, the Sharks have also revealed that three out of the four players who picked up injuries last weekend will now return to South Africa for further assessments.



Esterhuizen – who recently captained the Springboks- sustained a right ankle injury, and he is set to be ruled out of the November Tests.

Phatu Ganyane suffered an injury to his right elbow, and Jurenzo Julius picked up a right hamstring injury.

“All three players will undergo scans and consult with specialists on their return home to determine the severity of their injuries,” the Sharks added in a statement.



Springbok players among the walking wounded

In addition to the injury worry over Pollard, the Bulls released the following injury report.

Canan Moodie (wing/centre): Moodie has returned to training under the Head Injury Assessment (HIA) return-to-play protocols. He will not be considered for selection this week.

Moodie has returned to training under the Head Injury Assessment (HIA) return-to-play protocols. He will not be considered for selection this week. Cheswill Jooste (wing): Jooste has undergone an operation for a broken cheekbone. Having been concussed during the match against Ulster, he faces a mandatory two-week stand-down under HIA protocols, and extended rest has been recommended.

Jooste has undergone an operation for a broken cheekbone. Having been concussed during the match against Ulster, he faces a mandatory two-week stand-down under HIA protocols, and extended rest has been recommended. Sango Xamlashe (centre): Xamlashe will not be considered for selection this week after he completed HIA protocols following a concussion in Saturday’s match.

Xamlashe will not be considered for selection this week after he completed HIA protocols following a concussion in Saturday’s match. Embrose Papier (scrumhalf): Papier is recovering from an ankle operation and will be out for several weeks.

Papier is recovering from an ankle operation and will be out for several weeks. Thaakir Abrahams (wing): Abrahams is expected to recover from a hamstring injury within one week.

Stormers also assessing injured players

Fourie is expected to be out of action for an extended period, and it could ultimately spell the end of his time at Springbok level, Hacjivah Dayimani will be sidelined for at least one more week due to a head knock, while André-Hugo Venter suffered an elbow injury.

Stormers boss John Dobson praised his players for overcoming a series of injuries before holding on for a 52-40 victory over the Scarlets in round four of the URC competition.



“That’s our game, the set-piece. And then minutes 60 to 80 is when the hurt is meant to be done, and then suddenly we had that taken away (due to injuries).

“It was absolutely bizarre. That’s where I give them credit, because they weren’t getting it from the guys in the coaches’ box.

“I thought actually the way we closed it, we were in ascendancy for the last 10 minutes, which was remarkable given no set-piece for a set-piece team.



“The way we defended at the end there, it was probably our best period of defence.”

World.title: Gayton McKenzie makes BOLD Joslin Smith claim
World.content:
ayton McKenzie has made a bold claim about his role in keeping missing Joslin Smith’s disappearance in the public spotlight. Image: X

Patriotic Alliance (PA) leader Gayton McKenzie claims South Africans would have forgotten about missing Joslin Smith if he and his party had not kept her disappearance in the headlines.

The Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture made the claim during a Facebook Live broadcast on Sunday evening, 25 October.

According to a report, McKenzie credited himself and the PA with keeping Joslin’s case in the public eye, more than two-and-a-half years after she vanished from Saldanha Bay.



His comments came days after Joslin marked her ninth birthday on Friday, 23 October.

GAYTON MCKENZIE DEFENDS PA MEDIA BAN

McKenzie made the remarks while defending the PA’s decision to stop granting interviews to South African media outlets.

He announced the ban on Sunday, 18 October, after accusing the media of negative reporting about his party.

During his latest live, McKenzie argued that the PA had played a crucial role in drawing national attention to Joslin’s disappearance.

He claimed the public would have moved on from her case without his party’s involvement.

The outspoken politician has faced criticism over his involvement in the investigation, but he insists he remains committed to finding the missing girl.



‘I BELIEVE JOSLIN IS STILL ALIVE’

McKenzie also dismissed suggestions that Joslin had died, insisting he still believes she is alive.

“The moment I think Joslin is dead, I have to stop looking for her,” he said, translated from Afrikaans.

“I believe Joslin is still alive. You may believe Joslin is dead, but I believe she is still alive.”

McKenzie previously claimed to have obtained new information about Joslin’s disappearance and launched a foundation in her name earlier this year.

JOSLIN SMITH STILL MISSING

Joslin disappeared from her Middelpos home in Saldanha Bay on 19 February 2024. She was just six years old.

Her mother, Racquel ‘Kelly’ Smith, Jacquen ‘Boeta’ Appollis and Steveno van Rhyn are serving life sentences for human trafficking.

The Western Cape High Court sentenced the trio on 29 May 2025 and handed them additional 10-year sentences for kidnapping, which run concurrently.

Despite the convictions, investigators have yet to find Joslin.

Her disappearance continues to raise questions about what happened to her and whether she is still alive.

Police have kept the investigation open.

World.title: Yellow Level 4 warning issued for severe thunderstorms in Mpumalanga
World.content:
SAWS has issued a Yellow Level 4 warning for severe thunderstorms in southern Mpumalanga. Image: AI illustration

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) has issued a Yellow Level 4 warning for severe thunderstorms in southern Mpumalanga.

Heavy downpours and damaging winds could cause flooding, damage to infrastructure and major travel disruptions.

The warning takes effect at 14:00 on Monday, 26 October, and remains valid until 23:59 on Tuesday, 27 October.



SAWS warns that severe thunderstorms could bring significant impacts to affected communities, although it considers the likelihood of these impacts low.

Which areas are affected?

The Yellow Level 4 warning covers southern parts of Mpumalanga, including areas around Ermelo and Emakhazeni, as indicated on the SAWS warning map.

These areas face a higher impact level than those covered by the Yellow Level 2 warning in other parts of the province.



What impacts can residents expect?

According to SAWS, heavy downpours and strong, damaging winds could cause flooding and damage to infrastructure, homes, vehicles and other property.

The weather service warns of possible injuries and danger to life, particularly in areas vulnerable to flooding.

Severe weather could also disrupt major transport routes, with some roads and bridges potentially closing because of flooding.



Municipal and essential services, including electricity, healthcare, education and communications, could experience disruptions.

Farmers could also face agricultural losses, including damage to livestock and livelihoods.

Staying safe during severe thunderstorms

Residents should monitor weather warnings and avoid travelling through flooded roads or bridges.



Motorists should reduce their speed during heavy rain and avoid unnecessary travel when conditions become dangerous.

People living in areas at risk of flooding should remain alert to rising water levels and follow instructions from local emergency services.

SAWS advises residents to keep checking official weather updates as conditions change.

World.title: Proteas select 'enforcer' Coetzee for Australia decider
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - Fast bowler Gerald Coetzee will replace injured fellow paceman Anrich Nortje in the South African team for the series-deciding third Test against Australia, starting at Newlands on Tuesday.

Australia, meanwhile, are waiting on the fitness of key batsman Steve Smith, who is recovering from a neck injury.

"He's the closest we've got to a like-for-like replacement for Anrich Nortje," South African captain Temba Bavuma said of Coetzee at his pre-match press conference on Monday.

Like Nortje, Coetzee is capable of bowling at speeds of up to 150km/h.

And, like Nortje, bowling at high pace has led to lengthy periods on the sidelines because of injuries.

Nortje played in the first two Tests against Australia after a three-year lay-off – and was ruled out of the third Test by a groin injury.

Coetzee last played in the Test team two years ago but played in two of the three one-day internationals between South Africa and Australia last month.

"It's about the balance of the attack," said Bavuma, who said Coetzee and the medium-paced Wiaan Mulder added different strengths to the strike duo of Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen.

"Gerald's got that extra bit of pace. You need someone in that enforcer role who can pick up a wicket when the wicket is flat."

Mulder made crucial breakthroughs during South Africa's innings and 31 runs win in the second Test by bowling with tight control. "When you want someone who brings the stumps into play Wiaan comes into the conversation," said Bavuma.

Australia will delay naming their team until the morning of the match but are set to make changes in their batting line-up.

Opening batsman Nic Maddinson has been released from the squad after three failures in four innings. Matt Renshaw, player of the match in Australia's 214-run win in the first Test, is set to return to his accustomed position as an opening batsman after batting at number five in the first two Tests.

Australian captain Pat Cummins said Cameron Green would return in the middle order after recovering from an abdominal injury, while Smith would be given "every chance" to recover from a neck injury which hampered him in the second Test in Gqeberha.

Smith only faced gentle throwdowns on Sunday and his availability depended on how he feels on Tuesday after a more thorough examination in the nets on Monday.

"Hopefully it all goes well and he will be there," said Cummins.

World.title: Govt raises concern over unregulated water tankers
World.content:
PRETORIA - Government says it is concerned about the source of water supplied by some private tanker operators.

Currently, the City of Tshwane has deployed 36 water tankers to help restore access to safe water in Bronkhorstspruit.

This is as an investigation into the interruption of chlorine supplies and the failure to warn residents in time continues.

But government has noted the emergence of private tanker operators, with Deputy President Paul Mashatile saying there will be intervention to follow up on those water tankers.

READ | Tshwane water crisis: Parliament calls for wider accountability

The same concerns were flagged by Water and Sanitation Minister Pemmy Majodina, who said some of the private tankers are not regulated.

She said this is not only unique to Tshwane but across the country.

“When people see water in a desperate environment, they will buy water everywhere, not knowing whether that water has been treated…”

Tshwane mayor Nasiphi Moya said Tshwane Metro Police Department has received all registration numbers to follow up on the water tankers around to ensure they know where they source the water and who has tested it.

READ | Bronkhorstspruit Water Crisis: Tshwane deploys 36 water tankers

To date, the city has temporarily shut down the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Plant to allow for cleaning and the installation of equipment.

It has also begun flushing and disinfecting the affected water network and is conducting daily water-quality tests.

More than 800 Bronkhorstspruit residents have been affected by gastrointestinal illness, with three people hospitalised.

World.title: M1 freeway reopens after SAMWU protest
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The M1 freeway has been reopened following a protest action by the South African Municipal Workers' Union (SAMWU) on Monday.

The closure caused heavy congestion around Braamfontein and the CBD area.

Johannesburg Metropolitan Department (JMPD) spokesperson Xolani Fihla said the protest action was over ongoing wage disputes.

“Demonstrators marched onto the M1 freeway, forcing a total closure in both directions at the Smit Street on- and off-ramps near Braamfontein. The blockade caused severe back-ups along the main north-south arterial corridor, impacting travel into and out of the Johannesburg CBD,” he said.

Fihla said JMPD officials have been deployed to monitor the situation and ensure that there are no further disruptions.

“We can confirm that the crowds have been dispersed, the freeway has been reopened and traffic is flowing but we will still be on the ground to ensure that we avert any further disturbances.”

Motorists have been urged to proceed with caution as residual delays clear.

World.title: Bronkhorstspruit Treatment Water Plant temporarily shut down
World.content:
PRETORIA - The City of Tshwane has temporarily shut down the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Plant to allow for cleaning and the installation of equipment.

The City has begun flushing and disinfecting the affected water network and is conducting daily water-quality tests.

It says its chlorine supply has been secured for the next six to seven weeks.

More than 800 Bronkhorstspruit residents have been affected by gastrointestinal illness, with three people hospitalised.

An investigation has been ordered into the interruption of chlorine supplies and the failure to warn residents in time.

Following a preliminary report, the plant manager was suspended last Friday.

Tshwane mayor Nasiphi Moya said an external investigation had also been commissioned to examine several aspects of the incident and identify ways to improve the municipality’s systems.

To help restore access to safe water, the City has deployed 36 water tankers. Coca-Cola has also provided three standard-sized tankers and a 34,000-litre tanker, which is currently servicing the Bronkhorstspruit community.

“The focus is we must provide water in all the households so that we be able to reduce the number of infections,” said Moya.

Moya said all water storage facilities would be cleaned, disinfected and refilled.

“There are areas that are also receiving water through boreholes, there is testing that is happening there. Even for those buying from spaza shops, there is also testing through the environmental health colleagues.

READ MORE | Mayor needs to go - political expert over Bronkhorstspruit water crisis

“In terms of private tankers, TMPD has received all registration numbers to start following the tankers around to make sure we know where they get the water and who has tested that water.”

Moya said water-quality testing across the City would continue.

“The issue of chlorine has now been sorted while we deal with contractual issues. Rand Water is on site, and they have assured that they will be able to help us to get more so that we never run out. I can assure you that there is enough chlorine across the City of Tshwane.”

World.title: Parents protest over pupils' sexual abuse claims in Naturena Primary school
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Parents have staged a protest outside a primary school in Naturena, Johannesburg, following allegations of sexual abuse involving pupils.

A group of Grade 4 boys alleged that they have been sexually assaulted by older Grade 7 pupils, reportedly in the school toilets.

Parents and community leaders are demanding the school principal be removed.

READ | Soweto teacher denies rape allegations

The allegations have sparked outrage, prompting a visit from Gauteng Education Department officials.

Gauteng Education spokesperson Onwabile Lubhelwana said they are concerned about the incident and have since deployed a trauma counselling unit at the school.

He also confirmed that police are in the process of opening two cases in this matter.
