World.title: South Africa: Ready to Vote? Know What to Expect On Election Day
World.content:
South Africans will head to the polls on 4 November 2026 to elect local government representatives in the Local Government Elections.

According to the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), special voting will take place on 2 and 3 November 2026 from 8am to 5pm.

On Election Day, voting stations will open from 7 am to 9pm.

Prior to Election Day, voters can check that their voter registration details are correct and confirm their voting station. According to the IEC website, for municipal elections, voters must vote at the voting station where they are registered.



Voters can check their details through the IEC website at www.elections.org.za, SMS their 13-digit ID number to 32810, or send "Hi" to the IEC WhatsApp number 060 088 0000.

Voters are reminded to take an acceptable identity document: a smart ID card, green barcoded ID book or valid temporary identity certificate.

The Electoral Commission cautioned South Africans not to bring driver's licenses, passports, student cards or photocopies of ID documents, as these are not accepted for voting purposes.

What happens at the voting station?

Upon arrival at a voting station, an election official will verify your identity and registration details. Your name will then be checked against the voters' roll.

Your thumbnail will be marked with indelible ink to prevent double voting. You will then receive your ballot papers.

Know your ballot papers

The number of ballot papers you receive depends on the municipality where you are registered.

If you are registered in a metropolitan municipality, you will receive two ballot papers.

These are:

- A ward ballot to choose a ward councillor.

- A proportional representation (PR) ballot to choose a political party for representation in the metropolitan council.

If you are registered in a local municipality, you will receive three ballot papers:

- A ward ballot to choose a ward councillor.

- A PR ballot to elect a political party for the local municipal council.

- A district PR ballot to elect a political party for representation on the district municipal council.

Take the time to understand each ballot before making your choice.

How to cast your vote:

- Take your ballot papers into the voting booth and vote in private.

- Make one clear X (cross) inside the box next to your chosen candidate or political party on each ballot paper.

Close 

- Do not write your name, sign the ballot or make unnecessary marks, as this could make your ballot invalid.

- If you make a mistake, do not place the ballot in the ballot box. Return it to the Presiding Officer and ask for assistance.

- After voting, fold your ballot papers to keep your choice private and place them in the ballot box as directed by election officials.

*This article first appeared in Vukuzenzele

World.title: Uganda: How Uganda's Sugarcane Boom Leaves Families Hungry
World.content:
opinion

What needs to change: First, the sugar mills should stop signing contracts with males only

Busoga, in eastern Uganda, is a low, fertile plateau surrounded on three sides by Lake Victoria, the River Nile and Lake Kyoga. Most of its 4.3 million people farm small, rain-fed plots. Yet hunger is common: in the 2024 census, about a third of Busoga households reported going whole days without food.

Sugarcane has been grown commercially here since the 1920s, when one family established a large sugar processing facility. New investors followed after the government stopped setting sugar prices and opened the industry to the private sector in 1991.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Seven mills now operate in and around the Busoga region, with the amount of sugar cane planted tripling in size between 2000 and 2024. Tens of thousands of families also grow cane on their own land as "outgrowers", selling this on contracts to the sugar mills.

I spent over 20 years working in Uganda's civil service before becoming an academic. For my doctoral research, I set out to understand why decades of sugarcane growth had not reduced hunger in Busoga. I visited two parts of Busoga - the Jinja and Buyende districts - and interviewed 27 officials, local leaders and farmer representatives. I also asked four groups of farmers for their views.

I asked who decides how land is used, who signs contracts, who receives the money, and how households eat while waiting for the harvest.

My research found that the hunger in Busoga isn't caused by farmers not growing enough sugarcane to sell. The prices of sugarcane are dropping, but my research found that the main problem is that sugar mills mainly sign contracts with men.

This means that decisions about what to use land and cash for are solely in the hands of the men. They don't always use the cash to feed their families. The work of feeding families falls mainly on women, who are left only with the option of planting what little land is left with food crops.

To solve the problem, the government and sugar companies all need to end the practice of only contracting with men, set up contracts with women farmers too and make sure that women from sugarcane farming families inherit contracts automatically when their husbands die.

One fifth of the land, all the responsibility

Only about 20% of the available farmland in the Jinja and Buyende districts of Busoga is available to grow food crops. Up to 80% of farmland owned by families is used to grow sugarcane to sell.

Mills recruit sugarcane farmers through male household heads, whose names appear on the contracts. In one focus group, women described husbands signing multi-year contracts covering the family's entire land without consulting them. When they questioned this, the women were told the decision was not theirs.

The payment, a lump sum at harvest, is made to whoever signed the contract. A political leader in Buyende, speaking anonymously, told me that many men now keep the cane money and don't use it to buy food for the home.

Uganda's Land Act says family land cannot be sold, leased, or mortgaged without a spouse's written consent. But cane deals rarely go through a land office, so no one checks if consent is being given.

A widow inherits the cane, but not the contract

Uganda's constitution recognises the right of women to inherit land. Yet my research found that when an outgrower dies, the contract usually remains in his name, and his widow has no standing with the mill.

The mill's recruitment agent, who signs up farmers, might decide not to allow her to take over her husband's contract. A clan meeting may instead hand the land to a male relative. A bank may refuse her credit without a man's signature. Although this is not legal, my research found that it is common practice and the government hasn't put in place any way of stopping it.

Government extension officers, who advise farmers, visit only registered contract holders, and don't advise the wives of contract holders. Researchers call this the gap between holding a right and being able to use it.

In some cases, young men inherit the family's land but then sell it to pay for a motorcycle, school fees, or a family obligation. With the land gone, many end up cutting and loading cane for daily wages. A technical officer in Buyende told me that most of those workers are children. Uganda's employment law bars this, but enforcement is weak: one study found that there were only 83 labour officers in Uganda, but that 1,344 were needed to make sure that labour laws were not being broken.

What needs to happen next?

All the different organisations in the sugar industry have a role to play in protecting the rights of women in sugarcane growing families.

Close 

First, the sugar mills should stop signing contracts with males only. Kidera Sugar, a new mill in Buyende that opened in 2026, is now recruiting outgrowers, and has not set its contracting rules yet, so there's an opportunity for at least this sugar mill to introduce practices where women benefit equally.

Second, the Sugar Industry Stakeholders Council, the sugar industry regulator, gives mills their licences. It could change the situation by refusing to approve contracts without both spouses' signatures in the case of married couples. It could also start a new practice of requiring that all contracts pass on to widows. It could even make a rule that widows should retain a share of each farm's food crops.

Third, district land offices could register cane agreements so the Land Act's consent rule applies. Fourth, the labour ministry should fund the jobs of more inspectors in cane-growing areas.

As contract farming spreads, who signs the contract can determine who controls the income and whether the family has enough to eat.

James Kintu Is the Postdoctoral Research Fellow, Centre for Governance and Sustainability, Umass Boston.

World.title: Kenya: Nubian Community Wins Kibos Land Dispute Against Kenya Railways
World.content:
Joshua Odiambo Nyamori, the advocate who represented the community, addressed residents on Monday, saying the Supreme Court decision left intact an Environment and Land Court ruling that recognised the communityâs claim to the land/CFM

Kisumu — The Nubian community in Kibos, Kisumu, has won a long-running land dispute against Kenya Railways after the Supreme Court upheld earlier court decisions recognising the community's rights to the contested settlement.

The ruling, delivered on Friday, October 23, marks a major milestone for families who have lived on the land for generations but lost their homes, a nursery school and a mosque during a demolition operation in 2021.

Joshua Odiambo Nyamori, the advocate who represented the community, addressed residents on Monday, saying the Supreme Court decision left intact an Environment and Land Court ruling that recognised the community's claim to the land.

Nyamori said the community had been allocated the settlement in 1937, decades before Kenya Railways was granted the land it claimed to own.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"We are here with excitement after the Supreme Court of Kenya pronounced itself on Friday that the land on which we stand belongs to the Nubian community living in Kibos," he said.

He explained that the community's settlement in Kisumu dates back to the colonial period, when the railway reached the lakeside town in the early 20th century.

According to Nyamori, Nubian elders met the colonial administration in 1937, leading to the allocation of the current settlement to the community.

He said the Environment and Land Court established that Kenya Railways was granted its land in 1963, after the community had already been allocated the settlement. The court also found that the boundary separating the community's settlement from railway land had been clearly marked.

The dispute escalated in 2021 when homes and community facilities were demolished in an eviction operation that Nyamori said was carried out at night during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"When the bulldozers started rolling over their houses, the nursery school and even the mosque, they reduced a thriving settlement to total ruins," he said.

Nyamori recalled meeting elderly residents who had been left without shelter after the demolitions, describing the destruction as a severe blow to their dignity and livelihoods.

He said the community subsequently moved to court seeking protection from eviction and recognition of its land rights.

The Environment and Land Court found that the manner in which the demolitions were conducted violated residents' constitutional rights, including the rights to housing, property and human dignity, according to Nyamori.

The court also allowed the community to pursue a separate case seeking compensation for property destroyed during the operation.

Close 

Kenya Railways challenged the decision at the Court of Appeal, which dismissed its appeal before the matter proceeded to the Supreme Court.

"The effect of that decision is that the Environment and Land Court decision that gave the land to the community stands as the valid decision," Nyamori said.

The ruling offers the community greater certainty over its claim to the settlement after years of legal uncertainty. However, residents are also seeking formal title documents to strengthen their tenure security.

Kisumu Muslim Association chairman Sheikh Musa Ismail Haji, who accompanied Nyamori, called on President William Ruto's administration to facilitate the issuance of title deeds to affected families.

"We are asking President William Ruto to help this community secure title deeds, just like other minority communities in the country," Haji said.

He said formal ownership documents would provide lasting security and help protect residents from future disputes over the land.

Haji also said he was engaging well-wishers to support the construction of decent houses for families whose homes were demolished in 2021.

He called for urgent assistance to help residents rebuild their homes and restore their dignity after years of hardship.

"We want the title deeds issued to the families before the 2027 General Election so that they can live here with security and peace," he said.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria Has No Ebola Cases After Patient's Evacuation to Switzerland - WHO
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, says Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases following the medical evacuation of the patient and her husband to Switzerland.

Janabi disclosed this in a statement on his official X handle on Monday, adding that Nigeria would continue monitoring 52 contacts, while Switzerland would manage the patient and follow up with her husband.

He said the evacuation took place earlier in the morning, noting that both the patient and her husband were Swiss citizens.

According to him, the patient was clinically stable after Nigerian medical teams successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilised her condition.

Janabi congratulated the Federal Government, health workers, clinicians, emergency responders and other partners involved in the Ebola response, describing the development as a remarkable achievement.

He said the successful management of the patient demonstrated Africa's expertise, resilience and leadership in public health, particularly when countries worked together to respond to health emergencies.

However, the WHO regional director stressed that vigilance remained critical despite the evacuation, urging continued attention to contact monitoring and other response measures.

He said Nigeria would maintain close follow-up of 52 contacts, while Switzerland would assume responsibility for the continued management of the patient and monitoring of contact number 53, her husband.

(NAN)

President Donald Trump is considering giving the White House press corps the boot from its longtime briefing room — and has another use in mind for the space that doesn't involve the swimming pool he insists was never on the table.

Trump said Sunday he is thinking about relocating reporters to make room for other White House needs, a day after suggesting the press could be moved to a "less obnoxious location."

"I am not building a swimming pool in the White House Briefing Room, and never had any intention of doing so," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location, but I will use that location for very badly needed space."

The president’s comments come after The New York Times reported on Oct. 20 that Trump had discussed replacing the White House’s James S. Brady Press Briefing Room with an indoor swimming pool.

DAVID MARCUS: KAROLINE LEAVITT’S LASTING LEGACY IS OPENING THE WHITE HOUSE TO INDIE PRESS

When reached for additional comment, the White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's Sunday Truth Social post.

"There is a Fake News report out there that I am going to remove the White House Press Room and bring back the old Swimming Pool, which lies directly underneath," Trump wrote in the social media post. "Although I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location, the old swimming pool will never be brought back."

TRUMP THREATENS TO ADD NY TIMES' 'TREASONOUS' IRAN WAR COVERAGE TO $15B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT

TRUMP BYPASSES MEDIA GATEKEEPERS AS GOV SANDERS REVEALS LEGACY OUTLETS ARE LOSING THEIR GRIP

World.title: Michael Douglas doesn't 'feel bad' about affair revelations from 'before Catherine'

Michael Douglas gave a cheeky response when asked how his wife, Catherine Zeta-Jones, had reacted to his new tell-all, "One Helluva Ride."

The 82-year-old actor's new memoir, published Oct. 6, contained revelations about his life, including his secret affairs with his former co-stars Kathleen Turner and Jeanne Tripplehorn, as well as his past cocaine use and struggles with addiction.

During an appearance on the "Happy, Sad, Confused" podcast on the day of the book's release, host Josh Horowitz asked Douglas whether Zeta-Jones, 57, knew "everything" that he revealed in the book.

MICHAEL DOUGLAS GETS EXPLICIT ABOUT HOW HE FILMED SEX SCENES BEFORE INTIMACY COORDINATORS

"I'll be home to ask her because she just got the book two days ago. I told her this was all, as I say, B.C., before Catherine," Douglas said in the interview, which was published on Oct. 19.

"And you know, we have a 25-year age difference, so I'm looking at some of these films, like with Kathleen, and Catherine would have been seven years old," he joked.

"I don't feel bad," Douglas added. "I think she understands."

In "One Helluva Ride," Douglas confirmed that he and Turner, 72, had an affair in 1983 while filming the hit 1984 romantic adventure movie "Romancing the Stone," a rumor they denied for over 40 years.

At the time, Douglas was legally married to Diandra Luker, with whom he shares son Cameron, though he said in his memoir that they were separated when production on the film began, and they were both having extramarital affairs.

Douglas recalled that he and Turner continued to deny rumors that they were romantically involved during production of the sequel and even years later when they reunited on "The Kominsky Method."

SALLY FIELD SAYS BURT REYNOLDS WAS ‘WONDERFUL’ BUT ‘FRIGHTENING,’ CLAIMS HE TRIED TO CONTROL HER CAREER

The two told the public that while they "had amazing chemistry" and were "both tempted," they never acted on their feelings.

"The truth is that during the production of ‘Romancing the Stone,' Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship," he wrote. "It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen."

PHIL COLLINS GETS FRANK ON MARRIAGE FAILURES AND LIFE REGRETS: 'I REGRET MY MARRIAGES FALLING APART'

He noted that he and Turner kept their affair a secret for 40 years to protect Luker and Cameron. Douglas wrote that the two decided to end their relationship after Luker visited them on set with Cameron "and made it clear to her [Turner] that we were still married."

After reports circulated about Douglas' admission, Turner said in a statement to People, "Good heavens, what a fuss about something 40 years ago! I love Michael, and I look forward to enjoying the book."

SHARON STONE SAYS SHE 'NEARLY DIED' AFTER 'BASIC INSTINCT' OPENED THE DOOR TO HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE

Douglas also disclosed that he and Tripplehorn, 63, who was almost 20 years his junior, had an affair during the filming of their 1992 movie, "Basic Instinct."

"The truth is, I fell very hard for Jeanne despite our nearly 20-year age difference," he wrote. "In fact, I was ready to officially leave my wife for Jeanne. I was crazy about her."

Douglas recalled that his "relationship with Jeanne lasted through production," but that they "went our separate ways" once production ended.

"But I will always think of her as an amazing actress and a truly terrific woman that I was very fortunate to spend time with," he added.

'CADDYSHACK' STAR MICHAEL O'KEEFE CLAIMS COCAINE WAS BUDGETED ON SET, ADMITS FILMING SCENES HIGH

Douglas maintained that he and Luker were still separated at the time. Luker filed for divorce in 1995, and their split was finalized in 2000.

Tripplehorn has not publicly commented on Douglas' memoir, though the actor previously said she approved of him including their relationship in the book. During an interview with Page Six, Douglas said, "I talked to her before I put it in the book," adding that "she was fine" with it.

The memoir also explored Douglas’ struggles with substance abuse, his complicated relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, and Cameron’s battle with addiction.

Zeta-Jones previously confirmed that she had not yet read "One Helluva Ride" during an Oct. 8 appearance on "Today."

"As much as I love my husband, when I’m tired at night, I have no intention of reading about him. At all," she joked.

The Oscar winner cited her exhausting schedule, having just wrapped up seven months of filming the third season of her Netflix series "Wednesday" in Dublin, while also working on her new Prime Video show "Kill Jackie" in London and traveling to Bilbao, Spain, before her press tour.

"But everyone else should [read it]," Zeta-Jones told the audience. "The book is called ‘One Helluva Ride,’ and I think everyone should hold on to their cowboy hats, because I think it is."

During a subsequent appearance on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!," Douglas was asked if it "was for the best" that Zeta-Jones had not read his memoir.

"Oh, yeah," Douglas quipped.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

In an Oct. 7 interview with Page Six, Douglas confirmed that he had already "talked" to Zeta-Jones about the book and expressed his confidence that she would be "very understanding."

Douglas first fell head over heels for Zeta-Jones when she caught his eye in the 1998 movie "The Mask of Zorro." He went on to meet Zeta-Jones at the Deauville Film Festival in France. At the time, Zeta-Jones was aware of his reputation as a Hollywood womanizer and wary of starting a relationship with him.

In his memoir, Douglas recalled that Zeta-Jones demanded monogamy, and he called five other women that day to end their relationships before committing to her.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The couple, who share the same birthday, Sept. 25, though 25 years apart, became engaged in December 1999 and tied the knot in November 2000. Douglas and Zeta-Jones, who are parents to son Dylan, 26, and daughter Carys, 23, separated in 2013 before reconciling eight months later in 2014.

In "One Helluva Ride," Douglas wrote candidly about their separation and shared that he never gave up hope that they would reconcile.

"I love Catherine in a way that I have never loved any other woman," he wrote. "She's my wife, my best friend, and my life partner. I could never lose her."

OHIO STATE MOVES SENIOR DAY AWAY FROM MICHIGAN GAME IN AN EFFORT TO REMOVE 'DISTRACTIONS'

World.title: Democrats far less likely than Republicans to prioritize patriotism as key value, poll finds
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democrats are far less likely than Republicans to prioritize patriotism as a core value the nation needs, marking the single widest partisan divide in a new survey examining the country’s values.

According to a Gallup and With Honor survey released Sunday, 46% of Republicans ranked patriotism among the top three values the nation needs most, compared with just 6% of Democrats – a 40-percentage-point difference that dwarfs every other ideological disagreement in the poll.

"Democrats are far more likely to say the country needs equality, fairness and kindness, while Republicans are far more likely to say the country needs responsibility and patriotism," according to Gallup.

ONLY 27% OF DEMOCRATS WILL DISPLAY AMERICAN FLAG ON JULY 4: POLL

Overall, Americans view honesty (34%), responsibility (32%) and integrity (31%) as the values most urgently needed. Beneath that surface, though, the parties see starkly different remedies for what is most needed in the nation.

STUNNINGLY LOW PERCENTAGE OF ADULTS IN US THINK AMERICA STANDS ABOVE EVERY OTHER NATION: POLL

Republicans place the highest priority on patriotism (46%), followed by responsibility (41%) and honesty (38%). Democrats as a whole valued equality highest (44%), followed by fairness (34%) and honesty (32%).

DEMS PUT ON BLAST OVER POLL THAT SHOWS RECORD-LOW PATRIOTISM IN US: 'TEAR OUR SOCIETY APART'

Independents land between both sides, most frequently selecting honesty (34%), responsibility (32%) and integrity (31%), with only 15% selecting patriotism.

Despite the large disparity between Democrats and Republicans on the value of patriotism, it was one of the most selected values that participants said they believed was shared by most Americans regardless of their political leanings. When given a list of 12 choices, 32% said they believed most Americans shared patriotism as a value, trailing only freedom at 38%.

Those 12 values were: freedom, patriotism, service, kindness, respect, equality, fairness, responsibility, integrity, courage, honesty and humility. More than three-quarters of Americans (76%) believed people shared at least one of those values regardless of politics, while 59% said at least two, and 46% said at least three.

INDEPENDENT VOTERS AREN’T PICKING A POLITICAL TEAM, THEY JUST FEEL PICKED ON

Beyond patriotism, the second-largest partisan divide emerged around equality, chosen by 44% of Democrats compared to just 10% of Republicans – a 34-point spread. Fairness similarly split the electorate, chosen by 34% of Democrats versus 15% of Republicans.

The findings also reveal an age divide that mirrors the political split. Adults aged 65 and older are nearly three times as likely as adults aged 18-39 to say the nation needs more patriotism (32% vs. 12%).

Despite the deep differences in priorities, the survey revealed broad consensus on political tolerance. Nearly eight in 10 Americans (79%) – including 84% of Democrats, 81% of independents and 72% of Republicans – said respecting different values matters more than sharing the same ones. Additionally, 70% of respondents said elected leaders must be willing to compromise across party lines, even at personal political cost.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Perhaps, then, the ultimate shared value is that Americans agree to disagree," the Gallup analysis concluded.

The survey was conducted May 12–22 among a nationally representative panel of more than 3,000 U.S. adults.

World.title: LA mayoral hopeful Nithya Raman calls herself both a 'capitalist' and 'democratic socialist'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman declared herself both a capitalist and a democratic socialist during an interview Friday, raising questions about her political ideology as the Democratic Socialists of America considers challenging her endorsement from the organization just days before the election.

Raman, a Los Angeles city councilwoman and DSA member challenging incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, defended the two labels when Michaelson pressed her about capitalism and the organization's political positions.

"I am a capitalist, and I'm also a democratic socialist," she told CNN's Elex Michaelson. "I want the city to work and when the government is doing its job, it needs to work really effectively, and we need to make sure capitalism works without harm to workers, without worker exploitation, without exploitation of poor people. That's what I'm going to focus on."

Los Angeles County Republican Party Chair Roxanne Hoge criticized Raman's remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital, questioning how the mayoral hopeful could embrace capitalism while maintaining ties to an organization that advocates replacing it.

DEPROGRAMMED: FORMER DSA INSIDER REVEALS ‘FRIGHTENING’ SOCIALIST AGENDA DROVE HIM FROM ‘EXTREME’ IDEOLOGY

"It's no surprise that Nithya Raman is confused by two mutually exclusive concepts. Perhaps she was in a fugue state when she agreed to co-govern with the DSA who proudly proclaim their desire to expropriate private property and to abolish the police," Hoge said.

The Los Angeles Times reported Saturday that DSA national leadership was considering action against the Los Angeles chapter's endorsement of Raman over accusations she doesn't fully support the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement targeting Israel. At a forum last month, according to the LA Times, Raman referred to BDS as a "legitimate form of peaceful protest " without explicitly saying she supports the movement.

Lisa Cusack, president of the Don't LA My Burbank PAC, criticized Raman's affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America, pointing to the organization's communist roots and its current political program advocating greater worker control over private industries.

"The founder of DSA-LA, Dorothy Rea Healey, was a longtime leader of the California Communist Party in California," she told Fox News Digital. "Her autobiography is titled: 'A Life in the American Communist Party.' The current Democrat Socialist Program for Los Angeles states, 'Capitalists extract massive profits by stealing the surplus value of working-class labor.'"

She claimed the program's mantra involves organizing to rebuild worker militancy, expanding union density, dismantling the gig economy, and asserting democratic worker control over municipal and private industries.

"This is who Nithya Raman will be expected to co-govern with. When people tell you who they are, believe them," Hoge said.

'DSA JIHADI': LA MAYORAL CANDIDATE TORCHED AFTER DEFENDING 'GENOCIDE' COMMENT DURING JEWISH FORUM

Raman's remarks contrasted with the DSA's official description of democratic socialism, which calls for replacing capitalism with an economic system in which workers exercise greater control over businesses and major industries.

The organization explicitly rejects capitalism in its explanation of its political philosophy.

"Capitalism is a system designed by the owning class to exploit the rest of us for their own profit. We must replace it with democratic socialism, a system where ordinary people have a real voice in our workplaces, neighborhoods, and society," the DSA states on its website.

DNC CHAIR KEN MARTIN DEFENDS 'BIG TENT' STRATEGY WHEN PRESSED ON DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS

Raman's latest comments also marked a change from how she answered the same question during a July interview with Michaelson. At the time, she declined to directly identify herself as a capitalist, instead emphasizing the existing economic system and the responsibilities of local government.

When Michaelson asked whether she considered herself a capitalist, Raman acknowledged the economic structure under which Los Angeles operates.

"You know, we are in a capitalist system. It's a city government," Raman said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Michaelson also asked Raman whether she supported abolishing police departments, prisons or the U.S. Senate. She rejected all three proposals. When Michaelson pressed her on how she reconciled her political affiliations with those disagreements, Raman defended the ideological diversity within the organization.

"I don't, you know, I think democratic socialism is a big tent," she said. "The DSA is a big tent organization, and I'm in part of that tent and I think a lot of Angelenos are in that tent with me."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA, Raman and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

World.title: Trump's brutal Truth Social attack on Bill Maher after dinner sparks confusion online
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump set social media ablaze on Sunday night with a lengthy Truth Social post slamming HBO host Bill Maher on the heels of a recent dinner between the two of them, leaving onlookers baffled at the sudden about-face.

Trump hosted Maher for dinner at the White House earlier this month, marking the second time they have dined together. Afterward, Trump told reporters that the HBO comedian was "great," and that it "was a very informative dinner," but the president changed his tune on Sunday night.

"Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher. He’s got a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO, which was once, long ago, a Network of Quality and Excitement — But that’s all gone. It’s not 'HOT' anymore!" Trump wrote.

Trump also described his past relationship with Maher's "Club Random" show producer Chuck LaBella from his days on NBC's "The Apprentice," claiming that LaBella would frequently encourage Trump to appear on Maher's show.

BILL MAHER CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP FELT 'BETRAYED' BY HIM WITH 'SILLY' FEUD AFTER CORDIAL 2025 DINNER

"When I became President, I agreed to meet, after the first one, and the last one, but never agreed to do his show, which he wants me to do, DESPARATELY [sic] — It won’t happen! When I have watched the show, which isn’t often, it always ends with dishonesty, about me at least, but, who cares?" Trump wrote.

He described LaBella and singer Kid Rock arguing in favor of inviting Maher to the White House for a meeting in what ultimately became their April 2025 dinner, though Trump claimed Maher "invited himself."

The president also wrote that Maher was in worse condition during their more recent meal.

"Also, I wanted to tell Bill that he’s a major POTHEAD. He’s got to stop, it’s very bad for his health. He looked like hell this time. Bill was drunk and had alcohol in his hand as he walked through the White House. Stephen A. Smith and Kid Rock came along with him. Overall, I thought it was a good meeting. It didn’t last four hours, it lasted two hours, maybe less, and everybody was happy. We have the timestamps. I learned nothing, and felt it was a waste of time," Trump wrote.

Trump claimed that since their second dinner, Maher's show has become "worse" than before and implored Maher and his team not to reach out to him again in the near future.

TRUMP HOSTED A DINNER WITH – WAIT FOR IT – STEPHEN A SMITH, KID ROCK AND BILL MAHER

"There were so many other falsehoods Bill spewed, but I won’t waste time in FACT CHECKING him. He isn’t worth it. Bill: Don’t call anymore. It’s useless, and tell Chuck LaBella not to call so much, and say how much you love 'TRUMP,' and want to get together, because you’re a hopeless guy, who is just trying to cater to your small group of 'fans.' You’re also a coward who is afraid to tell the truth about how well our Country is running because of your few 'fans,' and how badly the Dumocrats have done, almost destroying the U.S.A.," Trump wrote.

He concluded, "You’re not transformative, you’re a Loser! I never watched your show much, but I will never watch it again, because it is nothing more than FAKE NEWS that America, and the World, is unfortunately subjected to."

When reached for comment, the White House pointed Fox News Digital back to Trump's Truth Social Post. Maher did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was the longest post Trump has ever sent, according to CNN.

Comedian Tim Young — the Heritage Foundation’s media fellow — feels there is only one explanation for the 1,300-plus word takedown.

World.title: Judge orders DOJ to reinstate former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director
World.content:
A federal judge ruled Monday that former Assistant United States Attorney Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was “unlawfully terminated” and ordered that she be reinstated.

The Justice Department’s abrupt firing of Comey in July 2025 violated the Constitution’s separation of powers and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman found. The Trump administration’s assertion that it can fire career prosecutors at will would “unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system,” the judge wrote.

He granted Comey back pay effective from the date of her termination through Dec. 20, 2025, when she began a new job.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department said DOJ “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.”

In a joint statement, Comey’s attorneys Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said that “this decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”

They added that the “hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law.”

Then-Assistant U.S. Attorney Maurene Comey outside court during the Sean "Diddy" Combs' sex trafficking trial in 2025. Ted Shaffrey / AP

Comey had worked on a number of high-profile cases in the Southern District of New York, including the prosecutions of disgraced music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, former Sen. Bob Menendez, D-N.J., and the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his co-conspirator, Ghislaine Maxwell.

Comey filed suit in September 2025, alleging the Trump administration provided “no legitimate explanation” for firing her after almost 10 years of service, and that it had only done so because of President Donald Trump’s “well-known and longstanding vendetta against James Comey, whom he fired as FBI Director in 2017.”

Maurene Comey said the only thing she was told about her firing from her boss was that it “came from Washington.”

The Justice Department later said in a court filing that she was removed at the direction of then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.

The judge found Bondi did not follow the law when she fired Comey, depriving Comey of her rights to due process.

“Congress granted the Attorney General power to remove Comey,” the judge wrote, but “Congress imposed limits on that power — limits that, even Defendants concede, were violated in Comey’s case.”

Among DOJ’s arguments were that Bondi had the authority to fire Comey “at will” and for no reason at all, and that Congress does not have the authority to put limits on that authority.

Furman roundly rejected those arguments. DOJ has staked out a “sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority,” he wrote, and its position “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”

The Trump administration has routinely fired career federal prosecutors along with FBI employees, particularly focusing on individuals involved in prior investigations of Trump or with the massive investigation into the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

Furman seemed to take note of those firings while declaring Comey’s firing unlawful.

“Defendants invented a new and expansive theory of executive power. And they have also utilized that theory to remove other Executive Branch employees who have long held protections from removal,” he wrote, adding the declaration should “serve a useful purpose in clarifying or settling the legal issues involved.”

The administration is also continuing to push forward with a federal criminal case brought against Comey’s father over a photo of seashells that it contends amounted to a threat against Trump.

The seashells case has been delayed until at least early 2027 as a judge weighs whether to dismiss it. James Comey’s team has argued the case is a product of Trump’s retribution campaign rather than a good faith application of federal law and that “dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense” show the seashells photo was not a true threat.

World.title: How Democrats could win the House, how the GOP could hang on, and where to look for a wave
World.content:
Districts to watch: NC-14, KY-6

Another way to estimate the possible size of November’s swing is to look at the partisan shifts in elections held in 2025 and 2026, ever since Trump returned to office. These races include the 2025 governor’s elections in New Jersey and Virginia, other high-profile statewide elections and several special elections for the U.S. House.

Although Trump lost Virginia and New Jersey, the other recent elections have tended to occur in places that supported Trump in 2024. Averaging across all of these states and districts, Trump won them by an average of about 3.5 percentage points in 2024. In the 2025 and 2026 elections, however, those states and districts supported the Democratic candidate by an average of about 11 points. This amounts to a shift of 14.5 points in the Democrats’ favor.

If the Democrats are able to shift the vote in every district by such a historically massive margin in 2026, they could win as many as 263 seats to the Republicans’ 172. That would be the largest majority that either party has held in the U.S. House since the 1990 midterm elections.

Such a shift could put into play districts like Florida’s 27th District, represented by GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar. Republicans in Florida left this district nearly unchanged when they redrew the state’s congressional map, believing that a district that Trump won by 14.6 points would be out of reach for the Democrats.

But it appears the race in this heavily Hispanic district is tightening, as polls show Latino voters nationwide turning against Trump and Republicans, with economic concerns weighing heavily on their minds. These voters were critical to Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, and indications that they are moving back toward Democrats are helping drive the party’s competitiveness in Republican-leaning, heavily Hispanic districts in states like Texas, too. Salazar outran Trump’s win margin by nearly 6 percentage points in 2024, and her survival in the 2026 election may require a similarly strong overperformance.

A 14.5-point national swing toward Democrats could also make North Carolina’s 14th District competitive. Republican Rep. Tim Moore’s district is one that North Carolina Republicans did not bother changing when they redrew their maps last year. Trump won the district by 15.1 points, and Moore himself won it in 2024 by 16.1 points.

Another district to watch is Kentucky’s 6th District. Republican Andy Barr has held this open Lexington-based seat since 2013, and Trump carried it in 2024 by 15 points. Barr is running for the U.S. Senate this year. Republican- and Democratic-aligned groups are spending heavily here, reflecting the importance of the race, as Republican Ralph Alvarado faces off against Democrat Zach Dembo.

The NBC News Decision Desk rates this race as lean Republican. In 2024, this district reported almost 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m. ET. If Democrats are on track for a massive national shift, this district may provide one of the best pieces of early evidence.

National trends don’t mean every district shifts the same amount

To be sure, all of these scenarios assume that the partisan shift in 2026 will be the same in every district. This may be true on average, but some districts will have a larger shift than the national average and others will have a smaller one.

Demographics of a specific district may play a role in the size of the shift. For example, if Hispanic voters shift more dramatically toward the Democratic Party than non-Hispanic voters, then districts with higher concentrations of Hispanic voters will vote more favorably for the Democrats than the underlying partisanship of the district would predict.

Incumbency can also play a large role in causing a district to shift more or less than the national average. In 2024, the incumbent members of Congress outperformed their party’s presidential candidate by an average of 2.5 percentage points.

This year, there are slightly more Democrats seeking re-election than Republican ones. This means that the Democratic Party as a whole stands to gain more from the benefits of incumbency compared with the Republican Party.

On the other hand, there are more Republicans who represent districts with evenly divided underlying partisanship. For example, an “incumbency bump” matters a lot more to a Republican in a district Trump won by 5 points than to a Democrat in a district Harris won by 25 points.

Finally, redistricting has also played a key role in this year’s midterms. By redrawing districts in several states, Republicans stand to win as many as 10 more seats than if the map remained unchanged after 2024.

Redistricting impacts the role of incumbency, too. When the lines for a district are redrawn, incumbents are fighting for the votes of people whom they’ve never represented and who may be less familiar with their records. This tends to diminish the size of the incumbency advantage. Republican incumbents in Texas and other red states and Democratic incumbents in California must lean heavily on the “D” or “R” next to their names when they try to win the support of their new potential constituents.

World.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers as it invests more in AI
World.content:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, or roughly one-quarter of its global workforce, as the technology giant invests more in artificial intelligence, according to Agence France-Presse.

So-called voluntary exit offers are available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the U.S., Microsoft said in announcing the buyout program on Monday. Employees must be at the vice president level or below to qualify for a buyout.

"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's chief people officer, said in a memo to employees.

The exit program is the second voluntary buyout offer Microsoft has offered workers this year. In April, the company reportedly offered around 7% of its U.S. workforce the option to retire early.

Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings. Around 27% of Microsoft's workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer, according to AFP.

The offer is available to mid-level workers for what Microsoft said was a limited period of time. It's designed to let them leave the company with financial padding and career-planning resources, while allowing the company to save on labor costs.

Eligible employees will be made aware of the offer by email on Monday, Coleman said.

Workers in some business units are ineligible for the buyout, the company said. They include employees focused on data centers and those who work in sales and marketing, Bloomberg reported, citing a company spokesperson.

World.title: Walter Koenig, actor who played Chekov on "Star Trek," dies at 90
World.content:
Walter Koenig, the actor who played Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" series and several movies, has died, his rep confirmed to CBS News. He was 90.

Koenig died Sunday night at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent rep Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.

In "Star Trek," Ensign Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.

Walter Koenig is seen playing Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" series. CBS via Getty Images

Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty.

"Star Trek" ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive.

World.title: Pope cleared for South America trip after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Only two weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV has been given the medical green light to embark on an ambitious 12-day tour of South America next month.

"Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned," the Vatican said in a statement on Monday. "The Pope is following medical recommendations with great care and diligence, and with a deep determination to continue serving the Church."

The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling. The 71-year-old pontiff plans to travel to 10 cities, board 14 flights, and attend many public appearances and religious ceremonies.

The Vatican also confirmed that the trip would proceed "according to the program previously published," which means that a visit to the Peruvian city of Cuzco, Peru, situated at more than 11,000 feet above sea level, remains on the schedule. The thinner air there could pose difficulties for someone recovering from lung surgery.

Pope Leo XIV addresses the crowd from the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St.Peter's Square during his Sunday Angelus prayer at the Vatican on Oct. 25, 2026. Alberto PIZZOLI /AFP via Getty Images

Doubts about the pope's ability to undergo the South American trip surfaced again last week, when, on the advice of his doctors, Leo canceled a visit by helicopter to Assisi for an international peace gathering to take place Tuesday. Doctors said they advised him to do so preventively, because of the unpressurized air on the helicopter journey.

The upcoming journey carries particular personal significance for the first American-born pope, who spent more than two decades working as a missionary and bishop in Peru.

"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a statement Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy."

Leo was operated on Oct. 13, when doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.

Since leaving the hospital, Leo has gradually resumed his public duties, including his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square and meetings with visiting church leaders.

World.title: Maurene Comey, James Comey's daughter, was unlawfully fired, judge rules
World.content:
Washington — A federal judge on Monday found that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her post as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York.

U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman said in a 55-page decision that Comey's removal violated the constitutional separation of powers and federal law. The judge retroactively reinstated Comey to her role as a federal prosecutor and ordered the Trump administration to provide her back pay from the date of her firing in July 2025 through Dec. 20, when she accepted a different job.

Comey's lawsuit was one of several filed by former government employees who were fired without cause that tested the limits of the president's power to fire federal officials.

The Trump administration had argued that Article II of the Constitution gives the president unrestricted removal power, and said Congress could not limit the removal of federal prosecutors.

But in his decision, Furman ruled that Comey's firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, a landmark law enacted in 1978 that provides protections for federal workers. The Trump administration, he wrote, is attempting to "upend" long-settled case law allowing Congress to regulate the removal of so-called inferior officers.

"Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," Furman wrote.

Comey's legal team cheered the decision as a "hard-earned victory" for her and all civil servants.

"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system.' This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law," lawyers Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said in a statement.

A Justice Department spokesperson said it "disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."

Comey had served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan since 2015, handling high-profile criminal cases against figures including Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and former Democratic Sen. Robert Menendez.

In a letter to her former colleagues at the time of her dismissal, Comey said she was "summarily fired via memo" by the Justice Department's headquarters in Washington, and was not given a reason for her termination.

The letter she received stated, "Pursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States, your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately."

It was initially unclear who made the decision to oust Comey, but in May, the Trump administration said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi "directed" her removal, and her successor, Todd Blanche, "ratified" her termination.

Comey sued the Justice Department over her firing last year, alleging she had probably been fired because President Trump dislikes her father, who has been indicted twice during the second Trump administration. One of the criminal cases was tossed out, and James Comey has denied wrongdoing in the second.

"Ms. Comey's termination — without cause, without advance notice, and without any opportunity to contest it — was unlawful and unconstitutional," Comey's attorneys wrote in their complaint.

The Trump administration attempted to dismiss the lawsuit on the grounds that Comey was required to bring her claims before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the agency tasked with adjudicating appeals from federal employees regarding adverse actions taken against them, but Furman denied the government's motion and allowed the case to continue.

Furman found that because Comey's firing rested on Article II of the Constitution — not a federal law governing the civil service — the federal court had jurisdiction to hear the case.

In court filings, the Justice Department admitted that Comey had received a rating of "outstanding" on her performance reviews from 2019 through 2024, but said that her firing had been carried out under legal authority Congress granted to the attorney general to fire assistant U.S. attorneys.

In defending Comey's firing, the Trump administration relied, in part, on the Supreme Court's June decision allowing the president to fire members of certain independent agencies without cause. In that case, the high court overturned a more than 90-year-old decision that allowed Congress to restrict the president's ability to fire officials from multimember agencies at will.

But Furman said the Justice Department's argument amounted to a "sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority."

World.title: These factors could decide Netanyahu's fate in Israel's election
World.content:
Tel Aviv — After three years with their country at war on multiple fronts, Israelis will go to the polls Tuesday in a hotly contested election that will shape their next government. Polls show it is an incredibly tight race, and as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to hold onto his job, there's no guarantee of a quick, definitive outcome for him or his political opponents.

Polls vary widely regarding the expected outcome. Right-leaning pollsters give an advantage to the right-wing and religious bloc led by Netanyahu, while left-leaning pollsters show an advantage for the so-called change bloc opposing the incumbent.

Most polls show neither side is likely to win a decisive majority of the 120 seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, which would enable it to unilaterally form a new government. The tight margins mean the voting may end in a stalemate, which could lead to protracted negotiations across ideological lines, the formation of a minority government, or even an election do-over.

"It looks like an indecisive outcome is the most likely outcome," said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute.

This will be the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis will go to the polls Tuesday with their country still — fighting in the subsequent multi-front war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for a third.

Against that backdrop, there are a few key issues that could determine the election outcome, even if it does take days or weeks to shake out. But first, here's a look at the two main factions vying for the votes.

The Netanyahu camp

Netanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.

He has two main pitches to voters: First, that only he can form a government without the support of Israel's Arab parties, which he argues would be a danger to the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts.

Netanyahu's second argument to voters is that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.

"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said.

A campaign billboard depicting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump is seen in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 26, 2026. JACK GUEZ/AFP/Getty Images

Since that endorsement, Netanyahu has argued that only he can work with Mr. Trump to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, which many Israelis see as an existential threat.

Netanyahu's campaign slogan, which rhymes in Hebrew, is: "Either right wing or Palestine, either right wing or a nuclear bomb."

Over the weekend, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv on social media, with a caption reiterating his insistence that Iran poses an existential threat to Israel.

Netanyahu's supporters see him as a top-tier global leader.

"Bibi can handle the whole world," restaurant owner Benny Abraham told CBS News, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him."

"He's the king of Israel," Abraham added.

The (anyone but Netanyahu) "change bloc"

Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of Arab, right, left and center parties that have one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at a campaign rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Tel Aviv, Israel. Erik Marmor/picture alliance/Getty Images

Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.

Eisenkot responded Monday to Netanyahu's rhetoric about Iran posing a nuclear threat by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv."

"This time, it won't work for him," he said.

Eisenkot's key campaign promises include launching a state inquiry into the intelligence and security failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas — something Netanyahu has thus far blocked.

Uzi Aharoni, 73, an engineer from Tel Aviv, told CBS News he saw Eisenkot as the only real alternative to Netanyahu.

"Eisenkott is not left, he's not right. He's straight and honest. He's the kind of leader who will take care of us, the people of Israel, and not himself or his corrupt family," Aharoni said.

The Arab vote and the ultra-Orthodox draft

There are a few factors analysts believe could hand a victory to either side.

One thing polls can't predict well in Israel is voter turnout. Past elections have shown voters backing Netanyahu's Likud party, and Arab-Israeli voters, vary the greatest in their enthusiasm to come out on election days, so there could be room for turn-out surprises that significantly change the electoral math in favor of either side.

Arab Israelis, also referred to as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up around 20% of Israel's population.

"The higher the Arab turnout, the less likely that Mr. Netanyahu, within the current coalition, can form another government," said Plesner at the Israel Democracy Institute.

More Arab voters will head to voting booths this year because of their strong desire to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government with far-right allies, who have made life difficult for them over the last four years, Jehad Abomoch, a cafe owner in the predominantly Arab city of Baqa al Gharbiya, told CBS News.

"The last four years were a real catastrophe, both socially and in terms of wars," he said, adding that many Arab Israelis feel that under Netanyahu, they have "no hope, no future."

There are also two new parties entering this election, and polls show each is hovering around the threshold of support required to gain seats in the Knesset. Whether either party ultimately crosses that threshold could also tip the scales — in either direction — toward a new coalition government.

Both parties are focused on challenging Netanyahu's alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties by demanding that ultra-Orthodox Jewish citizens be formally included in Israel's mandatory military service.

Ultra-Orthodox Jewish leaders of the Breslev Hasidic community take part in a rally against mandatory military conscription on Oct. 12, 2026, in Netanya, Israel. Amir Levy/Getty Images

It's a key issue that cuts right through Netanyahu's traditional support base and coalition partners.

Not all election outcomes are neat and tidy

In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in parliament, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is that the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than 50% of the 120 available. Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.

If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.

Plesner told CBS News that, if all the politicians running effectively stick to their campaign promises and refuse to swap sides in the event of a stalemate "we will roll into another election."

"I'm sure that most politicians are not interested in that," he added.

World.title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
World.content:
Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.

In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.

Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."

Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.

Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.

Anthropic shares will list on the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.

Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.

Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.

In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

World.title: Notable Deaths in 2026
World.content:
Tom Skerritt as Dallas in the 1979 film "Alien." | 20th Century Fox/Stanley Bielecki Movie Collection/Getty Images A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity. By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery. Actor Tom Skerritt (Aug. 25, 1933-Oct. 21, 2026) was an indelible presence in such films as "M*A*S*H," "Alien," "Top Gun" and "A River Runs Through It." He won an Emmy Award for the 1990s series "Picket Fences." A ruggedly handsome actor with an easy-going presence, the Detroit native had originally planned on working behind the camera, and attended UCLA film school. After watching "Citizen Kane," he determined that, if he wanted to write and direct well, he'd need to know how to act. Mentored by rising talents Robert Altman and Hal Ashby, he soon found himself in front of the camera. Skerritt's roster of nearly 200 films and TV roles began in the early 1960s, with the World War II drama "War Hunt," which co-starred Robert Redford. He played an Army surgeon in Altman's "M*A*S*H," a motorcycle cop in Ashby's "Harold and Maude," the captain of a fated outer space tug in "Alien," a sheriff investigating murders on the Stephen King thriller "The Dead Zone," an instructor at the Navy's school for elite fighter pilots in "Top Gun," and a strict minister and father in "A River Runs Through It" (directed by Redford). He received the National Board of Review's best supporting actor award as Shirley MacLaine's husband in "The Turning Point." Even as he was landing starring roles in popular films like "Ice Castles" and "Alien," Skerritt was also making appearances on TV in shows like "Cannon," "Barnaby Jones" and "Baretta." He told The A/V Club in 2019 that his journeyman actor ethos was born of necessity: "I had to make a living, you know. You have to do what you have to do — I had three kids. I had to raise the kids myself, so it's a very delicate balance. … I never could imagine myself as a movie star because that's not what I wanted to do. ... I just wanted us to get by. I didn't want us to have to move into a trailer park camp because I couldn't afford any rent, you know?" But his rough-hewn good looks and naturalistic talent made him a welcome addition to films like "Up in Smoke," "Steel Magnolias," "SpaceCamp," "The Rookie," "Contact," "Smoke Signals," and "Texas Rangers." He starred as small-town Sheriff Jimmy Brock in the 1990s series "Picket Fences," and played the patriarch of the Kennedy family in the TV series "Jackie Bouvier Kennedy Onassis." He also made appearances in "Cheers," "Chicago Hope," "Will & Grace," "The West Wing," "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit," "The Good Wife," and "Madam Secretary." Skerritt made his Broadway debut at age 80, in an adaptation of John Grisham's "A Time to Kill." At 88, he was lead in the film "East of the Mountain," playing a retired doctor who tries to hide his terminal cancer diagnosis. Skerritt also co-founded TheFilmSchool, a training program for filmmakers, in Seattle; and the media companies Heyou Media and Triple Squirrels. He was still working into his 90s. His last credit was a 2025 film about a rodeo rider, "Broke," starring Wyatt Russell and Dennis Quaid. And as he told Variety in 2021, he was nurtured by the nature surrounding his home in Seattle: "I live in a place that's like going on vacation," he said. "I look up, I see Lake Washington. I may see an otter on the neighbor's dock, an eagle flying in the air, mountains in the distance, a little smoke from a forest fire. All of this stuff is a beautiful world. This is all creative input. That's the way I've lived my life since I've been an adult."

Martina Arroyo Martina Arroyo in the title role of "Aida." | Louis Melancon|Met Opera Metropolitan Opera singer Martina Arroyo (Feb. 2, 1936-Oct. 13, 2026) was a sparkling talent acclaimed as an interpreter of Verdi and Mozart, starring as the heroine in productions of "Aida," "Don Carlo," "Il Trovatore," "Macbeth," and "Don Giovanni." She was named a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2013. Arroyo was born in Harlem to a father raised in Puerto Rico and an African-American mother who gave her a love of culture and a pioneering spirit. Her first exposure to opera came via radio. "My parents used to listen to the Metropolitan Opera on Saturday afternoon," Arroyo told "CBS This Morning" in 2013. "And I couldn't see them and I couldn't care less what they looked like. I just liked the sound and making music." She studied the arts as a child, and took voice lessons while teaching Italian in a Bronx public school and serving as a case worker in the city's welfare department. In 1958 she won a radio competition to audition for the Metropolitan Opera's training program. The soprano would go on to sing at Carnegie Hall, and in the 1960s performed on stages in Europe. Her big break came in New York in 1965, when Met star Birgit Nilsson fell ill; Arroyo was called in at the last minute to perform Aida. At the end, there was a standing ovation — and everything changed. She became a Metropolitan Opera contract singer, and over 20 seasons starred in a run of 199 performances, including major Verdi and Mozart roles, as well as Puccini ("Madama Butterfly"), Ponchielli ("La Gioconda"), and Wagner, becoming the first Black woman to perform Elsa in "Lohengrin." She also sang in Berlin, Chicago, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, London, Paris, Prague, San Francisco, Vienna and Zurich. A prolific recording artist, she also performed in recitals and oratorios, and appeared regularly on "The Tonight Show." Arroyo gave her last opera performance in 1991, but she continued to give lectures and lead master classes around the world. She also established the Martina Arroyo Foundation in 2003 to aid artists at the beginning of their careers. In 2013 she spoke of the impact of teaching singers starting out: "Because I think that it all led to this. It's knowing that it doesn't end with you. It's going to go on, and you want it to go on even better than when you were working in that profession."

RJ Mitte A portrait of actor RJ Mitte, in Hollywood, Calif., April 21, 2009. | Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic via Getty Images Actor and disability rights advocate RJ Mitte (Aug. 21, 1992-Oct. 12, 2026) was best known for playing the son of Bryan Cranston's chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer on the series "Breaking Bad." The character of Walter White Jr. had been inspired by a college friend of series creator Vince Gilligan. Mitte drew from his own experience living with cerebral palsy to bring authenticity to the role. He told the Associated Press in 2014 that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all key subjects on the show — made him better at his job. "You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world," Mitte said. "You're able to use that. And I think it's an asset instead of something that would hinder." He had faced struggles since childhood. Raised in Jackson, Miss., by adoptive parents who divorced when he was 9 months old, Mitte was 3 when he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy. He used crutches and braces until his teenage years. "I didn't know anything was wrong with me when I was growing up," he told The Guardian in 2016. "I thought everyone went to occupational and speech therapy, I thought these were common things. I thought I was quite normal, until I went to school and someone told me it wasn't normal to have a disability." When he was 12, his mother was in a car accident that paralyzed her for six years. He helped raise his baby sister, and after the family moved to Los Angeles, he became a breadwinner working as an extra. Mitte was 14 when he was cast in "Breaking Bad," which ran from 2008 to 2013. It was recently ranked as the best TV series of the 21st century in a New York Times poll. Mitte's other credits included the TV series "Switched at Birth" and "Guardians of Justice," and the films "Dixieland," "Triumph" and "Westhampton." He also produced the independent films "The Unseen" and "Love Me Dead." As an advocate, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He was also president of the Mitte Foundation, which supported community initiatives around disabilities. In 2025 he spoke to CBS News Minnesota while promoting the service dog organization Can Do Canine. "I have cerebral palsy. I'm very lucky with my disability that I have worked very hard to have the mobility I have today. … I see in many people's lives, they don't get the same opportunities," said Mitte.
