If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental health crisis, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing or texting "988."

Mike Ditka Head coach Mike Ditka of the Chicago Bears gets carried off the field following his team's 46-10 Super Bowl victory over the New England Patriots, Jan. 26, 1986. | Focus on Sport/Getty Images NFL Hall of Famer Mike Ditka (Oct. 18, 1939-Oct. 9, 2026) became a tough and fiery symbol of Chicago as both a player and coach of the Super Bowl-winning Bears. Nicknamed "Iron Mike," Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then – as Chicago's coach – led his team to the championship with one of the game's most dominant defenses ever (and a lineup that was even featured in a rap video, "The Super Bowl Shuffle"). Born in Carnegie, Pa., the son of a welder, he was a talented three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt. Selected by Chicago in the 1961 draft, Ditka earned Rookie of the Year honors, and multiple trips to the Pro Bowl. In 1963 the Bears won the NFL Championship. After six seasons in Chicago, Ditka played for the Philadelphia Eagles, and then the Dallas Cowboys. He moved to the sidelines as an assistant to coach Tom Landry (as the Cowboys won three NFC championships and a Super Bowl), before becoming Chicago's head coach in 1982. His 10 years leading the Bears brought Ditka five straight NFC Central titles and a Super Bowl ring – as well as a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan, and a new nickname: "Da Coach." After several years in the NBC booth, Ditka returned to coaching the Philadelphia Eagles and the New Orleans Saints, leaving the game behind after the 1999 season. After retiring as a coach, Ditka became an NFL analyst and color commentator at CBS and ESPN, as well as a restaurateur and TV pitchman. He also made appearances as himself on such shows and films as "L.A. Law," "Cheers," "3rd Rock From the Sun," "Entourage" and "Kicking & Screaming." He was also a forceful advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players. Unafraid to share his opinions about the game, in 1987, Ditka told "Sunday Morning" that he was against playing football in climate-controlled domed stadiums. "Domes have no place in sport, none," he said. "Unfortunately, people waste a lot of money building them … indoor domes should be used for roller rinks."

Eva Marie Saint A portrait of Oscar-winner Eva Marie Saint c. 1964. | Screen Archives/Getty Images Academy Award-winning actor Eva Marie Saint (July 4, 1924-Oct. 6, 2026) starred in such classics as "On the Waterfront" and "North by Northwest," but she also bucked Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career. A regal-looking blonde who ricocheted from playing sultry spies to Southern belles and Superman's stepmother, Saint made her motion picture debut opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's "On the Waterfront" (1954). Her performance earned Saint one of the film's eight Academy Awards, becoming only the fourth person to win a best supporting actress Oscar for their film debut. On the night she received her award, she was visibly pregnant. "I may have the baby right here!" she said. (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.) Saint married director-producer Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, and the couple stayed together for 65 years until his death in 2016. They had two children. Saint had made it clear that family was more important to her than her career. "I had an agent once who wanted me to make many more movies," she told CBS' "Sunday Morning" in 2014. "I said, 'I can't. I can only do one a year, if that. I have children, young children.' And he said, 'Well, I guess you won't be a superstar.' And I said, 'Well, I guess not.'" And what happened to that agent? "Fired him," she said. She kept up her self-imposed limit on films; she also brought her extended family to the set of Otto Preminger's "Exodus" while filming in Cyprus and Israel. Despite not cranking out movies, Saint followed her Oscar win by appearing in many prestige projects, including "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "All Fall Down," "The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," and the eponymous TV miniseries based on "How the West Was Won." She also received five Emmy nominations, and won for the 1990 TV movie "People Like Us." At age 97, she appeared on a podcast series. But perhaps her most memorable performance was as Eve Kendall, a mysterious blonde who crosses paths with Cary Grant's Roger Thornhill as he runs from murderous spies in the 1959 Alfred Hitchcock thriller "North by Northwest." Little does Thornhill realize that Kendall herself is a secret agent. Saint said Hitchcock's direction to her playing a sexy spy was simple: "Three things: Lower your voice. Don't use your hands. And look directly into Cary Grant's eyes at all times," she recalled. Though playing a femme fatale was new to her, Saint said she wasn't surprised upon watching her performance. "No. I don't think actors are surprised," she said. "I mean, that's what we do."

Marjoe Gortner A 1972 portrait of evangelist and actor Marjoe Gortner. | Jack Mitchell/Getty Images Marjoe Gortner (Jan. 14, 1944-Oct. 2, 2026) began his public life at an extremely young age, in a performative and highly influential role: as a child evangelist in a Pentecostal church. Born in Long Beach, Calif., his parents pushed him into the role. At age four he was ordained. He officiated a wedding, and toured the country preaching. But as he entered adolescence, he became disillusioned with the evangelical world. In the 1960s he quit the pulpit, taking on California's counterculture movement. He made a final return to preaching in 1971, this time with a film crew in tow, aiming to pull back the curtain on the revival tent circuit. In the 1971 documentary "Marjoe," Gortner recalled how he'd supported his parents as a child preacher. [His mother even sewed extra pockets into his clothes so that he could fit more donations.] He estimated that, beginning at age four, he brought in about $3 million, before his father disappeared with it. [His father disputed that account, opining to People magazine in 1972 that Gortner had come "under the influence of Satan."] The resulting documentary, which spotlighted exploitation of the public by traveling evangelists, won the Academy Award. He pursed acting and music careers, recording a folk-rock album, "Bad, But Not Evil," and starring in the TV movies "The Marcus-Nelson Murders" (which introduced the detective character Kojak) and "The Gun and the Pulpit," a western. He also appeared on "Barnaby Jones," "Medical Center," "Police Story," "Airwolf," "T.J. Hooker," "The A Team," "Fantasy Island," and several editions of "Circus of the Stars." His longest-running role was on the CBS drama "Falcon Crest," playing Vince Karlotti, a fake psychic, on 17 episodes. Gortner also starred in the 1974 disaster film "Earthquake" (playing a wacko National Guardsman), "When You Comin' Back, Red Ryder?," "Viva Knieval!," "Bobbie Joe and the Outlaw" (with Lynda Carter), and "Starcrash." He also organized "Celebrity Sports Invitationals," raising money for charities (such as medical research and environmental conservation).

Margaret Hamilton Computer programmer Margaret Hamilton sits in a mockup of the Apollo command module at MIT, Nov. 25, 1969. | AP Photo Groundbreaking computer scientist Margaret Hamilton (Aug. 17, 1936-Sept. 30, 2026) led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo program. A graduate with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, Hamilton went to work for MIT in 1959, assisting with computing weather prediction software (which became key in the development of chaos theory), and with developing satellite tracking software. In the 1960s, at MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory, she was director of the Software Engineering Division, responsible for the on-board flight software of NASA's Apollo missions. Hamilton is credited with coining the term "software engineering" for what her team was generating. In 2009, Hamilton told MIT News that, for her and her colleagues (many of whom had started in their 20s), "Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. … Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners." And, as Hamilton pointed out in a 2018 conference presentation, their software was vital to keeping the astronauts alive: "It had to work, and it had to work the first time. Not only did the software itself have to be ultra-reliable, but it would need to be able to detect an error and recover from it in real time. … Hardware engineers had come to the project with rules; we didn't. Problems had to be solved that never had been solved before." She explained that, leading up to Apollo 11's approach to the moon, software managed to compensate for a switch being placed in the wrong position by the astronauts – consuming valuable computer processing time, and potentially jeopardizing the landing. "The mechanisms the software used for this emergency were thought by many to have saved the Apollo 11 mission," Hamilton said. Not only had Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin become the first humans to walk on the moon, Hamilton said, "Our software became the first software to run on the moon." After working at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s, Hamilton founded two software companies. In 2016, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama. Upon Hamilton's death, her daughter Lauren described her mother to The Associated Press as a reserved person. "The spotlight wasn't necessarily a natural thing for her," she said. "She encountered a lot of sexism in her field, but she didn't come back aggressively. She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly."

Duncan Sheik Duncan Sheik ("Spring Awakening") at the 61st Annual Tony Awards in New York City, June 10, 2007. | Peter Kramer/Getty Images Grammy-winning singer-songwriter Duncan Sheik (Nov. 18, 1969-Sept. 17, 2026) earned two Tony Awards for the 2006 Broadway musical "Spring Awakening." Working with playwright Steven Sater, Sheik challenged the conventional notions of musical theater by mixing a story set in 19th century Germany with contemporary pop-rock, as its young characters defy a repressive society. The show, which starred Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff and John Gallagher Jr., offered a frank portrayal of abortion, incest and suicide. Sater, who met Sheik while both were practicing Buddhists, was collaborating on Sheik's 2001 album, "Phantom Moon," when he mentioned he was working on a new production. Neither had done a musical before. "With the exception of our director, we are all kind of Broadway outsiders," Sheik told The Associated Press in 2007. "We wanted to shake things up a bit. And we just set out to make this really cool piece of theater." The show went on to win eight Tonys, including best musical, and a Grammy for its cast album. Duncan had emerged in 1996 with a self-titled debut album, which featured the hit single "Barely Breathing." He ultimately released nine studio albums, plus a live 2017 recording. And while none of his later albums achieved the success of his debut and its Grammy-nominated lead single (which factored in an intense episode of the series "Girls" and was covered on "Glee"), Sheik's retro folk-rock-pop sound blended introspective lyrics and thoughtful melodies with electronics. But his body of recorded music continually changed in genre and tone. Critics called his music both ambitious and "unpredictable," and they were right. 2009's "Whisper House" featured songs for a stage musical that premiered the following year at the Old Globe Theatre in San Diego. He released a 2011 album of covers of British pop songs by such acts as Thompson Twins, Depeche Mode, Tears for Fears and The Psychedelic Furs. During the COVID pandemic, he recorded his experimental 2022 album "Claptrap" in a 250-sq.-ft. New York City studio apartment. Sheik also wrote music for stage adaptations of "American Psycho," "Alice in Wonderland," and "Because of Winn-Dixie," for productions of "The Taming of the Shrew" and "Twelfth Night," and for the films "A Home at the End of the World" and "Through the Fire." In a 2015 interview with BMI, Sheik was asked how writing for musical theater influenced him as a singer-songwriter. "I just think it's really helped broaden my palette," he said. "Especially as a lyricist, it's enabled me to understand that's it OK to write from the perspective of a different persona. Every song that you write doesn't have to be this exercise in navel-gazing, this kind of self-analysis. Every song doesn't have to be about, 'Oh, this girl doesn't like me anymore,' which ultimately starts to get incredibly boring. Working with Steven Sater has certainly opened me up to using more poetic and enigmatic language and not worry about being so literal all the time, which is my pet peeve with the current pop music scene."

Peter Max Artist Peter Max, pictured in 1983 at a Beverly Hills, Calif., gallery, shown with his 1968 poster "The Different Drummer." | Artwork © ALP, Inc.; Photo by Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images The signature vibrant colors and playful designs of pop artist Peter Max (Oct. 19, 1937-Sept. 14, 2026) became synonymous with the psychedelic '60s. His designs danced across a variety of media, from posters and illustrations to advertising, ocean liners, postage stamps, and the New York City yellow pages directory – an aesthetic that was frequently co-opted. (The look of the 1968 animated Beatles film "Yellow Submarine" was inspired by his work.) Born in Berlin, Peter Max Finkelstein's Jewish family fled Nazi Germany for China when he was a baby. They lived in Tibet, Israel and Paris, before moving to New York City when Max was 16. There he studied at the Art Students League, the School of Visual Arts and the Pratt Institute, and opened a graphic design studio in 1961. Max's vivid images proved a success in both advertising and pop culture, and perfectly encapsulated the burgeoning "Flower Power" fashion of the decade. His graphics also adorned commercial products – dresses, scarves, bedsheets. "My work was really, I would say, almost exploited," he said. To devote more time to painting, he shut down his graphic business in the early 1970s. In 1981 he was asked by first lady Nancy Reagan to paint a series of 8-foot-tall portraits of the Statue of Liberty at the White House. Despite changing tastes, his standing in the art world endured his guilty plea to tax fraud in 1997, and legal battles over his work, which has been featured in museums around the world – from New York's Museum of Modern Art to the Corcoran Gallery of Art and National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C., the de Young Memorial Museum in San Francisco, the Künstlerhaus in Vienna, and the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia. Max never cared about maintaining relevance. "I just think about, what do I want to paint, what am I gonna do now, what am I gonna do later," Max told "CBS This Morning" in 2015. "I just love the moment." And his thoughts about legacy blurred the creative and the personal. "Some people remember me for my color, some people remember me as a friend," Max said. "You know, different, whatever."

Bob Mackie Fashion designer Bob Mackie poses with the limited-edition "Gold Barbie" doll in New York City, 1990; Pictured also are designs by Mackie for such personalities as Marilyn Monroe, Diana Ross, Cher, Tina Turner and Carol Burnett. | Photo by Sonia Moskowitz/Getty Images; designs © Bob Mackie Fashion designer Bob Mackie (March 24, 1939-Sept. 14, 2026) created stage costumes and red carpet gowns for such glamorous stars as Cher, Diana Ross, Barbra Streisand, Bernadette Peters, Tina Turner, Madonna, Beyoncé, Miley Cyrus, Zendaya, Sabrina Carpenter, and Elton John. A film-struck boy growing up just outside Hollywood in the 1940s who was enamored with visions of Carmen Miranda and Betty Grable, Mackie brought his art school portfolio to movie studios, where he was hired as a sketch artist for Edith Head at Paramount and Jean-Louis at 20th Century Fox. It was for Jean-Louis that he drafted a sketch of a very sheer gown for Marilyn Monroe – one she ended up wearing to a birthday celebration for President John F. Kennedy. But it was in TV variety specials that Mackie made his mark, creating clothes for Mitzi Gaynor and then Carol Burnett – designing everything Burnett and everyone else on her show wore, every single week, for 11 years. Mackie told "Sunday Morning" in 2003, "Very often at the run-through, Carol would say, 'Oh, we're gonna cut that sketch, it's just not working.' And I would beg her. I would say, 'Don't cut it. Wait 'til you see what you're going to wear. It's going to make the whole thing work.'" He met Cher on "The Carol Burnett Show." Their collaboration – encompassing "The Sonny & Cher Show," as well as Cher's other TV and stage performances – would last decades, reaching a pinnacle with his design for her 1986 Oscar gown, a so-called "revenge dress," after her performance in "Mask" was ignored by the Academy's voting membership. It featured a feathered headdress and bare midriff. ("As you can see, I did receive my Academy booklet on how to dress like a serious actress," Cher told the audience.) Two years later, when she was recognized by the Academy with an Oscar for "Moonstruck," Cher wore another stunning Mackie creation of glittering sequins (and not much else). Mackie won nine Emmy Awards and earned three Oscar nominations (for "Lady Sings the Blues," "Funny Lady" and "Pennies From Heaven"). Other TV work included specials starring Ann-Margret, Neil Diamond and Bette Midler. With a client list that ran from Cher to Streisand, Mackie said he did not mind working with divas. "There's nothing wrong with being a diva," he said, "because, you know, you can be talented, but if you have no ambition, you have no whatever that it takes to be a diva, you're boring. The ones that are really interesting have that drive and that style and that little bit of crackle that makes people interested in them." Outside of Hollywood and Las Vegas, Mackie also launched a line on QVC's Home Shopping Network, started a couture collection, and even designed Liza Minnelli's gown for her fourth wedding. But for sheer outrageousness, perhaps nothing topped Mackie's costume for Carol Burnett's 1976 send-up of "Gone With the Wind," in which she wore Scarlett's gown fashioned from curtains ("I saw it in the window and I just couldn't resist it"). "Well, it's probably my most famous costume," Mackie told "Sunday Morning." "You know, all these gowns and elegant clothes and beautiful, glamorous clothes, and I'll probably be known [as] the guy that designed the curtain-rod dress for Carol Burnett."

Gloria Steinem Gloria Steinem is pictured at the office of Ms. Magazine in New York, Nov. 24, 1980. | Mel Finkelstein/New York Daily News via Getty Images Journalist, activist, and author Gloria Steinem (March 25, 1934-Sept. 2, 2026) was a trailblazing figure of the women's liberation movement, and a co-founder of Ms. Magazine, the first major publication to be owned, run, and written by women. Ms. was a spearhead for the promotion of equal rights, helping to raise awareness about issues of inclusion, media representation and social justice affecting women and girls. As a journalist, Steinem exploded the notions that "women's issues" were confined to women. She was also a tireless advocate for women's voices in politics – at the ballot box, and in the halls of power – by fighting for voting rights, and promoting female candidates for office. Steinem told "Sunday Morning" in 2023 that, as the women's liberation movement picked up steam, the very word "feminism" seemed to threaten people for two reasons: "One, because they didn't understand it, and two, because they did understand it!" Born in Toledo, Ohio, to a traveling salesman, Steinem lived an itinerant life as her family moved about, until her parents' separation and divorce when she was a teenager. Steinem ended up caring for her mom, who suffered from mental illness. Steinem's career as a journalist began in New York City, where she contributed to several publications, including The New York Times and Esquire. She made a splash with her two-part 1963 exposé in Show magazine, for which she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny at Hugh Hefner's Playboy Club. The article, which exposed sexual harassment on the club's floor and the toll on female employees behind the scenes (including mandatory blood tests and gynecological exams), was a sensation. After helping found New York Magazine (a news, pop culture and style publication), publisher Clay Felker volunteered to publish a sample issue of Ms. within the pages of New York magazine in 1971. The issue promptly sold out. The publication's first full issue appeared on newsstands on July 1, 1972. In addition to having Wonder Woman on its cover, the issue featured a petition signed by women of various backgrounds announcing that they had had an abortion and were demanding that it become safe and legal. [It would be another year before the Supreme Court's decision in Roe v. Wade.] The magazine courted controversy (a cover photo advertising a story about sexual harassment on the job, depicting a man fondling a doll, got the magazine pulled off newsstands), while some advertisers shied away (the head of a major cosmetics company told Steinem that women who read Ms. don't buy makeup). Still, the magazine persisted, while Steinem also helped nurture groups and publications dedicated to advancing civil rights, from the Ms. Foundation for Women (which created the Take Our Daughters to Work Day initiative, later expanded to include sons), to the Women's Action Alliance, and the National Women's Political Caucus. She was president and co-founder of Voters for Choice (which later merged with the Planned Parenthood Action Fund), and was co-founder of the reproductive rights organization Choice USA (now URGE). In 1999, Steinem was asked by the "CBS Evening News" whether technological advances were responsible for women's advancement. Steinem discounted that: "There's nothing automatic about political change, about liberation," she said. "There's no substitute for self-respect, banding together with other people, standing up for ourselves. Liberation does not come from outside. Power can't be given to you. The process of taking it is part of the empowerment." In 2000, Steinem (who once thought marriage was demeaning) did the unexpected: she married David Bale, a human rights activist and father of actor Christian Bale. But their life together ended three years later, when Bale died of lymphoma of the brain. In 2006, she told "Sunday Morning" that losing her husband made her understand the difference between sadness and depression. "Yes, because people would say to me, 'Aren't you depressed?' And I realized that in depression, nothing matters. And in sadness, everything matters. It makes everything poignant." Steinem continued writing and lecturing into her 90s, as some of the topics introduced long ago by Ms. Magazine, such as sexual harassment in the workplace and domestic violence, took on new force with the rise of the #MeToo movement. Steinem told "Sunday Morning" that the revolution for women's equality is still being fought today. "There's a barrier that has moved, but there's still a barrier," she said. "So, what used to be you couldn't get a job, now you hit a ceiling after a few years. What used to be an unequal marriage is now unequal after children are born. The barrier has moved, thank goodness. So, there's more room back here that's liberated. But the barrier is still there to be pushed.

Cassandra Wilson Frans Schellekens/Redferns via Getty Images Two-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer Cassandra Wilson (Dec. 4, 1955-Sept 1, 2026) was once called America's best singer by Time magazine. The daughter of musician Herman Fowlkes (who stopped going on the road when Cassandra was born) and teacher Mary Fowlkes, Cassandra studied piano from age 6 until 13, at which point her father encouraged her on the guitar. In addition to her love of Motown, Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk, she was also exposed to folk and rock music. "That was the beginning of my interest in people like Joni Mitchell and Judy Collins, Richie Haven," she told "Sunday Morning" in 1997. "It allowed me to step outside of the box, so to speak. You're placed in a box naturally – I think most of us are. And listening to this music gave me an opportunity to see possibilities." She performed at coffeehouses and in cover bands while studying at Millsaps College and Jackson State University, and mentored under jazz greats in New Orleans before moving to New York City, where she joined Steve Coleman's M-Base collective. Wilson's art, and her contralto, crossed folk, pop, R&B, and country. She recorded 20 albums, and was also a featured performer with Wynton Marsalis, Greg Osby, The Roots, Terence Blanchard, Elvis Costello, Luther Vandross and the Count Basie Orchestra, among others. She earned four Grammy nominations and won two for best jazz vocal album (for "New Moon Daughter" and "Loverly"). She released her last album, "Coming Forth by Day," an homage to Billie Holiday, in 2015. In 2022, Wilson was named a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master. Though she was most frequently described as a jazz artist, Wilson called labels mostly stifling and altogether unnecessary. "It's a matter of testing yourself, pushing yourself, challenging yourself and not accepting the status quo, not accepting what everyone says you should be doing," she told "Sunday Morning."

Tim Curry A 1974 portrait of English actor Tim Curry. | Evening Standard/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Actor Tim Curry (April 19, 1946-Aug. 25, 2026) was famed for a roster of entertaining miscreants and villains, from a campy cross-dresser in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," to the manipulative butler Wadsworth in "Clue," to Pennywise, the sinister, murderous clown, in the Stephen King thriller "It." The fact that even his most devilish characters were crowd-pleasers was a testament to Curry's overpowering charisma. Acting, he told "Sunday Morning" in 2025, gave him "the freedom of being somebody else, and I think that I was (like everybody else) drawn to the idea of fame probably, although I came to kind of rather despise it." Curry's first professional stage role was in the London production of "Hair." But it was the cult favorite "Rocky Horror" that lit up his career. He said that what made the role of Dr. Frank-N-Furter unique was his power: "He gave a lot of teenagers permission to be different, and I'm very happy that he did have that power," Curry said. Other roles included a prince of darkness opposite Tom Cruise in "Legend"; Carol Burnett's scheming and duplicitous brother in "Annie"; a put-upon hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York"; a Soviet officer in "The Hunt for Red October"; Cardinal Richelieu in "The Three Musketeers"; and Long John Silver in "Muppets Treasure Island." He was also the voice of Nigel Thornberry in the Nickelodeon series "The Wild Thornberrys" and its movie spin-offs. Curry also starred on Broadway in "The Rocky Horror Show," Tom Stoppard's "Travesties," "Amadeus," "My Favorite Year," and "Monty Python's Spamalot," earning him three Tony Award nominations. His life went sideways when, in 2012, he suffered a stroke (the same malady that his father had suffered before dying when Curry was 10), and a paralysis on his left side. He underwent invasive brain surgery, and had rehabilitation to learn how to speak again. "That was very weird," Curry said. "I hated not being able to speak." In 2025 he told "Sunday Morning" he was not remotely afraid of dying. "I don't fear death," he said. "I try to avoid it, as I think we all do! But I suspect that in the end, I will welcome it." Why? "Well, I think it may be very comforting to go bye-bye – and I want to earn it!" he laughed.

Dolly Parton A publicity photo of Dolly Parton for the 1988 CMA Awards. | CBS via Getty Images She was a singer-songwriter who lit up stages and screens for decades – who, beginning as a child, composed more than 3,000 songs and sold more than 100 million records. But Dolly Parton (Jan. 19, 1946-Aug. 25, 2026) was remembered for gifts beyond her sheer talent: as a philanthropist who donated millions of books to children, and whose charities benefited local communities, graduating seniors, and public health; and as a savvy businesswoman whose enterprises included her own recording company, theme parks, a chain of dinner theaters, and a downtown Nashville hotel, which includes a "Life of Many Colors Museum." Born in the foothills of the Smoky Mountains in eastern Tennessee, Parton grew up dirt-poor, the fourth of 12 children raised in a cabin with no electricity or indoor plumbing. But Parton's family was rich with music, and she showed a talent for it early on. "When I started writing these songs, my mom was real impressed with how I could write," Parton told "Sunday Morning?" in 2019. "And she would say, 'Oh honey, go get that guitar. I want you to sing them.' And she'd say to people, 'I want you to hear this song this little thing wrote.' And so I thought, Ooh, I'm getting a whole lot of attention now! "But also, I loved the sound of that music. I loved the sound of the instruments. I loved being able to create something, and it gave me a little space, and a little world of my own that I could just live in, and be creative in." The first of her family to finish high school, Parton graduated on a Friday, headed to Nashville on Saturday, and never looked back. Her first big hit, released in 1966, was "Dumb Blonde," which was not an apt description of Parton herself: "I'm pretty sharp," she told "Sunday Morning" in 2004. "I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. I'm country smart. You know how they say somebody's street smart? I feel like, you know, if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart." Those country smarts led her from her big break, in 1967, as a regular on a popular local music program, "The Porter Wagoner Show," to when she left Wagoner in 1974 to make it on her own. She turned the heartache of her professional split into art, penning the song "I Will Always Love You." "So I just started, you know, writing what was coming out, like, 'If I should stay, I would only be in your way. So I'll go, but I know I'll think of you...,'" Parton said. "So that song just flowed completely out. It just came out … I'll bet that song didn't take me more than an hour to write." Writing, to Parton, was seemingly effortless: "I mean, I've got boxes, dresser drawers, chests, trunks, Army trunks. I write something almost every day. Things just come to me, funny things, sad things. Depending on my mood, I have to write that. It's like my therapy. It's like my doctor." Songs like "Jolene," written in response to a bank teller's flirtatious behavior towards Parton's husband, Carl Dean; or "If You Hadn't Been There," released shortly after Dean's death, in 2025, ending their 59-year marriage. Parton's songs – of memory, love, painful wounds, and fierce humanity – included "Just Because I'm a Woman," "Yellow Roses," "In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad)," "My Tennessee Mountain Home," "Coat Of Many Colors," "Love Is Like a Butterfly," "The Bargain Store," and "9 to 5," which she recorded for her first film role, a comedy about female workers fighting back against a chauvinistic boss. She appeared in other films, including "Steel Magnolias," and recently co-wrote a biographical musical, "Dolly," set to begin previews on Broadway in December. Parton won 11 Grammy Awards, 13 Academy of Country Music Awards (including Entertainer of the Year in 1978), 14 CMT Music Awards, 10 Country Music Association Awards (including its lifetime achievement award in 2016), and an Emmy (for the TV movie "Dolly Parton's Christmas on the Square"). She was nominated for two Oscars (for best original song, for "9 to 5" and "Travelin' Thru"), and a Tony (for the 2009 stage musical based on "9 to 5"). Parton was Ms. Magazine's Woman of the Year in 1986, and was made a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2006. But her most inspiring accomplishment was to champion literacy through her Imagination Library, which has donated more than 300 million books to children in five countries. It was, she said, a response to her own father's illiteracy – and to the larger-than-life role that books played for her while growing up. For her philanthropy, Parton received the motion picture academy's Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award in 2025. And through it all, Parton maintained an embracing, big-hearted outlook that was as invigorating as her music – and she did it with lots of humor, too. When asked how she wanted people to remember her 100 years from now, she replied, "I want 'em to say, 'God, don't she look good for her age!'"

Bill Rasmussen Bill Rasmussen, the co-founder of ESPN, in 2018. | John Woike, Hartford Courant/Tribune News Service via Getty Images Bill Rasmussen (Oct. 15, 1932-Aug. 18, 2026) worked in the advertising services business, and in radio and television broadcasting, before serving as the public relations director for the New England Whalers, a World Hockey Association team, in Hartford, Connecticut. Fired along with other front-office staff in 1978 when the Whalers didn't make the playoffs, Rasmussen was sitting in idled traffic when he came up with the idea of a 24-hour sports network on cable TV with his son, Scott. The nascent channel secured 24-hour satellite time, which was initially planned to air Connecticut college sports. Backers were hard to come by. The head of one broadcasting company rejected his proposal to carry 24-hours sports, pronouncing that cable would be dead in a few years. After Rasmussen maxed out his credit card for a $9,000 advance, he received financial backing from Getty Oil; the channel also worked out a deal with the NCAA for exclusive rights to selected games, which expanded the range of their offerings. The Entertainment and Sports Programming Network — EPSN — went on the air on Sept. 7, 1979, while their Bristol, Conn., studio was still under construction. "SportsCenter" debuted, as the channel carried college football, basketball, soccer, tennis, bowling, and exhibition games in advance of the 1980 Winter Olympics. You want American Legion baseball? Sprint car racing? Full contact karate? The Royal International Horse Show? ESPN had you covered. The network began televising the NFL draft in 1980; inaugurated the ESPY Awards in 1993; and in 1995 launched the X Games competition. Over time, sports schedules were shifted to accommodate viewers, who in 2011 numbered more than 100 million. The number of postseason bowl games exploded. Rasmussen was ESPN's first president and CEO, but he and his son were forced out in 1980 by Getty, which owned 85% of the network. (The controlling interest was later sold to ABC.) Rasmussen and ESPN were estranged until 1999, when company executives invited him to the 20th anniversary celebration. He has since been recognized for his innovation, and has toured the country speaking at events for ESPN and the Walt Disney Company (the network's current owner). He was inducted into the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame in 2025. "A salesman once told me that every sale starts with a 'no.' We knew we were going to be really big because we got lots of 'no's' in the beginning," Rasmussen told Forbes in 2012. "Now there are over six U.S. networks and 46 international networks that have grown from the original ESPN."

Frank Beard An undated photo of drummer Frank Beard of the band ZZ Top. | Ed Spinelli for CBS News In the summer of 1969, drummer Frank Beard (June 11, 1949-Aug. 17, 2026), then 20, and guitarist Billy Gibbons got together to audition bass players at a Houston club called the Catacombs. When Dusty Hill strode in and began playing, "we wound up playing one song for about three hours straight!" Gibbons told "Sunday Morning" in 2019. The three would perform together for more than 50 years as the band ZZ Top. "I'm dumbfounded!" laughed Beard, the only member of the band without a beard. "It's longer than we've been married, by a long shot." Known for hits like "Legs" and "Sharp Dressed Man," ZZ Top had six No. 1 singles on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Airplay chart, and sold more than 50 million records. They earned three Grammy Award nominations, and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Beard, originally from Frankston, Texas, met Gibbons in a band called The Moving Sidewalks. With Hill (who died in 2021), they released their debut album in 1970, called "ZZ Top's First Album," a mix of hard rock, Southern rock, boogie and blues. Their heavy touring schedule — as many as 300 concerts a year — featured elaborate stage shows involving Texas longhorn steers, rattlesnakes and buzzards. By 1983, ZZ Top released their eighth album, "Eliminator," which featured three Top 10 hits: "Gimme All Your Lovin'," "Sharp Dressed Man" and "Legs." Their success was driven in part by their music videos on MTV, featuring a hot rod, pretty girls and catchy tunes, while sporting their signature look: fulsome beards (except for Beard himself), dark glasses, and flashy playing. Of the early music videos, Beard told "Sunday Morning," "We started out with some simple ideas. One, we thought, okay, the three of us are not, like, prima donna-looking rock stars, you know? So, let's be the ones watching what's goin' on in the background." Their video for "Legs" won them the MTV Video Music Award. Other ZZ Top hits included "La Grange," "I Thank You," "Sleeping Bag," "Tush," "Stages," "Doubleback," "My Head's in Mississippi," "Burger Man," "Give It Up," "Pincushion," and "What's Up with That."

Hayden Panettiere A 2013 photo of Hayden Panettiere as Juliette Barnes in the TV series "Nashville." | Bob D'Amico/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images Hayden Panettiere (Aug. 21, 1989-Aug. 16, 2026) was best known for starring in the TV series "Heroes" and "Nashville," and for the films "Remember the Titans," "I Love You Beth Cooper," "Bring It On: All or Nothing," two entries in the "Scream" franchise," and the 2011 biopic "Amanda Knox." Panettiere began her acting career as a child, appearing in 50 commercials by the time she was 5. At age 4 she was on the soap opera "One Life to Life." She later played recurring characters on "Guiding Light," "Ally McBeal," and "Malcolm in the Middle." She also voiced the character of Dot in Pixar's animated "A Bug's Life." Her breakout role was the 2006 TV series "Heroes," in which she played a high school cheerleader, Claire Bennet, who possessed the superhuman power of indestructability. In 2008 Panettiere told the Associated Press that the sci-fi series' appeal was that audiences could dream of something bigger: "And at the core of it are these human stories that people can relate to, very rugged. And it's just grabbed everyone in every age group." Panettiere won two Teen Choice Awards for "Heroes." In 2012 Panettiere starred in the series "Nashville," playing rising country singer Juliette Barnes. Over six seasons, Panettiere did her own singing, earning two Golden Globe nominations and hitting the Billboard country charts. (She'd earlier earned a Grammy nomination for the children's spoken word album, "A Bug's Life: Read-Along.") Meanwhile, she was struggling with mental health, addiction and postpartum depression following the 2014 birth of her daughter. Panettiere entered rehab in 2015 while filming "Nashville," putting herself into a treatment center. "I was drowning," she told Women's Health magazine in 2023. In her 2026 memoir "This Is Me: A Reckoning," she was candid about her long struggles with mental health and addiction, and her issues with paparazzi. Panettiere told "CBS Mornings" that the emotional challenges began as a young actress: "Once people figured out that I could cry on cue the way that I did, it was in everything, literally every scene," she said. "And it went from being a kid and having to imagine just that your pet passed away or something, but then as I got older, the imagery became darker and darker and darker, and the emotion that I had to hold within me in order to get those trigger tears going, it became harder and harder to jump out of it. I didn't know where my character started and where I ended … I was, you know, feeling just this deep sadness, and then the people were so happy afterwards. And you do that over such a long period of time — years after years after years — that of course it's going to take its toll on you emotionally." She credited finding the right therapist to helping her heal. She also served as an activist for environment causes, including protesting the hunting of dolphins and whales, and advocating for the victims of domestic violence. In her memoir, Panettiere described herself as an "optimist to the core" who refused to be defined by tragedy. She told "CBS Mornings" that her impetus to write the book was to address the stigma of postpartum depression and the backlash she received when she gave up custody of her daughter to the girl's father, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko. "I had spent so many years trying to hide as much of my life as I could that it was just, you know, a habit," she said. "I really wanted to share with the world that they don't have to be afraid, that they can live their truth, that they can be imperfect, that being perfectly imperfect is being brave, and it's okay."

Tommy John Tommy John, of the Los Angeles Dodgers, pitching in the 1970s against the Phillies at Veterans Stadium in Philadelphia. | Focus on Sport/Getty Images During his 26 seasons in the majors, four-time All-Star pitcher Tommy John (May 22, 1943-Aug. 15, 2026) won 288 games, most while wearing the uniform of the Chicago White Sox, New York Yankees and Los Angeles Dodgers. But despite a career ERA of 3.34, notching 2,245 strikeouts and the second-highest number of wins of any pitcher since 1900 not yet elected to the Hall of Fame, John was perhaps best remembered for the groundbreaking elbow surgery that came to bear his name. Born in Terre Haute, Indiana, he was a top athlete in high school, and was recruited by the University of Kentucky to play basketball. However, John chose baseball and signed with the Cleveland Indians. In 1974, while playing for the Dodgers, the left-hander, then 31, tore the ulnar collateral ligament, or UCL, in his pitching elbow. At the time it was considered the death knell for pitchers' careers — that is, until Frank Jobe, the Dodgers' team physician, invented a procedure to fix John's arm, changing baseball forever. "I just said, 'You do what you have to do to get me back playing baseball again,'" John recalled for "Sunday Morning" in 2024. John allowed Dr. Jobe to replace the ligament with a tendon from his right forearm. The procedure had been done on others before, although it was usually performed on wrists and hands; John was the first pitcher to have it done on his elbow. Jobe gave the surgery 100-to-1 odds of being successful. John became the first pitcher to successfully return after undergoing the procedure — which is now called Tommy John surgery. He won 124 games before his UCL repair, and 164 after, with his final appearance in 1989, just days after his 46th birthday. Since John's return to the mound, more than 2,600 big leaguers and thousands more amateurs have had UCL reconstructions. Among active MLB pitchers, an astonishing 35% have had the surgery, including Shohei Ohtani and three-time Cy Young Award-winner Justin Verlander. But with advanced training methods, pitchers of all ages are throwing harder than ever, with the average speed of a major league fastball now close to 95 mph — about 6 mph faster than it was in 2002. And just as MLB pitchers are throwing harder, so are Little League pitchers. Today, about 60% of Tommy John surgery recipients are under 19. "I am sick my name is attached to a surgery happening in kids more than pros," John tweeted in July 2018.

Yayoi Kusama Visions of artist Yayoi Kusama (left, second from top, in 2013 in New York City). Pictured, clockwise from top left: "My Soul Blooms Forever" (2019) at the New York Botanical Garden; "With All My Love for the Tulips, I Pray Forever" (2017); "Infinity Room-Gleaming Lights of Souls" (2017); The Yayoi Kusama Retrospective Exhibition at The Whitney Museum of American Art (2012); "Pumpkin" (2019); the Yayoi Kusama exhibition at National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne, Australia (2024). | All photos via Getty Images: Timothy A. Clary/AFP; Roslan Rahman/AFP; Suhaimi Abdullah; J. Countess; Francois Goudier/Gamma-Rapho; Graham Denholm for NGV; Andrew Toth Pop artist Yayoi Kusama (March 22, 1929-Aug. 14, 2026) had an instantly identifiable style: a prodigious use of polka dots – on paintings, sculptures, even the human body. Her fixation with polka dots, she told "Sunday Morning" in 2012, stemmed from lifelong hallucinations. "I had a very miserable childhood and have been fighting against mental stress that comes from that," she said. "Producing art has been my cure for many years. I feel better when I make things and draw. So, I make more." Raised in a conservative, dysfunctional family on a flower farm in Matsumoto, Japan, Kusama was frustrated by the traditions of the Japanese art world. At 27, she wrote to artist Georgia O'Keeffe, whose words of encouragement were enough to set Kusama off for New York City. There, her vast "Infinity Net" paintings, along with her art "happenings," gained her notoriety within the avant garde world. She returned to Japan in the early 1970s, and lived voluntarily for decades in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital, where she continued to produce artwork that was noted for its obsessiveness. Whitney Museum curator David Kiehl described to "Sunday Morning" the "amazing control" of her art, which he held as extraordinary as a drip painting by Jackson Pollock: "She's repeating over and over again gestures or filling up all the spaces. The idea of layering something, and also the constant repetition as you repeat that gesture over and over again, you're saying, I am here, I am here." Kusama's artwork, sculptures and installations were featured in exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City, and the Museum Ludwig in Germany. She also joined with fashion brand Louis Vuitton to design dotted fashion accessories. For a time, Kusama's paintings auctioned at the highest prices ever paid for a living female artist. In 2014, Christie's New York auctioned her "Infinity Net" painting "White No. 28" for $7.1 million, while in 2019 another "Infinity Net" painting went for $7.9 million. In 2022, Phillips New York sold her "Untitled (Nets)," from 1959, for $10.4 million. Kusama told "Sunday Morning" she still wore polka dots all the time, though, interestingly enough, never to bed. "When I go to sleep, I take off my polka dots nightgown," she said. "In the morning, I wake up, I see polka dots again, and it makes me happy."

Glen Hansard Irish musician Glen Hansard photographed at the Auditorium Parco della Musica, Rome, Nov. 12, 2019. | Luciano Viti/Getty Images Singer-songwriter Glen Hansard (April 21, 1970-July 29, 2026) started playing Dublin street corners at age 13 — just him and his guitar. But at least he had the permission of his grade school principal, Frankie Byrne, to quit school in order to pursue music. "So for me, that was just, you know, the wings I needed," Hansard told "Sunday Morning" in 2013. "So I went home, and basically announced to Ma, 'Listen, it's OK. Frankie told me it's OK!'" Busking led Hansard, at 18, to form a band, The Frames (named after the piles of bicycle frames in Hansard's backyard). Their music video for the 1995 song "Revelate," made using a post office security camera for less than $5, was picked up by MTV. Over the next 24 years, The Frames released nine studio and live albums, but while Hansard maintained ties with the group, he also worked with Czech singer-musician Markéta Irglová, forming another collaboration called The Swell Season. At the same time he was recording his first album with Swell Season, Hansard was asked by one of his former Frames bandmates ,John Carney, to help with a small film he was making, "Once," about a songwriter recording a demo and the tentative relationship he develops with a fellow musician. During filming, Hansard and Irglová became romantically involved. "I think part of what made 'Once' on the screen kind of work was that there was always this energy between us," Hansard told "Sunday Morning." "You'd be a fool to deny it." The film became an international hit, and Hansard and Irglová shared the Academy Award for writing the best original song, "Falling Slowly." "When we won that award, it was just, like, the most amazing thing," Hansard said. "And then my thing was like, 'OK, thanks, now let's get on with our lives.' And then when there was talk of it going to Broadway, I remember being very nervous, and honestly I was against it. "For me, Broadway meant sort of hamming it up," he said. "'Course, you're tempted by the idea of people saying, whispering in your ear, going, 'Do you know if this does well, like, you're gonna be seriously rich?' And going like, 'That was never why we did this.'" But Hansard relented, and the musical "Once" won eight Tony Awards, including best musical. Hansard and Irglová continued touring as The Swell Season and releasing new recordings, even after they broke up. "It was hard, and it was something we addressed all the time," Hansard said. "If you said to me, you could have all this success or you could just have a great relationship with Mar, I'd have took the relationship," Hansard said, "because it was the most profound and beautiful thing I had been through." The two were featured in a 2011 documentary, "The Swell Season," which examined the media attention on them following the success of "Once," and traced how the couple's romantic relationship ended. Each went on to marry others and have children; their most recent album was 2025's "Forward. In 2013, Hansard released the first of five solo albums, "Rhythm and Repose." And he continued busking for charity in Dublin with other Irish artists, like Sinead O'Connor and Bono. Playing music in the streets was, he said, a constant reminder of his origins. "You can climb all the levels of success and of celebrity or fame. But you're never more than a step away from the guy who's just making his money for the day," he said.

Charles Gaines Charles Gaines, co-creator of the sport of paintball. | adkisaac/Wikipedia Charles Gaines (Jan. 6, 1942-July 21, 2026) was a writer, documentarian, teacher, bodybuilder and outdoorsman, who studied creative writing at the University of Iowa under Kurt Vonnegut. His 1972 novel, "Stay Hungry," about the world of bodybuilding, was adapted to a film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. Gaines also wrote and narrated the 1977 documentary, "Pumping Iron," based on his bestselling photo book. Over his career he wrote 25 books and more than 300 magazine articles. An avid fisherman, Gaines also helped found the U.S. Fly Fishing Team, and wrote and directed segments for ABC's "American Sportsman." But it was a disagreement over survival that led to his most notable innovation. Gaines, who'd grown up in the woods in the South, had long argued with his friend and tennis rival Hayes Noel, a New York City stockbroker, about whom would more likely survive in the wilderness. This led to a cat-and-mouse hunt in the woods, each wielding a paint gun used by farmers to mark livestock. What followed was devising structured gameplay out of their duel. On June 27, 1981, in Henniker, New Hampshire, Gaines and Noel, along with Bob Gurnsey, a local ski shop manager, put their challenge to the test by organizing the first paintball game. With 100 acres of forest staked out, and referees keeping score, a dozen camouflaged participants, armed with CO2-powered guns, paint pellets, goggles, and a compass and map, had to capture colored flags without being painted themselves. Players ran the gamut from hunters, an ex-Green Beret and a trauma surgeon, to a New York venture capitalist, a film producer, and an amateur boxer. Some played aggressively, racing through the course, snapped twigs be damned. Others stalked through the woods quietly, or set up defensive positions in abandoned buildings. "How people played the game reflected who they were," Gaines told NPR Boston in 2018. Ritchie White, a certified forester, stealthily accumulated four flags and exited the course first in just over two hours, without ever having fired a shot. Gaines, Noel and Gurnsey later commercialized the sport by forming the National Survival Game. Today, paintball and its variations (including speedball) have been played by millions, in amateur, professional and tournament competitions, in a market valued at greater than $1 billion. As the sport's co-creator, Gaines was inducted into the Paintball Hall of Fame in 2024.

Peter Lassally Producer Peter Lassally is photographed at CBS Television City in Los Angeles in 2013. | Liz O. Baylen/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Fabled TV executive Peter Lassally (Oct. 14, 1932-July 19, 2026) was the executive producer for such late-night stars as Johnny Carson, Tom Snyder, David Letterman and Craig Ferguson. He also championed many rising comedians, from the duo of Mike Nichols and Elaine May, to Mort Sahl, Garry Shandling and Steven Wright (who, Lassally said, would call him every year on the anniversary of Wright's first "Tonight Show" appearance to thank him). Despite being a kingmaker of late-night comedy, Lassally's background was exceedingly dark. Born in Hamburg, Germany, his Jewish family fled the Nazis to Holland. For a time, he attended the same grade school as Anne Frank. When he was 10, Lassally's father died. Soon after, he and his sister and mother were sent to the first of two concentration camps, witnessing terrifying brutality and enduring psychological torture. After the war. Lassally emigrated to the United States. He started out as a Radio City Music Hall usher (alongside Regis Philbin), and then as an NBC page. By the mid-1950s, he was working for America's biggest TV star, Arthur Godfrey. He served as a producer of "The Tonight Show" for more than two decades, as well as "Late Night With David Letterman." Lassally told "Sunday Morning" in 2018 that Johnny Carson, the king of late-night talk shows, was very uncomfortable with people: "If he'd have to go to a party, he'd sit at the end of the couch, wouldn't talk to anybody," Lassally said. "He was not a social animal." Lassally said that once Carson retired in 1992, the former star was finally able to relax — but missed giving a monologue every night. "He loved the monologue," Lassally told David Letterman in 2005. "And he would pick up the papers in the morning and write jokes from the paper for his own amusement, and then he would call me. It's true! He would call me and read them to me over the phone. And I thought they were hysterical, and I'd laugh like crazy." In 1993, after Letterman was passed over as "Tonight Show" host for Jay Leno, Lassally transitioned with Letterman from NBC to CBS, where they created the network's late-night programming block. Lassally was also executive producer of "The Late Late Show." His decades guiding TV's late-night stars earned Lassally the nickname "The Host Whisperer." In a 2009 interview for the Television Academy Foundation, Lassally said, "The most important thing for a talk show host is to listen. If they don't listen they're going to miss great opportunities. Try to make the guest look good, not necessarily make yourself look good."

Jennifer Finch Jennifer Finch performs with the punk band L7 in Belgium, 1992. | Gie Knaeps/Getty Images Punk musician Jennifer Finch (Aug. 5, 1966-July 18, 2026) played in bands alongside Courtney Love and Kat Bjelland, and was a member of the 1980s group L7, often performing bass while barefoot. As a teenager Finch began photographing Los Angeles punk bands; an exhibition of her pictures of such acts as Red Hot Chili Peppers and Bad Religion appeared at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 1986 she joined L7, which had formed as a duo the prior year with Donita Sparks and Suzi Gardner. With drummer Roy Koutsky, they recorded their first eponymous album in 1987. By 1989, when drummer Demetra "Dee" Plakas came on board, L7 had become one of the leading all-female punk groups, their songs "Pretend We're Dead," "Everglade," "Monster" and "Andres" charting in the U.S. and U.K. Fearless renegades and feminist icons, L7's music was dubbed by Vice magazine "unforgiving, aggressive, and chaotic." In 1991 the band founded Rock For Choice, which produced pro-choice benefit concerts that ran for 10 years. Finch recorded three more albums, and appeared in the "Doll Parts" music video with Hole, before leaving L7 in 1996. She formed OtherStarPeople with Xander Smith, then founded the bands The Shocker and Sex in Progress. In 2014 she reteamed with Gardner, Sparks and Plakas to record another L7 album, "Scatter the Rats." In a 2025 Guitar World interview, Finch said, "L7 ain't over yet. I'm in my 50s now and we still get to be examples. But also we get to fail publicly in a way that we couldn't do in our 20s. I've never felt directly responsible for anyone picking up a guitar — pick up your own f****** guitar! It's a thing you gotta do or do not. I'm very heart-warmed when particularly women say, 'Because of you, I got into politics,' or 'I got my medical degree because of you.' You know, fighting for housing rights — that's awesome."

Pat Oliphant Cartoonist Pat Oliphant at his drawing desk in Washington, D.C. in 1980. | Diana Walker, Getty Images; Maansi Srivastava, The Washington Post via Getty Pulitzer Prize-winning cartoonist Pat Oliphant (July 24, 1935-July 13, 2026) skewered the high and the mighty in cartoons syndicated to hundreds of publications around the world. Hailed for his acid humor and unforgiving pen, Oliphant once remarked to The New York Times about the politicians that were his frequent target, "They're all guilty until proven innocent." Born in Australia, he began working as a teenager at newspapers in Adelaide, producing cartoons and illustrations. By focusing his attention on international figures rather than locals, he managed to avoid censorship. In the early 1960s, eager to emigrate to the United States, he sent his portfolio to the Denver Post and was hired. His work lampooning President Lyndon Johnson, Barry Goldwater, Ho Chi Minh and others was soon syndicated internationally. In 1975 he moved to the Washington Star, positioned in the locus of American and global politics. Republicans, Democrats, military officers, pedophile priests — all were fair game to Oliphant, who was frequently criticized for offending segments of the public with his caricatures. "I usually stay away from presidents or politicians in general, because I might like them," Oliphant told an audience at the Yale University Art Gallery in 2014. "I did meet, after he was in office, Gerald [Ford]. He was a very good fellow, nice fellow. And that really gave me pause. You shouldn't hobnob with the enemy!"

Sam Neill Sam Neill as Dr. Alan Grant in Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" (1993). | Murray Close/Getty Images Actor Sam Neill (Sept. 14, 1947-July 13, 2026) exuded suave, Old Hollywood glamour, which he displayed in some of his best-known roles, from blockbusters like "Jurassic Park" and "The Hunt for Red October" to "The Piano" and "Dead Calm." Born Nigel Neill in Northern Ireland to a New Zealander officer in the British Army, he emigrated to New Zealand as a child, and called himself Sam because, he said, there were too many Nigels at his school. At a boarding school in Christchurch, he developed a love for acting. He had roles in local productions, including the thriller "Sleeping Dogs" (which helped revive the dormant New Zealand movie industry), before his breakout Australian film alongside another rising star, Judy Davis, 1979's "My Brilliant Career." Neill spent subsequent years gliding among Australian, European and American films and TV, receiving a Golden Globe nomination for the series "Reilly: Ace of Spies." He portrayed Damien the Antichrist in the third "Omen" film, "The Final Conflict," and Cardinal Thomas Wolsey in the miniseries "The Tudors." Starring alongside Sean Connery, Neill played a Soviet submarine officer in "The Hunt for Red October" who dreams of living in Montana, or maybe Arizona. Neill also starred opposite Meryl Streep twice, in "Plenty" and "A Cry in the Dark." In Jane Campion's "The Piano," his character's jealousy over his wife's affair — abetted by her beloved piano — is so consuming he commits a particularly nasty act of revenge.



"With 'The Piano,' you know, I had terribly mixed reactions," Neill told "CBS This Morning" in 1999. "Some people would come up and say, 'I really loved the character that you play and I understood him and I bled for him.' And that's the way I felt about him. But on the other hand, a lot of people said, 'I hated you in 'The Piano.' People have this odd way of confusing you with the character that you play. A guy that chops off his wife's finger isn't going to make a lot of friends with those sort of people." Neill won over all audiences, however, in Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" (1993), as paleontologist Dr. Alan Grant, whose visit to an island containing cloned dinosaurs sets the stage for deadly dinosaur-human clashes. He came back to the role in the sequels "Jurassic Park III" and "Jurassic World: Dominion." Along with his acting career, Neill was a country farmer. His organic winery, Two Paddocks, on New Zealand's South Island, produced pinot noir and riesling wines, while his social media account featured pictures of his farm animals named after his actor friends, such as Laura Dern the chicken. In a 2010 interview with Country Life, Neill said what he loved, more than anything, was planting things, "in particular, trees. Then I wander about them and take great satisfaction from their growth. … I do admire and emulate those who plant knowing they will never see the full fruits of their labor in their lifetime."

Bonnie Tyler Singer Bonnie Tyler performs c. 1980. | Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler (June 8, 1951-July 8, 2026) was best known for her chart-topping hit "Total Eclipse of the Heart," and "Holding Out For a Hero" from the "Footloose" soundtrack. Her trademark powerful and husky voice came about following surgery to remove nodules from her vocal cords. Ordered to rest her voice, she altered it permanently by screaming. The result: a gravelly sound reminiscent of Rod Stewart that carried her first major hit, 1978's "It's a Heartache," to worldwide acclaim. Born Gaynor Hopkins, in a small town outside Swansea, she was a coal miner's daughter living in public housing, who recorded "Top of the Pops" on her dad's reel-to-reel tape recorder. She also emulated her musical idols like Janis Joplin, Nina Simone and Tina Turner by singing into her hairbrush. "I fell in love with singing just from doing that," she wrote in her autobiography, "Straight from the Heart." "Looking back, even then my voice had a husky tone to it, but I didn't think much of it. I thought everyone's voices were different from each other's." Her debut album, 1977's "The World Starts Tonight," featured "Lost in France," and earned her a breakthrough artists nomination at the Brit Awards. Working with Meat Loaf songwriter-producer Jim Steinman, she recorded "Total Eclipse of the Heart," the debut single for her fifth studio album, "Faster Than the Speed of Night." "Eclipse" hit No. 1 on the U.S. Billboard chart in 1983 (and over time accumulated more than 1 billion streams). The following year her "Holding Out For a Hero" was a standout on the bestselling soundtrack to the movie "Footloose." Later releases included 1984's "Here She Comes" (from Giorgio Moroder's reimagining of "Metropolis"). She also recorded duets with Rod Stewart ("Battle of the Sexes"), Cliff Richard ("Taking Control"), Francis Rossi ("Someone's Rockin' Your Heart"), Vince Gill ("What You Need From Me"), and Mike Oldfield ("Islands"). Her 2013 album, "Rocks and Honey," a country album recorded in Nashville, featured the ballad "Believe in Me," which Tyler sung as the U.K.'s entry in that year's Eurovision Song Contest. Over the course of her career, Tyler recorded 22 studio and live albums, earning three Grammy nominations. In 2023 Tyler told the BBC she never got fed up with singing "Total Eclipse of the Heart." "Of course I don't! I love it!" she said.

Wally Funk Wally Funk speaks at a press conference following her flight aboard the Blue Origin spacecraft, July 20, 2021. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images Aviation pioneer Wally Funk (Feb. 1, 1939-July 8, 2026) spent her life in the clouds. After getting her first flight lesson at age nine, she became a licensed pilot at 17, and logged more than 19,000 flying hours. But her lifelong dream of going to space eluded her, until 2021, when – at age 82 – Funk became the oldest woman to travel beyond the Earth's atmosphere. In the early 1960s, Funk was a member of the Mercury 13 – female pilots who were put through the same training program with NASA as the all-male astronaut corps. "We had no idea what we were going through; we didn't know where it was taking us," Funk told "CBS This Morning: Saturday" in 2021. Among the strenuous tests they were forced to endure: "X-raying all over your body, every bone, every tooth, sticking water into your ears. I had to drink radioactive water." The women of Mercury 13 met, and often surpassed, the results of the men. But NASA required astronauts to be military test pilots, and at the time the military did not allow women to fly. [It wasn't until 1983 that an American woman, Sally Ride, flew into space.] Funk became the first female inspector for the Federal Aviation Administration, and the first female air safety investigator for the National Transportation Safety Board. But the dream of going into space never died. "That is my quest. ... I love flying, that's my job, that's what I love. And I'm not a quitter," Funk said. In 2021, she got her chance aboard Blue Origin's New Shepherd rocket, riding alongside Amazon founder Jess Bezos and two others (including 18-year-old Oliver Daemon, who became the youngest person to fly into space). There was a delay at Blue Origin's Texas launch site; Funk, sitting in the capsule, grew impatient. "Time's passing, and so I hit the button, I said, 'What's the holdup?'" she told CBS News Texas. But shortly after, the six-decade wait was over. "We're lifting off, and we're going up, and I'm looking out the window, I said, 'Wow! There goes the ground!'" Then came capsule separation, and weightlessness. "Oh, I love it, I love it," she exclaimed, as she floated in zero G. After landing in the Texas desert, she said, "I feel so lucky that my dream has come true." But she was eager for another invitation: "I want to go back up in space. That's where my brain has been, in space, ever since I came back."

Louise Lasser Louise Lasser as the title character of the 1970s TV satire "Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman." | Hulton Archive/Getty Images Actress Louise Lasser (April 11, 1939-July 6, 2026) was an early second banana to her husband, Woody Allen, even after their 1970 divorce. She starred in his comedies "Take the Money and Run," "Bananas," and "Everything You Wanted to Know About Sex* (But Were Afraid to Ask)." But Lasser reached celebrity of the first banana variety by starring in the 1976 satire of TV soap operas, "Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman." Produced by Norman Lear and distributed via syndication, the show ran five nights a week, portraying life in the Ohio suburb of Fernwood. Lasser's character, a housewife overloaded with consumerist messages, endured ever-wild situations of the soap variety – from marital problems, infidelity, religious cults and UFOs, to being held hostage by a mass murderer, to being institutionalized in a psychiatric ward. On top of it all, she bemoaned, "My floor has a waxy yellow buildup." In a 2013 profile for Interview magazine, Lasser said the producers asked her what she thought should happen to Mary next: "I was surprised when they asked me. I remember taking a beat and thinking, 'I think she's got to have a nervous breakdown, because you can't be this bombarded without…' Do you know what I mean? And this was equivalent to America's nervous breakdown that we were all starting to go through too fast, and you didn't know what anything meant, and nothing meant anything. … I once said that I thought she was like a survivor that lived in a world that might not be worth surviving in, you know?" "I know people think it was this very light, funny show, and it was this funny show, but the humor came from a great angst inside," she said. Though it only ran two seasons, the series developed a cult following. Lasser earned an Emmy nod for her performance, though the Television Academy was hard put in which category to list "Mary Hartman." They settled for "Special Classification of Outstanding Program and Individual Achievement." "People always say it's way ahead of its time," Lasser told Interview. "I never thought it was ahead of its time. I always thought it was of its time." Her other film and TV roles included "Slither," "Coffee, Tea or Me?," "It's a Living," "Modern Love," "Mystery Men," "Happiness," "Requiem for a Dream," and appearances on "Saturday Night Live," "Taxi," "St. Elsewhere," "Empty Nest," "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation," and "Girls," Lasser's stage credits included "Thieves," and replacing Barbra Streisand in "I Can Get it for You Wholesale."

Victor Willis A promotional photo of lead singer Victor Willis (front), of the group Village People, March 1980. | CBS via Getty Images Singer-songwriter Victor Willis (July 1, 1951-June 30, 2026) was co-founder of Village People, and co-wrote several of the disco group's greatest hits, including "Y.M.C.A.," ″Macho Man" and "In the Navy." In 1977, producers Jacques Morali and Henri Belolo, inspired by visits to gay dance clubs, put together songs for an album to be titled "Village People." Willis (who had appeared on Broadway in "The Wiz") was hired after they heard his demo tape, and he belted out such songs as "San Francisco (You've Got Me)" and "In Hollywood (Everybody Is a Star)." But once the record took off, dancers were needed for TV and live appearances, hence the ads in trade publications: "Macho Types Wanted: Must Dance And Have A Moustache." The final lineup of Village People – all very macho-looking men – featured Willis dressed as a policeman, Alex Briley as a soldier or sailor, Glenn Hughes as a leather-clad biker, David Hodo as a construction worker, and Randy Jones and Felipe Rose as a cowboy and Native American – the only two members of the group who were openly gay. "Each of us represents American images that have been around for a long time," Willis told Rolling Stone in 1979. In 1978, Village People released two albums, "Macho Man" and "Cruisin'," which featured "Y.M.C.A." The song, which Willis co-wrote, was inspired by his visit to a Y.M.C.A. in Manhattan when he moved from San Francisco to New York City. "Y.M.C.A." hit No. 2 on the Billboard chart, and No. 1 in the U.K., Canada, Japan and other countries. It was later added to the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry, and in 2021 it was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Willis left the band before they appeared in 1980's "Can't Stop the Music," a disco movie that bombed. As Village People's lineup changed, Willis returned to the group to record the 1982 album "Fox On the Box/In the Street." But he focused on a solo career. (His album "Solo Man" was released in 2015.) He also fought over the rights to his Village People songs, until a federal jury ruled in 2015 that Willis was entitled to 50% copyright of 13 of the group's songs (including "Y.M.C.A."). "I've always made a living off my (songwriting) royalties, which is the reason I was able to stay in and fight so long with the lawsuits," Willis told news.com.au in 2017. "It has cost me millions to fight this case. I've recaptured my writing credits now and I own them for life. … Now a lot of other artists are realizing they can recapture the copyrights to their songs. Other people are following in my footsteps." He then returned as the group's lead singer to record and tour, including performing his most popular song, one he insisted was not meant to be a gay anthem. "I wanted to write a song that could fit anyone's lifestyle," he said. "I'm happy the gay community adopted ['Y.M.C.A.'] as their anthem, I have no qualms with that."

Penelope Keith Actress Penelope Keith in the 1970s British sitcom "The Good Life." | Don Smith/Radio Times/Getty Images A familiar comedic presence in British sitcoms, Penelope Keith (April 2, 1940-death announced June 29, 2026) starred in the series "The Good Life" and "To the Manor Born." Her career in television, film, radio and theatre, including with the Royal Shakespeare Company, spanned decades. Beginning in the 1960s she had small roles on TV, including "The Avengers" and "The Pallisers," and starred on stage in "The Norman Conquests," before starring in "The Good Life," as the proper and snobby Margo Leadbetter, next-door neighbor to a pair of self-sufficient homesteaders who've made a farm out of their suburban tract. Keith won the first of her two BAFTA Awards for her performance. She starred for three seasons in the BBC comedy "To the Manor Born, as Audrey fforbes-Hamilton, a widowed aristocrat forced to sell off her palatial estate to a wealthy commoner. Other TV roles included "Executive Stress," "No Job for a Lady," "Moving" and "Death Comes to Pemberley," and the film "Priest of Love." On stage she won an Olivier Award for the 1976 play "Donkey's Years," and starred in "Blithe Spirit," "The Importance of Being Earnest" and "The Rivals." In 2014 Keith was made a dame for her services to the arts and charity. She told the Radio Times in 2011, "Of course, the fact that 'Manor Born' and 'The Good Life' have stayed in people's memories that long is wonderful. It's an extraordinary thing, but somehow films always date, television drama always dates, but comedy – the good comedy – seems to weather the storm."

David Clayton-Thomas David Clayton-Thomas performs with Blood Sweat & Tears in 1970. | Steve Morley/Redferns via Getty Images In the 1960s and early '70s, David Clayton-Thomas (Sept. 13, 1941-June 24, 2026) was lead singer of the band Blood, Sweat & Tears, his husky and urgent voice carrying such gold-record hits as "Spinning Wheel," "And When I Die" and "You've Made Me So Very Happy." Clayton-Thomas replaced original lead singer Al Kooper in 1968, and his debut album with the group, the eponymous "Blood Sweat & Tears," won the Grammy for album of the year. Born David Henry Thomsett in Surrey, England, and raised in Canada by his father, a pianist, he fought violently with his dad, and by his mid-teens was living on the streets. He was incarcerated for vagrancy and assault by the age of 20. But he taught himself to play a guitar left behind by another inmate, and later spent time playing clubs in Toronto. Changing his last name to Clayton-Thomas, he performed with several bands, and in the mid-'60s had a hit single with the anti-war rocker "Brainwashed." He befriended other rising stars, including Joni Mitchell and John Lee Hooker, who encouraged Clayton-Thomas to move to New York, where he was recruited to replace Hooker at the Cafe Au Go-Go in Greenwich Village, when Hooker left for a European tour. After Judy Collins brought Blood, Sweat & Tears member Bobby Colomby to the club to hear him perform, Clayton-Thomas was invited to join the band, which had started splintering following the release of their debut album, "Child Is Father to the Man," but which still had a recording contract with Columbia Records. "We rehearsed for about a week and we opened at the Cafe Au Go-Go and we started recording basically our set," Clayton-Thomas told The Wire magazine in 2020. "What we were doing at night down in the village, we'd go up to 52nd Street and record the songs in the daytime. Everything we put on that album, we played live before we recorded it. We released that album in October 1968 and by New Year's '69, it was the number one album in the world. It happened that fast." One of the biggest hits off that album was "Spinning Wheel." "It's an old theme: everything comes around, right?" Clayton-Thomas said. "I actually wrote that song about two years before I went to New York. I wrote it here in Canada and recorded it for a Canadian record company, and they heard it and they were horrified. They said, 'It's jazz. It will never sell. You can't do this.'" The band's recording of "Spinning Wheel" topped Billboard's Adult Contemporary chart and was nominated for three Grammys; the song would be covered by such artists as Sammy Davis Jr., Shirley Bassey and James Brown. After recording their second album, the group performed at the 1969 Woodstock festival, and toured Eastern Europe on behalf of the State Department. But Clayton-Thomas, burned out, left the group in 1972 to pursue a solo career. He released more than a dozen solo albums, but rejoined Blood Sweat & Tears at various times over the next several decades

Ann Blyth A studio portrait c. 1950 of actress Ann Blyth. | Screen Archives/Getty Images Her most famous film role earned her an Academy Award nomination at age 17. Actress and singer Ann Blyth (August 16, 1927-June 24, 2026) shot to stardom for her performance as Joan Crawford's unscrupulous (and murderous) daughter in the film noir "Mildred Pierce." Her career during the height of the Hollywood studio system found her acting opposite Burt Lancaster, Tyrone Power, Gregory Peck, Robert Mitchum and Paul Newman, and in the 1950s she sang opposite Mario Lanza and Howard Keel in musicals such as "The Great Caruso," "Kismet," "Rose Marie" and "The Student Prince." Born Anne Blythe in Mount Kisco, New York, she was a radio singer at age 6, and trained with the San Carlo Opera Company. At 13 she appeared on Broadway as Paul Lukas' daughter in Lillian Hellman's anti-Nazi play, "Watch on the Rhine." When the show toured in Los Angeles, Universal signed her to a contract, showcasing her in low-budget musicals like "Bowery to Broadway" and "Babes on Swing Street." Auditioning for the Warner Brothers adaptation of the James M. Cain crime novel "Mildred Pierce," Blyth screen tested opposite Crawford herself and won the role. For her performance as the scheming and amoral Veda Pierce — who slaps her mother across the face, and dares to have an affair with her new husband (Veda's stepfather!) before killing him — Blyth received an Oscar nomination for best supporting actress, one of the film's six nominations.
