Crawford won for best actress. "Mildred Pierce" led to more substantive and darker roles for Blyth in such films as "Brute Force," when she played her part in a wheelchair, having broken her back in a sledding accident. But she also appeared in lighter fare, like "Mr. Peabody and the Mermaid." By the end of the '50s she had stopped appearing in films to raise her family, but she occasionally worked in TV (including "Wagon Train," "The Twilight Zone," "Quincy, M.E.," and "Murder, She Wrote"), and toured in productions of "Show Boat" and "The Sound of Music." In a 2013 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Blyth was asked how she hoped she would be remembered by film fans: "That I made them happy. That would make me very happy."

Clive Davis Singer Whitney Houston and music executive Clive Davis at a party c. 1989. | Lester Cohen/Getty Images Record executive Clive Davis (April 4, 1932-June 22, 2026) had an ear for divining hits through his more-than-half-century career. In the 1960s, he signed Janis Joplin; in the '70s, he made a star of Barry Manilow; he guided Whitney Houston to seven straight No. 1 songs in the '80s; he engineered Carlos Santana's comeback in the '90s; and in the 2000s, he discovered Alicia Keys. The winner of five Grammy Awards, Davis was an indisputable icon, winning the trust of leading artists and steering musical tastes, even though, he told "Sunday Morning" in 2011, he wasn't an avid music fan as a child, and never learned how to play an instrument. He described his music career as "an accident." The son of a Brooklyn tie salesman, Davis lost both his parents to sudden illnesses within a year of each other when he was a teen. He learned an early lesson: "There was no substitute for hard work. You had to earn it. I earned every scholarship that I had to get me through law school as well as college." After studying at Harvard Law, he got a job in the legal department at CBS. Within a few years, he was tapped to be head of Columbia Records. "This was a challenge," he said, "and I poured myself into it. Not to say I had an ear, I never even thought of that, but to learn the record business as well as anybody who had ever been involved with it." At CBS Records helped nurture the careers of Billy Joel, Bruce Springsteen, and Earth, Wind & Fire. Accusations about misusing company funds led to his dismissal, and a guilty plea to tax evasion. But Davis made a stunning comeback, taking over a struggling record label, Bell, and renaming it Arista. His first release: Barry Manilow's "Mandy," which topped the Billboard chart. David signed or supported such artists as Lou Rawls, The 5th Dimension, Melissa Manchester, Gil Scott-Heron, Patti Smith, Lou Reed, The Grateful Dead, Aretha Franklin and Luther Vandross. He signed Whitney Houston when she was 19; her debut album, 1985's "Whitney Houston," sold 23 million worldwide, while her follow-up, 1987's "Whitney," made Houston the first female artist to debut an album at No. 1 on the Billboard charts. He also conceived of the Santana album "Supernatural" (1999), which went on to win nine Grammys, including album of the year. He became the first music executive to be voted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2000. Davis also launched J-Records, with such artists as O-Town and Alicia Keys, whose 2001 debut album, "Songs in A Minor," earned four Grammys. In 2002, he became Chairman and CEO of the RCA Music Group; six years later, he was named Chief Creative Officer of Sony BMG Worldwide. In his 70s and 80s, Davis was still directing the careers of such artists as "American Idol" winners Carrie Underwood and Kelly Clarkson. In 2021, when New York City was trying to recover from the COVID pandemic, Davis was asked by the city to spearhead a concert on the Great Lawn in Central Park. "We Love NYC - The Homecoming Concert" featured such artists as Santana, Manilow, Jennifer Hudson, Earth, Wind & Fire, and Jon Batiste. "We're using music to not only change the mood, but we're using music to symbolize rebirth, revival, recovery," he told "Sunday Morning" then. "And that is why it's so special." Sadly, a lightning storm shut down the concert midway, before Springsteen, Paul Simon and Elvis Costello could perform. The influential music executive who almost didn't get into the industry credits his career to a fluke: "I'm indebted to a lucky break — an accident — that brought me into music and that has given me a life of incredible fulfillment and pleasure," he said.

Alan Greenspan Alan Greenspan testifies before the Senate Banking Committee on January 26, 2000 in Washington, D.C., on his nomination for a fourth term as Chairman of the Federal Reserve. | Marshall, Liaison Agency/Getty Images As chairman of the Federal Reserve for more than 18 years, Alan Greenspan (March 6, 1926-June 22, 2026) worked with four presidents. When he left the Fed in 2006, America was in its greatest period of economic growth in its history — and Greenspan was the economy's rock star, heralded as a "maestro" and an "oracle" whose visits to Fed meetings carrying an overstuffed briefcase would lead to massive media conjectures about possible changes in economic policy. But then came the economic shocks of 2008 — a burst housing bubble, a collapse of banks, a plunge in the stock market. Greenspan told "Sunday Morning" in 2013 that one article in particular struck him: "It said basically, 'Do we economists know anything?' And it is a very legitimate question. Because if you don't know enough to capture the most extraordinary event, economic event, in all of our lifetimes, what in the world do we really know? It's like a mystery story to me. You know, how in the world did I miss it? And I said, 'I'm gonna find out why.'" He spent two years studying data and charts, and wrote "The Map and the Territory" (2013), which explored how irrational human behaviors — guided by fear or euphoria — were not factored into the Federal Reserve's computer models, but played a role in the crash that some thought should have been foreseen. "Bubbles go up very slowly as euphoria builds," Greenspan told The Associated Press. "Then fear hits, and it comes down very sharply. When I started to look at that, I was sort of intellectually shocked." A native New Yorker, Greenspan studied music at Juilliard and toured for a year with the Henry Jerome Swing Band, playing saxophone and clarinet. He accepted that he was never going to be a great musician. "I mean, I had played next to Stan Getz — I was 16, he was 15 — and I played for a year side-by-side with him in a band. And he was basically pretty much determined I was gonna become an economist!" Greenspan laughed. A disciple of libertarian philosopher Ayn Rand, Greenspan studied at New York University and Columbia and earned his doctorate from NYU. After having served as President Gerald Ford's chief economic adviser, he was named by President Ronald Reagan as chairman of the Federal Reserve in 1987. He was credited with helping restore stability after the "Black Monday" crash on Wall Street in October of that year. During his tenure at the Fed, Greenspan drew praise for presiding over an economic expansion with little inflation. He also believed financial markets could largely regulate themselves, and helped block efforts to increase federal oversight of derivatives, which allowed speculators to make bets on the market, from oil prices to mortgages. That climate proved fateful. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, assigned by Congress to investigate the 2008 crash, concluded: "More than 30 years of deregulation and reliance on self-regulation by financial institutions, championed by former Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan and others ... had stripped away key safeguards, which could have helped avoid catastrophe." Greenspan admitted he'd made a mistake in assuming that banks could regulate themselves. After leaving the Fed just weeks before turning 80, Greenspan ran a consulting business, Greenspan Associates. Retirement, he told "Sunday Morning" in 2013, was not an option: "I don't know what it means," he said. "I mean, what do we do, stop thinking?"

David Hockney A portrait of English artist David Hockney at his home in Los Angeles, 1987, alongside his 1972 painting, "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)." Acrylic on canvas. | Photo by Anthony Barboza/Getty Images; painting © David Hockney, courtesy Christie's British-born artist David Hockney (July 9, 1937-June 11, 2026) was one of the most vital artists to emerge in the era of mid-20th century pop art. Noted for his portrait and figurative works, Hockney was also recognized for his paintings of California swimming pools, landscapes, photo-collages and scenic designs for opera productions. But he had a particular affinity for portraits. Asked why, in a "Sunday Morning" interview in 2006, Hockney replied, "Well, I like people. They're rather fascinating. They're all a bit different, especially faces." Born in Radford, England, Hockney was encouraged by his parents, who frequently modeled for him. As the artist recalled, his father, using a mirror, would watch and comment on Hockney's progress: "'Is that a right color?' he'd go." After moving to the United States, Hockney fell in love with the light and lifestyle of Southern California. Collectors snapped up his work from the beginning. "They weren't very expensive — you know, $300, $500," he said. "The moment I earned a living as an artist, I felt I was rich, which I was, actually, because you're doing what you want to do. I could look at the world and interpret it and get paid for it as well. … What else would I want to do?" His portraits often displayed a sense of humor, which might explain why he usually refused to accept commissions for portraiture. "You need to be a bit of a flatterer, I think," he said, "and some people can do that. I'm not very good at that, no." One frequent subject of his was a former lover, Peter Schlesinger, featured naked in his 1966 painting "Peter Getting Out of Nick's Pool." Hockney, who was always open about being gay, said, "I don't want to live a deceitful life, you know? I mean, you're an artist, you want to be honest. You've got to be." Over the years, Hockney's lush California landscapes and cool blue swimming pools earned him an international reputation. His 1972 painting "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)" sold at auction for $90.3 million in 2018. He also experimented with "joiner photographs," creating montages of fragmented photographic details depicting an object or setting. He told "Sunday Morning" in 1984 it was to impart movement: "What it led me to believe, now, [is] that it wasn't volume that gives something life, it was time, in a way … It makes you look at it for a long time, if you fragment it. … "I think the beauty is in the looking, not in the thing itself," Hockney said. "In fact, if you can see and look, you've got life, and that's the beautiful thing."

Marjane Satrapi "Persepolis" author and filmmaker Marjane Satrapi poses during the Rome Film Festival, Nov. 16, 2012. | TIZIANA FABI/AFP via Getty Images Iranian-French cartoonist and filmmaker Marjane Satrapi (November 22, 1969-June 4, 2026) won worldwide acclaim for her graphic

World.title: AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records
World.content:
AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records

toggle caption i Patrick Sison/AP Photo



The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.

Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.

Sponsor Message

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks.

Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.

Sponsor Message

Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."

U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.

AI stocks have been hit by volatility

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice, with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.

But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.

In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

Concerns remain about the AI sector

The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.

Sponsor Message

Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.

Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to "pace the frontier," or to slow the development of their most capable models.

Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.

In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a "supply chain risk" — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.

World.title: Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
World.content:
Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban

toggle caption i Rick Rycroft/AP

MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state's ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian."

Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.

He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to "enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background," court documents showed.

Sponsor Message

Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities' refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite "limited his cultural rights" under the charter.

But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities' goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.

"The limitation on Mr. McKechnie's ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner," Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.

Prison officials testify Vegemite could impair drug sniffer dogs and be used to make alcohol

Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state's 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs' ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.

McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were "less restrictive means reasonably available" to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.

Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren't raised on it.

Sponsor Message

The last U.S. president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: "It's horrible."

Prisoner argues Vegemite ban contributed to vitamin deficiency

McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency.

He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn't eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin.

Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9) which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children.

But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as "not important," after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence.

Prisoner said Vegemite ban left him feeling 'deprived, sad and disconnected'

McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel "deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community."

The judge responded that "it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community."

McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal "Gastronomica" in 2003 that said, "Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world."

The article, based on research by Australia's Queensland University in 1995, found that a "taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry."

McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning an Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing.

He cited Australian band Men at Work's 1980s international hit "Down Under" that mentions a "Vegemite sandwich."

On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man's unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs.

Sponsor Message

Judge rejects evidence that Vegemite doesn't interfere with drug sniffer dogs

The judge upheld prison authorities' argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs.

McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained "no live yeast" and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread.

A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly.

Vegemite's owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

World.title: What to know about China's plenum as Xi seeks stronger party discipline
World.content:
What to know about China's plenum as Xi seeks stronger party discipline

toggle caption i Xie Huanchi/Xinhua via AP

HONG KONG — China's political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party's discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption.

This week's closed-door gathering, known as the fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader and personnel changes to key leadership bodies.

Xi began the meeting by delivering a work report and speaking about a draft policy decision on advancing "full and rigorous party self-governance," according to China's official Xinhua News Agency. The policy aims to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.

Sponsor Message

While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will offer him an opportunity to further align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants.

"The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising the ranks share Xi's assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces," said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

Here's what to know about one of Beijing's most significant political meetings this year.

Xi targets underperforming cadres and corruption

Xi's anti-graft drive has been a defining feature of his rule since he came to power in 2012. Purges of officials — including some viewed as his political rivals — have been carried out on a scale that led critics to argue the campaign was also used to consolidate his power.

But his focus has expanded to cracking down on underperforming cadres too. In recent years, the number of officials punished for "formalism" and "bureaucratism" — misconduct such as dereliction of duty, inaction and reckless acts that seriously hinder development — has surged.

Xi's policy proposals reflect his emphasis on the party's "self-revolution," a concept centered on the party reforming itself through efforts such as rooting out corruption and building ideological commitment, analysts say.

Sponsor Message

Osman said the disciplinary crackdowns are now aimed more at institutional longevity.

"It's less about purging elite rivals and more about building a disciplined system that can sustain Xi's political priorities across leadership cycles," she said.

Record-high disciplinary campaigns also do not necessarily mean a rebound in corruption, but rather that Xi has been steadily raising the bar for the party's expectations of officials, she added.

Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group's China practice, said Beijing has been building its agenda for months.

"The message is clear: the anti-corruption campaign is not winding down. Officials are not only tested for loyalty, but also for compliance and action," he said.

Xi said in a January meeting that while decisions by the party's top leadership were smoothly implemented in general, inspections and audits found problems such as failures to comply and improper execution, according to an October article in the Qiushi Journal, a publication of the central committee.

Xi warned against "two-faced people" who might profess political loyalty while privately defying orders and doing as they please.

"During leadership transitions, we must keep our eyes sharp, elevate good cadres who are truly loyal and reliable, consistent in word and deed, and willing to take responsibility, and never allow 'two-faced people' or those driven by self-interest to slip through," Xi was quoted as saying.

Xi's purges of top army officials will be put on display

The number of empty seats in the conference hall this week will help observers gauge how widespread Xi's purges have been.

Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, and his colleagues Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang noted that while Xi's civilian purges are record-breaking, 42 out of 44 officials affiliated with the military elected as full central committee members in 2022 have also been purged or disappeared.

Sponsor Message

The central committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 full and alternate members. Thomas and his colleagues estimated turnout this week could be less than 80%, potentially setting a record low at any plenum since the end of former leader Mao Zedong's rule in 1976.

Attention will also be on new demands on the officials who remain.

Thomas expects tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption, and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi's priorities.

New personnel appointments are possible, though Xi may wait until a once-in-five-years Communist Party Congress next year to anoint his picks, said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London. If he does fill any openings, it will be with loyalists, he added.

Hints at a Xi successor are unlikely

The underlying theme of the fifth plenum is that it will be another opportunity for Xi to position himself for an unprecedented fourth term in office.

Xi, who removed presidential term limits in 2018, is viewed by some as the most powerful Chinese leader since Mao. He is widely expected to be confirmed as party leader for the next term in the fall of 2027.

Ahead of that, Thomas said new ideological language reinforcing Xi's authority might emerge at this week's meeting.

He said the plenum should prepare the ground for Xi's fourth term and reinforce expectations of political and policy continuity.

"After Xi has purged so many of the people that he promoted at the last congress, watch for tougher scrutiny of the officials competing to join his next leadership team," he said.

World.title: Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term
World.content:
Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Republicans had a plan to keep control of the House in the midterms: Redraw congressional district lines to favor the GOP and avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses. President Trump began pressuring Republican-led states to do just that last year, but it isn't working out as expected. Republicans could now be spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to be easy wins, and end up losing anyway. Of the 15 districts drawn specifically to favor Republicans, only five are rated by the Cook Political Report as either likely or solid Republican. Most are toss-ups or lean toward a Democratic win.



🎧 One reason the Republicans' redistricting push hasn't been as successful as expected is that some district lines were drawn based on the 2024 Trump electorate, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. Since then, his support has weakened, particularly among young and Latino voters. Several Democratic incumbents targeted by redistricting have stuck it out to fight for their seats. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the characterization that redistricting didn't work, saying that it "creates new battlefields" but doesn't "create outcomes."

Several Democratic incumbents targeted by redistricting have stuck it out to fight for their seats. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the characterization that redistricting didn't work, saying that it "creates new battlefields" but doesn't "create outcomes." ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Sponsor Message

In a stunning political comeback, leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in the presidential runoff election in Brazil. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, by more than 4 million votes. It's the first time since Brazil restored democracy in 1989 that a candidate who finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidency.



🎧 Lula's win appears to have put the brake on a right-wing sweep in Latin America, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Seven conservative presidents have been elected in the past 18 months. Kahn says one message helped rally voters in the final weeks of Lula's campaign: that the return of a Bolsonaro to power would be an existential threat to Brazilian democracy.

Large demonstrations against the government continued over the weekend in France, where more than 100,000 people showed up in Paris, and more than 400,000 came out nationwide. What started with students demanding better conditions has grown into a much bigger movement. Unions and public-sector workers have joined, calling for more public spending and protesting growing inequality. Similar protests have erupted across Europe, from Spain to Serbia.



🎧 The reasons behind the protests vary, from schools and housing costs to corruption, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. But they have something in common: most are leaderless movements by young people frustrated with the world they're being left to. In Serbia, crowds celebrated in the streets of Belgrade after a student-led movement known as the "student-list" defeated the party of longtime strongman Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's parliamentary elections. The win followed two years of protests over government corruption and lack of accountability.

Sponsor Message

Healthcare helpline

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

Out-of-pocket maternity expenses are difficult to predict. A federal requirement for insurers to provide personalized cost estimates under the No Surprises Act was supposed to take effect in 2022, but federal regulators haven't made it happen despite pressure from Congress. Until the cost of maternity care gets more transparent, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy:

👶 Enroll your baby in your insurance before your deadline. For most employer health plans, that's within 30 days of birth.

👶 Check what your maximum out-of-pocket expense is. That's the most you'll pay each year for covered, in-network expenses before your insurance pays 100% of the costs.

👶 Choose in-network providers whenever possible.

👶 Go over every bill, and don't be afraid to appeal errors.

👶 Ask your hospital or other providers about financial assistance.

Deep dive

toggle caption i National Oceanic and Atmospheric/National Oceanic and Atmospheric

When Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm, Google DeepMind's AI model outperformed the traditional model, correctly predicting it would hit the Florida Panhandle rather than head west toward Louisiana. Hurricane forecasters say they're increasingly relying on AI technology, and that it's rapidly transforming the field.



🌀 The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating Google DeepMind into its official forecasts last year. By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was among the best at predicting a storm's strength and path.

🌀 Traditional physics-based prediction models use real-time atmospheric data like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear. AI models rely more on history and patterns from analyzing thousands of past storms.

🌀 AI models can feel like a black box; meteorologists depend on them but don't always know why their predictions are correct.

🌀 Humans still interpret the results of these models and translate them into clear guidance people can act on.

3 things to know before you go

The latest edition of NPR's Breakfast Around the World series takes us to the ancient city of Aleppo in northern Syria, where a sweet semolina pudding called mamounieh evokes memories both bitter and sweet. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 4,588 confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year through Oct. 22 — more than double the number for all of 2025. Cases are particularly high in Pennsylvania. The general fertility rate for U.S. women fell by 1% to a record low in 2025, according to the CDC. Birth rates declined among women in their 20s but rose among women ages 30 to 45.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
World.content:
Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

PORT HURON, Mich. — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.

Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.

El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country "shameful" and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president's remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.

Sponsor Message

"The president's statements are out of line," he said in a phone interview. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."

With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan's Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.

Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn, a city with one of the nation's largest concentrations of Arab Americans.

Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday's rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan "to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."

Responding to Trump, who also regularly mocks his name, El-Sayed told supporters at a rally in Grand Rapids later Sunday that he doesn't care how Trump pronounces or misrepresents it.

Sponsor Message

"I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," El-Sayed said, drawing cheers. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro."

El-Sayed's faith, associations and past statements become campaign flashpoints

Central to Republicans' strategy against El-Sayed in the final weeks of the campaign has been an effort to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations.

There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that "my family has long been MB" and described a conversation with her mother about her involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.

El-Sayed was born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother.

Trump on Sunday also targeted El-Sayed's ties to popular streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared alongside the Democrat multiple times during the primary campaign, including at his election night event.

Piker in the past has said that "Hamas is a thousand times better" than Israel, describing some Orthodox Jews as "inbred" and that "America deserved 9/11."

El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric. He has repeatedly refused to answer questions about whether Iran or Israel poses a bigger threat to the country. Earlier this year, he said "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened.

"To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry," he said. "That was not my intention."

Sponsor Message

Founder of Arab Americans for Trump calls the president 'racist'

Bahbah, whose organization has since changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace, said Trump's remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs.

"The remarks are out of line and crazy. I mean, no sane individual would say these things," Bahbah said.

Dearborn helped Trump win Michigan in 2024 after many voters in the city were outraged by the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza.

"The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable," said Bahbah. "And people are going to remember that on Nov. 3."

Sen. Bernie Sanders, speaking at the Grand Rapids rally, said Trump and his allies were using Islamophobia because they have "nothing to say" about the issues most important to working people, such as health care, housing and income inequality.

"All they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness," Sanders said.

The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year

Rogers and El-Sayed have been locked in a bitter race to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed's loyalty to the United States.

"Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked.

El-Sayed said that questioning was "shameful."

"I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray," he said.

Speaking before Trump's appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year," Rogers said on stage. "Abdul El-Sayed's."

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

Rally doesn't deliver a new economic handout, but gets boost from Minaj

Trump has routinely announced new investments in factories at his campaign rallies, but he did not do so as part of his speech in Michigan, a state defined by the auto industry.

Sponsor Message

The president instead repeated investments already being made by domestic automakers. Those automakers could see their finances slump if the president expands his trade war with Canada, which has been an essential partner for the U.S. automotive sector.

While it lacked a fresh promise for Michigan's economy, Trump's rally did deliver a bit of star power.

Rapper Nicki Minaj appeared on stage and urged people to get out and vote for the state's Republican ticket. Her appearance followed an awkward moment from Trump, who has increasingly been fixated on commenting about other people's body parts.

After praising the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican in a close election contest, Trump turned his eye toward Minaj and commented on her posterior.

The president then signaled for Minaj to stand for the crowd and she did, after which Trump said, "I hope Nicki wasn't insulted, but we love Nicki. She's been with us for a long time."

World.title: Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments
World.content:
Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments

toggle caption i LA Johnson/NPR

One of Kathleen Tejeda's students began freshman year just trying to get by. High school can be tricky for any teenager, but she was navigating it as a blind person.

By the end of her junior year, with support from Tejeda and other school staff, the student had gone from getting by to going big: She made the cheerleading squad and the school choir. She even sang the national anthem in front of the whole school.

Tejeda, who has been a special educator for 20 years in Riverside County, Calif., said that kind of advocacy is just as much a part of her job as teaching her students. But teachers like her can be hard to find.

Sponsor Message

There is a shortage of special educators in 45 out of 50 states, according to the Learning Policy Institute, an education research organization. That shortage is growing because the number of special education students is climbing: It's now more than 8.2 million — about 1 out of 6 public school students.

While turnover worsened sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, the shortage isn't new. It has existed since special education became embedded in federal law with the passage of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1975. Half a century later, a fundamental question remains: Why is this shortage of special education teachers so persistent?

Myths and realities about teaching special education

Let's start with a common misconception: The kids are hard to work with, so teachers don't want to do the job. "That is not the case," said Liz Bettini, a former special education teacher who is now a researcher and professor at Boston University. "That has not borne out in our research at all."

Loading...

What Bettini's research does show: Special educators can feel isolated from other school staff and feel they have too many student needs to manage. The volume of required paperwork can be crushing. These educators are often responsible for teaching across several subjects and grade levels. Many feel they don't get paid enough to do this essential work.

"That's a very heavy weight to carry as a teacher," Bettini said.

NPR set out to hear directly from about a dozen special educators from around the United States' public schools to learn what it takes to do their jobs day to day. They have been sharing snippets of their lives through voice memos since the start of the school year, and some will open their classroom doors to NPR in the coming months.

"No teacher does this for the paycheck," said third-year high school teacher Diana Swanson, who works in Vail, Ariz., as she sat at her desk the day before her school year began in July. "Just the students, that fulfillment, seeing them fill their cup a little bit, seeing them smile, be a member of society and part of their community. That's what fulfills me."

Sponsor Message

"I feel like I was coming into this school year more prepared this time around," fourth-year elementary school teacher Danalyn Garcia said late one school night from her living room in Chicago. "Yet, I feel the needs are even greater than the year before."

"Honestly, I had no life outside of school and outside of being a teacher," said Kaori Anderson-Walker, looking back on his first year of teaching middle school in Philadelphia. Now in his fourth year, he said he has finally learned to manage his time more effectively but said the work is still never-ending. "When my students aren't performing where I want them in the classroom, my mind is just constantly moving."

Much of the day isn't spent on teaching

Being an educator of any kind is demanding and requires immense skill. Research shows that burnout among all kinds of public school teachers is high, but it's even more acute for special educators. These teachers work with students who have an incredibly diverse set of needs, including those with autism, learning disabilities such as dyslexia, developmental delays and physical disabilities.

Special educators also do a lot more than teach — in fact, one study found that they spent only about a third of their day on instruction. They spend the rest of their time tracking student goals, coordinating specialized services for students (say, speech therapy or extra reading help), training support staff and writing individualized education programs (IEPs), which are legal documents that track each special education student's needs at school.

In many states, that means teachers must have specialized certification and training, but they typically aren't paid more. In 32 states, teachers get no extra pay for the hardest-to-staff positions, including in special education, according to a recent study.

While all 13 special educators NPR has spoken to said building relationships with students is their favorite part of the work, they also described the realities of those students' needs being more complex than those of many general education students.

Sponsor Message

"Special educators have reported, 'I can't teach this kid and respond to the student's crisis simultaneously. So I'm abandoning instruction because the crisis has to take priority,'" Bettini said.

For example, Grace Fitzgerald, who teaches elementary school in Peoria, Ill., shared on a drive home from school that one of her students had an emotional crisis that forced her to evacuate the rest of her class for their safety. "It's been challenging mentally and emotionally to kind of go through that at the very end of the first quarter, my first year of teaching," she said. "No one gets a road map to deal with that kind of situation."

Several teachers shared that behavioral challenges with individual students can make it harder to meet the needs of their many other students.

Loading...

"Our school doesn't have walls. So we have six classes per grade level in one ginormous room, and it's separated by dividers," Garcia, in Chicago, said. "So when one kid is screaming and crying and begins to escalate, it disturbs the whole pod and then other kids react to it." Getting students back on track can be difficult in these kinds of situations, she said.

Essential but time-consuming paperwork

Individualized education programs are a key part of special education. These written plans, required by federal law, are managed by teachers and other school staff and serve as a kind of road map for each special education student. IEPs outline the student's unique needs and their annual goals. For example, a goal of a student with autism may be to maintain eye contact for a certain period of time.

IEPs help families hold schools accountable, and they also help enforce a primary aim of special education: to teach students in the "least restrictive environment," meaning students with disabilities are taught alongside students without disabilities as much as possible. But IEPs also require regular meetings with families, an understanding of special education law and time spent away from teaching students — time that teachers often don't have.

Sponsor Message

Then there's the work of putting the IEP into practice in the classroom. Tejeda, of Riverside County, said when she's "pushing in" to other teachers' general education classrooms, she provides targeted support without singling out special education students. "We're going to walk the classroom and check in with everybody, but at the back of our minds, we know that we need to make sure we're [making] accommodations for that particular student."

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

For Anderson-Walker, in Philadelphia, "the biggest struggle" was feeling like he had to juggle IEP paperwork with teaching duties. Then, last year, his school, Boys' Latin of Philadelphia, hired staff members who are responsible for the paperwork part of IEPs, leaving teachers more time for the classroom. "Not having that stress is amazing," Anderson-Walker said.

Searching for solutions

In addition to the workload, at the core of the special education teacher shortage are pay and the sheer number of qualified people. Research shows that paying teachers more can help attract and retain them.

For example, in 2020, Hawaii raised special education teacher salaries by $10,000 annually. That cut the state's vacancies by 35%, but it wasn't enough to keep many special education teachers in their jobs. Seventeen states now pay teachers additional money to work in hard-to-staff subjects, including special education. That's down from four years ago, when 22 states did so.

The pipeline of qualified special educators is another big problem. According to education policy researcher Chad Aldeman's analysis of federal data a few years ago, about 46,000 special ed teachers leave public schools every year, while teacher preparation programs train fewer than 30,000 annually to replace those teachers.

Aldeman calls it a crude estimate but said that the rapid increase in demand for special education teachers is outpacing the supply of people trained to do those jobs. Many schools end up resorting to hiring teachers who aren't fully qualified for the work.

Sponsor Message

But research has found that "grow-your-own" programs that focus on recruiting people who already live in the community may be effective at filling special education jobs. Bettini and her research partners also found that supportive administrators and adequate planning time can help make the work feel more sustainable for teachers.

For example, Fitzgerald, the first-year teacher in Illinois, said she was feeling overwhelmed by her workload at the start of the year. So she worked with her school leadership to build more dedicated planning time into her day.

"I think that's going to be very beneficial and will hopefully lead to a decrease in time spent after school," Fitzgerald said. She uses that time to focus on lesson plans, logging data and writing IEP goals.

It allows her to be more present in the classroom, working with her students.

Visuals and graphics design by LA Johnson and Julianna Conley

World.title: How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts
World.content:
How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts

toggle caption i NOAA/NOAA

Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field.

When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.

In early October, Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm. Conventional forecasting models initially predicted it would head further west, toward southeastern Louisiana.

But Google DeepMind's artificial intelligence model called it right out of the gate: the hurricane was going to hit the western Florida Panhandle.

"Google DeepMind, in particular, has really proven itself the last few years as the gold standard model," says Michael Lowry, a longtime meteorologist and hurricane expert in Miami, who has previously advised both the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

Sponsor Message

"That model has been, by far and away, the best performing computer model that we've ever seen. Period."

A different kind of model

The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating the Google DeepMind model into its official forecasts last year.

By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was already one of the best at predicting a storm's path and strength, says Brian McNoldy, a hurricane researcher for the University of Miami.

Usually, new models take years to refine after first being introduced.

"It's something we're not used to – to have a model, the new kid on the block, very quickly becoming the best model out there," McNoldy says. "This pretty much came out of the gate in first place, and that's a pretty impressive feat."

Traditional physics-based hurricane models use real-time atmospheric data, like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear, as measured by satellites and aircraft. Then they use complicated equations to predict what path a storm might travel and how strong it could get.

An AI model operates very differently: it relies more on history. It identifies patterns by analyzing thousands of past storms along with atmospheric data.

"The AI models don't really know anything about the atmosphere other than the current picture," Lowry says. "Beyond that, it's not leaning on the governing equations of the atmosphere, the physics, to make predictions."

Sponsor Message

Most of the people designing and developing these models aren't even meteorologists, Lowry notes: "They're software engineers, and they're developing neural networks."

A "neural network" is a set of computer algorithms modeled on the human brain and trained to find patterns in massive amounts of data.

As a result, the models can seem like a "black box," Lowry says: "We don't know why they might get a forecast right. We also don't know why they might get a forecast wrong."

It can be unsettling for meteorologists to depend on a system they don't totally understand – especially during storms when millions of people might be relying on their forecasts.

"It makes us a little uncomfortable, because we like to know why you're getting the right answer," McNoldy says. "And I feel like we don't – or at least I don't know why."

Not all AI models have performed well, though. There are lots of unproven weather forecasting AI models out there, Lowry says.

The two that have so far proven to be the most accurate, despite some pitfalls, are the models developed by Google DeepMind and by the U.K.-based European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).

toggle caption i Gerald Herbert/AP

Relying on a "blend" of models

Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center use several proven models – both AI and traditional – when putting together their official forecasts.

"Every storm has different forecast challenges," says NHC Director Michael Brennan. "That's why we take that consensus approach and use that blend of the best models."

And it's still humans who have to interpret the results of those models before deciding what to tell the public.

The NHC provides updates every six hours during active hurricanes. The models by themselves can sometimes show drastic changes from one update to the next. Forecasters have to translate those shifting predictions into clear guidance that people can act on.

Sponsor Message

"That's one thing that the human forecaster provides a lot of, is continuity," Brennan says. "We're using our expertise and our understanding to translate that hurricane forecast into the hazard space, and that's what people really need to pay attention to."

Scientists expect rapid advances

The Google DeepMind model still needs some work, Brennan says. While it topped other models in tracking the path of Isaias, it didn't do as well as the NHC's blended forecast in determining the intensity, or strength, of the storm.

Brennan's team gives regular feedback to Google DeepMind to help improve the model. Google didn't respond to questions from NPR for this story.

The "future of forecasting has always been changing," Brennan says. "It's never just one thing that's driving those improvements."

It wasn't that long ago when forecasters couldn't predict how strong a storm would be even within a couple of days, he notes. That changed, because of advances in prediction models and better data collected by satellites and planes.

"Errors are about half of what they were, say, at the time of [Hurricane] Katrina, in terms of intensity forecasting," Brennan says.

The exciting thing about AI, says meteorologist Michael Lowry, is how quickly it's improving. AI updates take only months or even weeks, unlike traditional models, which are updated annually at best.

"They are making advancements in skill and hurricane predictions over the course of a year that would have taken us 10 years, a decade or more, to make," Lowry says.

But even with AI coming in fast and strong, Lowry says he's not worried about artificial intelligence replacing people.

"For me, I don't feel some sort of existential crisis with AI," Lowry says. "If anything, I think it is a boon for our business."



Edited by Rachel Waldholz

World.title: Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges
World.content:
Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges

toggle caption i Kirk Siegler

EUGENE, Ore. - President Trump is widely expected to soon open up some 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests in a move he says will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown lands.

Trump signaled the move with executive actions last year aimed at dramatically boosting timber sales on U.S. Forest Service land and reversing the agency's 25-year-old Roadless Rule, which blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forestlands.

Today with the formal repeal of the Roadless Rule rule expected early next year, the picture on the ground in timber country looks messier. Those who make a living in the forests say the problems are much bigger than access to more trees.

Sponsor Message

"I'm not saying these EOs [Executive Orders] are useless, they set the tone," says Sean Smith, CEO of the family owned Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Ore.

Smith, standing in a bustling lumber yard with the sawmill cranking behind four story high stacks of freshly cut timber, says the industry has more pressing challenges now, starting with the record high price of diesel fuel. Economists largely blame that on Trump's war with Iran. And then there's inflation, which is driving up the costs of just about everything.

"Steel, you know, we have to buy sawblades, we have to buy ball bearings," Smith says. "We have to buy a million different parts to keep this mouse trap going."

So repealing the Roadless Rule - which has largely banned new road building and logging projects on some 44 million acres of pristine national forests since 2001 - is lower on the priority list.

toggle caption i Kirk Siegler

Smith, a burly man with a dry sense of humor and a neatly trimmed salt and pepper beard, does support the reversal saying it will eventually give industry a more reliable local timber supply. He says a lot of the nearby Willamette National Forest, roaded or not, is dangerously overgrown. That built-up fuel makes these forests more prone to catastrophic wildfires.

Sponsor Message

"This is not a 'gee I sure want more cheap timber volume,' you know, this is not me promoting an agenda," Smith says. "This is a guy who lives here and is tired of seeing these beautiful places burn up."

Trump says a boom is coming but the industry is a fraction of what it was

The administration alongside the timber industry and some local officials are pushing for the repeal, saying it will give the Forest Service more flexibility to carry out wildfire prevention, including tree thinning, on land that's largely functioned as wilderness since 2001.

But under recent Republican and Democratic administrations, the Forest Service has struggled to get those projects going on forests that already have roads. Lawsuits and red tape are an ongoing challenge, as is finding enough workers.

"Right now, there's not a ton of people that want to wake up at 2 a.m. and drive a log truck for the same price that you could go work at McDonald's for," says Jeff Brink, a second generation logger near Eugene, Ore.

Brink says the industry is a fraction of what it was when his dad and uncles started Brink Land Development in 1981. The company is getting by ok, for now he says, due to a steady stream of forest restoration projects on private land as well as some recent salvage logging timber sales from nearby wildfire burn scars.

But for many smaller, less established loggers already struggling, Brink says, labor shortages and high diesel prices could be the tipping point.

"For an industry already operating on low margins, this is a tough one," Brink says.

Due to tightening environmental laws and other market forces including cheaper Canadian lumber imports, timber sales on U.S. federal land dropped by close to 90% since the 1990s. Brink says today the infrastructure just isn't there for the forest work that needs to be done, let alone a promised timber boom.

Sponsor Message

"Rural Oregon is struggling and all the mills that aren't along the I-5 corridor or near urban centers that can source wood are closing," he says.

Since the 1990s, an estimated 400 mills across the broader Northwest have closed, amounting to the loss of about 35,000 jobs. Seven mills have closed in Oregon since 2024 alone.

Industry experts project that overturning the Roadless Rule could lead to a five to ten percent boost in federal timber sales. That's hardly enough to boost much enthusiasm on the ground.

"We're in an industry that for decades has been in a state of contraction," Brink says.

Several national environmental groups have also already signaled they plan to sue once the administration formally repeals the rule, which is expected to happen by early next year.

Some fear a revival of the bitter Timber Wars

Timothy Ingalsbee turns his hybrid station wagon onto Forest Service Road 2408, near the scene of an infamous year-long tree sit and blockade that he helped lead against a Forest Service old growth timber sale in the nineties.

"The industry [back then] was headed for a crash, they had exhausted the supply," Ingalsbee says, as he stops the car and gets out at a vista.

Today, his hair cropped shorter and greying, Ingalbee notes that many of those towering, old growth trees, their bark cloaked in moss, have burned in recent wildfires. Ingalsbee, a retired Forest Service firefighter, today runs a national firefighter safety and advocacy group.

"The claim that they're going to do all this new road building and logging in roadless areas on behalf of wildland firefighters, and make it more efficient for them, is just a big lie," Ingalsbee says. "Not in our name you don't."

toggle caption i Kirk Siegler

Ingalsbee fears that punching even more roads into these forests will lead to more human-caused wildfires, which have been rising steadily for decades. But he doesn't think any of this is really about wildfire prevention or creating more logging jobs.

Sponsor Message

"What's driving a lot of Trump's executive orders for public lands management is not real economic drivers. I don't hear industry clambering for this," he says. "It's more ideology."

For Ingalsbee, the U.S. government is just racing to open up as much of the West as possible so industry can squeeze out maximum profits on timber, oil and coal.

Everyone is tired of policies 'whipsawing' from one president to the next

One thing that almost everyone on the ground in the Northwest agrees on is that Congress has largely failed to act on either protecting or opening up federal forest lands to more development.

When President Clinton signed the Roadless Rule by executive order at the end of his second term, Republicans controlled both the Senate and the U.S. House where appetite for passing more wilderness legislation was slim. The rule was the culmination of a sweeping inventory of land conducted by the Forest Service in which the agency had marked certain forests as prime acreage for wilderness protection.

Congress never codified it, and since then, the administrative rule has become an environmental flashpoint in a polarized country.

Back at Starfire Lumber, CEO Sean Smith is tired of federal forest and timber policy whipsawing from one presidential administration to the next.

"Sometimes the cynical side of me says, 'hey, what could be better than a do-nothing Congress at least they're not screwing anything up," Smith says, with a sardonic chuckle. "But that's no way to run a country long term."

Not to mention, he adds, it makes for a hard environment to keep a business going in.

World.title: Alberta referendum tallies reveal rural-urban divide on 'the 9'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Elections Alberta officials are finishing counting referendum ballots, but the results so far suggest Albertans in rural areas seem to hold different views on immigration and constitutional fights than those living in urban areas.

The agency confirmed its unofficial count Saturday night. Results suggest more Albertans overall support the proposals in questions 1 to 5, which focused on immigration and access to services for non-permanent residents, and oppose the proposals in questions 6 to 9, which pertained to various constitutional issues.

Most support for any of the questions that have come to be known as “the nine” — because so much focus was on Question 10, which asked about Alberta’s place in Canada — came from rural ridings, while voters in Calgary and Edmonton were more divided, if not firmly against them.

“We've long seen urban-rural divide over things like immigration, and that partly tracks with the fact that … rural places tend to be more conservative than urban places,” Feodor Snagovsky, an associate professor of political science at the University of Alberta, told CBC News, adding that those on the political right tend to have “more restrictive views” on immigration.

The immigration questions focused on ideas like requiring voters to prove their Canadian citizenship to cast ballots in provincial elections, the provincial government taking more control of immigration — more of a federal responsibility, historically — and imposing conditions on non-permanent residents’ access to services like health care and education.

The constitutional questions regarded issues like provinces — not the feds — being able to make judicial appointments and trying to abolish the federal Senate.

Given the results so far, political analysts suggest Premier Danielle Smith’s government did not get a strong mandate on the proposals it put forward in the referendum. During an interview with CBC podcast West of Centre Friday, Smith said she believes voters told her government to proceed with caution, but that there is a desire to get more control over economic migration.

The referendum was worth holding, she said, and it showed her that Albertans are more concerned about immigration policy than pursuing constitutional change — and her government will prioritize taking action on those proposed measures.

“People want to be fair, they want to be generous, but we can solve a lot of the problems by focusing our newcomer population on the jobs that are available,” Smith said, adding that someone landing in the province with a well-paying job probably relies less on social services.

“When somebody makes a commitment to being a permanent taxpayer, as a permanent resident, they’ll get the same programs as everyone else. If we can fix that part, then I think it will reduce some of the stress on our health-care and education and other systems.”

When asked about the dissension in Alberta’s two largest cities, Smith argued that most of the jobs that the province needs to attract people from elsewhere to fill are located outside of those centres, thus rural voters might have felt more strongly about immigration.

WATCH | Alberta referendum reveals rural-urban divide for 'the 9': A rural-urban divide for 'the 9' in Alberta referendum | Duration closed caption 2:12 Elections Alberta is finalizing the count of referendum ballots, but so far, results suggest rural voters seem to hold different views on immigration and constitutional fights than those in urban areas. CBC’s Nicole Healey has the details.

Opposition to immigration in rural areas, at least in part, stems from concerns about Canada’s Temporary Foreign Worker Program, Snagovsky said, adding he believes there is room for a conversation about ensuring employers are using that appropriately.

Moving forward, however, the referendum’s apparent rural-urban divide forces Smith to walk a political tightrope, said Lisa Young, a University of Calgary political science professor.

Most MLAs for the governing United Conservative Party represent rural ridings, but 11 of them represent Calgary ridings. Edmonton’s districts are all represented by the Opposition NDP.

Data suggests Question 5 — about proving Canadian citizenship to vote in provincial elections — was the only one of “the nine” that a majority of voters supported across all UCP-held ridings. But for the rest, some of the UCP’s Calgary ridings — including those held by cabinet ministers like Demetrios Nicolaides and Mike Ellis — either objected to, or narrowly supported, the proposals that were put forward.

“The results of the referendum suggest that [Smith’s] hold on Calgary seats is maybe not as strong as it was in the past, so the viability of her coalition strategy now is in question,” Young said.

The next general election is set for October 2027. For the governing UCP to hold on to power, Young said, the premier must figure out how to maintain rural support, while also appealing to at least some urban Albertans.

Elections Alberta is set to release its official referendum results Thursday, two days after the fall session gets underway in Alberta’s legislature. The provincial government issued a news release Friday that listed multiple issues about which it intends to propose legislation.

Young said she assumes the government has already drafted legislation related to the referendum issues. She said she will be watching for whether the government hesitates to introduce anything because of the referendum results, and if it uses Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedom — the notwithstanding clause — to pass certain items.

“It’s going to be telling whether this legislation now comes forward — and in what form,” Young said.

World.title: Judge rules Trump administration illegally fired prosecutor Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday.

Maurene Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the country's highest-profile cases and consistently receiving "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found.

After her firing, Comey sued the U.S. Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment.

She asserted she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom U.S. President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.

The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to "make her whole" and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the "unlawful termination."

In her lawsuit, Comey asked for the retroactive pay so that she could get back pay and qualify for retirement benefits. In February, she was hired as a partner at New York law firm Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler.

Firing violated constitution, statutes: judge

Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" powers.

He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."

Furman added: "Indeed, to accept defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system."

The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled.

WATCH | 'Well, they're back': Comey vows to fight indictment, again: Former FBI director James Comey indicted again over social media post | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 4:21 Former FBI director James Comey was indicted again on Tuesday over a social media post of seashells arranged on a beach reading the numbers ‘86 47.’ The Department of Justice says this post was a ‘call to violence’ toward U.S. President Donald Trump.

Furman reserved judgment on Comey's First Amendment claim pending further arguments to be submitted by each side, though he said he was inclined to dismiss the claim because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement.

Comey's lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.

"This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the president is not above the law," they said.

The Justice Department, during the Trump administration, has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration's agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.

The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father's longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.

The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican's successful 2016 campaign for the White House. In the years since, Trump has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.

An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

When James Comey was originally indicted, his son-in-law, Troy Edwards Jr., resigned from his position as assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. He is married to another daughter of Comey's.

The Justice Department and the FBI are facing a number of court challenges related to the ouster of dozens of attorneys and agents who were dismissed after participating in earlier investigations of Trump, or because they were perceived as insufficiently loyal to the Republican president's agenda.

World.title: Horse-drawn carriages are still a tradition in some Canadian cities
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The horse-drawn carriage industry is again getting a lot of neigh-sayers, after New York City council passed a bill last week that would ban the rides by June 2028.

The vote came after a teenage tourist died last spring when he was thrown from the carriage as a horse bolted away from its driver.

The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers and the rest of the industry find other jobs, and it's revived an ongoing debate in North America over the practice of using horses to pull tourists on city streets.

In Canada, several large cities still permit horse-drawn carriage rides — or calèches, as they're known in Quebec — though this hasn't been without controversy.
