Toronto banned the carriages in its downtown core in 1998, but Montreal didn't look into doing so until 20 years later. In 2018, a horse collapsed and died in the middle of a guided tour, prompting then-mayor Valérie Plante to propose a ban on the calèches that took effect in 2020.

The city worked with the provincial labour department to help calèches drivers find other work and offered to pay owners $1,000 per horse to retire the animals.

The move drew outcry, with horse carriage owner Denis Murray telling CBC at the time it was "stupid." Murray said he and his horse Sissi shared a close bond and that she enjoyed the work.

She was later adopted by a veterinarian couple in Quebec's Eastern Townships, where Murray said he was happy to see she appeared to be doing well.

Denis Murray with his horse Sissi. (Submitted by Denis Murray)

Canadian cities should 'take note': animal rights group

The tours have persisted elsewhere in the country, including Victoria, Vancouver, Quebec City and Charlottetown.

"It's time for other Canadian cities to take note," said Bianca Del Bois, a spokesperson for the Animal Alliance of Canada, who added that while the group is "delighted" to see Manhattan undertake a ban on the carriages, it also welcomes the measures for workers accompanying the legislation.

"I don't think the humans are lost in this," she added.

Sinikka Crosland of the Canadian Horse Defence Coalition agrees.

"T his is an important consideration, making the end of the industry more fair and palatable," she told CBC.

'Hot-button issue' in Victoria

The opposition in Victoria has been spirited in the past decade, to say the least. In May 2018, a video showing two Victoria Carriage Tours horses slipping, tangling harnesses and collapsing near the Ogden Point cruise terminal after a minor bump with a bus went viral and caused outrage.

The B.C. SPCA called on Victoria City Council to ban horse-drawn carriages from busy downtown streets or restrict them strictly to park environments.

Activist groups like the Victoria Horse Alliance and the Animal Protection Party of Canada — which shares many members with the Animal Alliance — gathered tens of thousands of signatures and pushed for a complete phase-out or ban.

A horse-drawn carriage is seen in Victoria on March 24, 2016. Victoria councillors at the time considered tightening city regulations governing horse-drawn carriage tours as part of proposed wholesale changes to its animal control bylaw. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

In May 2019, councillors weighed phase-out proposals and carriage operators threatened legal action against the city. Victoria's council ultimately struck down a motion to ban the horse-drawn carriage industry by a six-to-two vote in March 2020, allowing the operations to continue.

Protests continued, but Donna Friedlander, the owner and operator of Tally-Ho Carriage Tours, decried animal activists in The Times Colonist newspaper for harassing her employees.

She said protesters filmed her staff throughout their work day and surrounded them as they set out on tours, " hurtling unrelenting verbal assaults at my staff who are horse professionals, working tirelessly out of love to ensure the safety, health and happiness of the carriage horses," Friedlander wrote.

Colleen Mycroft, a spokesperson for the City of Victoria, recalled the issue being a "hot-button topic," with some of the protests taking place outside city hall.

"There were motions from councillors. There was pleading from those that were supporting the businesses. And then there were folks that thought it was cruelty to the horses … but nothing came of it," Mycroft said.

Changing practices ahead of city legislation

Two horse-drawn carriage tour companies continue to operate in Quebec City, where the 400-year-old buildings in the old quarters draw tourists from around the world.

One of them, Calèches Québec, notes in a voice message on its phone line that since 2025 it no longer offers last-minute or day-of tours, in the best interest of its horses.

The company did not immediately reply to CBC's request for more information.

A horse-drawn carriage carries people on the Plains of Abraham as part of Quebec City's winter carnival on Feb. 4, 2010. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

In Vancouver, park board staff considered removing "animal-powered transportation" in 2025 from Stanley Park, where it is permitted. But, according to a statement from the board to CBC, "a review of recent Park Board records did not identify any motions from recent years seeking to end horse-drawn carriage tours in Stanley Park."

Whether the New York ban will convince these Canadian cities to rein in the horse carriages remains to be seen. Until then, the push and pull of those for and against this storied tradition is bound — just like time and the tides — to carry on.

World.title: Air Canada blamed maintenance issues to deny compensation. Records show it wanted planes for other routes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Air Canada denied Juan Rojas compensation for a cancelled flight after it swapped the aircraft assigned to his flight with one that needed safety-related maintenance.

The Gatineau man challenged the airline through the Canadian Transportation Agency and won — and the evidence raises questions about the information Air Canada provided to justify denying him compensation.

"I felt like they were trying to cheat the system," Rojas told Go Public.

Under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations, passengers can be entitled to up to $1,000 for delayed flights, but only if the delay is within the airline's control and not required for safety.

Rojas's case is not the only one raising questions about airlines' use of the safety exemption.

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

Go Public has uncovered three other instances in which Air Canada told passengers their flights were cancelled because of safety-related maintenance while flight records show the aircraft they were scheduled to fly on were subsequently used on other routes. In all three cases, Air Canada maintains it does not owe compensation.

What is the maintenance 'loophole'?

The maintenance "loophole" is a simple way for airlines to potentially deny compensation for countless passengers every year, said Montreal lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille.

"It's a huge duffel bag in which they can put anything and everything," said De Bellefeuille, director of legal services for Option consommateurs, a Montreal non-profit that advocates for consumer rights.

"Most passengers do not have enough information to counter whatever is said by the airline."

WATCH | How a 'maintenance loophole' is costing air travellers | Go Public: How a 'maintenance loophole' is costing air passengers compensation | Go Public | Duration closed caption 2:11 Air Canada has been accused of using a safety maintenance 'loophole' to deny compensation for cancelled flights. Advocates are urging the government to adopt regulations from other countries that prevent airlines from citing safety maintenance to avoid payouts.

Air Canada declined Go Public's request for an interview.

But in a written statement, it acknowledged that in all four cases, it made a commercial decision: reassigning a functioning aircraft to another route where the scheduled plane required safety-related maintenance, leaving passengers on the original route without their scheduled flight.

Air Canada argued that an aircraft's schedule is fluid, and it must be able to make "operational adjustments" to "minimize the overall impact on passengers." The airline said it was within its rights to deny compensation.

Gabor Lukacs, founder of Air Passenger Rights, strongly disputes that interpretation. He points to a 2022 CTA decision, which said mechanical issues must be "a direct cause" of a cancelled flight and cannot be considered a "knock-on effect."

"I am finding it stunning that Air Canada continues to pretend as if the law has not been settled," said Lukacs.

Air Canada 'misrepresents' info to federal regulator

When Rojas's September 2022 flight to Bogotá from Montreal was cancelled, Air Canada denied his request for compensation, citing safety-related maintenance.

When Rojas challenged the airline before the Canadian Transportation Agency, Air Canada submitted documents claiming a catering truck had struck his plane, damaging it.

A complaints resolution officer with the CTA found that Air Canada's claim it cancelled a flight due to safety issues was unfounded and ordered the airline to pay $1,000 in compensation. (CBC)

It wasn't until a friend suggested he check the public Civil Aviation Daily Reporting System , that he realized the Air Canada plane struck by a catering truck was not the same one assigned to Rojas's cancelled flight.

In other words, the incident Air Canada cited to justify denying Rojas compensation involved a different aircraft.

It's "outrageous," said De Bellefeuille, the lawyer.

"They were clearly misrepresenting the information," said Rojas, who submitted his discovery to the CTA.

Air Canada told Go Public Rojas's aircraft was moved to cover for the one that had been damaged.

This past January, a complaint resolution officer ruled in the case, ordering Air Canada to pay Rojas $1,000 for the "inconvenience."

"The decision to swap aircraft to avoid or minimize delays for one group of passengers at the expense of another is a commercial decision," the officer wrote. The airline could make that decision, per the ruling, but it was required to compensate affected passengers.

'A real black mark on Air Canada'

Michael Bociurkiw was flying from Bangkok to Vancouver last February when he received an email from Air Canada mid-flight. His connecting flight from Vancouver to Newark had been cancelled because of safety-related maintenance, the airline said.

But the plane with supposed safety concerns had the exact registration number of the very aircraft Bociurkiw was seated on.

"I wasn't too concerned about a safety issue," said Bociurkiw. "I was more concerned about what the hell is going on? And why is Air Canada giving me this story?"

Michael Bociurkiw had his flight cancelled for safety-related maintenance. He found out the plane assigned to his flight was perfectly fine, but the airline needed it for another flight. (Submitted by Michael Bociurkiw)

Go Public found two more cases in which Air Canada cited safety-related maintenance to deny passengers compensation, while flight records showed the aircraft originally assigned to their flights were perfectly fine and used on other routes.

Carlos Fernandez accuses Air Canada of "blatantly lying" after his May flight from Las Vegas to Toronto was cancelled 10 minutes after his aircraft was swapped for one needing safety-related maintenance. Alison Monaghan's July flight from Toronto to Vancouver was similarly impacted.

"It's a real black mark on Air Canada as far as ethics and integrity go," said Monaghan.

Alison Monaghan's flight to Vancouver was cancelled after Air Canada used the plane to replace an aircraft on a different route that had developed maintenance issues. (Submitted by Alison Monaghan)

How often does this happen?

Go Public has previously reported on WestJet using the safety-related maintenance exemption to deny passengers compensation. But the full extent of the practice among Canada's two largest airlines remains unclear.

The CTA, which launched an investigation in the WestJet cases, does not publish its decisions on air passenger disputes — despite a recent court order requiring them to be made public. The agency declined Go Public's request for past decisions.

A CTA spokesperson cited privacy concerns and said the agency planned to begin publishing decisions early next year, once those had been addressed.

But Lukacs said airlines have little financial incentive to comply with passenger protection rules if they face no meaningful consequences for violating them.

"Right now, it is just more economical for an airline to deceive passengers than to actually comply with the law."

The CTA said no fine has been issued in Rojas's case, nor has it ever issued a penalty against Air Canada "for incorrectly characterizing a flight cancellation as safety-related maintenance."

It should have issued a "hefty" fine in Rojas's case, Lukacs said, "because Air Canada was not only mistreating the passenger, it was also maintaining the same fraudulent falsehood even when it came before a decision-maker."

Feds need to do more to protect air passengers, advocates say

De Bellefeuille says Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations need to change so passengers are not left to rely on airlines' own explanations when flights are cancelled or delayed.

"It's really David against Goliath," said the Montreal lawyer and consumer advocate.

Lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille says Ottawa should close a maintenance 'loophole' airlines use to deny paying compensation for delayed or cancelled flights. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

In the European Union , airlines can only avoid paying compensation for a qualifying disruption caused by a mechanical problem in limited situations, such as extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided, such as an act of terrorism.

But Lukacs – who has also called for an overhaul of air passenger protections – said the government has shown little appetite for reform.

Documents obtained by Go Public through an Access to Information request show previous transport ministers telling the CTA to maintain the airlines' ability to deny compensation for safety-related maintenance.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon declined an interview request.

Rojas says he's angry that the current rules can leave air passengers in the dark when airlines cite mechanical problems to deny compensation. He's now been compensated, but wonders about the other people who were booked for the same flight?

"The least the government can do is ensure that our rights are protected."

World.title: The 2 crises haunting the Bank of Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story is part of Mind Your Business, a weekly analysis of the biggest business stories emailed to subscribers on Monday mornings. If you haven't subscribed yet, you can do that by clicking here.

The Canadian economy is facing two very distinct problems right now.

On the one hand, inflation is high and rising. So far, at least, price increases have been contained to energy. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent last month, but core measures (which strip out more volatile components) remained subdued.

But as we saw in the U.S., the containment doesn't hold forever — and once price increases spill over into other sectors, it can be tough to rein them back in.

On the other hand, the economy is weak. And we haven't even really started to get a measure of the impact of the latest tranche of tariffs.

Those two duelling crises pose a difficult riddle for the Bank of Canada.

Weak growth would usually prompt the central bank to cut interest rates to spur some economic growth. But rising inflation makes the bank want to raise rates to slow the economy and keep prices from increasing too quickly.

Two problems — with two solutions in complete contradiction to one another.

WATCH | Bank has held interest rates 7 times in a row: 'We have to be realistic' about Canada-U.S. situation, Bank of Canada governor says | Duration closed caption 1:52 Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says while he hopes for a return to a 'more normal' Canada-U.S. relationship, he doesn't anticipate getting back to 'where we were' when dealing with an American administration that favours tariffs and protectionism.

One by one, most of the major economic outfits in the country have switched their forecasts. Most now believe that on Wednesday the Bank of Canada will increase its key overnight lending rate.

They all lay out the economics of the matter, but as Frances Donald and Nathan Janzen from RBC Economics remind us, the bank is seeing this year's surge in inflation through the prism of the last surge — the pandemic shock of 2022 to 2023.

"The cautionary lessons of the post-pandemic inflation surge ... demonstrated how supply-side shocks and persistent cost pressures can overwhelm an economy surprisingly quickly," wrote Donald and Janzen in a note to clients last week.

So, most economists now believe the bank will increase rates, even though they don't all feel the bank should make such a move.

Donald and Janzen say a quarter-point increase won't materially move the needle on where they think the economy is headed. (They had, after all, built their forecast on the assumption that rates were going to rise next year.)

"Ultimately, the signal of a rate hike on Oct. 28 has a larger meaning we shouldn’t ignore: Central banks do not have the same patience for inflation they might have had in the past, and are willing to act pre-emptively to guard against it," they wrote.

If we could wave a magic wand, we would probably like the economic data this week to come in opposite order. We have the interest rate decision on Wednesday and GDP numbers on Friday.

GDP stalled in July (zero per cent growth) and the economy is expected to have grown by 0.1 per cent in August. But new tariffs kicked in that month, so the risks to the forecast remain firmly planted on the downside.

Uncertainty is the new ... everything.

The Canadian economy and the Canadian consumer have both proven themselves to be far more resilient than expected. But each new obstacle takes a fresh swipe out of the Canada's potential growth.

On the upside, we will also get an update on the Bank of Canada's forecasts this week. The Monetary Policy Report is the central bank's deep dive into where it sees the economy headed.

World.title: U.S. officials accuse Canada of midterm meddling — but Trump has endorsed foreign candidates
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite U.S. officials repeatedly warning Canada not to get involved in the upcoming U.S. midterms, President Donald Trump has his own track record of weighing in on foreign elections.

Trump has endorsed about half a dozen candidates across the globe since he returned to the White House in early 2025 and even boasted earlier this year that he has "a very good record of endorsing candidates within the United States," before touting a number of foreign candidates he backed.

"I'm not supposed to be endorsing people," Trump said during the February inaugural meeting of his Board of Peace. "As long as it works, it's OK with me."

Since early 2025, Trump has backed presidential or prime ministerial candidates in Poland, Honduras, Colombia and Japan.

Most recently, he voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing an election on Tuesday.

The U.S. president also put his support behind former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán's failed re-election bid, which included Vice-President JD Vance appearing at a rally in Budapest.

Trump also weighed in to last year's midterms in Argentina, suggesting that a financial support package would hinge on a good result for President Javier Milei's party.

WATCH | The Power Panel on U.S. meddling claims: U.S. election meddling fears just 'distraction politics': ex-AG | Duration closed caption 18:48 Global Affairs Canada instructed Canadian diplomats in the U.S. on Tuesday to avoid meeting with, attending events with or appearing in photos or promotional materials alongside U.S. midterm election candidates. The memo came after U.S. President Donald Trump accused Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections. The Power Panel stops by Power & Politics to unpack the election interference concerns.

Daniel Drezner, a professor of international politics at Tufts University in Massachusetts, said U.S. officials suggesting Canada is interfering in the midterms is a situation of the "pot calling the kettle black," given Trump's track record.

"The truth is that this administration has had a long track record of intervening directly into the elections of official allies," he told CBC News in an interview.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" on Wednesday pointing to instances that could amount to "potential interference in U.S. elections" after Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian politicians dismissed previous suggestions that Canadian officials are trying to influence the vote outcome on Nov. 3.

WATCH | 'No merit' to U.S. claims, Carney says: 'No merit' to suggestion Canadian politicians interfering in U.S. election, Carney says | Duration closed caption 3:37 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from Istanbul on Friday, says there are deep diplomatic ties between Canada and the U.S., and engagement happens no matter the timing, including during elections. 'We have no intention to interfere' with their democratic processes, Carney said.

The embassy's release pointed to Liberal MP Anthony Housefather canvassing for a Florida Democrat, whom he's said is a friend, during a primary vote earlier this year and comments made by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly regarding Canada's counter-tariff strategy, some going back to March 2025 when she was in charge of foreign affairs.

The embassy's list also included the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Reagan ad that ran in the U.S. last year and a federal government billboard campaign from early 2025.

In an exclusive interview with Rosemary Barton Live, former U.S. ambassador to Canada James Blanchard said the administration has "no credibility" given Trump's list of public endorsements.

"If this accusation had come from the Reagan administration or the Bush administration or the Obama administration, the Clinton administration, I would take it seriously," Blanchard said. "But I can't from this current administration."

Embassy declines to comment

CBC News reached out to the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa and pointed out Trump's track record of endorsing foreign candidates. The embassy declined to comment when asked if a Canadian official offering a similar endorsement to a midterm candidate would amount to potential election interference.

Trump also jumped into the Canadian political fray during the 2025 campaign, writing on social media that he'd "rather deal with a liberal than a conservative."

The current president is not the only notable U.S. politician to talk Canadian electoral politics during a campaign. Former president Barack Obama publicly endorsed former prime minister Justin Trudeau in 2019 and 2021, albeit after he had left the White House. Sen. Bernie Sanders also backed former NDP leader Jagmeet Singh in the 2021 campaign.

Drezner said those examples are different from Trump's endorsements because neither were a part of the executive branch at the time. He pointed out that typically it's the norm for heads of states or heads of government not to weigh in on foreign elections.

"The idea was that surely you can do business with whoever wins and you might have to do business with whichever party wins. So therefore you shouldn't be seen as campaigning overtly for one side or another," he said.

Trump officials also appeared to take an interest in the recent Alberta referendum. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in January that Alberta would make a "natural partner" for the U.S. while discussing the possibility of a separation referendum.

WATCH | Canadian diplomats told to be cautious during midterms: Canadian diplomats told to avoid appearances with U.S. midterm candidates | Duration closed caption 2:04 Global Affairs Canada has advised Canadian diplomats in the U.S. to be careful on social media and to avoid appearances with midterm candidates as American warnings about election interference ramp up.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

The U.S. Embassy's list came after Ambassador Pete Hoekstra and Trump adviser Peter Navarro warned against Canada getting involved in the midterms.

Carney and other government officials have pushed back on the suggestion that Canada is looking to interfere.

"There is no merit to these claims, so I'll call it out that way," Carney told reporters during a news conference in Istanbul on Friday.

"I'm disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions," the prime minister said of Hoekstra in particular.

WATCH | Joly denies U.S. election interference claims: Joly denies U.S. election interference claims by Trump administration | Duration 0:54 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters on Thursday that she regularly meets with both Democratic and Republican politicians, after the Trump administration accused her of planning to 'influence American politics.'

While Drezner said Housefather's canvassing for a candidate might be "slightly unusual," other instances the embassy mentioned — like Joly and Bernadette Jordan, Canada's consul general in Boston, meeting with American politicians — amounts to "garden variety diplomacy."

Joly herself has pushed back against the accusations saying she has met with Republicans and Democrats in recent months.

The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates in border states like Michigan and Maine.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997 and has tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs, said Friday that she "secured" some exemptions to those levies.

"I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner," she said in a social media post.

WATCH | Trade war a major issue in midterms: Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:18 The Canada-U.S. trade war is solidifying itself as a major ballot-box issue in pivotal states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.

Drezner said he could "easily see" a situation where the Trump administration blames bad midterm results on Canada.

"They're going to blame anyone and everyone. That is the modus operandi of this White House," he said.

When asked on Friday if the Trump administration might blame Canada for a poor midterm result and slap more tariffs on Canadian exports, the prime minister said he doesn't "see that coming to pass."

World.title: Gamers, developers praise BioWare's envelope-pushing games following 'heartbreaking' closure
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

To video game players, developers and industry watchers, the sudden closure of Edmonton-based BioWare came as a shock but not necessarily a surprise.

"I knew BioWare wasn't long for this world, so I had already done my mourning for that studio. And so when this news came down, I was like, yep, that's pretty much what I expected," said Ash Parrish, a writer for the gaming news site Kotaku. "This sucks super hard."

The studio, founded in Edmonton in 1995 by three doctors and acquired by U.S.-based games publisher Electronic Arts in 2007, was shuttered as part of company-wide layoffs on Wednesday.

Its developers specialized in role-playing games with a heavy emphasis on storytelling and player agency, including Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age and Mass Effect.

"Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this news, along with their families and colleagues. Canada’s video game industry is home to an exceptional depth of talent and creativity, and the contributions of the people who built BioWare will remain an important part of our industry’s story," said Paul Fogolin, president of the Entertainment Software Association of Canada, in a statement.

Gamers, developers and critics lamented the news online, with many crediting its works for kickstarting their own careers in the games industry. They also noted that while BioWare may be no more, its impact on video games will continue into the future.

Financial pressures after Saudi buyout

The recent fortunes of EA made BioWare's closure less shocking. BioWare's staff was slashed from about 200 to less than half that in 2025, after Dragon Age: The Veilguard failed to meet internal sales expectations.

Earlier this year, Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund and a private equity firm owned by U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner finalized a $55-billion US buyout of EA. It included $20 billion borrowed from U.S. bank JPMorgan, which now hangs over EA as leveraged debt.

Alyssa Mercante, a digital trends writer for Digiday and a former games journalist, said EA likely thought it was more important to maintain its "biggest moneymakers," like sports games and online multiplayer shooters with live service elements, than the titles with a "lengthy development cycle" and the deep role-playing games (RPGs) that BioWare is known for.

WATCH | BioWare co-founder Trent Oster on company's closure: The Edmonton-based video game company BioWare is being shut down | Duration closed caption 2:42 Edmonton-based gaming company BioWare is shutting its doors for good. Its owner Electronic Arts, said the company is shifting its focus to developing larger shooters and action-adventure titles moving forward. That news meant EA's shutting down BioWare and stopping its early development for the next Mass Effect title — one of the company's biggest video games. BioWare has been around for more than 30 years and has made many games considered staples in the video game world. Trent Oster is one of the companies original co-founders and is now the CEO of the gaming company Beamdog.

Live service games offer additional content, which can sometimes include randomized trading card-like content packs, that costs more money or subscriptions on top of the initial retail price. EA credited live service games like Battlefield 6 and the soccer franchise EA Sports FC for reaching live service revenues of $1.47 billion US in the previous quarter.

RPGs like Dragon Age or Mass Effect, meanwhile, are sold like a single book or movie, with few avenues for additional monetized content.

Groundbreaking narrative, diverse stories and characters

BioWare's games have long been celebrated for featuring characters of diverse gender identities and backgrounds. For example, players can choose whether the main character Shepard in Mass Effect or Hawke in Dragon Age is male or female. Some games also have optional same-sex romantic storylines between main characters and narratives featuring transgender characters.

Gaming writer Parrish credits Dragon Age: Origins (2009) for pulling her out of an emotionally difficult time in her life.

"I'm like, let me try it and see, you know, if this sparks joy. And it did," she said. "It just rewrote my brain chemistry in ways that I'm still experiencing ... to this day."

A promotional screenshot from Dragon Age: The Veilguard. (BioWare/Electronic Arts)

She credits it for inspiring her to become a games journalist and Dragon Age fan communities online for connecting her with lifelong friends who would go on to attend her wedding years later.

Mercante had a similar journey when she first played Dragon Age's sci-fi sister series Mass Effect.

"It had wrapped itself around my core personality and kind of stayed there for a while in my teens, early 20s," she said.

Voice actor Jennifer Hale is photographed in her studio on Vancouver Island, B.C., in 2024. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

Players at the outset chose whether to play as a male Shephard, voiced by Mark Meer, or "FemShep" (as she's known by fans), played by Vancouver Island-based Jennifer Hale.

"Being FemShep means an enormous amount to me," said Hale, who called it "an extraordinary privilege" to play a main character whose female version was treated on an equal footing as her male counterpart.

"That means the world to me. I love me some kicking down barriers."

Natalie Checo, a Vancouver-based video game designer originally from the U.S., says she connected particularly with the genetically enhanced operative Miranda Lawson in Mass Effect 2.

"What resonated for me was the story about a woman who is biologically engineered to be perfect, and yet she still can't really attain that, because being perfect is a human impossibility," she said. "I think women grow up in a society that pushes us to be as perfect as possible."

Checo says that many of her game developer friends are from marginalized communities, and BioWare's games "pushed us to dream more than our real world has allowed us to feel like we can."

Ongoing legacy

Osama Dorias, a Montreal-based developer at HeartLoop Games, says BioWare's games taught him important lessons when working on narrative-based games of his own.

"I played Mass Effect 1, and I was really surprised by the level of agency that they were able to give the protagonist Shepard, and how the characters still had their own personality," he said.

Varric the dwarf and Solas the elf are seen in Dragon Age: Inquisition. (BioWare/Electronic Arts)

Dorias, Mercante and others pointed to successful RPGs by other studios that have carried on that format, including CD Projekt Red's The Witcher series and Baldur's Gate 3, a direct sequel to BioWare's games of the same name made by Belgian studio Larian.

Dorias calls BioWare's closing "heartbreaking," estimating that at its peak, the company may have employed half of all full-time employees in Edmonton's games industry.

He noted that several independent studios have formed over the years from former BioWare developers, building games that may stray significantly from its role-playing game blueprint but still have "the same really strong character development and storytelling."

"I can't understate how influential those franchises from BioWare were to the industry at large. It really, really had a big impact."

Hale hopes Bioware's IPs will live on

In the days after BioWare's closure, a trailer for the now-cancelled Mass Effect game was leaked online, reportedly by a former BioWare employee.

An image from a reportedly leaked trailer for an upcoming Mass Effect game from BioWare. The studio was closed down by its parent company Electronic Arts on Oct. 21 and the game was cancelled mid-development. (Dejahvoe Ivoe/YouTube)

After watching the trailer for the first time, Hale called it "gorgeous," and said she holds out hope that if EA has no plans for one of its other studios complete the game, that it might sell the IP and let another team finish the work.

"I think the fans would be overjoyed if that IP found a place to live that was just some small, little maverick place.... They would engender a great deal of good will," she said.

"So let that thing go, and let us, the community, play and let us do beautiful things with this story that is still wanting to be told."

World.title: Toronto’s mayoral campaign is ending in a tight race. Here's how it got so close
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s the end of a Toronto mayoral campaign that arguably started when the byelection ended three years ago.

On Monday voters will select their mayor and council for the next term, with polls suggesting either Brad Bradford or Olivia Chow will lead the city.

Voting opens at 10 a.m. across Toronto and will close at 8 p.m. School board trustees are also on the ballot.

The challenger’s primary

When former mayor John Tory resigned in 2023, both Chow and Bradford ran to replace him.

In that election, Chow pulled 37 per cent of the vote, while Bradford came away with one per cent.

Not to be deterred, Bradford announced in October 2025 he would run again, offering an opposition voice to Chow’s three-plus years as mayor.

Political strategist and Bradford supporter Bob Richardson said the decision to announce early was key to raising his support.

“It was very smart to do that and I think it was smart to be steadfast about it,” he said.

WATCH | Mayoral challenger Brad Bradford joined Metro Morning to make his pitch to voters in the final week of the campign: Brad Bradford's pitch for Toronto: Property tax freeze, safer streets | Duration closed caption 19:07 Brad Bradford is making his pitch to be Toronto’s next mayor, centring his platform on property tax relief and public safety. The mayoral candidate joined Chris Glover on CBC's Metro Morning days ahead of the vote. We will be speaking with incumbent Olivia Chow on Friday, October 23.

His early declaration may also have deterred other candidates.

Through the spring a number of potential challengers — including Premier Doug Ford’s nephew, Michael, and former finance minister Rod Phillips — all ruled themselves out of running.

After mulling a campaign of his own, Tory also announced he wouldn’t launch a bid to return.

That, Richardson said, allowed Bradford to "effectively set himself up as the standard bearer for the moderate centrist crowd.”

Safety, affordability dominate

Chow didn’t confirm she would run for re-election until May, officially launching her campaign in September. By the time she did, Bradford was well-established as her main rival in a race that focused increasingly on safety and affordability.

Public safety, in particular, took a front seat as two contradictory issues emerged. Statistically, Toronto is safer than it was when Chow took office, but polling shows residents think safety is actually worsening.

“Both are true,” Clayton Campbell, the president of the Toronto Police Association, said.

His organization hasn’t endorsed either candidate, but heaped praise on Chow’s public safety plan, while questioning the logic of Bradford’s proposals.

“Over the last three years, you're seeing those crimes start to head in the right direction,” he added. “But statistics say one thing, people can [still] feel unsafe.”

Erin Morrison, a political strategist and Chow supporter, suggested the Bradford campaign has also exaggerated the problem.

“He talks as if you can't open your door and walk out onto your sidewalk in any neighborhood in this city, in any ward of this city without being shot at,” she said.

WATCH | Mayoral incumbent Olivia Chow made her pitch to voters on Metro Morning in the final week of the campaign: 'The cost of living is a problem': Olivia Chow's pitch to Toronto (in her own words) | Duration closed caption 18:37 Olivia Chow is making her pitch to stay in office, anchoring her platform on affordable housing and a city-wide lunch program. Speaking on CBC Radio's Metro Morning with Chris Glover, the incumbent detailed her vision for a second term — following our interview earlier this week with candidate Brad Bradford

If you want to dig into the public safety question, we’ve covered the disconnect between how people feel and what the statistics say.

CBC Toronto’s Olivia Piercey has also examined both candidates’ police plans.

New promises roll out

Bradford rolled out a number of high-profile policies on affordability as election day approached.

The challenger vowed to cut the land transfer tax, pledged a one-year property tax freeze (the Chow campaign argues that promise is misleading) and to replace sections of track on the Toronto subway.

He also promised he would not cut services, while doing a line-by-line audit of finances at city hall.

Polls suggest Brad Bradford (right) or Olivia Chow will be Toronto's next mayor. Both contested the 2023 byelection to replace John Tory, with Chow winning and Bradford only winning one per cent of the vote. (CBC)

Myer Siemiatycki, professor emeritus in politics at Toronto Metropolitan University, said Bradford followed a well-trodden path through the campaign — one that may be easier to promise than to deliver.

“I think Coun. Bradford has focused on what in many ways are the tried and true formula for getting yourself elected: promise lower lower taxes and better service,” he said. “Now, how you square that is a real challenge.”

Chow has said she will introduce a fare cap on the TTC, with customers only paying for their first 10 rides of the week. She’s also pledged to introduce free school lunches and help independent grocery stores, along with support for renters.

Morrison said the incumbent is right to have run on her record, complimented by retail politics promises.

“She's been challenged to present herself also as somebody who's pragmatic, who's cautious with taxpayer dollars,” she explained.

“When you look at programs like school food … she's talking about it in terms of a money-saving program that puts $900 in the pockets of Toronto families every year.”

Tightening polls, high advance voter turnout

In the final weeks of the race, polls narrowed.

A Liaison Strategies poll in February (before Tory ruled himself out of the race) had Bradford at 18 per cent and Chow at 40. A study from the polling firm released last Wednesday, put Bradford at 49 per cent, Chow at 47.

The Liaison study was conducted using interactive voice response. It surveyed 1,000 city residents between Oct. 18 and 19, with a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. You can read about that poll here.

“There's no question [Bradford’s] made progress,” Richardson said. “He's made progress in the parts of the city where he has to — in Etobicoke, in North York.”

WATCH | If you're just tuning into the Toronto mayoral race, here's a look at the campaign, the two leading candidates and their key promises: What to know about Toronto’s mayoral race ahead of Monday’s vote | Duration closed caption 2:47 Toronto’s mayoral race is tightening ahead of Monday’s election, with recent polls showing candidates Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford in close contest. CBC’s Isaac Callan looks at what the candidates are promising voters.

Morrison disagrees, arguing the Chow campaign is succeeding in getting her message across at a pivotal time.

“In a good campaign, you find your way back to your message in the closing 10 days or so — and that's what I'm seeing from the Chow campaign,” she said.

Siemiatycki thinks a nail-biting end to the race was always inevitable.

“I'm not sure that it's been blunder versus a strong performance playing out here,” he said. “I think it's more sort of the ebb and flow of timing.”

If you haven’t voted yet, you can consult the CBC’s promise tracker to see where Bradford and Chow stand on a range of key issues. Remember, there are 50-plus other candidates also running for mayor, you can see the full list here .

World.title: What authors of the Alberta ‘firewall’ letter think of Smith’s referendum: Full Comment podcast
World.content:
Article content

Twenty-five years ago they rewired the province’s political thinking with their landmark “Alberta Agenda,” a.k.a, the “firewall” letter: a manifesto for the premier to assert sovereignty within a systemically inequitable federation. Days after Alberta’s referendum on some of the same issues they raised — but also going drastically further in considering separation — Brian Lilley speaks with letter-writers Ted Morton, who went on to become a provincial cabinet minister, and Ken Boessenkool, now a strategist and lobbyist. With voting results showing a hard no to separation and more narrow losses on questions of greater provincial powers in justice, social services and regulation, they discuss whether Premier Danielle Smith’s tactic helped the cause of a more assertive Alberta, or set it back.
