World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election
World.content:
A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:39 UTC Full article

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques said

The president of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Federal Court by former president Jair Bolsonaro in 2020, said on Monday that the extension of voting hours did not change the result of the runoff won by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president’s son, had cited the extension in refusing to recognise his defeat and calling for the election to be annulled.

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques told a press conference.

On Sunday night, Bolsonaro called it “unacceptable” that Supreme Court Judge Cristiano Zanin, whom he called “Lula’s lawyer” for having defended him in the Lava Jato cases, ordered at 5.01 p.m., when polls were due to close, an extension of voting until 7 p.m. “There is a lot to clarify before Brazil recognises this outrage that has just happened,” he said. “I will never know how many votes I could have had.”

Zanin ordered the extension at the request of Lula’s coalition, which reported a lack of buses to carry voters in cities such as Salvador and São Paulo. Bolsonaro’s campaign, for its part, had asked the electoral courts to extend voting in municipalities affected by rain, flooding and power cuts in states such as Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul. The measure applied only to polling stations still open; those that had closed at 5 p.m. did not reopen and followed the usual counting procedure.

Lula won with 51.78% of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.22%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes. There is no record yet of the senator’s campaign having filed a formal challenge.

World.title: Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term
World.content:
Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:29 UTC Full article

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will begin his fourth term as Brazil’s president on January 1 with an economy that has grown more than expected and record-low unemployment, but with fiscal imbalances that markets punished heavily on Monday, the first trading day after his re-election. The dollar rose more than 12% at one point to 5.60 reais, the Ibovespa index triggered an automatic trading halt at the open and long-term interest rates jumped almost two points.

The reaction reflects investors’ bets on a victory by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who promised sharp spending cuts. On Friday, the dollar had closed at 4.99 reais and the Ibovespa at 205,082 points, close to the record it reached after the first round. Analysts agree that the president’s first test will be the make-up of his economic team and his fiscal framework. These are the five main challenges he faces.

Debt

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending, which leaves less than 8% of the federal budget for adjustable items. Lula has at times played down concerns over debt, arguing that stronger growth will solve the problem. His team has pledged to keep the current fiscal rules, which cap spending growth and set primary surplus targets, but meeting them will be harder given the commitment to raise the minimum wage above inflation, which also increases pension costs, and the new benefits announced during the campaign.

Inflation and interest rates

The Central Bank has cut the Selic rate five times in a row to 13.75%, but annual inflation exceeded the 4.5% tolerance ceiling in September, against a 3% target. The Monetary Policy Committee meets on November 4, and the real’s depreciation complicates further cuts. Lula proposes lowering rates through greater fiscal discipline without touching social programmes, while most economists argue a faster decline would require spending cuts.

Household debt

According to credit agency Serasa, nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million companies are behind on payments, a record attributed to high interest rates. The government is preparing new relief measures, such as buying distressed mortgages from banks at a discount and forgiving tax debts for small business owners, which analysts see as temporary relief.

A hostile Congress

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party will hold the largest bloc in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, in the most conservative Congress since the return to democracy. That will hamper the government’s plans to cut tax exemptions and the approval of appointments to the Central Bank, regulators and the Supreme Court, which were already difficult during the current term. Bolsonaro, moreover, does not recognise the result and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Tax reform

The new value-added tax, approved in 2023, takes effect in January, but the government has yet to set its effective rate, which independent analysts put at around 28%. The government also postponed during the campaign a bill for a selective tax on products harmful to health or the environment, such as tobacco and alcohol.

World.title: Trump insults Norway and rejects its immigrants for not giving him the Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
Trump insults Norway and rejects its immigrants for not giving him the Nobel Peace Prize

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:24 UTC Full article

Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize

US President Donald Trump lashed out at Norway at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, saying Norwegian immigrants are not welcome in the United States because the Nobel Committee did not award him the Peace Prize. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide replied that the committee is independent.

“Frankly, Norway stinks. Norway has become a shithole country, in fact,” Trump said at a campaign event a week before the November 3 midterm elections. The president said he would welcome immigrants from certain countries but not from Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize. So I don’t want anybody from Norway.”

“He knows very well that the Nobel Committee is independent. We have reminded him of that, in case anyone had any doubts, and that remains the case,” Barth Eide told Norwegian public radio NRK on Monday.

Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize. This year the Nobel Committee awarded it to South African jurist Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, a decision Trump called “shameful and embarrassing”. Last year, when the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, he also expressed anger at not being recognised. In 2018, during his first term, he was heavily criticised for using similar language about Haiti and several African countries.

World.title: Trump questions Lula’s victory as most of the region, including the right, congratulates him
World.content:
Trump questions Lula’s victory as most of the region, including the right, congratulates him

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:16 UTC Full article

“They just applied the Biden playbook in Brazil. Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite. But communists don’t give up power once they get it,” Trump said

US President Donald Trump cast doubt on Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election in Brazil and compared it with the 2020 US election, while most Latin American governments, including several right-wing allies of Washington, congratulated the Brazilian president. In Argentina, President Javier Milei remained silent.

“They just applied the Joe Biden playbook in Brazil. Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite to win the second. But communists don’t give up power once they get it,” Trump said, according to the EFE news agency, without offering evidence of irregularities. Trump has never acknowledged his defeat by Biden in 2020. The White House has not formally commented on the result, which Senator Flávio Bolsonaro also refuses to recognise and has said he will seek to annul.

One of the first to congratulate Lula was Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi: “I have just spoken with Brazil’s president-elect, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a friend. I congratulated him on his victory and on the democratic celebration that an electoral process represents.” Governments of the opposite ideological stripe also did so. Chile’s José Antonio Kast, an ally of the Bolsonaros, said the two countries “have a lot of future in common”; Paraguay’s Santiago Peña hailed “this great democratic day”; and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz noted that Bolivia and Brazil are “neighbouring and brotherly countries”. Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa called for working together against “common enemies”, and Panama’s José Raúl Mulino pledged to keep “working together”. Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.”

In Argentina, Milei, who backed Bolsonaro during the campaign and even accused Lula of seeking to “steal” the election, had issued no congratulations. The Peronist opposition, by contrast, celebrated. Former president Cristina Kirchner spoke of “a genuine electoral 17 October”, referring to Peronism’s founding date; Buenos Aires governor Axel Kicillof of “a historic night”; and former presidential candidate Sergio Massa wrote: “Today, as yesterday, on Lula’s side of life.”

Former Chilean president Gabriel Boric, who followed the vote in Brazil, thanked Lula “for never giving up the fight”. Congratulations from right-wing leaders such as Kast, Peña and Paz reflect the weight of Brazil, the region’s largest economy and the main trading partner of several of its neighbours. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 1.

World.title: Milei stays silent on Lula’s victory as Kast and Peña congratulate him
World.content:
Milei stays silent on Lula’s victory as Kast and Peña congratulate him

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:05 UTC Full article

Neither the president nor Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno had issued a statement on the result, according to the Argentine press

Argentine President Javier Milei had not congratulated Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on his re-election in Brazil by Monday, unlike other right-wing South American leaders such as Chile’s José Antonio Kast, Paraguay’s Santiago Peña and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz. Milei, who publicly backed Senator Flávio Bolsonaro during the campaign, met his cabinet at the Casa Rosada first thing in the morning.

Neither the president nor Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno had issued a statement on the result, according to the Argentine press. “We have to wait,” official sources said. During election night, Milei shared social media posts questioning the extension of voting hours in Brazil, and on Monday he shared a message against the “average leftie”. Bolsonaro does not recognise Lula’s victory and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Kast, for his part, said he had spoken with Lula: “I have just spoken with the President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and congratulated him on the election result.” The presidents of Mexico, Panama and Uruguay also congratulated the Brazilian leader, according to the newspaper La Nación.

Within the Argentine government, Bolsonaro’s defeat came as a surprise. “The rejection of Bolsonaro was very strong,” an official told the Noticias Argentinas news agency. At the Casa Rosada, the result is attributed to Lula’s latest economic measures, the shorter working week and the rejection the candidate generated among women and young people. A political figure who regularly visits government headquarters told Infobae the defeat weakens the idea of an international right-wing alliance that Milei had promoted. The Peronist opposition, by contrast, celebrated the re-election: Cristina Kirchner, Axel Kicillof and Sergio Massa linked it to Argentina’s 2027 elections.

Relations between the two presidents are strained. Milei repeatedly called Lula a “thief” and last week said he hoped he would not “steal” the election. In July, Brazil recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations after earlier insults from the Argentine president. Brazil is Argentina’s main trading partner, and the two countries are Mercosur’s largest economies.

World.title: Brazil’s real plunges more than 8% and São Paulo stocks slump after Lula’s victory
World.content:
Brazil’s real plunges more than 8% and São Paulo stocks slump after Lula’s victory

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:03 UTC Full article

The fall in Ibovespa futures hit the permitted limit shortly after the open and forced a temporary halt in trading, prompting the São Paulo stock exchange

Brazil’s real lost more than 8% against the dollar and futures on the Ibovespa index plunged 15% on Monday, in the first session after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in the election runoff, a result markets had not expected. The dollar opened up 8.64% at 5.42 reais.

The fall in Ibovespa futures hit the permitted limit shortly after the open and forced a temporary halt in trading, prompting the São Paulo stock exchange, B3, to widen the daily fluctuation band to 20%. Brazil’s Treasury also cancelled the debt auctions scheduled for October 27 to 29. Brazilian assets trading abroad had anticipated the move: the exchange-traded fund of Brazilian stocks in Tokyo fell as much as 15%, according to Bloomberg. According to El País, it is the real’s steepest decline since 1999.

The sell-off reflects investors’ bets on a victory by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after his first-round win, which on October 5 drove a 7.7% rise in the Ibovespa on expectations of greater fiscal discipline. “Markets were broadly positioned for a Bolsonaro victory,” said Eirini Tsekeridou, an analyst at Julius Baer. A Citibank survey of 73 fund managers showed 80% expected a fall of more than 5% if Lula won.

Analysts say attention will now turn to the stance of Bolsonaro, who does not recognise the result and has said he will seek to annul the election, Lula’s ability to build majorities in an opposition-dominated Congress and, above all, the make-up of his economic team. “Investors need a revised fiscal framework that generates primary surpluses sufficient to stabilise debt,” said Viktor Szabó of Aberdeen Investments. Brazil’s public debt exceeds 80% of GDP, and the ten-year bond yields around 6.5%, second in the region only to the 12% demanded on Argentine debt, according to the same analyst.

World.title: Lula wins Brazil’s presidency for a fourth time with 51.8% of the vote
World.content:
Lula wins Brazil’s presidency for a fourth time with 51.8% of the vote

26th Monday, October 2026 - 09:01 UTC Full article

Lula is the first candidate to win the presidency after coming second in the first round since Brazil returned to direct presidential elections in 1989

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Sunday’s presidential runoff with 51.78% of valid votes against 48.22% for Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with 99.97% of the vote counted. Lula, 80, will govern the country for a fourth time, from 2027 to 2030, after overturning his first-round deficit.

The Workers’ Party candidate won 64.2 million votes, some 4.4 million more than the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who received 59.8 million. The court declared Lula mathematically elected shortly after 9 p.m. Brasília time, following a count in which the president overtook his rival when about half the votes had been tallied and never lost the lead. In Brasília, Bolsonaro supporters gathered on the Esplanade of Ministries left in silence as the result became known.

Lula is the first candidate to win the presidency after coming second in the first round since Brazil returned to direct presidential elections in 1989, and the first Brazilian elected to the office four times. He governed from 2003 to 2010 and returned to power in 2023 after defeating Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election with 50.90% of the vote, a narrower margin than Sunday’s. He will be 85 at the end of this term and will not be able to run again.

The result defied the polls, which until the last day showed a statistical tie with a slight edge for the senator. The latest Datafolha poll gave each candidate 50% of valid votes. Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, had won the first round on October 4 with 47.03% of the vote, some 56.1 million, against Lula’s 45.16%, a result that also surprised pollsters.

After that setback, Lula’s campaign threw itself into mobilising the roughly 33 million voters who stayed away in the first round, with particular attention to those over 70 and 16- and 17-year-olds, for whom voting is optional. In the final stretch, the government raised the Bolsa Família social programme, received by 20 million families, by 15%, and Congress approved the 40-hour working week with two days off, one of the president’s flagship pledges. Lula also announced subsidies, fuel tax cuts and debt relief programmes which, according to calculations by the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, add up to almost 300 billion reais through 2027.

Bolsonaro, who received the backing of almost all right-wing and centre-right parties after the first round, focused his campaign on security, the cost of living and a promise to cut public spending while maintaining social programmes. He had pledged to pardon his father, sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after the 2022 election, and during the campaign committed to respecting the result.

Voting day was marked by the extension of polling hours in some areas, ordered by a judge at the request of Lula’s campaign over public transport problems, according to El País, a decision criticised by opposition figures. The campaign was also shaped by the legal dispute with Meta, which both candidates accused of unequal treatment on its platforms, and by the agreement both signed at the electoral court to mutually lift the secrecy of their bank, tax and phone records.

Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, will take office on January 1 alongside Vice President Geraldo Alckmin and will have to govern with a Congress in which the Liberal Party will hold the largest bloc in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, foreshadowing strong parliamentary opposition.

Regionally, the Brazilian president will govern alongside neighbours that have mostly aligned themselves with Donald Trump’s administration, such as Argentina, Chile, Paraguay and Bolivia. Argentine President Javier Milei backed Bolsonaro during the campaign, repeatedly insulted Lula and even accused him of seeking to “steal” the election, while Lula used Milei as an argument against his rival in both debates. Relations with Washington, marked by the tariffs Trump imposed on Brazilian goods, which Lula blamed on the Bolsonaro family, will be another major challenge of his new term. Former Colombian president Gustavo Petro was among the first to congratulate him.

World.title: Bolsonaro refuses to recognise Lula’s victory and says he will seek to annul the election
World.content:
Bolsonaro refuses to recognise Lula’s victory and says he will seek to annul the election

26th Monday, October 2026 - 04:26 UTC Full article

“It is impossible to recognise the result of the election in the context in which these things happened. We are going to ask for these elections to be annulled,” Bolsonaro said, taking no questions

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro announced on Sunday night that he does not recognise President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s presidential runoff and will seek to have it annulled, arguing that the extension of voting hours ordered by a Supreme Federal Court judge was irregular. Lula won with 51.78% of valid votes against 48.22%, a margin of some 4.4 million votes.

“It is impossible to recognise the result of the election in the context in which these things happened. We are going to ask for these elections to be annulled,” Bolsonaro said in Brasília at around 10.40 p.m., taking no questions. “I will not accept the rules of the game being changed in the middle of the game,” he added. The Liberal Party candidate described the decision as “a disgrace” and said it caused a “total breach of equality” between voters in different states. He also alleged that his party’s monitors had been removed from the vote-tallying room, without presenting evidence.

At 5.01 p.m., when polls were due to close, Supreme Court Judge Cristiano Zanin ordered voting extended until 7 p.m. nationwide at the request of Lula’s coalition, which reported a lack of buses to carry voters in cities such as São Paulo and Salvador. Zanin later clarified that the extension applied only where polling stations were still open and that votes from those already closed would be counted normally. It was the first time voting hours in a presidential election had been extended nationwide. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also asked the electoral courts to extend voting in municipalities in several states affected by rain.

Bolsonaro referred to Zanin as “Lula’s lawyer”: the judge defended the president in the Lava Jato cases before Lula appointed him to the Supreme Court. There is no record yet of the campaign having filed a formal challenge. According to the Brazilian press, Supreme Court President Edson Fachin called for respect for the election result and said the country needs peace.

In 2022, Jair Bolsonaro, the candidate’s father, also failed to publicly recognise his defeat by Lula, although he authorised the start of the transition. On January 8, 2023, a week after the inauguration, thousands of his supporters stormed the seats of the three branches of government in Brasília. The former president was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 1.

World.title: Mexico sends ultrarunners and a photo exhibit to El Salvador to promote Indigenous sporting culture
World.content:
A delegation of high-performance Mexican athletes will travel to El Salvador to participate in next month’s Cordillera Challenge, a 130-kilometer mountain race with over 6,300 meters of positive elevation gain.

The participation of the four runners is part of a government-sponsored agenda seeking to strengthen sporting and cultural ties between both countries.

María Lorena Ramírez Hernández, an Indigenous ultramarathon runner originally from the Sierra Tarahumara in the state of Chihuahua, will lead the delegation.

The 31-year-old Ramírez, a 2025 National Sports Award recipient, gained international recognition after winning the UltraTrail Cerro Rojo in 2017, an ultra-distance race of 80 kilometers (50 miles), while wearing huaraches, a type of traditional sandal. She finished with a time of 7 hours, 20 minutes.

The Cordillera Challenge — a 130-kilometer, multi-day endurance race taking place from Nov. 6-8 — will traverse some of El Salvador’s most stunning natural landscapes, including Lago de Coatepeque (a 115-meter-deep crater lake), the Izalco and Ataco volcanoes and the coastal sandbar known as Barra de Santiago.

Mirna Beatriz de la Cruz, leader of México Imparable, a government initiative that links sport and cultural identity to promote athletic talent and give visibility to Mexico’s Indigenous peoples, will also attend the 3-day event.

Upon establishing México Imparable in August 2025, President Claudia Sheinbaum described the initiative as “a symbolic action that represents the strength and resilience of all the Mexican people, particularly the indigenous communities.”

México Imparable’s agenda in El Salvador includes the photo exhibition “Mexico, Land of Champions,” which will be inaugurated on Nov. 3 at the National Library in San Salvador.

The exhibition — sponsored by the Mexican Embassy — includes images of daily life, traditions and the rich cultural heritage of the Sierra Tarahumara’s Indigenous communities.

Through portraits of its inhabitants, their customs, their relationship with the land and their connection to sport, the exhibit seeks to introduce the Salvadoran public to the cultural diversity of the Rarámuri and highlight their contribution to Mexico’s heritage.

With reports from El Mundo and Diario Latino

World.title: Mexico in 10 objects: Stone heads, silver dollars and tacos
World.content:
In January 2010, Neil MacGregor of the British Museum started to broadcast his new series, “A History of the World in 100 Objects.” It was a magnificent success, and a bestselling book followed. Since then, there have been numerous other titles, from “The History of Football in 100 Objects” to “A History of Food in 101 Objects.”

The idea is such fun that MND asked contributor Bob Pateman to put together his very own “A History of Mexico in 10 Objects.”

1. The Olmec stone heads — the start of Mexican civilizations

The Olmecs, the Mexican mother culture, thrived in the lowlands of southeastern Mexico between 1500 and 400 B.C. San Lorenzo and La Venta became the biggest communities on the continent, the builders of palaces and pyramids.

The most striking of their artwork was the giant heads carved from boulders that had been brought from the distant Sierra de los Tuxtlas mountains. Mysterious and haunting, 17 of these heads have been discovered.

Item selected: Colossal Head 1 was the first to be discovered and is the largest, at 2.84 meters (9 feet 4 inches) and 25.3 metric tons. With its direct stare and elaborate headdress, it is also one of the most haunting.

Where it is: Colossal Head 1 can be seen in the Xalapa Museum of Anthropology in the city of Xalapa, Veracruz.

2. The Mexica statue of Coatlicue

Pre-Hispanic Mexico was a mosaic of different societies that interacted through trade, politics and war. The Mexica flourished for little more than 200 years, but during that time they acquired previously unheard-of levels of wealth and power.

There is no lack of amazing objects to represent them, with gems ranging from feather headdresses to giant stone calendars.

Item selected: The giant statue of the earth and mother goddess Coatlicue. This was carved around A.D. 1500 at the height of Mexica power. It stands 2.5 meters tall and weighs between 2 and 3 metric tons. It is an interwoven collage of snakes, claws, skulls, and human hearts and hands. Threatening and powerful, Coatlicue was clearly a god you didn’t mess with!

Where it is: The National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City.

3. A memory of a lost empire — the Florentine Codex

Although the Mexica did not have an alphabetic writing system, they produced wonderful books that recorded their myths, economic records, history and laws in pictograms and glyphs. Written on bark, skin or cloth, they were targeted by the Spanish, and only a handful escaped the flames.

Item selected: Ironically, the Spanish, who tried so hard to burn all the Mexica “books,” produced one of the finest. Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún worked with Nahua elders and artists to document the culture and history of the Mexica people. It was a mammoth work, 2,500 pages organized into 12 books, recording the story of an empire that was in the process of being destroyed.

Where it is: The Florentine Codex is housed in the Laurentian Library of Florence.

4. A Spanish silver dollar

The Spanish colonies in the Americas became rich from their silver mines, and for 350 years Mexico led the way. Much of the raw metal was turned into coins known as the Spanish dollar or, later, the Spanish peso. The amount of silver in each coin was equal to eight Spanish reales, and for smaller purchases, a coin could be cut into bits, which is why pirates referred to them as pieces of eight.

Mexico sat at the center of an international trade network that stretched from China to the Ottoman Empire, and the Spanish dollar became the world’s first international currency.

Item selected: Produced in the millions, the coins can be acquired for as little as US $100. However, everything depends on rarity and the history of the coin, and the highest auction price is US $587,500 for a coin minted in Mexico in 1538. This was the first dollar-sized silver coin ever struck in the New World, and this particular example was salvaged from the underwater wreckage of the Golden Fleece, a vessel that sank in the northern Caribbean around 1550.

Where it is: Only three coins of this standard are known to exist, and all are in the possession of unknown private collectors.

5. Bell of Dolores — Campana de Dolores

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JBorcegui (@borcegui)

On Sept. 16, 1810, the Roman Catholic priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla entered the parish church in Dolores and rang the bell to gather the villagers. This is seen as the symbolic start of an 11-year war that would bring Mexican independence from Spain.

Every year, the bell is rung on the night of Sept. 15 as the president of Mexico starts Mexico’s Independence Day celebration.

Item selected: The bell dates to 1768 and was cast in bronze in the small town of Dolores. It is 1.77 meters in height and weighs approximately 750 kilograms.

Where it is: Since 1896, the bell has hung above the central balcony of the Palacio Nacional.

6. The world’s oldest tequila bottle

Tequila can trace its roots back to the drink pulque. The Spanish brought in the technology to distill a clearer, more alcoholic version, which became known as mezcal.

This was displayed at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago, where it was labeled as “mezcal from the village of Tequila.” The name was reduced to simply tequila, and a legend was born.

Today, the tequila industry is worth around US $12 billion, and the drink is deeply interwoven into Mexican history and culture.

Item selected: The oldest known tequila bottle. Before 1880, tequila was sold in large wooden barrels to bars or to regional distributors, and you took it home in your own bottle or jug. A José Cuervo bottle dating to 1905 is the oldest verified surviving bottle of tequila.

Where it is: Displayed in The Tequila House in Parral, Chihuahua, as part of a collection of more than 3,000 vintage bottles.

7. Looking good! — A mariachi outfit

Mariachi music traces its origins to Jalisco, emerging from a combination of Spanish strings and Mexican folk music with just a trace of African influence.

The first mariachi bands performed in the simple white cotton shirts, trousers and leather sandals of the farms, but during the early 1900s, musicians started to adopt the dandy dress of the Mexican cowboy. Costumes reached a new height in the 1940s when mariachi bands appeared in Mexican movies.

Item selected: The iconic mariachi costume is the black charro suit and tejana hat that Pedro Infante wore in the 1955 movie “Los Gavilanes.”

Where it is: A collection of authentic costumes, hats and cinematic memorabilia — including the famous mariachi outfit — is on display in the Museo El Rincón de Pedro Infante, in the actor’s hometown of Mazatlán.

8. A painting from Mexico’s most beloved artist

Mexico has produced some wonderful artists, from the masterful landscapes of José María Velasco to the blending of styles and cultures in the work of Rufino Tamayo. However, nobody has captured the love of the country more than Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, and, as time goes by, it is Frida who is emerging as the real superstar of the partnership.

Her paintings have pride of place in art galleries around the world, and the auction record for one of her paintings stands at US $54.7 million for her 1940 self-portrait “The Dream (The Bed).”

Item selected: “Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird.” Painted in 1940, this is a complex work full of symbols. The thorn necklace is a reference to both Christ and her own pain. While the hummingbird is usually a symbol of love, this one is dead and still, a reflection of Frida’s own disastrous relationships. With its colors, animals and plants and the artist’s simple peasant dress, there is also something notably “Mexican” about the work.

Where it is: “Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird” is in the permanent collection of the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

9. Tacos — the food that fuels Mexico

The origins of the taco are debated. Some argue that they predate the arrival of the Spanish; others that the idea came across from Spain, perhaps with miners or even with Hernán Cortés himself.

Whatever the origins, there is nothing more Mexican than a small corn or wheat tortilla filled with a piping hot and juicy filling. It is the food that fuels the country every morning.

Item selected: What represents Mexican street food better than small, semi-mobile taco stands? It is not only a place to eat, but a spot to stand and chat.

Where it is: We are looking for a small stand with umbrellas, a few plastic chairs and a bright advertising sign. Shouldn’t be too hard to find!

10. The title belts of Julio César Chávez

View this post on Instagram A post shared by World Boxing Council (@wbcboxing)

Sport has a special place in Mexican society, from bullfights to lucha libre to the passion generated by big soccer games. Sport has also helped Mexico stake its place on the world stage, hosting the 1968 Olympics and three World Cup tournaments.

If there is one sport that is special to Mexicans, it is boxing, and for many, the greatest Mexican fighter of them all is Julio César Chávez. Over a 25-year career, he was a six-time world champion across three different weight classes. To get there, he had to go through many personal challenges, the kind of background that endears a fighter to Mexican fans.

Item selected: A world championship belt. When British fighter Tom Cribb defeated his American challenger, Tom Molineaux, in the early 1800s, King George III presented Cribb with the first championship belt in boxing history. There are no pictures of the gift, but it is said to have been made from lion skin with a silver buckle. This started a tradition that continues today, with boxers receiving a championship belt on winning a world title.

Where it is: Two of Chávez’s six belts are believed to have gone to private collectors. Four remain in his private collection.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Salman Rushdie to keynote the 2026 FIL Book Fair, Día de Campo Music Festival and plans for a new urban park
World.content:
Exciting music and book festivals are coming to town, while city leaders commit to addressing a critical shortcoming in Guadalajara: the lack of green spaces for public recreation.

A new urban park is coming to land that once housed the Oblatos prison

The Guadalajara City Council recently announced that it will renovate this public land with the aim of creating a new urban forest, with designated areas for sports facilities and family fun.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Verónica Delgadillo G (@verodelgadillog)

This initiative is critical to address the dire shortage of parks and other green spaces for residents’ enjoyment in the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA). On World Environment Day in 2019, María Guadalupe Garibay Chávez of the University of Guadalajara shared findings that the GMA has a mere 1.4 square meters per resident of public green space, falling well short of the World Health Organization’s recommended 9 square meters per resident.

The city plans to invest more than 100 million pesos (US $4.9 million) in the project, with work to be carried out in phases so that park activities can continue during construction.

One of the most visible — and welcome — changes will be the elimination of vast areas of concrete. The project calls for removing approximately 6,300 square meters of concrete, with more than 600 trees planted in its place.

A swimming pool and other sports areas

While the construction of a new swimming pool is a showpiece, the project also calls for the renovation of multipurpose courts, the frontenis area and the baseball diamond. There will be new spaces for calisthenics and boxing, with other areas repurposed to create children’s play areas.

In addition to sports facilities, the new park will provide a variety of areas to socialize and gather with friends and family. Park trails and walkways will be renovated, with the goal of expanding the availability of green spaces for city residents.

Outside park boundaries, improvements are planned for street lighting, sidewalks and intersections to make accessing the park safer and easier.

The new park, which has not yet been named, will be located at Calle Sebastián Allende 200, Colonia La Penal, on Guadalajara’s east side near the Cristóbal de Oñate station on Line 2 of the light rail.

The FIL Guadalajara prepares to welcome Salman Rushdie as keynote speaker

The FIL Guadalajara, Latin America’s premier book festival, has an exciting program in the works for its 40th edition. British American writer Salman Rushdie is slated to open the program with a keynote lecture Nov. 28 at the Juan Rulfo Auditorium of Expo Guadalajara.

The announcement was made earlier this month by the FIL’s director, Marisol Schulz, who noted that this year’s festival will encompass “more than 3,000 activities that over nine days will center the conversation on literature, thought, scientific outreach, art, music, film, gastronomy, comics, the publishing business, programs for professionals and, of course, the formation of readers.”

In total, more than 900 authors from 41 countries are expected to take part in this year’s FIL, where Italy returns as the guest country of honor after 18 years.

This year’s FIL will also pay tribute to Juan Rulfo, 40 years after his death, with an immersive pavilion devoted to the universe of “Pedro Páramo” and a panel featuring Juan Carlos and Juan Pablo Rulfo, writer Élmer Mendoza and photographer Rogelio Cuéllar.

Nicaraguan writer Gioconda Belli is set to receive the 2026 FIL Prize for Literature in Romance Languages, and Italian author Alessandro Baricco will open the Salón Literario Carlos Fuentes.

Ticket availability

No tickets will be sold specifically for Rushdie’s keynote address. Entry requires a general admission ticket to the FIL paired with mandatory online pre-registration due to the strict security protocols necessary to ensure the author’s safety.

Keep an eye on the official FIL Guadalajara website or its press announcements as the fair approaches for the exact date the pre-registration link goes live.

For more information about the general program and specific events, visit the website’s calendar page.

Dates: Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026 – Sunday, Dec. 6, 2026

Location: Expo Guadalajara, Jalisco

Cost: General admission tickets are available online from the FIL website or in person at FIL’s main office, with prices starting from 40 pesos (US $2) for adults and 30 pesos (US $1.50) for children.

Día de Campo Festival returns to Guadalajara

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aperol Día De Campo (@aperoldiadecampo)

Returning to Guadalajara next month for its fifth edition is the Día de Campo festival. Unlike the typical music festival experience these days, Día de Campo bills itself as an intimate, low-key event — a chill day in the park with fantastic music, not a drunken bacchanal.

This year’s festival is moving to a new venue, Titanes GDL, which sits across from Parque Metropolitano. It is reachable by taxi from downtown Guadalajara in about 20 minutes.

Headlining Día de Campo this year is Santa Pirata, a new side project by Arcade Fire’s frontman Win Butler. The band includes Haitian musician and Arcade Fire member Paul Beaubrun and DJ Cosmo Gonik. Santa Pirata blends DJ sets with live instrumentation, featuring Butler on drums and Beaubrun on bass and guitar.

Also performing this year in its Guadalajara debut is Chet Faker. Australian musician Nick Murphy has been performing under the moniker Chet Faker for the past 15 years, combining soul, R&B and electronic music with catchy, danceable beats. The artist is touring in support of his new album, “A Love for Strangers.”

Other confirmed artists for Día de Campo 2026 are Argentina’s Grammy-nominated Bándalos Chinos, known for its synth-pop, funk and indie rock, Norway’s Kakkmaddafakka, CocoRosie and Alanis Yuki.

Date: Nov. 29, 2026, starting at 1 p.m.

Location: Titanes event space next to Parque Metropolitano in Zapopan

Cost: Available on Boletomóvil starting at 1,323 pesos (US $65).

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Made in Mexico: How Carlos Fuentes captured Mexico’s political soul
World.content:
Mexican author Carlos Fuentes entered my life with the soft insistence of a truth you recognize before you can name it. In a house where books functioned as liturgy and political arguments were my family’s daily prayer, politics and fiction braided until nationhood itself could only be discussed through story.

Friends learned to avoid politics and religion in polite conversation. But at our table, it was compulsory.

Encountering Carlos Fuentes

Between my mother’s journalistic and analytic perception and my father’s artistic view of the world, I first encountered Carlos Fuentes. It was an introduction that felt less like discovery than initiation.

I first found “La Muerte de Artemio Cruz” (“The Death of Artemio Cruz“) rummaging through my parents’ bookshelves as a teenager, that furtive, holy act of taking what the house has to offer.

The book is a slow, terrible confession. It follows a revolutionary soldier who becomes a wealthy businessman and, on his deathbed, confronts the compromises that made his life

possible.

I asked my father if I might read it. He agreed with the tolerant risk of someone who knows the power of literature. I was too young to understand everything — too young for many of the dates and alliances and the dense historical scaffolding — but not too young for the voices.

The blunt honesty of Fuentes’ interlocutors cut into me. Their phrases echoed family stories, private grievances and the way a father’s silence sometimes explained more than his sermons.

I went to sleep that night with the book heavy under my pillow, feeling the first tremor of an allegiance.

Fuentes liked to say that the Latin American novel rescues what official history neglects. It is an attractive aphorism: literature as a salvage operation, novels as lifeboats ferrying the lives, rumors and embarrassments that governments prefer to let sink.

But his claim is more than rhetoric. Read Fuentes and you find not an inventory of facts but a map of forces — the informal routines, petty calculations and generational betrayals — through which Mexican politics actually works. He is not interested in vindicating every detail of the public record. He excavates the subterranean arithmetic of power. The small acts and grand illusions that produce regimes.

A ‘gypsy in a black tie’

If Fuentes’ vantage feels panoramic, it is because it was cultivated that way. Born in 1928 in Panama to a cultured, liberal diplomatic family, he spent his early years amid the humid expanses of Montevideo and Rio de Janeiro. Those tropical afternoons — book-lined, humid and full of foreign tongues — were where Fuentes first fell in love with literature. Alfonso Reyes, the Mexican humanist and a central pillar of the country’s intellectual life, became an early mentor who guided him through the literary world.

The young Fuentes absorbed European and Latin American canons with equal appetite, continued his journey to Washington with his family. They stayed eight years in the American capital amid tense Mexico–U.S. relations following President Lázaro Cárdenas’ 1938 nationalizations.

Made in Mexico: Carlos Fuentes

Watch this video on YouTube

Distance sharpened his sense of Mexico as a nation, and of his identity as Mexican in a foreign country, as he turned into a schoolyard enemy thanks to the “Tata Lázaro initiative.” Watching his country from abroad, he did not simply miss home. He began to interrogate it. He traced a family history animated by wider European convulsions — ancestors who fled Germany and Spain and settled in Veracruz, establishing a coffee hacienda, and he learned how much a personal identity could be a palimpsest of political choices and historical happenstance.

Then a pivotal evening at a New York cinema, where he watched “Citizen Kane” with his father, supplied a kind of formal revelation: narrative could reveal the way private lives braided into public histories. He decided then to write within those intersections.

The acquisition of a global perspective

Fuentes’ early reading list — Stevenson, Dumas, Miguel Zévaco, Jules Verne — reads less like a curriculum than a confession. He wanted plot and spectacle, but with an eye to the moral and historical sediment underneath.

A teenage posting in Chile broadened that sensibility further. Latin American politics did not respect borders. The authoritarian and reformist rhythms he observed in Chile and Argentina taught him that patterns reverberated across the continent, that the fate of one republic often presaged the anxieties of another.

He returned to Mexico, weary of the peripatetic diplomat’s life — the “gypsy in a black tie” as he called it — and enrolled at UNAM to study law at Alfonso Reyes’ encouragement. The law sharpened him. Fuentes would later borrow Stendhal’s praise for the Napoleonic civil code — “clear, concise and effective” — and insist that legal training gave a novelist a discipline of clarity.

Yet his impulse was to use that clarity to break forms with novels that could capture the messy simultaneity of Latin American time.

At age 26, he published his first book, “Los Días Enmascarados” (“The Masked Days”), 1954, a collection where myth and the fantastic meet a restless modernity. His true breakthrough came with “La Región Más Transparente” (“Where the Air Is Clear”), 1958, a book that announced, with a kind of civic thunder, a new way of seeing Mexico City.

From that moment, he was no longer an apprentice. He was a national habit.

A life stranger than fiction

Fuentes’ public life was as complicated as his fiction. His unique voice made him central to Mexican culture to the point where presidents listened carefully to what Fuentes and other Mexican intellectuals had to say about their regimes. Later, he accepted the ambassadorship to France (1975–1977), a decision tied to a friendship with President Luis Echeverría that earned both praise and censure.

When the following president, Gustavo Díaz Ordáz, took office, he resigned from his role as ambassador in protest to the Tlatelolco massacre in 1968, an act that marked him among writers who believed conscience could not be compartmentalized.

He would reflect on this episode as a reminder that the line between cultural influence and political entanglement is rarely neat. Fuentes moved in circles of power even as he remained a sharp critic.

The restless writer

He was, by any measure, prolific, writing more than seventy books — including novels, essays, short stories, scripts and plays — along with a steady stream of articles across the Americas.

Critics who catalog his work point to recurring obsessions: the mestizo nature of Mexican identity, the ways power shifts under pressure, and, when left to its own inertia, the precariousness of state narratives that tidy over contradictions.

But to reduce Fuentes to a set of themes is to miss his artistry, which is the ability to render political life in the language of human habit: betrayal as domestic pattern, corruption as genealogy and revolution as a choreography of broken promises.

If a reader wants a beginning, here are five texts that make his method and moral urgency plain.

1. “La Región Más Transparente” (“Where the Air Is Clear”), 1958

A portrait of Mexico City through a chorus of characters — peasants, intellectuals, opportunists, dreamers — this novel critiques a hopeful bourgeoisie who believes concentrated wealth will somehow be redistributed by fate. The city is staged as myth and machinery, a place where pre-Hispanic ghosts brush against neon and where national identity is debated in salons and tenements alike. Fuentes anticipates the rupture generation’s disillusionments, sketching a metropolis both magnet and mirror.

2. “La Silla del Águila” (“The Eagle’s Throne”), 2003

Set, proleptically, in 2020, told through letters after a communications collapse, it narrates a corrupt election, the corrosive compromises of those who seek higher office, and the blunt interventions of foreign powers — most pointedly the United States. It is less a speculative thriller than a study in how institutions erode when informal networks take precedence over civic duty.

3. “Tiempo Mexicano” (“Mexican Time”), 1971

An essayistic meditation on temporality and national memory. Fuentes argues that Mexican time is not linear but circular and overlapping. Epochs coexist and narrate one another. He examines who is given the right to remember and how state and culture conspire to shape collective consciousness. Here, his faith in youth and his hope that new generations could craft a more democratic nation glimmer most clearly.

4. “Nuevo Tiempo Mexicano” (“A New Time for Mexico”), 1994

Written in the wake of 1994’s ruptures — the Zapatista uprising in Chiapas and the peso’s collapse — this book is more sober. Where earlier essays were buoyed by the possibility of reform, “A New Time for Mexico” reflects on the hard limits of institution-building amid enduring inequality and the new economic realities shaped by NAFTA.

5. “El Espejo Enterrado” (“The Buried Mirror: Reflections on Spain and the New World”), 1992

Perhaps my favorite, a sweeping cultural history that traces five centuries of Hispanic America. Fuentes is at once historian and storyteller. He narrates the persistence of colonial and Indigenous legacies as the subterranean currents of identity. The book is elegiac and exuberant, a reminder that culture is not a surface polish but an accumulated architecture.

Why read Fuentes?

Because he converts complexity into clearness without flattening it. He is not a historian in the archival sense. Dates and citations are subordinated to moral geometry.

But he is remarkably precise in diagnosing how power, memory and myth conspire to produce national life. His prose wants to unsettle complacency. He hoped readers would argue with his books, not to annul them but to enlarge the conversation.

Fuentes belonged to an erudite generation that could look at Mexico from both inside and outside. The diplomat’s gaze that knows protocol and the exile’s view that knows perspective.

He understood how the Mexican Revolution’s promise had been domesticated: the postrevolutionary bourgeoisie reproducing prerevolutionary hierarchies, the Institutional Revolutionary Party’s (PRI) transformation from the Party of the Mexican Revolution (PRM) into an apparatus that welded party to state, and how industrial growth often masked social exclusion.

Clarity and cultural insight

But perhaps his clearest insight is cultural. The revolution’s deepest achievement was not the redistribution of land or the construction of institutions alone, but the knitting together of a fragmented populace so disparate communities could finally perceive one another.

To read Fuentes is to feel history as a kind of weather: sudden, changeable and always shaping the small gestures of private life. His novels let you listen to Mexico’s interiors — the whispered bargains, the private prayers and public betrayals. They teach patience.

Political truths are rarely delivered in headlines. They arrive through accumulations of habit and choice, through the intimate narratives that novels can, more truthfully than manifestos, deliver.

If you find a copy of his work, take it. Fuentes will not hand you a neat syllabus of reform. Instead, he will offer scenes and voices that make the stakes of politics unavoidable. His writing insists upon engagement.

Not mere consumption, but conversation, argument, indignation, laughter and, sometimes, renewal. In that stubborn insistence lies his lasting invitation: to read Mexico not as a place to be explained, but as a country alive with stories that refine what we think we know.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: El Jalapeño: US demands tariffs on top of tariffs in escalating Mexico trade negotiations
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

WASHINGTON, District of Columbia — Bilateral trade talks between the United States and Mexico came to a sudden halt Thursday after U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick submitted a revised 400-page framework requiring Mexico to pay a 25% duty on existing 25% tariffs, alongside a surcharge on the bilateral trade talks themselves.

According to sources familiar with the negotiations, the impasse arose when U.S. officials clarified that “tariff relief” was a procedural misunderstanding, proposing instead a compound tariff architecture in which every imported vehicle, steel beam or aluminum bracket would incur levies not only on its material value, but on the accumulated administrative cost of discussing those levies.

Under the proposed U.S. structure, if a Mexican-assembled automobile crosses the border into Texas, it will be subject to a baseline auto tariff, an additional fee for utilizing the border bridge, and a 12.5% “consultation duty” designed to cover the U.S. Department of Commerce’s operational expenses during the hours spent resisting tariff reductions.

“Our stance has always been entirely reasonable,” said a senior U.S. official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic friction. “Mexico asked for tariff cuts. We offered to cut the paper on which the tariffs are printed, but the ink used to print that paper remains subject to a 50% national security surcharge. If we do not tax the negotiations, we risk incentivizing future diplomacy, which could destabilize key domestic industries that rely heavily on trade deadlock.”

Mexican negotiators reportedly spent three hours attempting to calculate the effective compound tax rate on a single domestic brake pad before realizing the total duty exceeded the market value of the vehicle containing it. The Mexican delegation subsequently offered to suspend its own automotive parts tariffs for five years, only to be informed that concessions were subject to a 10% entry levy upon arrival at Washington Dulles International Airport.

Despite the procedural logjam, both governments publicly denied that negotiations had broken down. In a Thursday afternoon address to federal deputies, Ebrard maintained an unflappable optimism, assuring lawmakers that Mexico remains uniquely positioned to enjoy the most sophisticated, multi-tiered tariff relationship in the Western Hemisphere.

“We are making extraordinary, unprecedented progress toward defining the precise parameters of our disagreement,” noted a member of Mexico’s negotiating team. “Our position remains strong, our position remains favorable, and we fully expect that by Friday, we will have secured a formal agreement specifying the exact date on which we will resume failing to agree.”

At press time, U.S. officials were reportedly reviewing a proposal to implement a 5% ad valorem tariff on all future press releases issued by the Mexican Ministry of Economy that contain the word “constructive.”
