World.title: Mezcal production, Mother Earth and the enduring spirit of the Zapotecs
World.content:
Nestled between the Pan-American Highway and the Rio Grande, all along the Ruta Caminos del Mezcal, exist hundreds of palenques, or small farms that carry the ancient practice of mezcal production. Tourists come in droves to watch the mules pull the great stone wheel of the tahona in slow circles, crushing roasted agave before it is fermented, distilled and enjoyed.

I had the pleasure of learning about this age-old practice firsthand, a practice that existed long before it became a spectacle for curious travelers, while living and volunteering at one of these fabled farms.

How community and ecology sustain mezcal production

The land once belonged to the Zapotecs, an ancient civilization known for its profound connection to the natural and spiritual worlds. Inhabiting the land for more than 2,500 years, the Zapotecs were first overtaken by the Aztecs beginning in the late 15th century, and subsequently by the infamous Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés.

Although the group suffered decimation from disease and invasion, around 500,000 Zapotec speakers remain in the Oaxaca region. That air of tradition survives in the people and culture of Oaxaca today: in the emphasis on community, in farming and ecological initiatives, in spiritual practice and myth, and most notably, in mezcal.

Oaxaca, the mezcal capital of the world, is also known for its ecological initiatives and Earth-centered culture, and remains a place of continual education and philosophy for anyone passionate about a lifestyle that benefits the planet.

Indigenous and mestizo communities own nearly 82% of the state’s 6.1 million hectares of forest, managing them collectively rather than as private property. Zapotec is still spoken in several municipalities, and local mythology and spiritually driven land stewardship make the state an example of an ecologically sustainable community.

First sip goes to the Earth and ancestors

In Zapotec tradition, mezcal brings people closer to the spirits. Across Oaxaca, it is common to pour the first sip for the thirsty earth and for ancestors long gone.

As the glasses are raised and the offering given, participants speak the word “Dixeebe” over the anointed ground. Dixeebe is a Zapotec salutation used to express deep reverence for the spirit of Earth. The gesture is small, but it is a daily reminder to put the needs of the Earth, and of those no longer living on it, before one’s own. Repeated across a community, it builds a culture devoted to a better planet for all of us.

This inherent reverence and respect for the Earth reverberates through small, traditional mezcal-producing palenques across the Oaxacan region.

1 of 13

Protecting the land is protecting mezcal

For Miguel Ángel Zamora, mezcal maestro at Casa Cabrón in Unión Zapata, protecting the land and protecting mezcal are inextricably linked. Casa Cabrón is one of many family-run palenques in Unión Zapata that remain true to the traditional culture of mezcal production.

Regarding his production process, Zamora says, “That connection (to the Earth) is so important for life in general, and can also be achieved through mezcal. But first, we must be conscious of producing it in a conscious way.”

He goes on to say, “We must care for Mother Earth, because from her flows the medicine that heals our soul, mind, body and life.”

‘Revealing a bit of life’s magic’

The mezcal production process begins on monthly cycles.

During harvest day, jimadores use machetes to cut and carve the agave plants’ core and prepare them for pickup. After the batch is cut and ready, workers from the palenque or neighboring farms retrieve the haul from the mountains and bring it back to the palenques for production.

“For me, producing mezcal means revealing a bit of life’s magic, the magic of transformation,” Zamora says. “It means showing the world that processes rooted in great love and respect for Mother Earth foster life, enjoyment, bliss and joy.”

The following day the crew and I headed back to the harvesting site promptly at 4:45 a.m. to pick up the agave and deliver it. The trip to the Sierra Mixe mountains was a generous three hours, even with our skilled, quick driver.

As we maneuvered the mountains’ impressive turns, the men talked of the prior night’s full moon, healthy horses and newly bought motorcycles. My traveling companions would point out edible plants, dangerous cacti or friends’ palenques, all the while passing snacks over my shoulder.

Once we arrived at the agave harvesting site, beverages were shared over small coolers, while the workers formed assembly lines — one man lifted the cut-down plant, tossed it to the next, and finally threw it into the back of the exporting truck.

Despite the physically demanding work and intense heat, there was no shortage of laughter. It was easy to mistake our hard work for a friendly reunion.

Navigating the tradition-modernity divide

Although larger mezcal corporations have pitched their tent along the mezcal route in recent years, family-run mezcal farms remain, with their beliefs intact and traditions upheld. Contrasts between old and new, nature and machines, are everywhere in Oaxaca. Local ruins exist amongst modern towns. Spanish churches are built upon ancient Zapotec temples.

Nowhere is this divide clearer than at the Church of San Pablo in Mitla. An ancient Zapotec ceremonial site, this once-great temple was torn down and rebuilt by Spanish Dominican friars, turning the structure into a Catholic institution. However, the original Zapotec foundations remain, creating a haunting visual representation of religious syncretism within the region and the enduring Indigenous presence.

As I walked through the ruins, our guide, a local Zapotec historian and teacher, led us past fallen walls and shrunken tombs that once sheltered a people defined by their relationship to the natural world. Spirals of life and death decorated the low-hanging frames, and old women passed, the numinous melody of the Zapotec language drifting in their wake.

We had brought our guide freshly distilled mezcal to taste, and he insisted we pour the first sip for the thirsty ground and the ancestors. We stood together, surrounded by the imposing walls of the temple’s spiritual resilience, and poured the first sip of mezcal onto the ancient stone floors.

We saluted using the Zapotec word dixeebe, while remembering all those who had been at this very spot before us.

The Zapotec civilization may have been nearly lost to time, but its beliefs and the spirit of its people live on in Oaxaca and, evidently, around the world, carried in the smoky, sultry, handmade spirit of mezcal.

Abigail Rose is a journalist, archaeologist and storyteller with a hands-on, in-the-field approach to journalism. She reports on local environmental initiatives, cultural stories and frontline conflict through writing, photography and video. Her work has taken her across Colombia, Peru, Oman, Greece, Mexico, Ecuador, Germany, Italy and the U.S., with her next project bringing her to Oaxaca, Mexico.

World.title: Mexico Well-Read: A review of Sofía Robleda’s ‘The Other Moctezuma Girls’
World.content:
Anyone who has stood in Mexico City’s Zócalo has felt the weight of history; beneath the cathedral and the crowds lie Tenochtitlán and the blood and bones of conquest. The city has spent the succeeding five centuries deciding which parts of that story to tell. The usual cast is familiar: Moctezuma, Cortés, Cuauhtémoc and a Malinche as contested now as she was in 1519.

Rarely, however, does anyone linger on Tecuichpoch, Moctezuma’s favored daughter, baptized Isabel. She was consort to two Mexica emperors, Cuitláhuac and Cuauhtémoc, bore a daughter to Cortés, and later married three other Spaniards. Her life ran through nearly every famous name of the Conquest, yet she barely registers in the popular telling.

‘A disturbing tapestry’

Robleda decided to address that lack in her new novel, “The Other Moctezuma Girls,” an ambitious, often moving romp across history and the fascinating cultural geography of the Valley of Mexico.

The story opens in Tenochtitlán in 1551, 30 years after the Spanish Conquest, as Tecuichpoch’s will is read aloud after her death. Her daughter Isabel suspects that a second account of her mother’s life may be hidden, chapter by chapter. The clues to that inheritance are found in a disturbing tapestry bequeathed to Isabel and her younger sister in the will. Isabel sets out to follow them with her favorite siblings and a handsome young cook.

Alongside Isabel’s journey runs her mother’s own testimony, delivered in the first person by a woman who knows her time is short:

“Moctezuma, Cuauhtemoc, Cortés, Malintzin … they reshaped the order of the entire world. They may be dead, but by God, they are known. Yet no one but you will know me. I may be mentioned in passing as the child, the wife, the mistress … Listen to me, rambling on. Trying to carve out a pinprick of light in the darkness these people have cast over my life. It is very difficult, for I was also taught not to exalt myself, not to seek attention, lest I be judged, or mocked, or worse, publicly shamed. As my mother would say, Tlacoqualli in monequi — moderation is a must.”

Nearing death, Tecuichpoch wants to be known; she declares that she will not die silent. In a line that could serve as the book’s thesis, she observes that “men would leave us nameless, if they could.” That premise gives the novel real moral force.

‘Pure adventure’

Tecuichpoch recalls being married off three times by the age of 12. She was raised, as Nahua women of the age were, to keep her face serene, and she credits that discipline with her survival. The empress describes her father’s love as a weapon that cut both ways: She was Moctezuma’s cherished child, and he still handed her to his enemies. Yet she insists he was neither fool nor coward, and that he read the Spanish correctly, as men rather than gods, and as the vanguard of an innumerable and therefore unstoppable horde. It is a humane portrait, and it lets Moctezuma be a father without excusing him.

The domestic details do much of the work. There is the tank of axolotls that Tecuichpoch kept in her father’s zoo, the pranks she played on her father’s other wives, and the beloved brother who collected obsidian and volcanic stones in a wooden box. Anyone who has wandered the Museo Nacional de Antropología will understand why these touches matter. The Mexica are usually presented as a catalog of gods, glyphs and sacrifices, while here they are real people with siblings, grudges and favorite pets. Tecuichpoch’s prose is formal and lightly ornate, sprinkled with Nahuatl as well as Spanish.

Her daughter’s half of the book is more conventional but livelier. One of Isabel’s siblings, Catina, lost her hearing after an illness, and the siblings communicate through sign language, a welcome touch that keeps the teens from becoming a mere chorus of clue-solvers. The quest itself is pure adventure. It takes the young people through the viceregal court and then the chinampas of Xochimilco, into tunnels beneath the ancient pyramids of Teotihuacán, and even up the icy slopes of Iztaccíhuatl as nearby Popocatépetl threatens to erupt.

A highly entertaining mix of history and drama

Since Robleda is writing about a woman forced to live in two worlds at once, it is fitting that the book itself straddles these two modes. While guiding us through an exciting adventure — a deadly scavenger hunt — she also provides fascinating historical information about the colonial caste system, constraints on women, slavery and the lasting consequences of conquest. The country’s mestizo identity, after all, began in the negotiations, marriages and coercions that Tecuichpoch lived through.

Robleda assigns a high degree of respect to la Malinche, or Malintzin, from Tecuichpoch, who is said to have admired her spirit, her brilliance, and the long game this noblewoman-turned-slave-turned-noblewoman managed to play:

“(Malintzin), too, had been reshaped. Cortés had married her off to another of his captains, Juan Jaramillo, and she was no longer a slave but a free noblewoman again. This is what she had desired most in the whole world. Freedom for herself and her children—the young son she’d had with Cortés and Jaramillo’s newborn girl in her arms, who were now peers of the New World aristocracy.”

“The Other Moctezuma Girls” is not a scholarly reckoning, and it does not pretend to be. It is a novel of reclamation, intent on sharing the story of this utterly fascinating woman, the last Mexica empress. It is best suited to readers who enjoy their history with a mystery, a map and a pounding pulse. Take it with you on your next visit to Mexico City, and you may find yourself absorbing the history around you more energetically.

Ann Marie Jackson is a book editor and the award-winning author of “The Broken Hummingbird.” She lives in San Miguel de Allende and can be reached through her website: annmariejacksonauthor.com.

Oaxaca held its first Afro Guelaguetza in the coastal community of Chacahua Isla, bringing together 12 delegations to celebrate Afro-Mexican heritage through music, masked dances and traditional performances. World.title: Serbia Vote Was Uneven, Observers Say
World.content:
Key Facts Verdict: Observers from the OSCE, Council of Europe and European Parliament saw high turnout but a campaign tilted toward the outgoing ruling party.

Voting day: Observers rated voting positively at 96% of stations visited, but reported violence and family voting.

Count: Still preliminary: observers noted procedural gaps and mismatched result records, and final findings come later.

Next: Serbia’s electoral commission (RIK) has published a preliminary count but not yet the final result.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a crypto betting market, priced 97.6% that the student-backed Student List took 50% or more (1:10 p.m. ET, 26 Oct).

Published Monday, 26 October, 1:25 p.m. ET · Source: ODIHR, the OSCE’s election-monitoring office, and partner observer missionsSerbia’s students came out on top in the preliminary count, and on Monday the outside referees said the contest was real but the playing field was not level.International observers called turnout high and the count largely sound, yet they described a campaign tilted toward the outgoing ruling party.The verdict follows Aleksandar Vučić, the former president who led Serbia for more than a decade, saying on Sunday night that his list had lost.

The students’ Student List, a citizens’ group born of protests, leads the preliminary count. Our count coverage and our explainer on what happens next have the political picture.

Who Said This, and How Strong Is It?

Four bodies issued the statement together: the OSCE’s election office (ODIHR), the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, the Council of Europe’s parliamentary assembly and the European Parliament. The OSCE is a security organisation whose monitors are the standard international yardstick for elections in Europe.

Gilles Baum of Luxembourg led the OSCE short-term observers, and Piero Fassino of Italy led the Council of Europe delegation. Andreas Schieder of Austria headed the European Parliament team, and Eoghan Murphy heads ODIHR’s election observation mission.

File photo: Republic Square in Belgrade, Serbia’s capital.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Serbia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Was the Campaign Called Uneven?

Observers said the outgoing ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), Vučić’s party, enjoyed entrenched advantages, including misuse of state resources. They pointed to nearly one billion euros (about US$1.1 billion at 1.12 dollars per euro) of financial benefits announced before and during the campaign, which blurred the line between state and party.

They also cited intimidation and pressure on voters, candidates and civil society, and allegations of vote-buying. Contestants could still campaign vigorously, the observers added.

How Did the Media Treat the Two Sides?

ODIHR’s media monitoring found that RTS (Radio Television of Serbia), the state broadcaster, favoured “United Serbia”, the Vučić-led list, and singled out the “Student List” for negative treatment. National private channels did the same, and TV Informer, a pro-government channel, showed what observers called pronounced hostility.

Online, observers saw inflammatory rhetoric, coordinated fake activity and AI-generated disinformation. They said unresolved reports of illegal digital surveillance, including alleged use of Pegasus, a commercial phone-spyware tool, deepened public distrust of the security services.

What Went Right on Election Day?

Observers rated voting positively at 96% of the polling stations they visited, and they judged counting and tabulation positively in the vast majority. Citizen observers were present at nearly half of the stations observed, which added scrutiny.

The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), which runs the vote, generally worked transparently and on time. Observers did question how political affiliations of its members shaped contested decisions.

What Went Wrong?

Reported incidents of physical violence, including against polling staff, citizen observers and journalists, raised serious concern. Observers also found a statistically significant number of cases of group or family voting, weak protection of ballot secrecy and signs of pressure outside some stations.

Voters with physical disabilities lacked independent access at 61% of stations observed. Distrust in the voter register persisted, as the authorities gave no substantive public explanation for reported discrepancies.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, a Student List vote share of 50% or more traded at 97.6% at 1:10 p.m. ET on 26 October. The event covering all vote-share brackets has drawn US$114,311 in total trading.

Prices are bets, not polls, and this one tracks the vote count rather than the observers’ verdict.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For anyone with money or plans in the Balkans, a vote that was competitive but tilted means the incoming government will face pressure to fix the rules before the next election.The observers said significant recommendations from ODIHR and the Council of Europe’s legal-advice body, the Venice Commission, remain unaddressed.These include limits on misuse of state resources, journalists’ safety and media oversight.

What Is Not Known

This is a preliminary statement, and the mission’s final report, with detailed recommendations, comes later. RIK has published a preliminary count, but the final official result is still pending.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did international observers call Serbia’s election free and fair?

They did not use that phrase. They found high turnout, vigorous competition and mostly positive voting and counting, but a campaign with seriously compromised equal opportunities.

Who are the observers?

The mission combines ODIHR, the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, the Council of Europe’s parliamentary assembly and the European Parliament. Their statement is preliminary, and a final report follows.

Sources: ODIHR, “Serbia, Early Parliamentary Elections, 25 October 2026: Statement of Preliminary Findings and Conclusions” (26 October 2026); Polymarket; RT (EUR/USD).

World.title: Pope Leo Confirms Latin America Trip
World.content:
The Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary and Saint Benedict of Palermo in Paysandu, the city where Pope Leo XIV is due to celebrate Mass on 7 November, in a 2013 night-time file photo (Photo: Mverocai, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts Trip. Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, 6 to 17 November 2026, his sixth international trip as pope.

Health. The Vatican says there are “no contraindications”, after lung surgery on 13 October.

Why it matters. First US-born pope; first papal visit to Argentina and Uruguay in almost 40 years.

As of 26 October 2026, 17:00 GMT

Less than two weeks after lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV says he is going back to the continent he knows so well. He confirmed on Monday that he will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November.

The pope, who is 71, posted the message on Monday 26 October 2026 on his Spanish-language X account, @Pontifex_es. He wrote: “It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life.”

He added: “May this journey be an occasion to open our hearts to one another.” The Holy See Press Office, the Vatican’s official spokesman’s office, said the same day that there are no medical contraindications to the journey going ahead as planned.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 61.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

For US readers, this matters because Leo is the first US-born pope. The United States has a large Catholic community, and many of its members will follow the journey.

What We Know

The Holy See Press Office announced the trip on 5 August 2026. Its director, Matteo Bruni, said it would run from 6 to 17 November.

Uruguay comes first, from 6 to 8 November, with stops in Montevideo, Paysandú and the town of Florida. Argentina follows from 8 to 11 November, with visits to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and the pilgrimage town of Luján.

Peru closes the journey from 11 to 17 November, with stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa. At about a week, it is the longest of the three stops.

This is the pope’s sixth international trip. It is also the first papal visit to Argentina and Uruguay in almost 40 years.

Leo spent years as a missionary and bishop in Peru, so the final leg of the trip is a personal one. His own message speaks of returning to the continent where he has lived so many moments of his life.

Plaza de Mayo, Buenos Aires. Archive photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Pope Leo XIV (Argentina) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Health Question

On Tuesday 13 October 2026 the pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, as we reported at the time. The surgery confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He left hospital and returned to the Vatican on Saturday 17 October. His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora of Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, said: “As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place.”

The programme is demanding, with about a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. Cusco, one of the Peruvian stops, sits high in the Andes.

The Vatican’s statement points the same way. The surgeon’s view and the Holy See therefore agree on the main point.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether any events will be shortened or changed as the pope recovers. The Holy See has not said that any will be.

The Vatican has not said how the pope’s doctors will monitor him during the trip. Travellers should therefore treat the timetable as provisional, as we reported earlier this month.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Travellers heading to Lima, Cusco, Chiclayo, Buenos Aires or Montevideo around these dates should confirm flights and hotels directly with airlines and hotels. They should check the official programme before fixing plans.

Demand is already strong, because Uruguay’s tickets sold out in three hours. In Peru, the government has also given workers days off for the visit.

For US Catholics, the trip puts the first US-born pope on the continent he knows best. Readers can follow the background in our hubs for Peru, Argentina and Uruguay.

Entry rules and local advice differ by country. Checking them before booking is sensible for any traveller.

The trip starts on Friday 6 November. For now, the Vatican’s statement and the surgeon’s assessment are the facts on the table.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Pope Leo XIV visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru?

He will travel from 6 to 17 November 2026. Uruguay comes first from 6 to 8 November, then Argentina from 8 to 11 November and Peru from 11 to 17 November.

Is the pope healthy enough to travel?

The Holy See Press Office says there are no contraindications. His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, said there are no clinical reasons why the trip should not take place.

Which cities will the pope visit?

In Uruguay: Montevideo, Paysandú and Florida. In Argentina: Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján, and in Peru: Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa.

Why does the trip matter to US readers?

Leo XIV is the first US-born pope, and this is his sixth international trip. It is also the first papal visit to Argentina and Uruguay in almost 40 years.

World.title: Ethiopia’s Ruling Party Wins 438 Seats
World.content:
ETHIOPIA · POLITICS

Published Monday, 26 October, 12:39 p.m. ET · Source: Ethiopian parliament, National Election Board of Ethiopia, Ethiopian government statements

Key Facts — The result Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party won 438 of the 486 seats contested; no vote was held in Tigray.

— The government Abiy was sworn in for a second five-year term on 5 October.

— Tigray Federal forces took the regional capital Mekelle in early October; a six-month interim administration followed.

— The strain Drought is hurting crops and the US has warned it could sanction more leaders.

Ethiopia’s ruling party has won nine in ten of the parliamentary seats contested, handing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed a second term with little opposition in the chamber. The Prosperity Party took 438 of the 486 seats contested in the general election on 1 June, out of 547 in the House, and Abiy was sworn in on 5 October.

No vote was held in Tigray, where 38 seats stay empty.The result comes while the country is again tense in the north and short of rain.Fighting with forces linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) flared in late September, and drought is damaging crops in parts of the country.

How the Vote Went

More than 54 million people were registered, and 47 parties and more than 10,900 candidates took part. The African Union sent an observation mission led by former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, which gave its preliminary assessment on 3 June.

The result gives the party the majority it needs to form the government.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Ethiopia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Tigray Back in the Headlines

The TPLF is the party that ran Ethiopia for decades before Abiy came to power in 2018. After a large offensive by TPLF-aligned forces in late September, federal troops advanced and took Mekelle, the Tigray capital, around 3 or 4 October, and the TPLF said it had moved out temporarily and would keep fighting.

On 16 October the government announced a six-month interim administration for Tigray followed by regional elections.One local-language report says four TPLF leaders have been captured, but we could not confirm it.

Washington’s Warning

On 23 September the US ambassador, Ervin J. Massinga, warned that Washington had “tools to sanction additional leaders” after the offensive. We have found no new US sanctions so far.

Drought and Food

Parts of southern Tigray are in an official food crisis, a level the United Nations calls IPC Phase 3. A local report says drought linked to El Niño destroyed more than 250,000 hectares of crops in four months, a figure we have not independently confirmed.

What It Means for US Readers

Ethiopia is Africa’s second most populous country and a major recipient of US aid, and instability in Tigray, Amhara and Oromia can drive refugee flows, food shortages and sanctions debates. For a recent example of the violence in the south, read about the attack that killed more than 40 Orthodox Christians in Oromia.

What We Do Not Know

We do not know when Tigray will vote, whether more TPLF leaders have been detained, or how the interim administration will work in practice. We will update this story as the facts become clear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who won Ethiopia’s election?

The ruling Prosperity Party won 438 of the 486 seats contested in the House of Peoples’ Representatives on 1 June. No vote was held in Tigray. Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for a second term on 5 October.

What is happening in Tigray?

Federal forces took the regional capital, Mekelle, in early October after fighting with TPLF-linked forces. The government named a six-month interim administration on 16 October.

Is there a drought in Ethiopia?

Yes. Parts of southern Tigray are in a food crisis, and local reports say drought has destroyed large areas of crops.

Sources: National Election Board of Ethiopia · Ethiopian parliament and government · African Union observers · US embassy statements · UN food security data.

World.title: Algeria Votes to Send Troops to Niger
World.content:
NIGER · BREAKING

Published Monday, 26 October, 12:39 p.m. ET · Source: Algerian parliament, Niger defence ministry, Algerian and Nigerien officials

Key Facts — The vote Algeria’s upper house approved sending troops to Niger, 148 of 174 votes; the lower house followed.

— The mission Protecting energy sites, especially oil facilities tied to Algeria’s state company Sonatrach.

— A first Algeria’s first parliament-approved deployment abroad since the 1973 war with Israel.

— The unknowns Troop numbers, the start date and locations have not been published.

Algeria’s parliament has approved sending soldiers to Niger, the first approved deployment of soldiers abroad in more than 50 years. The upper house voted on Sunday, 148 of 174 senators in favour in a closed-door session, according to a senator quoted by AFP, and the lower house approved it by an absolute majority without publishing a count.

The constitution asks for two-thirds of each chamber, so the missing lower-house number is an open question.The stated aim is to protect energy installations, above all oil sites linked to Sonatrach, Algeria’s state oil and gas company.Neither country has said how many soldiers will go or when.

A Deal Signed Days Earlier

On 21 October Niger’s defence minister, General Salifou Mody, flew to Algiers, where he met President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and army chief General Saïd Chengriha. The two sides signed a military cooperation protocol that Niger’s government called a new framework for its armies, but neither side has released the text.

Chengriha said Algeria was ready to look at Niger’s proposals for deeper cooperation, and Mody welcomed what he called multidimensional coordination between the two armed forces.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Niger Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Now

Niger has been unstable since the army took power in 2023, and in late August mutinous soldiers reportedly tried to seize sites in the capital, Niamey, including an air base, before loyal troops regained control. On 30 August Algeria sent four Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jets, a transport plane and a refuelling tanker to Niamey at Niger’s request; four helicopters had already been delivered on 9 August.

President Tebboune had already said on 3 October that “we will protect Niger whatever it takes.” Algeria also has a stake in the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which is meant to carry Nigerian gas through Niger toward Europe, and the two countries share a desert border of about 960 kilometres.

What Algerians Say

Algeria’s 2020 constitution allows troops abroad only with the votes of two-thirds of the members of each chamber (Article 91), which is why the missing lower-house count matters. Critics ask what the mission is, how long it lasts and what it costs, and we have not found an official answer on the cost or the length.

What It Means for US Readers

The Sahel, the belt of countries south of the Sahara, has become one of the world’s main centres of jihadist violence, and Western forces have left much of it. A larger Algerian role in Niger shifts the balance toward regional powers and could affect gas supply plans for Europe and the fight against armed groups.

What We Do Not Know

We do not know the size of the force, the start date, whether it will fight armed groups or only guard sites, or how Niger’s military government will describe its role. We will update this story as the details come out.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Algeria sending troops to Niger?

Yes, parliament approved it. Algeria’s upper house voted 148 of 174 in favour in a closed session on Sunday, and the lower house approved it by an absolute majority. The size and date have not been announced.

Why is Algeria sending troops?

The stated aim is to protect energy installations, especially oil sites linked to Sonatrach. Algeria also backs Niger’s stability and a pipeline project that would cross it.

Is this the first Algerian deployment abroad?

It is the first parliament-approved deployment abroad since Algeria sent forces to support Egypt in the 1973 war with Israel.

Sources: Algerian parliament · Niger Ministry of Defence · Algerian presidency and army · statements by Algerian and Nigerien officials.

World.title: Egypt Approves Defence Aid to Saudi Arabia
World.content:
EGYPT · BREAKING

Published Monday, 26 October, 12:39 p.m. ET · Source: Egyptian House of Representatives, Egyptian presidency, Saudi Arabia

Key Facts — The vote Egypt’s parliament approved, by a two-thirds majority, a mandate for defensive military support to Saudi Arabia.

— What it means It is a permission, not an order: Egypt acts only if Riyadh asks and the president decides.

— The trigger Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including missiles aimed at the Mecca and Medina regions.

— The split The Egyptian Social Democratic Party’s 11 members abstained; the vote was held in closed session.

Egypt’s parliament has given President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi the power to send defensive military help to Saudi Arabia, after months of missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi cities. The House of Representatives approved the mandate on Monday, in a closed session, by a two-thirds majority, the level the constitution demands for any use of the army abroad.

The decision is a green light and not a deployment order. Egyptian forces would move only if Saudi Arabia asks and the president then decides, and officials describe the mission as purely defensive.

What the Mandate Allows

The wording covers support for Saudi Arabia against outside attack and the protection of its territory and its Islamic holy sites. A regional official briefed on the plan said Egypt would offer air-defence systems and aircraft to help shoot down missiles and drones, but no Egyptian ground troops in Yemen.

President Sisi has said the mission does not include an attack on Yemen.No numbers have been made public.We do not know how many aircraft, air-defence batteries or soldiers could be involved, where they would be based, or for how long.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Egypt Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Saudi Arabia Needs Help

The Houthis, an armed group in Yemen backed by Iran, have been firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia. The attacks have targeted Riyadh, its airport and facilities of the oil company Aramco, and Saudi authorities say missiles aimed at the Mecca and Medina regions were intercepted on 24 October.

The Houthis deny targeting the holy cities and say they hit only military and oil sites.Reports of attacks near Islam’s two holiest cities caused anger across the Muslim world, and Al-Azhar’s Grand Imam, Ahmed al-Tayeb, condemned the attacks, saying they offend nearly two billion Muslims.President Sisi asked parliament for the mandate on 17 October, and the National Defense Council he chairs pledged full support the next day.

Who Opposed It

The pro-government bloc has a comfortable majority, but the debate showed rare public cracks. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party’s 11-member bloc abstained, citing too little information on the goals, scope, duration, cost and risks to troops.

Some lawmakers reportedly objected, warning that a wider regional explosion would serve Israel. Egypt also has history here: it reportedly sent about 800 ground troops to Yemen in 2015.

Why Egypt Cares

Egypt’s economy depends on the Suez Canal, which is reached through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow gate at the southern end of the Red Sea that the Houthis can threaten. Saudi Arabia is also a major source of investment and aid for Cairo, so a clear show of support protects both interests.

What It Means for US Readers

A larger Arab role in Saudi Arabia’s defence could lower the load on US forces in the region, but it also raises the risk of a wider war involving Iran and Israel. Shipping and oil prices stay sensitive to any new attack near the Red Sea.

What We Do Not Know

We do not know the exact vote count, whether Saudi Arabia has asked for help, or when any Egyptian aircraft or air-defence units could arrive. We will update this story when Cairo or Riyadh gives details.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Egypt sending troops to Saudi Arabia?

Not yet. Parliament approved a mandate for defensive support, but Egypt acts only if Saudi Arabia asks and the president decides. A regional official said ground troops in Yemen are excluded.

Who are the Houthis?

They are an armed group that controls much of Yemen and is backed by Iran. They have fired missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.

Why did some Egyptian lawmakers object?

The Egyptian Social Democratic Party’s bloc abstained, citing unclear goals, duration and cost, and some lawmakers warned against being pulled into a regional war.

Sources: Egyptian House of Representatives · Egyptian presidency and National Defense Council · Saudi Arabia · Al-Azhar · regional officials.

World.title: Brazil Treasury Buys Back US$1.3B of Bonds
World.content:
The Planalto Palace in Brasilia, the seat of Brazil's presidency, lit at night in a file photo from 2013. It does not show the election or the statement. Photo: Leandro Neumann Ciuffo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Brazil Markets · Bonds · National Treasury

Published Monday, 26 October, 12:41 p.m. ET · Source: National Treasury (Tesouro Nacional), B3 exchange data, TSE electoral court data, RT market data

Key Facts —The buyback. Brazil’s Treasury bought back about R$7.1 billion (US$1.3 billion) of fixed-rate NTN-F bonds on Monday. —The cancellations. It scrapped Tuesday’s inflation-linked bond sale and Thursday’s fixed-rate bond sale. —The trigger. Long-term borrowing costs jumped after President Lula won re-election on Sunday with 51.79% of valid votes. —Still unknown. How far yields eased after the buyback, and whether more buybacks follow. —Prediction markets. Betting platform Polymarket prices “no change” at 74.9% for the central bank’s November rate decision (26 October, 12:36 p.m. ET). —Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Brazil Election Data Room Runoff poll average: Flávio Bolsonaro 51.0 %, Lula 49.0 % 45 national polls from 21 pollsters since 4 October, updated hourly. Every poll, free to download. Open the Data Room · Download the CSV · Embed the chart

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro – · Lula – (US$249 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 0.4% · Lula 99.6% As of 25 October, 11:40 pm ET (03:40 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Want prediction market reports on Brazil? Get yours free, right after you confirm →

When borrowing costs spike, a government can step into the market and buy back its own debt. On Monday, Brazil did exactly that, hours after investors reacted to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election.

The National Treasury, the agency that manages the public debt of Latin America’s largest economy, bought back about R$7.1 billion (about US$1.3 billion) of fixed-rate bonds late on Monday morning in Brasília. It also cancelled two of this week’s regular bond sales.

What the Treasury Actually Did

A bond is an IOU the government sells to investors. When the government buys some back, their price rises and their yield, the interest rate investors earn, falls.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The Treasury repurchased 5 million five-year, 2.4 million seven-year and 1 million ten-year NTN-Fs. These notes pay a fixed rate of interest twice a year, so their prices swing hard when investors expect higher rates.

At R$5.42 per dollar (RT market data, 12:35 p.m. ET), the R$7.1 billion is worth about US$1.3 billion. The dollar is up about 9% in reais from Friday’s R$4.98, so the real has weakened.

File photo: the Finance Ministry in Brasília, which oversees the National Treasury.

This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Why Long-Term Rates Jumped

Many investors had bet on a win by Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator who led the first round on 4 October. Lula, 80, won the runoff with 51.79% of valid votes, according to the TSE, Brazil’s electoral court (blank and spoiled ballots are excluded from valid votes).

By 9:23 a.m. in Brasília (8:23 a.m. ET), the rate on the January 2031 DI contract had climbed to 14.46% from 12.64% at Friday’s adjustment, data from B3, the São Paulo exchange, show. That is a rise of 182 basis points (1.82 percentage points) in a contract that traders use to bet on future interest rates; our report on the real’s slide covers the currency side.

Why Cancel the Bond Sales?

The Treasury cancelled the sale of inflation-linked NTN-B bonds set for Tuesday 27 October and the sale of fixed-rate LTN (Treasury bills) and NTN-F bonds set for Thursday 29 October. It said it would keep monitoring market conditions and act to ensure that public bond markets work properly.

In effect, the Treasury does not have to sell new debt at today’s higher rates. One auction stays: Tuesday’s sale of LFT bonds, whose payout follows the Selic, Brazil’s benchmark interest rate.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, traders put the odds of “no change” in the November rate decision of Copom, the central bank’s rate-setting committee, at 74.9%. A 25-basis-point cut is priced at 11.5% and a 25-basis-point rise at 5.2%, with US$100,150 traded (26 October, 12:36 p.m. ET).

These prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Government bond yields set the floor for borrowing costs across Brazil, including at companies listed in New York such as oil giant Petrobras (PBR), miner Vale (VALE), bank Itaú (ITUB) and Nu Holdings (NU). Higher yields can weigh on those shares and on the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ), on top of a weaker real.

Travellers see the other side: at R$5.42, a R$100 dinner costs about US$18.

What Is Not Known Yet

It is not yet clear whether more buybacks are planned, or how far yields eased once the Treasury began buying. The market also waits to learn who Lula picks to run the economy.

The next data point is Friday 30 October, when the central bank is due to publish September’s gross government debt, which economists expect at 83.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) against 82.9% in August (RT calendar data). World.title: Brazil’s Current Account Gap Shrinks 42%
World.content:
The National Congress and government ministries on the Esplanada dos Ministérios in Brasília, pictured in 2009. The photo does not show the election or any person in this story. Photo: Cayambe / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Brazil Economy · Trade · Published Monday, 26 October, 12:15 p.m. ET · Source: Banco Central do Brasil

Key Facts —The number. Brazil ran a current account deficit of US$5.1 billion in September, 42% below US$8.8 billion a year earlier. —Why it fell. Mainly a goods trade surplus of US$6.9 billion, up from US$2.5 billion in September 2025. —Still unknown. Whether September’s drop is a lasting trend or a one-month swing. —Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Want prediction market reports on Brazil? Get yours free, right after you confirm →

Brazil still spent more abroad than it earned in September, but the gap with the rest of the world shrank sharply. Brazil’s central bank, the Banco Central do Brasil, said on Monday that the current account deficit fell 42% to US$5.1 billion, down from US$8.8 billion in September 2025.

The current account is the broadest scorecard of a country’s money flows with the world, covering trade in goods, services and income. A smaller deficit means Brazil leans less on foreign financing to pay its bills. It is one more data point in the story of Brazil’s economy.

Exports Did the Heavy Lifting

Brazil sold US$34.6 billion of goods abroad in September, up 12.9% on a year earlier. Imports fell 1.7% to US$27.7 billion, so the trade surplus reached US$6.9 billion.

That swing of US$4.4 billion in the trade balance is bigger than the whole improvement in the deficit. In plain terms, Brazilian exporters earned more while the country bought slightly less from abroad.

Headquarters of Brazil’s central bank in Brasília. File photo. (Photo: Banco Central do Brasil, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Where the Money Still Leaks

Services, such as shipping, software licences and equipment rental, ran a deficit of US$5.2 billion, up from US$4.8 billion. Brazilians spent US$2.3 billion abroad on travel, up 19.3%, while foreign visitors spent US$0.9 billion in Brazil, up 8.3%.

Brazil also paid US$7.2 billion more in profits, dividends and interest (“primary income”) to foreigners than it received, up from US$6.9 billion. Profits and dividends sent to foreign owners of Brazilian companies rose 13.9% to US$5.1 billion, while net interest payments fell 12.2% to US$2.2 billion.

In Plain English Current account: the net total of trade, services and income flows between Brazil and the world.

the net total of trade, services and income flows between Brazil and the world. Primary income: profits, dividends and interest paid across borders.

profits, dividends and interest paid across borders. FDI: foreign direct investment, meaning money that builds or buys businesses in Brazil.

It also offers aeronautical services, such as passenger, aircraft landing, parking charges,…

Foreign Investors Covered the Gap

Foreign direct investment (FDI) was a net US$11.3 billion in September, up from US$9.6 billion a year earlier, with US$3.8 billion of it reinvested profits. Over 12 months, that investment totals US$88.3 billion, or 3.43% of GDP.

That is about 147% of the 12-month deficit, so long-term money more than paid for the shortfall. Investors in Brazilian shares and bonds sold a net US$2.1 billion in September, though over 12 months they bought a net US$5.1 billion.

The Yearly Picture Is Improving

Over the 12 months to September, the deficit stood at US$60.0 billion, or 2.33% of GDP. That compares with 2.50% in August and 3.57% a year earlier.

Brazil’s international reserves, the central bank’s stockpile of foreign currency, ended September at US$362.8 billion. They fell US$9.8 billion in the month, mostly on price and currency moves of US$6.2 billion, plus US$2.0 billion of dollar sales in the spot (immediate-delivery) market.

What It Means for US Readers

For dollar investors, a shrinking deficit means less dependence on foreign financing for the real, Brazil’s currency, a theme in our real-to-dollar guide. It matters to US holders of American depositary receipts (US-traded shares of foreign firms) such as Petrobras (PBR), Vale (VALE), Itaú (ITUB) and Nu Holdings (NU), and of the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ).

Travellers should note the other side of the data: Brazilians are spending more abroad, which adds to demand for dollars. Our Brazil stock market guide tracks how local shares react, and our interest rates guide covers the policy backdrop.

What Is Not Known

The central bank does not say whether September’s drop is a trend or a one-month swing, and we have no monthly market consensus to compare it against. Partial October data, through 21 October, show a trade-related foreign-exchange surplus of US$3.9 billion.

One risk to watch is profit and dividend payments, up 13.9% in the month even as interest costs fell. The next monthly report will show whether exports keep their lead.

World.title: Macron Warns Saturday Is High Risk in France
World.content:
File photo: French President Emmanuel Macron speaking at the United Nations General Assembly.

France in Turmoil

Published Monday, 26 October, 11:50 a.m. ET (4:50 p.m. Paris) · Source: President Macron’s remarks in Marseille, French government statements

France has five days to prepare for another tense Saturday. President Emmanuel Macron stood in Marseille on Monday and told the country that Saturday, 31 October, will again be a risky day.

He also said that future marches will be kept out of city centres, a new line in the France protests that have shaken France since mid-October. The aim, he said, is to protect shops, town halls and people, as explained in our guide to why France is protesting.

Key Facts Warning: Macron says Saturday, 31 October, will again be a risky day for French protests.

Rule change: Authorised marches will keep to routes outside city centres to protect shops and public buildings.

Admission: He conceded police were too few on 17 October and the violence was not anticipated.

Next: Yellow Vest (grassroots cost-of-living movement) rallies on 31 October and a national strike on Thursday, 5 November.

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: France Keeps Curfews After 1,435 Arrests

In plain English Since 17 October, cost-of-living marches have turned violent in several French cities. Macron’s message is that the next one could too, so the state will steer marchers away from shopping streets and keep police on guard.

Why Macron Is Moving the Marches

The weekend of 17 October was the shock. Cost-of-living protests drew about 550,000 people nationwide, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, the minister in charge of police, and in Marseille protesters forced their way into City Hall while shops were looted.

Macron said in Marseille that police were too few that day, “in Marseille as elsewhere”. “We had not anticipated what was going to happen,” he admitted.

A week later, on 24 October, marches were again steered away from the centres and security was stronger. Macron said preparation was better that day, and he wants the same arrangement to continue so protests stay calm.

He did not say how many cities the new routes will cover. The map for Saturday is likely to be settled locally over the coming days.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

No State of Emergency, but No Taboo Either

Macron was careful about the strongest tool available. He said order is being kept today without a state of emergency, adding that such a step is not a taboo if conditions deteriorate.

The government also signalled that curfews will be kept where needed. It promised concrete answers to students and unions on university access and school buildings, and help for shopkeepers and towns that suffered damage.

The Calendar Ahead for Protesters

The Yellow Vests, the grassroots movement that began in 2018 over fuel taxes and now centres on living costs, have called new rallies and sit-ins for Saturday, 31 October. The next big test after that is Thursday, 5 November, when a united front of unions has called a national strike.

That front groups five of France’s main union federations: CFDT, CGT, Force Ouvrière, UNSA and FSU. Strike calls usually hit trains, schools and public offices hardest, which matters for anyone travelling.

What It Means for US Readers

For Americans in or heading to France this week, the practical effect is local: expect closed shopfronts, diverted routes and possible curfews in big cities, especially on 31 October and 5 November. Our guide to travelling in France tracks the latest travel and strike notices.

For markets and politics, the question is whether Macron’s government can calm the streets without the heavier tools it has so far avoided. Our look at whether the French government could collapse covers that risk.

What Is Not Known

The routes for 31 October have not been published, and no one can say how many people will turn up. Whether unions beyond those already committed will join Saturday is also open.

It is also unclear whether Saturday will repeat the violence of 17 October or the calmer picture of 24 October. Curfew rules differ by town and can change at short notice.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Macron say about Saturday’s protests in France?

On Monday, 26 October, in Marseille, President Macron said Saturday, 31 October, will again be a risky day. He said authorised marches will follow routes outside city centres so protests stay calm.

Is France under a state of emergency?

No. Macron said on 26 October that order is being kept without a state of emergency, though he added that it is not a taboo if the situation worsens.

Sources President Macron’s remarks in Marseille (26 October 2026), Élysée Palace (the presidency) and the French government, plus union calls for the 5 November strike.

World.title: Puerto Rico’s Yannik Álvarez Makes History at 2026 Junior Tennis Finals
World.content:
Puerto Rican tennis player Yannik Álvarez has made history by becoming the first player from the island to qualify for the ITF World Tennis Tour Junior Finals, placing him among eight of the world’s leading junior competitors at one of the sport’s most prestigious youth tournaments.

The 18-year-old earned his place in the season-ending competition following a strong 2026 campaign that included three international singles titles and his first successful appearances on the professional circuit. The tournament, held October 21–25 at the Sichuan International Tennis Center in Chengdu, China, brings together eight boys and eight girls who have earned their places through results over the previous 12 months.

It is considered the junior equivalent of the ATP and WTA Finals, giving some of tennis’s most promising young players an opportunity to compete against one another before moving into the professional ranks. For Álvarez, simply qualifying represented a milestone for Puerto Rican tennis.

He entered the competition near the top 10 of the International Tennis Federation’s junior boys’ rankings, having built his standing through victories at tournaments in Brazil, Paraguay and Italy. His biggest junior title of the season came at the J500 tournament in Gaspar, Brazil. He also won J300 events in Asunción, Paraguay, and Santa Croce sull’Arno, Italy.

Those results demonstrated his ability to compete internationally and provided the ranking points needed to reach the elite eight-player field in Chengdu. Although Álvarez struggled against the strong competition in China, his participation marked another step in a season of significant progress.

He lost all three of his round-robin matches, finishing fourth in a group that included American Jordan Lee, Slovenia’s Ziga Sesko and Germany’s Jamie Mackenzie. The Puerto Rican then lost his opening placement match against Austria’s Thilo Behrmann, leaving him to face Mackenzie in Sunday’s seventh-place match.

The result of that final placement match had not been independently confirmed at publication time. Despite those defeats, Álvarez’s development has extended well beyond the junior circuit this year. In April, he made an impressive start in professional competition, reaching the semifinals of an ITF M15 tournament in Boca Raton, Florida.

He followed that performance with a quarterfinal appearance at another M15 tournament in Orlando the following week. At the Orlando event, he also captured a professional doubles title alongside American Ryan Cozad. Those performances are particularly important because the transition from junior to professional tennis can be difficult. Young players must begin competing against older, more experienced opponents while adapting to the physical demands and financial pressures of the professional circuit.

Álvarez has also gained experience representing Puerto Rico internationally. He was part of the country’s Davis Cup team as Puerto Rico earned promotion to the 2027 World Group II Play-offs, another encouraging development for tennis on the island. His junior Grand Slam appearances have provided additional opportunities to compete against leading players from around the world.

At the 2026 French Open, Álvarez reached the boys’ doubles semifinals. He had previously reached the same stage of the junior doubles competition at the 2025 US Open. In September, he competed in the US Open junior singles draw, defeating Japan’s Hyu Kawanishi in the opening round before losing to Kirill Filaretov.

Those experiences, combined with his success in junior tournaments and early professional results, have helped establish him as one of Puerto Rico’s most promising young tennis players. The Junior Finals also provide practical benefits for players preparing to move into professional tennis.

The ITF has allocated more than $220,000 in travel grants to participants, with payments determined by their finishing positions. The grants are intended to help young competitors cover the costs of future tournaments. Higher year-end junior rankings can also provide access to professional events through the ITF’s Junior Accelerator Programme, which helps leading juniors gain opportunities on the men’s and women’s circuits.

For Álvarez, those opportunities could become increasingly important as he continues his transition into professional competition in 2027. Puerto Rico has produced internationally recognized tennis players, most notably Olympic gold medalist Monica Puig, but establishing a consistent presence on the professional men’s tour has proved more difficult.

Álvarez’s qualification for the Junior Finals does not guarantee future success at the ATP level. However, his achievements across junior tournaments, professional events and Davis Cup competition show that he has already begun building experience beyond his age group. Whatever his final position in Chengdu, the 2026 season has given Puerto Rican tennis a new milestone and Álvarez a foundation for the next stage of his career.

World.title: BELTRAIDE: Women and young entrepreneurs among 95 businesses receiving $788,000 in grants
World.content:
BELTRAIDE: Women and young entrepreneurs among 95 businesses receiving $788,000 in grants

By Zoila Palma: BELTRAIDE and the CARICOM Development Fund (CDF) have officially concluded the Belize Enterprise Empowerment Program (BEEP), disbursing BZ$788,000 in non-repayable grants to 95 micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) across Belize.

The program’s completion was marked by a closing ceremony and lessons-learned workshop today.

Launched on August 14, 2024, BEEP evolved from the Belize Enterprise Revolving Fund, established in 2020. In April 2024, the initiative shifted to a grant-based model after partners recognized that businesses needed immediate financial support without taking on additional debt. In addition to funding, participants received business training, advisory services, and mentorship from BELTRAIDE personnel.

The program supported businesses in sectors including agriculture, agro-processing, manufacturing, tourism, creative industries, information technology, professional services, and business process outsourcing. Of the 95 beneficiaries, 61 businesses, or 64 percent, were women-owned, while 20, or 21 percent, were led by young entrepreneurs. Another 28 businesses operated in creative, cultural, and artistic industries.

Monitoring results show that 21 businesses expanded into new markets or introduced new products and services, while 16 reported more stable operations and greater confidence in pursuing additional financing. Beneficiaries across all groups also reported increases in sales.

BELTRAIDE and the CDF say the lessons gained through BEEP will help guide future support for local enterprises and contribute to a more competitive and resilient Belizean economy.

World.title: Tracy Panton calls on Alexis Rosado to step aside from Belize’s ICJ case amid serious criminal allegations
World.content:
Tracy Panton calls on Alexis Rosado to step aside from Belize’s ICJ case amid serious criminal allegations

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton is calling on Ambassador Alexis Rosado to voluntarily step aside from his involvement in Belize’s case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) while serious criminal proceedings against him remain unresolved.

In a strongly worded statement, Panton questioned whether Rosado should continue representing Belize following allegations involving the rape of a minor.

Her comments follow public debate over statements by the Speaker of the House of Representatives concerning Rosado’s continued involvement in Belize’s ICJ case.

Panton acknowledged that the allegations do not establish guilt and emphasized that Rosado is entitled to the presumption of innocence, due process and a fair hearing.

“Only the judiciary can determine criminal guilt,” she stated.

However, the UDP leader argued that temporarily stepping aside from an official appointment while criminal proceedings are pending should not be interpreted as a declaration of guilt.

Panton also questioned the Government’s decision to retain Rosado in his role, noting that Prime Minister John Briceño has defended his continued involvement based on his experience and the importance of Belize’s ICJ proceedings.

She called on the Government to explain how its decision meets appropriate standards of public accountability while safeguarding Belize’s national interests.

Panton urged Rosado to step aside voluntarily rather than wait for action from the administration.

The Opposition Leader also emphasized the importance of protecting the dignity and privacy of individuals who report sexual violence, particularly children.

Rosado remains entitled to the presumption of innocence, and the allegations against him have not been established as fact by a court.

World.title: International News: Pope Leo confirms upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
World.content:
International News: Pope Leo confirms upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru

By Zoila Palma: Pope Leo XIV has confirmed that he will travel to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from November 6 to 17, expressing “great joy and enthusiasm” ahead of his upcoming Apostolic Journey to Latin America.

The Vatican said the journey will provide an opportunity for the Pope to strengthen ties with local Catholic communities, encourage the faithful in their mission, and share messages of faith, hope, and peace.

Pope Leo also expressed his excitement about returning to the continent, where he has spent significant moments of his life, and said he hopes the visit will encourage unity among Christians and renew their commitment to proclaiming the Gospel.

The announcement also provided an update on the Pope’s recovery following surgery on October 13. According to the Holy See Press Office, his recovery continues to progress favorably, and medical examinations confirmed that his condition was localized and that no further oncological treatment was necessary.

The Pope has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his schedule in consultation with his doctors to allow sufficient time for rest.

The Vatican added that Pope Leo remains grateful for the prayers, support, and medical care he has received as he continues his recovery and prepares for the upcoming visit.

World.title: International News: French President pledges more measures as unrest continue
World.content:
International News: French President pledges more measures as unrest continue

By Zoila Palma: French President Emmanuel Macron has promised government measures in response to weeks of protests over the cost of living, public services, and other grievances.

Today, Macron said he had asked his government to address the demands driving the growing social movement while acknowledging the possibility of further unrest.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was expected to hold a news conference following a meeting with high school student unions demanding more resources for education and reforms to the university admissions system, which they say perpetuates inequality. The protests have expanded beyond students, attracting trade unions and “yellow vest” activists protesting economic pressures and the rising cost of living.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said authorities expected further disturbances during demonstrations planned for October 31.

Police deployed approximately 70,000 officers nationwide during Saturday’s protests, and Nuñez reported that 1,435 people were arrested. He also said organized far-right groups had confronted far-left activists in several cities, including Nice and Montpellier.

Despite the heavy security presence, business leaders warned that the unrest was continuing to hurt the economy.
