“They had no intention of blowing anything up or harming anyone. There is no basis for talking about any kind of organised activity,” he says.

The lawyer representing the second suspect has declined to comment to the media at this stage.

Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 225, parts 1 and 2, of the Criminal Code. The article covers organising group actions involving violence, looting, damage to or destruction of other people’s property, and the use of weapons. It also covers preparing to take part in such actions.

The article provides for a prison sentence of six to nine years.

School attack plot in Georgia

World.title: ‘Georgia without Ivanishvili’: Opposition launches new wave of protests – photos and video
World.content:
New wave of protests in Georgia

On 25 October, thousands of people gathered in Tbilisi for a major opposition-organised protest under the slogan ‘Georgia without Ivanishvili’.

Waving flags and blowing horns, protesters gathered outside Tbilisi State University before setting off on a mass march towards Rustaveli metro station.

With this rally, the opposition announced the start of a new wave of protests in Georgia. The next rally is scheduled for 28 November.

The date is symbolic: exactly two years earlier, the ruling Georgian Dream party publicly announced that it was suspending EU accession talks.

The announcement sparked ongoing pro-European protests, with demonstrators demanding fresh, free and fair parliamentary elections.

Key messages from opposition leaders

The rally’s organisers, leaders of the pro-Western opposition, addressed the demonstrators.

“This day, 28 November, represents a defeat for all of us as long as Bidzina Ivanishvili remains in power. The postponement of our integration into the European Union is a defeat for all of us. The indefinite delay of a brighter future for our children is a defeat for all of us,” said Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change.

“Ivanishvili’s group is trying to formally strip us of one of the most important achievements secured by the United National Movement – multiparty elections in Georgia. They now seek to legally establish a one-party dictatorship,” said Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of the Freedom Square party.

“It may seem that Bidzina Ivanishvili is making such a brazen decision that we should all despair. In fact, the opposite is true. By banning any alternative, Ivanishvili is acknowledging a crisis of his own legitimacy. He is admitting that he no longer trusts the Georgian people – that he fears the free choice of Georgian citizens, and quite rightly so,” said Tamar Chergoleishvili, leader of the Federalists movement.

Young people and other protesters were also among the speakers.

“Look at one another – you are surrounded by people who refuse to give up, who continue to fight for a better future for our country,” student Luka Mishveladze told the crowd.

Background

The 25 October rally was part of Georgia’s pro-European protest movement, which has been ongoing for nearly two years. The demonstration was announced and organised by the opposition.

The date was no coincidence: on 24 October 2024, Georgia held crucial parliamentary elections, with the country’s European future at stake.

The election results remain disputed both domestically and internationally. The vote marked the beginning of a major political crisis in Georgia, leading to strained relations with Western partners, sanctions and the suspension of multimillion-dollar aid packages.

The protests were met with violent police crackdowns, including beatings, torture and arrests of activists. Several packages of repressive laws were adopted, while pressure on the media and civil society intensified, including measures that effectively blocked access to funding.

Western institutions adopted numerous resolutions criticising these developments.

The political crisis entered a new phase when the ruling Georgian Dream party moved to ban pro-Western opposition groups it deemed unacceptable.

Almost all the parties that organised the 25 October rally and announced a new wave of protests were among those facing a proposed ban.

World.title: Why are Abkhazia residents with dual citizenship asked to show Russian passports at Moscow airports?
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s Foreign Ministry has said that some residents of the breakaway republic who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship are experiencing difficulties crossing the Russian border at Moscow airports.

Russian border guards have reportedly been refusing to allow dual nationals to enter or leave the country using their Abkhaz passports, instead demanding Russian documents.

As Abkhazia is a largely unrecognised republic, its passports are also not widely recognised internationally. Travelling on an Abkhaz passport is virtually impossible, except to a handful of countries, including Russia. For Abkhazians, obtaining a Russian passport is therefore practically the only way to travel internationally. However, this generally means a Russian international passport rather than a domestic identity document. Most do not hold Russian internal passports because they permanently reside in Abkhazia, where Russian passport holders account for around 70% of the population.

The ministry added that people holding only Abkhaz citizenship do not encounter such problems at airports. Similar incidents have not been reported at other border crossing points either.

Russia explains its position by saying that, for dual nationals, a Russian passport is not merely the primary document required to cross the border, but the only acceptable one. However, the explanation has been met with scepticism in Abkhazia, where some suspect the border guards may have other motives.

The issue was discussed by Abkhaz and Russian foreign ministers Oleg Bartsits and Sergei Lavrov during a recent meeting in Moscow. However, no solution has yet been found. According to Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry, the matter remains subject to “consultations with the competent authorities of the Russian Federation, taking into account the provisions of existing bilateral agreements”.

In the meantime, the ministry has advised Abkhaz citizens experiencing difficulties at border crossings to formally report the incidents to the ministry, providing detailed accounts of what happened.

From the perspective of international practice, border guards at Moscow airports are not doing anything unlawful.

As a general rule, people holding two or more citizenships are required to present the passport of the country whose border they are crossing, if they are citizens of that country. This requirement is enshrined in national legislation and strictly enforced in countries including Georgia, the United States and many others.

This raises the question: what exactly is the problem, why are Abkhaz citizens unhappy, and why are they reluctant to present their Russian passports at the border if they have them?

For some Abkhazians with dual citizenship, the right to use an Abkhaz passport is a matter of principle and national pride. While this argument carries little legal weight, it is highly significant in Abkhazia.

Others simply want the option of crossing the border using their Abkhaz documents in certain circumstances, such as when their Russian passport has expired and they have not yet received a replacement.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Making a living in dangerous waters: Challenges facing Azerbaijani sailors in Black Sea
World.content:
Azerbaijani sailors in Black Sea

Rufan Ahmadov was among the Azerbaijani sailors rescued from a vessel attacked off the coast of Romania on 23 October. According to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry, he sustained minor injuries and was accommodated in a hotel after undergoing a medical examination.

Russia was behind the drone attack on the Khoryv vessel. Two other Azerbaijani nationals on board were also rescued. This time, the sailors’ families received news that their loved ones had survived.

However, in recent months, families of other Azerbaijani sailors working in the Black Sea have received news of their loved ones being killed or going missing.

According to Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry statements on individual incidents, at least 48 Azerbaijani nationals were on board vessels targeted in attacks between June and October. Six Azerbaijanis were confirmed killed. Two others, initially reported missing, were subsequently declared dead. One person remains missing. At least 39 survived, ten of whom were injured or hospitalised.

Both Russia and Ukraine regularly launch strikes against merchant vessels in the Black Sea. Azerbaijani nationals work on these ships as captains, engine operators and in other roles. They transport civilian cargo, but their routes take them through areas affected by hostilities.

When a vessel comes under attack, the entire crew is put at risk. If a voyage is interrupted, the threat to their safety is compounded by other concerns: will the sailors receive their wages, will they be able to return home, and who will cover the cost of their repatriation?

Azerbaijani sailors killed or missing following attacks

Rustam Hasanov was killed on 5 October in an attack on the Royad Mammadov vessel. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the vessel had been struck by two Russian drones.

The victim’s father, Ismail Hasanov, last spoke to his son on 4 October, a day before the attack. In an interview with Khazar Khabar TV, he said Rustam had been working as the vessel’s captain since August.

Joshgun Mammadaliyev, a native of Digah village in Azerbaijan’s Masalli district, who worked as an engine operator on the same vessel, was injured and hospitalised in Romania. According to the broadcaster, he had worked in this role for three years.

In a statement issued on 6 October, Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry listed another Azerbaijani sailor, Muhammad Suleymanzade, born in 2002, as missing. At the time, three rescued Azerbaijani nationals were reported to be in hospital. There has been no further information about Suleymanzade’s fate.

Attacks continue

On 14 July, the Atlas Bey vessel, carrying 11 Azerbaijani nationals, came under attack off the coast of Odesa. Ukrainian officials described the incident as part of a series of Russian attacks on civilian vessels.

Ten sailors were brought ashore. The body of the vessel’s captain, Samad Nasrullayev, was recovered during a search operation and repatriated to Azerbaijan on 17 July.

Azerbaijani sailors were also affected by attacks on the Natra and Zirkon vessels in the Sea of Azov on 5 June. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the vessels had been struck by Ukrainian drones.

These incidents suggest that the threat is not confined to a single vessel or voyage. Over several months, Azerbaijani sailors have repeatedly faced attacks in the same region.

Crew awaiting wages and hoping to return home

The difficulties facing sailors extend beyond the threat of attacks. On 7 October, Sabukhi Salahov, captain of the Consul vessel, told Konkret that his crew had been stranded in Rostov-on-Don for several months without receiving their wages. According to the sailors, ongoing drone attacks near the vessel’s mooring location have prevented them from leaving the ship and returning to Azerbaijan.

“We want to get the money they owe us and return to Azerbaijan. But there’s nothing we can do,” the captain said.

According to Salahov, the crew have been waiting for their wages for several months and remain unable to return home. There has been no information about whether the sailors have since received their outstanding pay or been reunited with their families following their complaint.

“We were transporting dry cargo from Russia. Our last delivery was coal to Moldova. We then set off to collect a similar cargo, but the routes were blocked. Around 200 vessels have come under drone attack in the Azov-Black Sea region. Since then, we’ve been in the Russian city of Rostov-on-Don. We’ve been here for almost three or four months,” Salahov said.

The complaint also raises questions about how to ensure the safe return of Azerbaijani nationals from the dangerous region. If, as the captain claims, the crew are not receiving their wages and cannot return home, the sailors need consular assistance. However, there is no information about what steps Azerbaijani authorities are taking to repatriate the sailors or resolve the issue of unpaid wages.

Do all sailors have the right to refuse dangerous voyages?

The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has established rules for seafarers covered by certain collective bargaining agreements. Depending on the level of risk in the area of operation, these rules provide for additional payments, the right to refuse dangerous voyages and repatriation at the employer’s expense.

However, these protections do not automatically apply to all Azerbaijani sailors. To establish whether an individual seafarer is entitled to such protection, it is necessary to examine the terms of their employment contract, determine which collective bargaining agreement applies to the vessel and establish the risk classification of the area of operation.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry warns citizens about the risks of working in regions affected by war and instability. However, for those already working on vessels in such areas, it is important not only to be aware of the dangers but also to have a genuine opportunity to refuse to continue a dangerous voyage.

The ministry has also reported providing medical and consular assistance to sailors following attacks. However, measures to ensure their safety should not be limited to rescue operations and the repatriation of those affected.

It is also important to establish what support is available to Azerbaijani nationals who wish to leave dangerous areas, recover unpaid wages and provide for their families. For these sailors, warnings about the risks are not enough. They also need practical assistance that would enable them to refuse dangerous work.

World.title: Saturday march in Tbilisi “against oligarch Ivanishvili’s rule”. ‘Protests in Georgia’ video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for more than 700 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Baku hosted reception in honor of Austria's National Day (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. The Austrian Embassy in Azerbaijan hosted an official reception in Baku to mark the country’s National Day, Trend’s correspondent reports.

The event featured remarks by Etienne Berchtold, the Austrian Ambassador to Azerbaijan, and Nargiz Gurbanova, the Director of the Department of Economic Cooperation of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

Berchtold stated that Austria intends to expand the presence of its companies in Azerbaijan and develop bilateral cooperation.

According to him, relations between the two countries are based on trust, partnership, and shared values.

“Starting this year, we are purchasing gas from Azerbaijan. This is an important contribution to the energy security of Austria and Europe,” the ambassador noted.

He also highlighted the prospects for cooperation within the framework of the Middle Corridor and the opportunities for Austrian companies to participate in the development of railway infrastructure and the implementation of technologies.

According to Berchtold, approximately 2,000 Austrian citizens visited Azerbaijan in the first half of this year.

In turn, Gurbanova stated that Azerbaijan and Austria will hold the next round of inter-ministerial political consultations in Baku in November.

The parties will discuss the bilateral agenda and prospects for further cooperation.

She also noted that Azerbaijan has begun supplying natural gas to Austria. Thus, the number of European Union member states receiving Azerbaijani gas has reached ten.

According to Gurbanova, Austria’s expertise in industry and high technology, combined with Azerbaijan’s transportation and logistics capabilities, create opportunities for expanding economic cooperation.

World.title: Austria seeks to expand its companies' presence in Azerbaijan - ambassador
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Austria intends to expand the presence of its companies in Azerbaijan and develop bilateral cooperation, Austrian Ambassador to Azerbaijan Etienne Berchtold said at an event marking Austria’s National Day today, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

According to Berchtold, relations between the two countries are built on trust, partnership, and shared values.

"Our two countries maintain very close ties, founded on trust, partnership, and shared values. Austrian companies make a significant contribution to the development of bilateral relations. As of this year, we are purchasing gas from Azerbaijan. This represents an important contribution to the energy security of both Austria and Europe," Berchtold said.

He also highlighted the significance of energy cooperation between Azerbaijan and the European Union.

"Energy is a vital component and a cornerstone of the EU’s partnership with Azerbaijan. However, our cooperation isn’t limited to this sphere alone," the ambassador said.

Addressing the issue of transport connectivity, Berchtold mentioned the Middle Corridor and the potential for Austrian companies to participate in infrastructure development.

"Our companies, including those from Austria, have much to offer in the fields of railways and other technologies," the ambassador said.

He noted that direct flights operated by AZAL are highly beneficial in this regard. According to the ambassador, approximately 2,000 Austrian citizens visited Azerbaijan in the first half of this year.

"Our goal is to further strengthen the partnership, expand the presence of Austrian companies, and foster high-level contacts," he added.

World.title: Anthropic files to list on stock market in potential $US1.5tn float
World.content:
Anthropic has disclosed steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its US initial public offering filing, as the Claude-parent laid out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology.

The prospectus highlights the AI company's rapid growth over the past year, fuelled by Big Tech's breakneck spending that has driven a rally in AI stocks while raising concerns about lofty valuations and rising debt.

The company also flagged growing risks from AI technology, underscoring concerns over its potential to cause harm which had led chief executive Dario Amodei to call for a slowdown in development of advanced models.

Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $US80.7 billion ($114 billion), largely due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into company's shares. Revenue in this period stood at about $US16.3 billion.

The company's revenue grew a staggering 1,368 per cent in the three months ending June 30 from a year ago, but warned in the prospectus that revenue growth rate could decline over time and fluctuate from time to time.

Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei is among those warning about the need to limit the risks of artificial intelligence. (AP: Markus Schreiber/File)

The IPO, which is likely to be as early as later this month, is expected to establish Anthropic, the AI lab behind the viral Claude models, as a benchmark for how Wall Street values leading AI companies, including rival OpenAI.

The IPO push comes despite a once-busy fall listing calendar thinning out as choppy markets prompt companies to delay their offerings.

Analysts said that would give Anthropic access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions.

Growing investor uneasy with the debt-fuelled AI investment boom has led to a global sell-off in AI and tech stocks as they start to doubt if the trillions spent on data centres, chips and computing capacity will generate fast returns to support lofty valuations.

Increasing public opposition to data centres could limit investor enthusiasm for AI companies. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Investors assess Anthropic's value

Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $USUS1.5 trillion.

Anthropic said more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30 per cent of Global 2000 firms were customers generating at least $US100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30.

The case to go slow on AI is growing louder The federal government may have a big job ahead convincing voters that there are benefits to AI.

The IPO comes as Anthropic's own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviours including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation.

The findings have fuelled concerns about how companies can keep powerful AI systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially.

The ‌prospectus also highlighted risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit "self-preserving behaviours", including behaviour "resembling blackmail".

"Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures," it said.

Anthropic will trade on the Nasdaq after the IPO closes under the ticker symbol "ANT".

The filing did not reveal the terms of its offering, including the number of shares it plans to sell and the proposed price range.

Red hot growth predicted

Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers, was valued at $US965 billion in May in a funding round that drew some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and Wall Street.

"We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialisation, electricity, semiconductors and the internet," the prospectus said.

The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense for the foreseeable future.

Anthropic remains locked in a fierce battle with OpenAI to lead the race to build the most advanced AI systems.

The ChatGPT maker confidentially filed for an IPO in June and is expected to list by early 2027.

Anthropic's IPO follows that of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which rewrote the IPO record books in June, when it priced a $US75 billion offering that valued the company at $US1.75 trillion.

Reuters

World.title: Will Donald Trump or AI blow up financial markets first?
World.content:
It's an unpalatable choice.

But investors now are being forced to consider which poison will cause the least harm.

With civil unrest running rampant across the developed world, just as global investors are desperately seeking exits from the great artificial intelligence boom, a double dose of debt worries has suddenly infected the world of finance.

One is a problem decades in the making, as governments spent their way out of various crises with nary a care about the cost.

The other has arisen in a frighteningly short space of time, driven by a manic investment boom using trillions of dollars of borrowed cash to fund a technology with debatable benefits for society.

In the past eight weeks, the competing demands from those dual piles of debt have coalesced into a dramatic repricing on borrowing costs.

Financial markets are perennially worried about the next crisis.

But they now find themselves debating whether a sovereign debt crisis would be worse than an undoing of a technology boom that has driven stock markets since before the pandemic.

The one thing over which there is no dispute is that, if there is a meltdown, interest rates will provide the trigger.

Is the Firmus fiasco a crack in the AI boom? Amidst the wreckage of last week's failed mega capital-raising by data centre provider Firmus Technologies was a creeping sense that, once again, Australia had somehow fallen short.

The US Federal Reserve meets tonight and tomorrow, and while there is little chance of an official US rate hike this time around, markets are convinced that December will likely see an increase.

Either way, it's academic.

The US government has seen the cost of its long-term borrowings soar in recent months as bond markets, concerned about the mounting cost of its war in Iran coupled with massive tax cuts, have pushed debt costs higher.

America's debt is now equivalent to 126 per cent of its economic output, the highest it has been in the post-war era, with no plan to reverse the trend.

The annual interest cost on that $US40 trillion ($56 trillion) debt has topped $US1trillion, creating a snowballing budget deficit.

The great AI unravelling

They've been falling like bowling pins in recent weeks.

It began with the Firmus float flop, an audacious $44 billion grab for cash that may have gotten across the line just a few months earlier.

Last week, NextDC — a long-established Australian data centre builder with a strong track record — saw its share price plunge 42 per cent after Melbourne residents successfully delayed a monster computer shed in the suburbs.

Local dissent can delay or derail data centre projects, as NextDC found out. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

There was a similar incident in Sydney recently when Goodman Group canned a data centre in the northern suburbs.

It's a story resonating across the developed world.

CoreWeave, a US neocloud like Firmus that rents out its chips and computing power to AI firms, has seen its stock drop 36 per cent in the past month on concern over its mounting debts.

Being first on AI can come at a cost The federal government may have a big job ahead convincing voters that there are benefits to AI.

The Nasdaq exchange, which is dominated by global technology firms, has just endured its worst fortnight since April as developed nations collectively turn their backs on the build-out of AI architecture.

A recent Gallup poll in the US found 71 per cent of Americans opposed data centres. Of those questioned, only 53 per cent opposed nuclear power plants.

A continuation of those delays will dramatically slow the expected distribution of AI technology to businesses and firms.

That, in turn, could undermine revenue for AI firms and destabilise those that have taken on huge debts to fund their investment.

Those concerns have escalated dramatically in the past two months.

ASIC takes a deep dive

It's not all bad news.

Unlike the global financial crisis, where debt problems emerged out of left field, monetary authorities and market regulators are warning and preparing for the worst this time around.

In Australia, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is taking a helicopter view of national financial markets to ensure they are operating for the interests of all.

From the deeply troubled Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) to private credit markets, fixed income, commodities and foreign exchange, it is holding round table talks to improve their operation and eliminate friction points.

ASIC commissioner Simone Constant says the watchdog has two key themes running across all markets: resilience and transparency.

"Resilience gives you strength, transparency gives you trust," she says.

And the corporate watchdog is aware of the growing risk facing Australian investors and institutions.

Simone Constant says the regulator is observing market volatility not seen in a long time. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"Global markets are becoming more integrated and are open more hours than ever.

"Capital flows are going offshore as much as onshore because of the dominance of tech stocks.

" There's high and strategic risk … and giant pools of savings in Australia. "

During the 2008 financial crisis, a complete absence of transparency from ratings agencies, auditors and little-known corners of debt markets trading instruments that were mostly unregulated created panic across the financial system.

No-one knew who owed what or which bank held a toxic pile of worthless IOUs. As trust evaporated, the system ground to a halt.

Loading...

ASIC's overview won't stop a market crash. But it will limit the potential for regulators to be blindsided.

"We're seeing movements in spreads and volatility that we haven't seen for a long time," Constant notes.

The view from the helicopter may improve market efficiencies, she adds, the benefits of which will flow through to Australian investors, including those exposed through their superannuation funds.

"We don't want to be a regulator that fears the risk of the challenges ahead.

"It's about adapting to it with that trust and with that strength, that resilience and transparency give."

The AI payday

The prospect of a simultaneous blow-up of a sovereign debt crisis and a stock market collapse of hugely indebted companies terrifies many investors.

But there is a school of thought that argues that an implosion in one area may alleviate problems in the other, as interest rates would fall sharply.

Either way, it would still hurt.

Loading

In the early days, big tech companies funded their AI dreams through their enormous cash flows.

But as capital expenditures escalated and the boom expanded beyond the technology itself and into hardware like chips and then architecture like data centres, everyone turned to debt markets.

Even the giants, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, have raised more than $US200 billion between them this year alone.

Nvidia, the world's biggest company, has raised more than $US80 billion this year and routinely finances data centre firms like Australia's Firmus to roll out new data centres using its chips, making it a financier and supplier.

Bond market puts world on crisis trajectory If inflation remains stubbornly high in Australia, we can expect interest rates to rise and asset prices to go down. But it's that exact scenario that risks putting the global economy on the trajectory of another financial crisis.

Then there are the "innovative" financing arrangements such as "Special Purpose Vehicles" financed by industry suppliers and investors, along with what is known as "chip financing" as well as debt guarantees and lease arrangements that cloud the boundaries between financing definitions.

And these figures barely scratch the surface. Private credit firms, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and a host of financiers have gleefully handed over cash.

For years, technology and artificial intelligence have had investors enthralled and have driven stock markets to record levels.

Australia's superannuation funds have dived in with their ears pinned back, delivering double-digit returns to members.

But now comes the reckoning.

What if the rollout stalls because no-one wants a big humming data factory in their backyard?

What if China produces an ultra-cheap version of AI that undercuts Silicon Valley?

Or perhaps something more fundamental, like the pencilled-in sales revenue falls short and simply isn't enough to make the interest payments on the debt?

No wonder Wall Street is getting cold feet.

World.title: Economic pain collides with regulatory changes for small businesses
World.content:
Small businesses are unlikely to receive a reprieve from tough conditions, with another potential interest rate hike looming and fuel costs continuing to climb.

The unfavourable economic climate has collided with a string of policy changes facing operators, who say a growing regulatory burden has only increased their costs.

The changes include the introduction of payday super, a ban on debit and credit surcharges, an increase to minimum and award wages, and reforms to how trusts will be taxed.

Industry associations have voiced concerns about the cumulative impact on small firms, creating additional red tape at a time businesses were already navigating higher costs.

"It's just killing us, killing our industry," builder Steve Bright told The Business.

He went into construction for the love of the trade, but running his own firm, a typical day at work now looks very different.

"Instead of getting out and building a house, we're spending more than half our time in an office doing paperwork," he said.

New surcharge ban Surcharge bans are supposed to save consumers money but retailers say they're being forced to put prices up and are finding ways around the reforms.

He is one of about 2.7 million small business owners navigating the current conditions.

Mr Bright has hired extra staff to help implement the policy changes in his business.

" We've got full-time people that do it now ... it's just another cost that we've got to wear. "

Simon Croft from the Housing Industry Association said reforms have often been viewed in a "policy silo".

"It's that layering effect of simultaneous changes that then also … trickle down to their business operations."

Sunshine Coast designer and planner Debbie Johnson is rethinking her plans to pass her business onto her son after a tough year.

Debbie Johnson has run her small business on the Sunshine Coast for decades. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

"I really don't know that as a mother, I would like to see [my son] coming in and taking this business over. It's not like you work 38 hours a week and you get your holiday pay and your sick pay," she said.

"It's very difficult when you want to deliver services for your clients and, I suppose, the regulations that you're working within keep changing because it's disruptive to your focus of what your core business is."

Cashflow crunch worsening

The data demonstrates the cashflow crunch facing businesses at the same time as they adapt to regulatory change. An increasing number have fallen behind on payments.

Credit reporting agency CreditorWatch found "serious arrears" hit an 8.5-year high in September.

Its latest Business Risk Index showed more than 50 per cent of invoices were not paid on time.

One in 10 invoices were more than 60 days overdue, which CreditorWatch chief executive Patrick Coghlan said was the highest level of "serious arrears" since April 2018.

Patrick Coghlan warns more business insolvencies could come next year. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"Even though we're at almost record insolvency levels, the indicators that we're seeing show that that's likely to increase," he said.

"It's rarely one decision that gets made or one event that takes place that knocks a business over.

"It's generally [the] cumulative effect of all of these changes that really just continues to put pressure on small businesses."

Inflation and interest rate squeeze

In a week, the Reserve Bank's interest rate setting board will decide whether to increase borrowing costs for a fifth time this year.

Like households, many businesses have been squeezed by high inflation and rising rates.

Payday superannuation changes Payday super takes effect from next week, but some businesses are still unaware of the changes.

"The biggest single factor that is squeezing small business and the economy in general is higher fuel costs and therefore higher transport costs," said Westpac's chief economist, Luci Ellis.

The costs have then often been passed on to consumers, as with last month's ban on debit and credit surcharges, which saw hospitality venues increase their pricing.

"There have been a few instances of firms, particularly cafes, where it seems prices have increased even more [than the surcharge price]," Dr Ellis said.

" These are often places that have been dealing with other cost pressures, and this has just given them permission to adjust their prices. "

Luci Ellis says the biggest impact on inflation is fuel prices. ( ABC News: John Gunn )

Economic concerns overshadow regulatory changes

A survey by small business accounting platform MYOB found 38 per cent of small businesses have seen a drop in revenue from a year ago.

Loading...

Sixty-five per cent reported being concerned about cashflow for the coming year, and 69 per cent were worried about attracting new customers.

MYOB's chief executive, Paul Robson, said the payday super and surcharge policy changes have required small businesses to adapt.

"These two shifts have taken place within a relatively short period," he said.

"However, for the most part, our research suggests that concerns around regulatory changes are still behind cost factors including fuel, energy and interest rates."

The RBA estimates payment reforms will lower business costs by $910 million annually, but industry groups have reservations. (Unsplash: Blake Wisz)

Charlie Sheppeard, from competing accounting platform Xero, said slow sales growth in certain sectors made it harder to adapt to changes such as the surcharge ban.

"That leaves little room to absorb additional costs," he said.

"It is particularly challenging for sectors like retail and hospitality, where customer card transactions are common, and margins are already thin."

In a statement to the ABC, Small Business Minister Anne Aly said the government was aware businesses have been managing rising costs and adjusting to changes, and took the challenges seriously.

"That's why the Albanese Labor government is delivering billions in business tax relief," Dr Aly said, citing the $20,000 instant asset write-off being made permanent, and backing payment reforms, which the RBA has said will lower business costs by $910 million a year.

Watch The Business, Mondays to Thursdays 8:44pm on ABC News Channel, after the Late News on ABC TV, and anytime on ABC iview

World.title: US marine charged over Japanese woman's murder
World.content:
A US Marine has been charged over the murder and robbery of a woman in Japan's Okinawa prefecture while he was stationed there.

Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, has been accused of killing Anna Yagi in a hotel in the region's capital Naha and taking her wallet and backpack on October 3.

The 39-year-old woman appeared to have been strangled to death, according to police in local media reports.

Mr Ballard has denied the allegations.

"The case was indicted on October 25," a spokesman for the court in Naha confirmed to AFP.

The III Marine Expeditionary Force also said it was aware Mr Ballard had been charged.

"We recognise the seriousness of the charges and will continue to cooperate fully with Japanese authorities in their ongoing investigation as the legal process moves forward," it said in a statement.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by US military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions in the country to share the burden of hosting US troops.

US marine accused of murder in Japan Japanese police arrest a 20-year-old US marine in the Okinawa prefecture on suspicion of robbing and murdering a local woman.

Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi has said that officials were reviewing the off-base code of conduct for US troops following Ms Yagi's death.

The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of US military personnel, he said.

The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by US military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on US military personnel drinking in public off base between 1am and 5am or going to bars during those hours.

The US military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a month-long curfew.

The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Jordan arrests three relatives over deadly church attack
World.content:
Jordanian security forces have arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law following a shootout at an abandoned house.

The three are the suspected perpetrators of an attack at a Christian funeral that killed nine people and appear to have no ties to other cells, senior government security officials said.

"God willing, they only represent themselves," Jordan's Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah, said.

A map of the region the shooting took place. (Datawrapper)

Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East, and last week's attack on the Christian minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist".

Major-General al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism.

"The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells," Mr al-Faraya added.

The assault occurred during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, about 120km south-west of the capital, Amman, also wounded 34 others, alarming a Christian community.

At least 150 people were believed to be inside the church for a funeral when the shooting took place. (Reuters)

Witnesses said gunmen opened fire for several minutes.

The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials.

Video footage showed a building pockmarked by the exchange of fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate said in a statement carried by state media that security forces located the suspects while hiding in an abandoned house.

Nine were killed in the attack on the church with many more injured. (Reuters: Alaa Al Sukhni)

They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them.

No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects' possession.

There has been no claim of responsibility.

"Terrorism has no place among us," the directorate said.

It added the suspects had met their "just fate".

The Public Security Directorate did not name the suspects or publicly identify possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Mr al-Faraya said the authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable any participants in the attack.

Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past.

Reuters

World.title: Chris Brown avoids jail time over London nightclub brawl
World.content:
Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown has avoided prison time for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago.

The 37-year-old was given an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year.

He had faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to a count of affray in July for the attack on the dance floor of Tape, a private club in the swanky Mayfair neighbourhood in February 2023.

Video footage played in court showed Brown having to be pulled away from the victim, his former friend Abraham Diaw, after striking him twice in the head with a bottle.

"The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained," Judge Tony Baumgartner said in Southwark Crown Court.

Loading...

Despite the seriousness of the attack, Judge Baumgartner said Brown did not qualify for a custodial sentence because he pleaded guilty and there were several mitigating circumstances, including stable employment and charity work.

The judge acknowledged Brown's previous convictions but said he had maintained a clean record in recent years.

Previous brushes with the law

Brown has faced repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.

He has been arrested in several US states over altercations but was either not charged or prosecutors later dropped the charges. In 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape, but was released without charge.

Co-defendant rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who performs under the name Hoody Baby also pleaded guilty to affray. (Reuters: Jaimi Joy)

In return for his guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.

Brown's friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray and was given a four-month suspended sentence.

Affray is the use or threat of unlawful violence that leads someone to fear for their safety.

Brown apologises for the attack

Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said Brown played a leading role in the attack.

"By any circumstances, when one watches that footage, it is Mr. Brown that moves first," Ms Stonecliffe said.

Defense lawyer Sallie Bennett-Jenkins said Brown apologised to all those at the club that night, though she emphasised the attack lasted no more than 20 seconds.

"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Ms Bennett-Jenkins said.

"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr. Brown … offers a profound apology to all those present."

Mr Diaw was discharged from the hospital with head and knee injuries, Ms Stonecliffe said.

World.title: Liberal candidate's husband allegedly assaulted over campaign sign
World.content:
The husband of a Victorian Liberal Party candidate has allegedly been assaulted during a confrontation over election signs.

The party said the husband of Amanda Dow — the candidate for the seat of Yan Yean in Melbourne's outer north — was involved in an incident in Mernda on Sunday afternoon.

"We understand Ms Dow's husband approached a member of the public who was removing Liberal Party campaign signage and was allegedly assaulted," it said in a statement.

"He suffered facial injuries and was taken to hospital and was discharged today."

Amanda Dow campaigning in Mernda the day before the incident. (Supplied)

Police said a 59-year-old Mernda man was charged with recklessly causing injury, criminal damage and unlawful assault over an incident near Abundant Avenue and Bridge Inn Road at about 2pm.

"Police have been told the victim attended an address to retrieve political campaign signage when he was assaulted," a spokesperson said.

The accused has been released on bail to appear before Heidelberg Magistrates' Court on February 1.

The Liberal Party said it could not make any further comment on the matter.

"We ask that the privacy of Ms Dow and her husband be respected while he recovers," it said.

Yan Yean is held by Labor with a margin of 4.3 per cent.

World.title: Rescuers praised after hauling young dugong to safety
World.content:
Wildlife officials have hailed the "all hands" rescue of a young dugong tangled in a car fanbelt along Western Australia's north-west coast.

The globally vulnerable marine mammal was spotted struggling on Wednesday at Wapet Creek, a tidal estuary popular with flat fishers near Exmouth, 1,230 kilometres north of Perth.

Roughly two metres long, it took 15 responders less than 24 hours to return the dugong to deeper water.

"This was a smaller animal," said Sam Miles, acting marine program coordinator at WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA).

" But even a two-metre dugong can weigh a couple of hundred kilograms. "

The animal was wrapped in a cargo net before being hoisted over sand flats. (Supplied: DBCA)

The crew dubbed the dugong "Wapi" for the creek where it was found.

After assessing its health and contacting experts at Perth Zoo and the Sea World Foundation for advice, the group restrained the dugong before cutting it free.

They wrapped Wapi in a cargo net, hoisted it up from the shallows and over a sandbar back to sea.

Rescuers moved at a steady clip to get the marine mammal back in the water. (Supplied: DBCA)

Mr Miles said the team effort was "heartening".

"It took all hands on deck to lift the animal over the sand flats and back into the gulf," he said.

"Dugongs are endangered and we know that every dugong we save will help the overall population in the Exmouth Gulf."

Species under pressure

The dugong was caught in the rubber fanbelt of a car, bewildering its rescuers.

"We haven't seen entanglements in this kind of thing before, so we're not sure where it picked the entanglement up," Mr Miles said.

"It wasn't showing any signs of major distress, which was really important."

Sam Miles says a quick report from the public helped save the dugong. (Supplied: DBCA)

Exmouth Gulf is home to WA's second highest concentration of dugongs, behind Shark Bay.

But the gentle species is increasingly under threat around the country.

In the gulf, a record-breaking marine heatwave during the summer of 2025 devastated some seagrass stocks, scorching two varieties of the dugong's preferred food source.

Last month, aerial surveys of Queensland's Gulf of Carpentaria revealed its dugong population had suffered a 50 per cent drop in the past 20 years.

Huge dugong population decline The number of dugongs in the Gulf of Carpentaria has halved in the past two decades.

Helene Marsh, professor emeritus in conservation science at James Cook University, said she was "delighted" to see the animal move so strongly following its release.

"Australia's unquestionably the dugong capital of the world," she said, adding that they should be protected for animal welfare, scientific and cultural reasons.

"I think we're starting to understand we don't only need to protect animals because of their conservation significance, but we also need to think about their cultural significance."

Mr Miles said the rescue was a much-needed morale booster after a challenging year of entanglements off the remote Ningaloo coast.

"Sometimes we don't have the same positive outcomes," he said.

In a video captured by one of the DBCA staff, they can be heard calling out "yadiyarra”, or dugong in the language of the gulf's Baiyungu traditional owners, as it swims off.

"And stay out," one of the helpers said.

Cape Town: Nic Maddinson has been dropped and Steve Smith is yet to prove his fitness for the pivotal third Test against South Africa at Newlands. Maddinson, a late call-up to the team who made three low scores out of four innings as an opener, will join backup wicketkeeper Sam Harper in flying home early, with Josh Inglis and Cameron Green back to fitness. Smith, who batted briefly at the main session on Sunday, is still recovering from the neck injury that severely affected him in Gqeberha. Australia’s Nic Maddinson walks back to the pavilion after his dismissal in the second Test. AP His fitness status may also play a role in what happens with Marnus Labuschagne. Inglis and Green are both strongly in the mix to bat either in the top three or further down the order.



“He’s got a bit of a neck issue going at the moment. You guys would have seen that play out in the nets. I think he had about 20 odd minutes in the nets, give or take. Today he’ll progress that,” coach Andrew McDonald said of Smith. “He didn’t have his helmet on yesterday as well, so that’ll take part and hopefully progresses. We feel like it’s going to be a pretty steep progression in terms of he should be available. You’ll see that play out in terms of what happens. But we’re confident that he will be available.” Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Distinctly eerie’: Returning to Newlands for first time since ‘sandpapergate’ rocked cricket South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma confirmed on Monday that the hosts would choose firebrand fast bowler Gerald Coetzee to replace the injured Anrich Nortje. Coetzee has 14 wickets from four precious Tests at 23.57 and was notable for breaking the arm of Travis Head with a rising delivery in a 2023 ODI series, which forced Head to miss the early rounds of that year’s World Cup in India.



Australia's selectors are due to finalise their team later on Monday around their final training session ahead of a game they must win to retain the top spot on the ICC's Test rankings. Selection chair George Bailey said the panel would not be discarding Maddinson, and wanted him and Harper to return to Sheffield Shield ranks to make runs. “Would you like more runs? Yes, so that’s okay. Did it allow us to set the rest of the team up the way that we wanted to whilst we’re working with the group we have? Yes,” Bailey said. “We always talk about what do we see when we see players at their best. I think you saw a glimpse of that in the second innings in Durban. “With him going home, it was wanting to be clear to him it wasn’t a stopgap and that’s it, and it’s a discard. The same reasons that and process we work through to get him to be on the table for here, and ultimately to play.



“They’ll be the same questions that we’ll ask across the home summer to India as well. So, just being clear with he and Harps that, yeah, they were here for the right reasons, but yeah, more runs.” Bailey added that Labuschagne’s sequence of starts without making big scores was understandably being criticised, but the selectors had to weigh up whether his scores had value in the context of the forthcoming game. “We’re seeing some good things. Is there a block at the moment around 30s? Yes, still contributing in terms of his ability to get through a number of balls,” Bailey said. “So it’s a decision around what does that look like if it gets through there and again, what does it look like for the collective, is it helping others around him? Is it helping the team get a result that we ultimately want?” Matt Renshaw is set to return to opening after two Tests at number five, having prepared to play as an opener before the Green and Inglis injuries.

World.title: What’s up, what’s down: Which restaurants gained (and lost) hats in the new SMH Good Food Guide
World.content:
Eating outGood Food Guide What’s up, what’s down: Which restaurants gained (and lost) hats in the new SMH Good Food Guide Five eateries went from one to two hats, many won a hat for the first time, including a small gyros shop, and Sydney has its first Filipino hatted restaurant. Bianca Hrovat October 27, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Which restaurants gained and lost hats in the latest Good Food Guide? Dion Georgopolous; James Brickwood Restaurants didn’t need silver service, expensive wine pairings or even table reservations to receive a coveted chef’s hat at the 42nd annual Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide awards at Carriageworks on Monday as critics’ recommendations evolved to reflect the needs of contemporary Australian diners. More than 160 restaurants across NSW were recognised with at least one hat, many for the first time, after a team of anonymous restaurant critics spent six months independently reviewing more than 500 venues for the quality of their food, setting, value and hospitality. Among that number were five Sydney restaurants which rose from one to two hats - a four-fold increase from the previous year - including French bistro Porcine in Paddington, Crown restaurant Woodcut in Barangaroo and Neil Perry’s Italian phoenix Gran Torino, which replaced his Chinese restaurant Songbird in mid-2025. The Good Food Guide created the chef’s hat rating system more than 40 years ago to give readers a sense of what to expect in terms of food, service and experience, with value for money later added. Hats have been the cornerstone of Good Food’s rating system since.



Each restaurant reviewed in the guide is scored out of 20: 10 points for food, five for hospitality, three for setting and experience, and two for value. Restaurants scoring 15 or above are awarded one hat, those scoring 16 or 17 receive two hats, and those between 18 and 20 receive three hats. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Scores started to shift over the past three years as Good Food Guide co-editors Callan Boys and David Matthews encouraged a fresh approach to the unchanged 20-point scoring system: “We asked restaurant reviewers to consider the dining experience each venue aimed to achieve, rather than simply marking it against some imagined metric of fanciness,” said Matthews. The shift aimed to ensure the utility of the consumer guide by capturing exceptional venues across budgets, locations and cuisines. “Is Olympic Meats in Marrickville trying to do silver service or tweezer food?” he said. “Absolutely not, but its commitment to sourcing and DIY is almost unrivalled, with everything down to the pita made from scratch. And since it’s just a stone’s throw from Sydney’s Little Greece, it’s one of the most compelling places to see this city’s past and present collide.” The small, three-walled gyros restaurant overlooking Dulwich Hill station defied expectations this year by adding a wine service and delving deeper into chef-owner Timothy Cassimatis’ culinary roots with additional Peloponnese (southern Greek) dishes.



“There might be some pearl-clutching about it, but calling Olympic Meats a ‘gyros shop’ is like saying Cold Chisel is ‘just a pub band’,” Boys said. “Timothy Cassimatis puts as much work into his souvlaki and chips as any fine-dining chef.” It also takes a strong hospitality team to smooth over peak wait-times of more than an hour at the popular no-reservations venue, which relies on a QR-code queuing system. “Many were awarded a hat for the first time because they understood that making guests feel welcome and nourished, no matter how much they’re spending, is paramount,” Boys said. Olympic Meats was among the newly hatted in the 2027 edition of the Good Food Guide, alongside Tida Persian Food (North Willoughby), Avia (Darlinghurst), Farmhouse Kings Cross (Rushcutters Bay) and Takam in Darlinghurst, which became the first Filipino restaurant in Sydney to achieve 15/20, equalling a hat.



Takam head chef Francis Dela Cruz led the menu through several evolutions, landing the restaurant “right where it needed to be” at the intersections of familiarity, innovation and deliciousness, Boys said. It also served the tastiest skewers he’d eaten all year. Several high-profile restaurants regained their hat, including Potts Point legend Fratelli Paradiso, Paski Sopra (Paddington) and Arthur, which reopened its Surry Hills dining room with an a la carte menu in July. While there was a net gain to the number of hatted venues, CBD restaurants Loulou Bistro Martin Place, Tilda and The Gidley each lost theirs. Critics are instructed to maintain anonymity during their visits to ensure their dining experience reflects that of an everyday customer, and poor service was the greatest contributing factor to declining scores this year, Boys said.



“In one instance, a solo reviewer was mostly ignored in favour of the bigger tables of blokes ordering triple-digit bottles,” he said. “Plates weren’t refreshed, empty glasses were not refilled or removed, and staff offered little guidance … That restaurant no longer has a hat. “We understand that it’s important to look after the big-spender tables, but we also want to celebrate restaurants with staff trained to see a solo diner and think, ‘Right, I’m going to make sure this person eating alone has the best night possible.’ This is what real hospitality looks like.” The two-hat category gained 10 new entrants as “blistering hot first-timers” such as South End, Stanley and Omakase by Prefecture 48 entered the fray alongside fine-dining veterans such as Giovanni Pilu and Marilyn Annecchini, who opened Flaminia after two decades of success at Pilu at Freshwater, said Matthews. “Three Blue Ducks Burradoo winning two hats is huge for the group, but when the chefs’ CVs read Tetsuya’s, Quay and Sepia, anything less would almost have been a bigger surprise,” he said. Meanwhile, the upper echelon of fine dining contracted with the closure of acclaimed restaurants Quay and Oncore by Clare Smyth. For the first time since 1988, only two restaurants received three hats: Saint Peter (Paddington) and Sixpenny (Stanmore), the latter also named restaurant of the year.



Matthews said both restaurants had matured and strengthened their offering, becoming truly world-class. “What’s totally refreshing is that they’ve done it their own way,” he said. “It’s a generational shift happening right in front of us.” The winners of the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide Awards were announced on Monday, October 26, presented by Oceania Cruises and T2 Tea. Pick up a free 56-page Good Food Guide liftout in the Herald on Tuesday, October 27. The home of the Good Food Guide, the Good Food app is free for premium subscribers of the SMH and also available as a standalone subscription. You can download the app here.

World.title: The big mistake people with knee pain often make
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFitness The big mistake people with knee pain often make Gretchen Reynolds October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. As an orthopaedic surgeon for almost 30 years, Howard Luks has come to dislike one string of words that crops up constantly in his work. “Bone on bone,” he said. “I wish we could remove that phrase from medical discussions. I’ve seen it do so much unnecessary damage.” If there’s one thing you should do when you start to experience knee pain, it’s to keep moving. Getty Images Luks, 63, has built his medical practice, growing social media presence, and personal lifestyle and training around the idea that our joints, especially our knees, are capable of remaining strong and functional throughout life, with some basic care and feeding. He often writes and speaks about how knee pain, stiffness, tissue tears and even bone-on-bone osteoarthritis “don’t have to limit you”. They “don’t automatically require avoiding activities” you enjoy or need. They don’t mean you’re just getting old.



Related Article Wellness The exercise and lifestyle habits that can save your knees But they may signal that it’s time to rethink certain aspects of our lives and health. They almost certainly mean, Luks said, that it’s time to go for a walk. To learn more about how we can best protect and nurture our knees, I spoke to Luks about how knees work, why they sometimes fail, the surprising reasons they become arthritic – it’s not all wear and tear – the power of lifting and how he handles his own sometimes “cranky” knees. Why don’t you like the words “bone-on-bone”?



Over my career, I’ve had so many patients come to see me for a consultation or a second opinion, carrying an X-ray or an MRI scan, and they’ve been told they have bone-on-bone arthritis. So they think their knee is done, nonfunctional and they have to stop using it. They’re ready to quit running, playing tennis, using the stairs, even walking. And some of them weren’t feeling much, if any, knee pain before their diagnosis. But now they think they’re broken. They’re not? No. I tell people, “You are not your scan.” Just because someone has a meniscus tear [in the cartilage cushioning the knee bones], that doesn’t mean they’ll develop arthritis. And if they have some arthritis, it won’t necessarily progress to bone-on-bone. And if it does, even that doesn’t always mean they have to restrict activities. I have patients who are runners with bone-on-bone arthritis. They’re still running. But don’t running and other high-impact activities, even walking, wear away cartilage? I’m a runner, and people constantly tell me I’m ruining my knees. We’ve all heard that, but it’s a misconception. Moving and using the knee aren’t wearing away cartilage. Movement nourishes cartilage.



How so? Cartilage doesn’t have a blood supply, so it can’t get nutrients from blood. It gets nutrition only from synovial fluid [the viscous fluid filling the knee joint]. When you take a step, you bend and load the knee, which diffuses the synovial fluid around and through the cartilage, delivering nutrients. The same movement initiates cellular processes that prompt the cartilage to start building new collagen and repairing itself. Using your knees keeps them in shape. The biggest mistake people with knee pain make is not moving. Rest is a four-letter word for knees. Related Article Ageing The six biggest mistakes we make in midlife when it comes to knee health But if wear and tear aren’t causing arthritis, what is? It’s fair to say that the vast majority of cases of knee arthritis are not due to wear and tear. Some are. Knee injuries, like a torn ACL [a knee ligament] can change how people move, which contributes to wear and tear and, eventually, arthritis. Genetics play a role, too, though studies show it’s generally small. Being heavy also isn’t a major promoter of arthritis, which may seem counterintuitive. But people with obesity develop hand arthritis more often than people without obesity, which doesn’t make sense if arthritis is caused by excessive loading from body weight.



Then what’s left? For me, based on the latest [scientific] literature, osteoarthritis is primarily a metabolic disease. Remember, cartilage is replenished by synovial fluid. We now know that fluid reflects your metabolic state. If you have metabolic problems, such as diabetes or other conditions, your blood will contain inflammatory molecules. Some of them will find their way into the joint fluid and then into your cartilage and set off inflammatory processes there. They also change certain cells that line the joint. In a healthy knee, these cells release substances that help cartilage regenerate. But in an inflamed knee, they switch character and start pumping out substances that make it harder for cartilage to repair itself. Now you have a knee primed to deteriorate and become arthritic. That process didn’t start inside the knee, though. It began with whole-body metabolic issues. Going for a 10-minute walk every day is a small thing you can do to nurture your knee health. Getty Images So, what can we do to avoid or deal with aching knees if we do have them? My first ask with my patients is for them to walk 10 minutes every day. I tell them that exercise, almost any exercise, loads the joint and has benefits for metabolic health. But it’s good to start with something easy and achievable that most of us could do on the busiest or worst day of our lives. And if it winds up being seven minutes, not 10, that’s OK, and if it’s 12, that’s even better. Ultimately, I want them to walk for 30 to 60 minutes a day, if at all possible. Walking is medicine for arthritis. It improves metabolic health, lowers inflammation and decreases pain.



I also want them to strength train, which helps to stabilise and take some of the stress off the knee. Some of them worry they’re not capable of exercise, though. They’ll say, “Oh, I can’t do this; I’m old”, or they think it’ll hurt or make their joints worse. And I tell them the truth: that it may feel hard or uncomfortable. But that doesn’t mean they can’t do it, or that they’ll grind cartilage away. You can feel discomfort without causing damage. And getting older doesn’t mean you can’t still train and adapt and grow. Is that true even for people whose knee pain is intense? In that situation, I usually tell people that, with some work, their pain can probably get better. But it’ll take time. By the time we’re in our 50s or 60s, very few things get better in just a few weeks. But for most people, even those in pain, strength training or walking can pay huge dividends. And for those who tell me, “I did all that and my knee is still killing me”, that’s why we do knee replacements. What does your workout routine look like?



Well, I’m a bit of a lunatic. I regularly do 500 to 600 minutes a week of aerobic activity, but everything counts towards that. If I take my dogs for a hike, that counts. So does a six-kilometre walk. And I run three or four days a week, six to eight kilometres. I used to do a long run on Sundays, 16 to 24 kilometres. I don’t any more. I never want today’s workout to ruin tomorrow’s, and if I ran that long, I’d be wiped out the next day. Instead, to get my aerobic volume, I do long bike rides once or twice a week on an indoor trainer. It’s set up in front of a TV. I put on a movie and ride for two hours. It’s easy. I’m also a rock climber. I just love the functional movements when you climb. And the grip strength. I do that once or twice a week. That’s my treat. And I weight train, three days a week, minimum. I focus on adding muscle mass and strength, along with rotational work, power, balance and quickness. You need all of that for joint health and to maintain balance and avoid falls. Are your knees still in good shape? I have meniscus tears in both knees. The first happened 11 or 12 years ago. Most people over the age of 50 probably have a meniscus tear, even if their knees feel fine. So far, there’s no significant arthritis in either of my knees. My right knee does get a bit cranky on long runs. That hasn’t stopped me from running. I also do exercises at the gym that involve twists, turns and jumps, though they’re not always easy on my knees. But they’re foundational movements. If you don’t practise them sometimes, you’ll probably start avoiding them in your life, and then the narrowing starts.



Related Article Sponsored

Ageing The health costs nobody warns you about once you turn 60 Bec Wilson Money contributor The narrowing? I’m 63, and what I’ve seen in many people my age is that life starts to grow smaller as people rearrange their lives around what they see as limitations. They stop taking the stairs because stairs can be hard if you have sore knees. But then they don’t visit friends who have houses with stairs. Or they don’t go to the movies because they’d have to walk too far from the parking lot. Or they don’t take their grandkids to the park or play with them on the floor because they’re worried they won’t be able to get up. And their world starts to narrow dramatically. They may not see it at first. But the more you avoid things, the more you lose the ability to do them, even if you later decide you want to. You’re also not helping your knees because you’re moving less and less. I’ve seen this narrowing in my patients, my friends. I was worried about it in myself. So I made a conscious decision a few years ago to change my workouts, to make sure I was doing things that I might have thought I’m too old to do. So now I’m jumping on and off boxes and hopping from side to side at the gym. I want healthy knees, sure. But, even more, I want to build and strengthen the capabilities I need to broaden my life and keep it fun and interesting for years to come. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

World.title: Avoid the long drive: Where to stay near Sydney’s new airport
World.content:
InspirationNew South Wales Avoid the long drive: Where to stay near Sydney’s new airport Katherine Scott October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The takeoff of the first commercial passenger flight at Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport on Sunday marks a new chapter for the region, officially unlocking western Sydney as an emerging tourism hub for local and overseas visitors. Jetstar made history with the airport’s inaugural flight to the Gold Coast, and international services launched on Monday when Air New Zealand’s flight NZ165 arrived from Auckland. Singapore Airlines, Vietjet, Fiji Airways and Qatar Airways are set to roll out routes from now and into 2027. Right now, the journey from central Sydney to the airport takes about 50 minutes by car, or a whopping one hour, 45 minutes on public transport (or the airport shuttle bus takes about an hour and costs $55). So for the thousands of passengers soon to pass through Australia’s first major new airport in half a century, the question remains – where to stay? Efforts to bump up room capacity at the terminal have stalled following the collapse of the construction firm behind its only planned hotel, a Courtyard by Marriott. This has left a significant shortage of hotels within a 20-kilometre radius of the airport, prompting declarations of a hotel crisis.



The lack of immediate rooms means that, at least initially, travellers will have to look further afield. But that’s no bad thing – it gives passengers the perfect excuse to explore western Sydney’s dynamic and delicious surrounding hubs. 



Pullman Sydney Penrith One of the guest rooms at Pullman Sydney Penrith. Penrith’s new flagship five-star stay is proof the outer west is ready for its close-up. Wrapped in a rippling glass facade by acclaimed Turner Studio, its 152 high-design rooms feature luxe Hunter Lab amenities and an in-room tablet “Sleep Therapy Menu” for custom pillow orders. In-house Marcel Bar and Bistro plates up WA lobster linguine, while the surrounding Panthers Precinct offers a lively playground of dining and activities. For a limited time, guests can flash a WSI boarding pass at check-in for an airport launch Flight Recovery Kit with chamomile tea, caramel fudge, and a sleep mask. Distance to airport: 25 kilometres (20 to 25 minutes’ drive). See pullmanpenrith.com.au Novotel Sydney Cabramatta, Canley Vale Poolside tranquillity just moments from Cabramatta’s vibrant dining scene.



From lounging poolside to exploring Australia’s most dynamic Asian culinary enclave, this modernised stay delivers on all fronts. Cabramatta’s deep Vietnamese roots have earned it the title “Little Saigon” but its food scene stretches far beyond world-class pho to Laotian, Cambodian and regional Chinese flavours. Part of the $230 million Cabravale Club Resort redevelopment, the hotel is an ideal launchpad for food safaris – though staying in for fire-powered dining at Magma by Dany Karam is equally tempting. Distance to airport: 24 kilometres (25 to 30 minutes’ drive). See all.accor.com The William Inglis Hotel - MGallery, Warwick Farm Paddock-to-plate dining and equestrian charm at The Newmarket Room at The William Inglis Hotel. A deep-seated passion for thoroughbred racing doesn’t stop this Riverside Stables retreat from delivering serious luxury. The real highlight? A heated rooftop pool deck where you can soak up the sun while watching horses work the track below. Downstairs, grand staircases lead to paddock-to-plate steaks at The Newmarket Room, with tranquil Georges River walking trails right on your doorstep. Distance to airport: 28 kilometres (30 to 32 minutes’ drive). See williaminglis.com.au One Global Resorts Parramatta



An urban oasis in the city … One Global Resorts Parramatta. The name sounds more corporate insurance firm than boutique sanctuary, but for a stylish base in Parramatta, the rebranded One Global Resorts Parramatta (formerly Skye Suites) delivers. Set within V by Crown Group’s “vertical village”, its 72 spacious suites pair sleek architecture with resort-level perks – a 25-metre outdoor pool, a sauna and a gym – all steps from Parramatta Square, Westfield, and the station. Distance to airport: 33 kilometres (35 to 45 minutes’ drive). See oneresortsparramatta.com.au Astina Suites Penrith Twilight tones at Theo’s Rooftop Bar and pool, at Astina Suites Penrith. Related Article Aviation Wheels up for Australia’s newest major airport as first flight takes off Located moments from the Great River Walk and downtown Penrith’s dining hubs and artisan bakeries, this apartment-style sanctuary delivers serious resort-level indulgence. A special mention goes to Theo’s Rooftop Bar, where you can catch a superb sunset while sipping cocktails by an infinity pool and pretending you’re in Mallorca or somewhere equally Mediterranean-coded and lush. The on-site Reset Recovery Studio — complete with a spa, sauna, and ice baths — makes it almost impossible to leave the building. Distance to airport: 24 kilometres (22 to 25 minutes’ drive). See astinasuites.com.au
