Only one family attended a recent open home inspection of a contemporary four-bedroom house in Waverley for rent for $3750 a week. “Anthony Lark” and his wife, Hayley, wandered from room to room as their two daughters filmed videos to show their big brother what they hoped would be their new home. Everyone was delighted that each of the kids could have their own bedroom. The sunny open-plan living room and marble kitchen were a hit. Within 10 minutes of his arrival, Lark announced he wanted it. Kim Anthony Sarkin, also known as Anthony Lark, has defaulted on the rent on at least eight multimillion-dollar houses. Aresna Villanueva Lark’s rental application was as good as it gets: an excellent reference from his former Bondi landlord Charles Levy, a copy of his passport, a bank statement, a recent Origin Energy bill, and a reference from his manager at NovaData Consulting, Sandy Galvin. But it was all fake. There is no former landlord called Charles Levy, nor Sandy Galvin at NovaData Consulting; the passport had been doctored, as were the energy bill and bank statement, and there is unlikely to be any “excellent” reference from Lark’s former landlord in Bondi because he didn’t pay his rent.



That’s because Lark’s real name is Kim Anthony Sarkin, a serial rent fraudster who has defaulted on the rent he owes on at least eight multimillion-dollar houses across the eastern suburbs from Vaucluse to Bronte in the two years since he and his family moved to Sydney. All but one of Sarkin’s landlords have taken legal action through the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal in a bid to evict Sarkin and Hayley, their three children and two dogs from seven of those homes. In the process, they have revealed allegations of fake references and doctored receipts for purported rent and bond payments. Agents who have unwittingly handed over the keys of their top rentals to Sarkin say the backlog of cases before NCAT means Sarkin can live rent-free for three to four months before eviction orders are handed down. His unpaid rent bill has grown to more than $120,000. The four-bedroom house in Waverley that Sarkin applied to rent under his pseudonym Anthony Lark. Domain



Fortunately for agent Justine Kidnie, Lark’s application didn’t make it far before her suspicions were raised by a discrepancy on the payslip and Hayley Lark’s curious inability to recall her current address. “He didn’t actually get past first base with me, so I never worried about the fact his referee never responded. By that time I’d realised who he was,” said Kidnie. It wasn’t the first time Sarkin had allegedly lodged fraudulent documents in the name of his alter ego in a bid to rent yet another luxury residence in the beachside eastern suburbs. Anthony Lark’s name first appeared on a rental application in July, a few weeks after this masthead revealed Sarkin’s rental history. The application was for a four-bedroom house with a swimming pool in North Bondi on offer for $3500 a week. The North Bondi house that was listed for rent for $3500 a week when Anthony Lark applied to rent it. Domain



He wasn’t successful, but the doctored documents prompted leasing agent Henry Farage to take the matter to the police. A NSW Police spokesperson confirmed there was an investigation into alleged fraudulent activity, but no further action was taken. Sarkin, a data and AI governance specialist from South Africa, did not respond to questions. He has previously denied doctoring any bond payment receipts. Sarkin claimed this year that he intends to pay back the landlords once he gets his financial situation under control. “It’s not like I set out to create a problem. These things have happened, which is really unfortunate. There was never any intent to harm these people,” he said. Sarkin moved to Sydney from New Zealand in late 2024. At the time, his New Zealand business consultancy had been placed in receivership, and soon after ordered into liquidation by the Auckland High Court, owing almost $NZ1 million ($820,000) in unpaid taxes. He has since declared himself bankrupt in New Zealand.



Kim and Hayley Sarkin pictured in an Instagram post. Instagram The house in Auckland he claimed he owned as part of his rental application for the Waverley home is actually owned by his former landlord, Tony Wallace, who is still owed $NZ8000 in outstanding rent from Sarkin. Related Article Exclusive

Investigation The many multimillion-dollar homes of a ‘professional ratbag’ Corporate records show Sarkin recently set up a Sydney-based AI firm called NovaData Consultancy with an AI-generated website. The company is not to be confused with the Brisbane-based business intelligence and AI consultancy Nova Data, with which Sarkin has no relationship. The email address for the “manager” at the Sydney-based firm, Sandy Galvin, was registered this month by Kim Sarkin. World.title: Of all Melbourne’s sandwiches, these are the ones our critic happily drives an hour for
World.content:
Review Eating outBentleigh Of all Melbourne’s sandwiches, these are the ones our critic happily drives an hour for With Italian, Greek and Australian influences, Suburbia Deli’s sandwiches are “a perfect Melbourne story” between two slices of bread. And for Besha Rodell, they also take her straight back to New York’s delis. Besha Rodell October 27, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

1 / 8 Suburbia Deli makes some of the most generous sandwiches going around. Pete Dillon 2 / 8 Suburbia Deli’s Bentleigh location was added this year. Pete Dillon 3 / 8 The No. 3: Roast beef, provolone cheese, rocket, semi-dried tomato and sauerkraut. Pete Dillon 4 / 8 The No. 6: Mortadella, leg ham, salami, provolone cheese, tomato and pickled chillies. Pete Dillon 5 / 8 The menu includes 10 sandwiches, plus a few savoury and sweet baked goods. Pete Dillon 6 / 8 A friend of the owners bakes the brownies and cookies. Pete Dillon 7 / 8 Spanakopita is made to a family recipe. Pete Dillon 8 / 8 Both the Mordialloc and Bentleigh locations sell quality pantry goods too. Pete Dillon Previous Slide Next Slide 13.5 / 20 Critics' Pick How we score Suburbia Deli Cafe$$$$ We are living in a golden age of sandwiches here in Melbourne, a boom that shows no signs of slowing. But where, among all of this focaccia and Turkish bread, are the New York deli sandwiches? We have New York pizza and New York bagels, so why not the sandwiches? I’m not talking about the huge Reubens you get at Katz’s and other Jewish delis. I’m talking about the more workaday hoagie, hero and grinder, bought from a deli (or bodega, depending on the neighbourhood and, honestly, the ethnicity of the proprietor). My love affair with these sandwiches began during my first week of grade 12 when I, at a new high school in Tarrytown outside of New York City, was taken to the North Tarrytown Deli by a girl named Jackie. She ordered a sandwich on a hoagie roll with smoked turkey, muenster cheese, lettuce, mayo and salt and pepper. This sandwich was such a revelation – the bread soft, the lettuce cut on the slicer so it was shredded and crunchy, the turkey sliced thin but stacked thick – that it remains my order in New York delis to this day.



Suburbia Deli’s Bentleigh location was added this year. Pete Dillon In other parts of America, I’ll order some kind of Italian sub or grinder, usually multiple kinds of meat on that same long roll. In Australia, the closest we tend to come is a conti or continental roll, most prevalent in Western Australia but gradually becoming more available in Melbourne, too. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up What’s more common is the far more Italian panini or focaccia sandwich, which many establishments are doing beautifully. But I find focaccia too sproingy, too much of a distraction, and the filling never seems to be hearty enough to overcome the personality of the bread. Which is why, on a whim, I found myself driving an hour from home towards Suburbia Deli in Bentleigh on a recent rainy Wednesday, lured by the photos I’d seen on social media of something very closely resembling a New York Italian deli sandwich. Suburbia Deli scratches an itch for me and my own nostalgia, but it will do the same for someone else with a very different background, which is part of its beauty. What I found was something akin to a hybrid, a sandwich influenced by Italy and Australia and, interestingly, the weekend sandwich traditions of one Melbourne Greek family. What I was not, was disappointed. Suburbia Deli is a fantastic addition to Melbourne’s sandwich landscape, and it’s already growing.



The first shop was opened in Mordialloc in June of last year, with a second location added in May in Bentleigh. The deli is a multi-generational family affair. Maria and Angelo Georgopoulos, who have been in hospitality for decades, co-own the shops with their son Nico and his wife Marissa. Nico remembers his parents bringing home cold cuts, cheese and bread each weekend after he and his siblings played team sports, the whole family making sandwiches together. For Suburbia, a family friend makes all the cookies and brownies, and Nico’s best man does the shop fit-outs. They’re growing quickly, and are in the midst of building a third location in Parkdale, which they hope will allow for more in-house production of sweets and non-sandwich savoury goods. The No. 6 sandwich, with its deli meats and pickled chillies, is similar to a New York hoagie. Pete Dillon The defining characteristic of Suburbia’s sandwiches is generosity: meats and toppings are piled on so that there is far more filling than bread. The secondary feature is that bread, which is a soft oblong roll developed especially for the Georgopouloses by Bakery Lievito in Carrum Downs. It is soft inside, with a medium-crunchy exterior, engineered to be appropriate for fresh or grilled sandwiches. I prefer most of these sandwiches fresh, but that may be my New York nostalgia talking. There’s no turkey and muenster, and no build-your-own option, but the No. 6 – which comes with mortadella, leg ham, salami, provolone cheese, tomato and pickled chillies – does a lot to satisfy the Italian grinder itch. And some of them do beg to be toasted, like the No. 3, a roast beef, provolone and sauerkraut number that gets all melty in the best ways when given some heat.



I’m excited for the Parkdale location, if only because it might bring more of the Georgopouloses’ home cooking to the fore. Right now, the spanakopita – made from grandma’s recipe, all dill- and lemon-forward in a melting filo casing – offers a delicious glimpse into what that might entail. Spanakopita is made to a family recipe. Pete Dillon We love sandwiches for all kinds of obvious reasons, but one is that we don’t need chefs or even particularly ambitious home cooks to do them extremely well. They are part of our home life, part of our cafe life and a beautiful example of the ways in which our various ethnic traditions collide between two slices of bread. Suburbia Deli scratches an itch for me and my own nostalgia, but it will do the same for someone else with a very different background, which is part of its beauty. Mostly, these are some of the best sandwiches around, made by one family for their wider community with huge amounts of love. What a perfect Melbourne story. The low-down Atmosphere: Bright, modern, cheerful Go-to dishes: No. 6 ($18); No. 3 ($18); spanakopita ($12) Drinks: Italian and regular soft drinks, coffee Cost: About $40 for two



Related Article Crackling pork banh mi, half-kilo pastrami toasties: 15 must-try Melbourne sangas Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: NSW Liberals abandon YIMBY truce as housing goes on the ballot
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament NSW Liberals abandon YIMBY truce as housing goes on the ballot Max Maddison October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Minns government’s planning reforms will be on the ballot in March as Liberal MPs break from a pro-YIMBY stance to criticise developments in their backyard and argue Labor’s push for more housing is unsupported by the necessary infrastructure. A year after then-opposition leader Mark Speakman declared the party was “unashamedly YIMBY”, Liberal MPs have become increasingly vocal in their criticism of Labor’s planning reforms, with one labelling the policies “destructive” and another saying some developments “lack social licence”. The NSW Liberals have broken a pro-YIMBY detente ahead of the election, attacking the government for failing to deliver infrastructure. Steven Siewer As the state grapples to materially lift the construction of housing and vocal community groups oppose developments in their neighbourhoods, bipartisan support for the government’s suite of housing policies appears to be on the verge of shattering as Liberal MPs draw battle lines over development in Sydney. A Labor strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity to speak freely, said that a year ago, they believed housing could have been a defining issue at the state election. Today, with One Nation in the ascendancy and migration an increasingly toxic issue, they no longer believed full-throated support for greater supply was a guaranteed vote winner.



Liberal MPs in inner Sydney electorates confirmed to this masthead they would run local campaigns against aspects of the Minns government’s planning reforms at the next election, arguing infrastructure commitments had not kept pace with increased housing supply. Planning Minister Paul Scully attacked the party’s argument as evidence of having “settled back into their anti-housing NIMBY tendencies” and returning to a default setting that housing growth solely belongs in western Sydney. Liberal MP Stephanie di Pasqua says the government’s vision displayed contempt for her marginal Sydney seat. Rhett Wyman “While the Young Liberals appear to still believe in the need to fix our housing challenges, their elected representatives are crab walking away from it and waiting for policy direction from One Nation,” he said. First-term Drummoyne MP Stephanie Di Pasqua earlier this month attacked the “massive and unprecedented” proposal to build 60,000 more homes in her electorate over 15 years, saying the government’s vision demonstrated “contempt” for her inner-west electorate.



“I want my community to know that if they vote Labor, they will get 50 storeys in almost every suburb. Labor’s planning policy is destructive,” she said. Held by 1285 votes, Drummoyne will be heavily targeted by Labor as it seeks to offset expected losses elsewhere and retain power. Matt Cross – whose safe Davidson electorate covers swaths of the north shore – used a speech in parliament in June to criticise the government’s transport-oriented development policy and use of state significant development pathways as “controversial”. “I repeat: those SSDs (state significant developments) lack social licence and community support because they were in Labor’s controversial TOD (transport oriented development) zone and not in the Ku-ring-gai housing strategy. Before people jump to give the community and me a label, I remind them that we live in a vibrant democracy,” he said.



Opposition planning spokesman Chris Rath accused the government of playing “postcode politics”, saying they only supported density “so long as it’s not in their backyard”. Editor's pick Sydney beyond 2026 Sydney’s booming population won’t kill the great Australian dream, but it will change it “For local communities to embrace new developments and to make a dent into the housing crisis, the government must provide the funding to address schools that are already overcrowded, roads that are gridlocked, and local hospitals under strain,” he said. The government’s planning policies would be one of the top-tier issues at the March election, frontbencher Tim James confirmed, saying his electorate felt shut out of planning decisions. “The Willoughby community is deeply concerned about the scale of development being imposed without proper consideration of the infrastructure and services needed to support it,” he said.



In the neighbouring seat of Lane Cove, veteran MP Anthony Roberts said the government’s planning policies would deliver a “sugar hit” of supply followed by an “awful crash” which would require significant taxpayer funds to remedy the lack of strategic planning. “You can’t put in massive unit towers with little parking with the expectation people use public transport when there’s no public transport,” he said. North Shore MP Felicity Wilson said development was the No.1 issue in her electorate, saying the government had shoehorned a 35 per cent increase in housing supply into one Mosman suburb without investing in infrastructure. Similarly, Hornsby MP James Wallace also criticised the proposed rezoning around the Cherrybrook Metro station, which is slated to deliver 10,000 homes. “There is no plan. No transparency on what infrastructure is actually required. No accountability to ensure it is delivered,” he said. The case against the government’s planning reforms comes a year after Speakman used a speech at a housing conference to define his party as being pro-development after an unconvincing attempt to straddle both sides. He acknowledged his support was largely driven by the party’s lack of appeal to younger voters, saying: “A way to reverse that, I think, is to be aggressively pro-housing.”



Related Article City life The developers, the courtrooms and the battle over what gets built in Sydney In November, the opposition supported the government’s reforms of the planning system. A Labor strategist said housing had become a “no win” issue for both sides, despite spending three years establishing the party’s pro-development bona fides. “It’s not the thing we’re battling on or wanting to battle on,” he said. “You have to acknowledge it is an issue you don’t win votes on. I don’t think this election will be defined on our or the Liberals’ position on housing.” A senior Labor source argued the Liberals’ inconsistency on planning policy would be exposed during the campaign, saying their criticism of the government’s planning policies would require them to articulate a realistic alternative plan. In the latter part of last century, Melbourne’s inner south was the epicentre of its youth culture and Fitzroy Street – with its grand old George Hotel, cafes, bars and late-night clubs of varying respectability – attracted a mix of bohemians, backpackers, sex workers, musicians and assorted characters. These days, the city’s cool crowd may have migrated north to Fitzroy, Collingwood and Brunswick, but St Kilda has never entirely surrendered its rock’n’roll soul. Artist’s impression of Novotel St Kilda’s foyer area. Fitzroy Street, though, had been off the boil for some years, given over to closed shopfronts and unsavoury elements. After closing in 2015, the legendary Esplanade Hotel (AKA The Espy, not quite on Fitzroy Street but just around the corner), reopened in 2018 after a spectacular transformation that, some might argue, filed away its rough edges.



In 2021, the street gained a significant cultural landmark when Australia’s first purpose-built LGBTQIA+ community hub, the Victorian Pride Centre, was established. 



The former Novotel St Kilda was demolished to make way for the luxury Saint Moritz apartments in 2019, but the brand’s new incarnation is a more intimate affair, with 80 rooms and a $15 million transformation. The hotel, previously operated as Rydges St Kilda, has undergone a comprehensive redesign with public spaces by Rebecca Trenorden of Versa and guestrooms and corridors by Dezign. Artist’s impression of the Novotel’s food and beverage space. At the heart of the hotel is a reworked internal garden atrium, which brings natural light into the building and connects its public spaces. The ground floor is designed to engage locals as well as visitors, with the new Urban Kitchen & Bar which can accommodate up to 120 diners and includes private dining spaces.



There’s also a flexible coworking area, while conference and event facilities cater for groups of up to 140. A rooftop event space adds a fresh-air dimension. Related Article ★★★★

Hotel reviews As a travel writer, here’s where I stay in Melbourne when I’m paying Post refurbishment, its developer Erdi has donated furniture and fittings from the old Saint Kilda Beach Hotel to the Sacred Heart Mission and written cheques for local charities. Some things about St Kilda remain constant: the beach, St Kilda Pier, the Palais Theatre, Luna Park and trams that connect the neighbourhood to central Melbourne. And whatever its changing fortunes, there’s still nowhere else in Melbourne quite like it. See novotelstkilda.com.au

World.title: Labuschagne set to play, Smith battles injury after Maddinson dropped for Newlands
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Labuschagne set to play, Smith battles injury after Maddinson dropped for Newlands Daniel Brettig Updated October 27, 2026 — 5:00am ,first published 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Town: Marnus Labuschagne is set to play in the Newlands Test and Steve Smith has been challenged to push through a neck injury as selectors also ponder the inclusion of Cooper Connolly and Nathan Lyon for a showdown game against South Africa with the world number one ranking at stake. While Nic Maddinson has already been dropped and is with Sam Harper on his way home to the Sheffield Shield, Smith batted comfortably enough for around 35 minutes, but then needed a brief break to stretch his neck, before returning for another five minutes. Marnus Labuschagne during the second Test. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Labuschagne skipped the session entirely, as the tourists have decided his issues are largely mental in nature, and will be hoping he is refreshed for Tuesday’s first ball. Matt Renshaw will return to the top of the order, while Cameron Green is likely to return at number five. If Smith is not fit to play, his place would be taken by Josh Inglis.



“You don’t play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you’re not 100 per cent fit, so hopefully that’s the case this week,” captain Pat Cummins said. “Even though he’s probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he’s done many times before with other things, and can come out and ... contribute like he does every week.” Australia’s Nic Maddinson has been dropped. AP Coach Andrew McDonald, selection chair George Bailey, skipper Cummins and deputy Travis Head were seen in a thoughtful conference by the Test pitch, perhaps debating the merits of Nathan Lyon versus Scott Boland on a dry surface expected to require an attritional brand of cricket. Beau Webster later had a long chat with Bailey that seemed to strengthen the case for Cooper Connolly’s inclusion.



“I think that’s always the questions around anyone with selection really. If you’re going to bring in a known quantity versus someone that you’re not too sure about, both have positives to it,” Cummins said. “I said I think anywhere in the world, batting top three is really tough, and Marnus is doing the hard work. He’s facing quite a few balls, getting himself in. So, you think about all those things when you come up to the final 11.” Of Lyon, Cummins said it was most likely a straight-up duel with Boland for the final spot. “One is you’ve got Scotty Boland there, who averages whatever it is, something ridiculous, and it was storming and cloudy for a couple [of] days, and so largely conditions based,” Cummins said.“We know Nath’s quality, he’s played 140 Tests. We’re desperate for him to play as much as possible.” In a message that could have easily been directed at Labuschagne, Cummins said his batsmen needed to think in terms of partnerships for the team rather than career-affirming huge scores.



“That kind of investment in each other’s game and working together out there, I think that’s a pretty good path forward,” he said, referring to Boland’s Gqeberha union with Head. “Your tendency is if you’re a little bit out of form or out of runs, you try so hard again that next week. “You want to so desperately get the match-winning 100, you can sometimes lose sight of maybe what the team needs from you at that moment, or what’s the game demanding of you and that’s just been the chats around this week – What can you do for the team? How can you help each other out? “There’s no better feeling [in] cricket than when you’re having a beer after the Test after everyone’s made little contributions along the way that have added up to a match-winning effort, so yeah, don’t get caught up in the ‘I need 200 to kick-start my career again’. It’s what you can bring this week to help each other perform.” Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Distinctly eerie’: Returning to Newlands for first time since ‘sandpapergate’ rocked cricket South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma confirmed on Monday that the hosts would choose firebrand fast bowler Gerald Coetzee to replace the injured Anrich Nortje – victory would allow the Proteas to usurp Australia on top of the ICC Test ranking, having already claimed the World Test Championship.



Coetzee has 14 wickets from four previous Tests at 23.57 and was notable for breaking Head’s arm with a rising delivery in a 2023 ODI series, which forced Head to miss the early rounds of that year’s World Cup in India. Selection chair Bailey said the panel would not be discarding Maddinson, and wanted him and Harper to return to Sheffield Shield ranks to make runs. “Would you like more runs? Yes, so that’s okay. Did it allow us to set the rest of the team up the way that we wanted to whilst we’re working with the group we have? Yes,” Bailey said. “We always talk about what do we see when we see players at their best. I think you saw a glimpse of that in the second innings in Durban. “With him going home, it was wanting to be clear to him it wasn’t a stopgap and that’s it, and it’s a discard. The same reasons … and process we work through to get him to be on the table for here, and ultimately to play.”



Bailey added that Labuschagne’s sequence of starts without making big scores was understandably being criticised, but the selectors had to weigh up whether his scores had value in the context of the forthcoming game. “We’re seeing some good things. Is there a block at the moment around 30s? Yes, still contributing in terms of his ability to get through a number of balls,” Bailey said. “So it’s a decision around what does that look like if it gets through there and again, what does it look like for the collective, is it helping others around him? Is it helping the team get a result that we ultimately want?” Loading Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: What’s up, what’s down: Which restaurants gained (and lost) hats in the new SMH Good Food Guide
World.content:
Eating outGood Food Guide What’s up, what’s down: Which restaurants gained (and lost) hats in the new SMH Good Food Guide Five eateries went from one to two hats, many won a hat for the first time, including a small gyros shop, and Sydney has its first Filipino hatted restaurant. Bianca Hrovat October 27, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Which restaurants gained and lost hats in the latest Good Food Guide? Dion Georgopolous; James Brickwood Restaurants didn’t need silver service, expensive wine pairings or even table reservations to receive a coveted chef’s hat at the 42nd annual Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide awards at Carriageworks on Monday as critics’ recommendations evolved to reflect the needs of contemporary Australian diners. More than 160 restaurants across NSW were recognised with at least one hat, many for the first time, after a team of anonymous restaurant critics spent six months independently reviewing more than 500 venues for the quality of their food, setting, value and hospitality. Among that number were five Sydney restaurants which rose from one to two hats - a four-fold increase from the previous year - including French bistro Porcine in Paddington, Crown restaurant Woodcut in Barangaroo and Neil Perry’s Italian phoenix Gran Torino, which replaced his Chinese restaurant Songbird in mid-2025. The Good Food Guide created the chef’s hat rating system more than 40 years ago to give readers a sense of what to expect in terms of food, service and experience, with value for money later added. Hats have been the cornerstone of Good Food’s rating system since.



Each restaurant reviewed in the guide is scored out of 20: 10 points for food, five for hospitality, three for setting and experience, and two for value. Restaurants scoring 15 or above are awarded one hat, those scoring 16 or 17 receive two hats, and those between 18 and 20 receive three hats. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Scores started to shift over the past three years as Good Food Guide co-editors Callan Boys and David Matthews encouraged a fresh approach to the unchanged 20-point scoring system: “We asked restaurant reviewers to consider the dining experience each venue aimed to achieve, rather than simply marking it against some imagined metric of fanciness,” said Matthews. The shift aimed to ensure the utility of the consumer guide by capturing exceptional venues across budgets, locations and cuisines. “Is Olympic Meats in Marrickville trying to do silver service or tweezer food?” he said. “Absolutely not, but its commitment to sourcing and DIY is almost unrivalled, with everything down to the pita made from scratch. And since it’s just a stone’s throw from Sydney’s Little Greece, it’s one of the most compelling places to see this city’s past and present collide.” The small, three-walled gyros restaurant overlooking Dulwich Hill station defied expectations this year by adding a wine service and delving deeper into chef-owner Timothy Cassimatis’ culinary roots with additional Peloponnese (southern Greek) dishes.



“There might be some pearl-clutching about it, but calling Olympic Meats a ‘gyros shop’ is like saying Cold Chisel is ‘just a pub band’,” Boys said. “Timothy Cassimatis puts as much work into his souvlaki and chips as any fine-dining chef.” It also takes a strong hospitality team to smooth over peak wait-times of more than an hour at the popular no-reservations venue, which relies on a QR-code queuing system. “Many were awarded a hat for the first time because they understood that making guests feel welcome and nourished, no matter how much they’re spending, is paramount,” Boys said. Olympic Meats was among the newly hatted in the 2027 edition of the Good Food Guide, alongside Tida Persian Food (North Willoughby), Avia (Darlinghurst), Farmhouse Kings Cross (Rushcutters Bay) and Takam in Darlinghurst, which became the first Filipino restaurant in Sydney to achieve 15/20, equalling a hat.



Takam head chef Francis Dela Cruz led the menu through several evolutions, landing the restaurant “right where it needed to be” at the intersections of familiarity, innovation and deliciousness, Boys said. It also served the tastiest skewers he’d eaten all year. Several high-profile restaurants regained their hat, including Potts Point legend Fratelli Paradiso, Paski Sopra (Paddington) and Arthur, which reopened its Surry Hills dining room with an a la carte menu in July. While there was a net gain to the number of hatted venues, CBD restaurants Loulou Bistro Martin Place, Tilda and The Gidley each lost theirs. Critics are instructed to maintain anonymity during their visits to ensure their dining experience reflects that of an everyday customer, and poor service was the greatest contributing factor to declining scores this year, Boys said.



“In one instance, a solo reviewer was mostly ignored in favour of the bigger tables of blokes ordering triple-digit bottles,” he said. “Plates weren’t refreshed, empty glasses were not refilled or removed, and staff offered little guidance … That restaurant no longer has a hat. “We understand that it’s important to look after the big-spender tables, but we also want to celebrate restaurants with staff trained to see a solo diner and think, ‘Right, I’m going to make sure this person eating alone has the best night possible.’ This is what real hospitality looks like.” The two-hat category gained 10 new entrants as “blistering hot first-timers” such as South End, Stanley and Omakase by Prefecture 48 entered the fray alongside fine-dining veterans such as Giovanni Pilu and Marilyn Annecchini, who opened Flaminia after two decades of success at Pilu at Freshwater, said Matthews. “Three Blue Ducks Burradoo winning two hats is huge for the group, but when the chefs’ CVs read Tetsuya’s, Quay and Sepia, anything less would almost have been a bigger surprise,” he said. Meanwhile, the upper echelon of fine dining contracted with the closure of acclaimed restaurants Quay and Oncore by Clare Smyth. For the first time since 1988, only two restaurants received three hats: Saint Peter (Paddington) and Sixpenny (Stanmore), the latter also named restaurant of the year.



Matthews said both restaurants had matured and strengthened their offering, becoming truly world-class. “What’s totally refreshing is that they’ve done it their own way,” he said. “It’s a generational shift happening right in front of us.” The winners of the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide Awards were announced on Monday, October 26, presented by Oceania Cruises and T2 Tea. World.title: The big mistake people with knee pain often make
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFitness The big mistake people with knee pain often make Gretchen Reynolds October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. As an orthopaedic surgeon for almost 30 years, Howard Luks has come to dislike one string of words that crops up constantly in his work. “Bone on bone,” he said. “I wish we could remove that phrase from medical discussions. I’ve seen it do so much unnecessary damage.” If there’s one thing you should do when you start to experience knee pain, it’s to keep moving. Getty Images Luks, 63, has built his medical practice, growing social media presence, and personal lifestyle and training around the idea that our joints, especially our knees, are capable of remaining strong and functional throughout life, with some basic care and feeding. He often writes and speaks about how knee pain, stiffness, tissue tears and even bone-on-bone osteoarthritis “don’t have to limit you”. They “don’t automatically require avoiding activities” you enjoy or need. They don’t mean you’re just getting old.



Related Article Wellness The exercise and lifestyle habits that can save your knees But they may signal that it’s time to rethink certain aspects of our lives and health. They almost certainly mean, Luks said, that it’s time to go for a walk. To learn more about how we can best protect and nurture our knees, I spoke to Luks about how knees work, why they sometimes fail, the surprising reasons they become arthritic – it’s not all wear and tear – the power of lifting and how he handles his own sometimes “cranky” knees. Why don’t you like the words “bone-on-bone”?



Over my career, I’ve had so many patients come to see me for a consultation or a second opinion, carrying an X-ray or an MRI scan, and they’ve been told they have bone-on-bone arthritis. So they think their knee is done, nonfunctional and they have to stop using it. They’re ready to quit running, playing tennis, using the stairs, even walking. And some of them weren’t feeling much, if any, knee pain before their diagnosis. But now they think they’re broken. They’re not? No. I tell people, “You are not your scan.” Just because someone has a meniscus tear [in the cartilage cushioning the knee bones], that doesn’t mean they’ll develop arthritis. And if they have some arthritis, it won’t necessarily progress to bone-on-bone. And if it does, even that doesn’t always mean they have to restrict activities. I have patients who are runners with bone-on-bone arthritis. They’re still running. But don’t running and other high-impact activities, even walking, wear away cartilage? I’m a runner, and people constantly tell me I’m ruining my knees. We’ve all heard that, but it’s a misconception. Moving and using the knee aren’t wearing away cartilage. Movement nourishes cartilage.



How so? Cartilage doesn’t have a blood supply, so it can’t get nutrients from blood. It gets nutrition only from synovial fluid [the viscous fluid filling the knee joint]. When you take a step, you bend and load the knee, which diffuses the synovial fluid around and through the cartilage, delivering nutrients. The same movement initiates cellular processes that prompt the cartilage to start building new collagen and repairing itself. Using your knees keeps them in shape. The biggest mistake people with knee pain make is not moving. Rest is a four-letter word for knees. Related Article Ageing The six biggest mistakes we make in midlife when it comes to knee health But if wear and tear aren’t causing arthritis, what is? It’s fair to say that the vast majority of cases of knee arthritis are not due to wear and tear. Some are. Knee injuries, like a torn ACL [a knee ligament] can change how people move, which contributes to wear and tear and, eventually, arthritis. Genetics play a role, too, though studies show it’s generally small. Being heavy also isn’t a major promoter of arthritis, which may seem counterintuitive. But people with obesity develop hand arthritis more often than people without obesity, which doesn’t make sense if arthritis is caused by excessive loading from body weight.



Then what’s left? For me, based on the latest [scientific] literature, osteoarthritis is primarily a metabolic disease. Remember, cartilage is replenished by synovial fluid. We now know that fluid reflects your metabolic state. If you have metabolic problems, such as diabetes or other conditions, your blood will contain inflammatory molecules. Some of them will find their way into the joint fluid and then into your cartilage and set off inflammatory processes there. They also change certain cells that line the joint. In a healthy knee, these cells release substances that help cartilage regenerate. But in an inflamed knee, they switch character and start pumping out substances that make it harder for cartilage to repair itself. Now you have a knee primed to deteriorate and become arthritic. That process didn’t start inside the knee, though. It began with whole-body metabolic issues. Going for a 10-minute walk every day is a small thing you can do to nurture your knee health. Getty Images So, what can we do to avoid or deal with aching knees if we do have them? My first ask with my patients is for them to walk 10 minutes every day. I tell them that exercise, almost any exercise, loads the joint and has benefits for metabolic health. But it’s good to start with something easy and achievable that most of us could do on the busiest or worst day of our lives. And if it winds up being seven minutes, not 10, that’s OK, and if it’s 12, that’s even better. Ultimately, I want them to walk for 30 to 60 minutes a day, if at all possible. Walking is medicine for arthritis. It improves metabolic health, lowers inflammation and decreases pain.



I also want them to strength train, which helps to stabilise and take some of the stress off the knee. Some of them worry they’re not capable of exercise, though. They’ll say, “Oh, I can’t do this; I’m old”, or they think it’ll hurt or make their joints worse. And I tell them the truth: that it may feel hard or uncomfortable. But that doesn’t mean they can’t do it, or that they’ll grind cartilage away. You can feel discomfort without causing damage. And getting older doesn’t mean you can’t still train and adapt and grow. Is that true even for people whose knee pain is intense? In that situation, I usually tell people that, with some work, their pain can probably get better. But it’ll take time. By the time we’re in our 50s or 60s, very few things get better in just a few weeks. But for most people, even those in pain, strength training or walking can pay huge dividends. And for those who tell me, “I did all that and my knee is still killing me”, that’s why we do knee replacements. What does your workout routine look like?



Well, I’m a bit of a lunatic. I regularly do 500 to 600 minutes a week of aerobic activity, but everything counts towards that. If I take my dogs for a hike, that counts. So does a six-kilometre walk. And I run three or four days a week, six to eight kilometres. I used to do a long run on Sundays, 16 to 24 kilometres. I don’t any more. I never want today’s workout to ruin tomorrow’s, and if I ran that long, I’d be wiped out the next day. Instead, to get my aerobic volume, I do long bike rides once or twice a week on an indoor trainer. It’s set up in front of a TV. I put on a movie and ride for two hours. It’s easy. I’m also a rock climber. I just love the functional movements when you climb. And the grip strength. I do that once or twice a week. That’s my treat. And I weight train, three days a week, minimum. I focus on adding muscle mass and strength, along with rotational work, power, balance and quickness. You need all of that for joint health and to maintain balance and avoid falls. Are your knees still in good shape? I have meniscus tears in both knees. The first happened 11 or 12 years ago. Most people over the age of 50 probably have a meniscus tear, even if their knees feel fine. So far, there’s no significant arthritis in either of my knees. My right knee does get a bit cranky on long runs. That hasn’t stopped me from running. I also do exercises at the gym that involve twists, turns and jumps, though they’re not always easy on my knees. But they’re foundational movements. If you don’t practise them sometimes, you’ll probably start avoiding them in your life, and then the narrowing starts.



Related Article Sponsored

Ageing The health costs nobody warns you about once you turn 60 Bec Wilson Money contributor The narrowing? I’m 63, and what I’ve seen in many people my age is that life starts to grow smaller as people rearrange their lives around what they see as limitations. They stop taking the stairs because stairs can be hard if you have sore knees. But then they don’t visit friends who have houses with stairs. Or they don’t go to the movies because they’d have to walk too far from the parking lot. Or they don’t take their grandkids to the park or play with them on the floor because they’re worried they won’t be able to get up. And their world starts to narrow dramatically. They may not see it at first. But the more you avoid things, the more you lose the ability to do them, even if you later decide you want to. You’re also not helping your knees because you’re moving less and less. I’ve seen this narrowing in my patients, my friends. I was worried about it in myself. So I made a conscious decision a few years ago to change my workouts, to make sure I was doing things that I might have thought I’m too old to do. So now I’m jumping on and off boxes and hopping from side to side at the gym. I want healthy knees, sure. But, even more, I want to build and strengthen the capabilities I need to broaden my life and keep it fun and interesting for years to come. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

World.content:
InspirationNew South Wales Avoid the long drive: Where to stay near Sydney’s new airport Katherine Scott October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The takeoff of the first commercial passenger flight at Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport on Sunday marks a new chapter for the region, officially unlocking western Sydney as an emerging tourism hub for local and overseas visitors. Jetstar made history with the airport’s inaugural flight to the Gold Coast, and international services launched on Monday when Air New Zealand’s flight NZ165 arrived from Auckland. Singapore Airlines, Vietjet, Fiji Airways and Qatar Airways are set to roll out routes from now and into 2027. Right now, the journey from central Sydney to the airport takes about 50 minutes by car, or a whopping one hour, 45 minutes on public transport (or the airport shuttle bus takes about an hour and costs $55). So for the thousands of passengers soon to pass through Australia’s first major new airport in half a century, the question remains – where to stay? Efforts to bump up room capacity at the terminal have stalled following the collapse of the construction firm behind its only planned hotel, a Courtyard by Marriott. This has left a significant shortage of hotels within a 20-kilometre radius of the airport, prompting declarations of a hotel crisis.



The lack of immediate rooms means that, at least initially, travellers will have to look further afield. But that’s no bad thing – it gives passengers the perfect excuse to explore western Sydney’s dynamic and delicious surrounding hubs. 



Pullman Sydney Penrith One of the guest rooms at Pullman Sydney Penrith. Penrith’s new flagship five-star stay is proof the outer west is ready for its close-up. Wrapped in a rippling glass facade by acclaimed Turner Studio, its 152 high-design rooms feature luxe Hunter Lab amenities and an in-room tablet “Sleep Therapy Menu” for custom pillow orders. In-house Marcel Bar and Bistro plates up WA lobster linguine, while the surrounding Panthers Precinct offers a lively playground of dining and activities. For a limited time, guests can flash a WSI boarding pass at check-in for an airport launch Flight Recovery Kit with chamomile tea, caramel fudge, and a sleep mask. Distance to airport: 25 kilometres (20 to 25 minutes’ drive). See pullmanpenrith.com.au Novotel Sydney Cabramatta, Canley Vale Poolside tranquillity just moments from Cabramatta’s vibrant dining scene.



From lounging poolside to exploring Australia’s most dynamic Asian culinary enclave, this modernised stay delivers on all fronts. Cabramatta’s deep Vietnamese roots have earned it the title “Little Saigon” but its food scene stretches far beyond world-class pho to Laotian, Cambodian and regional Chinese flavours. Part of the $230 million Cabravale Club Resort redevelopment, the hotel is an ideal launchpad for food safaris – though staying in for fire-powered dining at Magma by Dany Karam is equally tempting. Distance to airport: 24 kilometres (25 to 30 minutes’ drive). See all.accor.com The William Inglis Hotel - MGallery, Warwick Farm Paddock-to-plate dining and equestrian charm at The Newmarket Room at The William Inglis Hotel. A deep-seated passion for thoroughbred racing doesn’t stop this Riverside Stables retreat from delivering serious luxury. The real highlight? A heated rooftop pool deck where you can soak up the sun while watching horses work the track below. Downstairs, grand staircases lead to paddock-to-plate steaks at The Newmarket Room, with tranquil Georges River walking trails right on your doorstep. Distance to airport: 28 kilometres (30 to 32 minutes’ drive). See williaminglis.com.au One Global Resorts Parramatta



An urban oasis in the city … One Global Resorts Parramatta. The name sounds more corporate insurance firm than boutique sanctuary, but for a stylish base in Parramatta, the rebranded One Global Resorts Parramatta (formerly Skye Suites) delivers. Set within V by Crown Group’s “vertical village”, its 72 spacious suites pair sleek architecture with resort-level perks – a 25-metre outdoor pool, a sauna and a gym – all steps from Parramatta Square, Westfield, and the station. Distance to airport: 33 kilometres (35 to 45 minutes’ drive). See oneresortsparramatta.com.au Astina Suites Penrith Twilight tones at Theo’s Rooftop Bar and pool, at Astina Suites Penrith. Related Article Aviation Wheels up for Australia’s newest major airport as first flight takes off Located moments from the Great River Walk and downtown Penrith’s dining hubs and artisan bakeries, this apartment-style sanctuary delivers serious resort-level indulgence. A special mention goes to Theo’s Rooftop Bar, where you can catch a superb sunset while sipping cocktails by an infinity pool and pretending you’re in Mallorca or somewhere equally Mediterranean-coded and lush. The on-site Reset Recovery Studio — complete with a spa, sauna, and ice baths — makes it almost impossible to leave the building. Distance to airport: 24 kilometres (22 to 25 minutes’ drive). See astinasuites.com.au

World.title: How one man managed to live in eight multimillion-dollar homes without paying rent
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWInvestigation How one man managed to live in eight multimillion-dollar homes without paying rent Lucy Macken October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Only one family attended a recent open home inspection of a contemporary four-bedroom house in Waverley for rent for $3750 a week. “Anthony Lark” and his wife, Hayley, wandered from room to room as their two daughters filmed videos to show their big brother what they hoped would be their new home. Everyone was delighted that each of the kids could have their own bedroom. The sunny open-plan living room and marble kitchen were a hit. Within 10 minutes of his arrival, Lark announced he wanted it. Kim Anthony Sarkin, also known as Anthony Lark, has defaulted on the rent on at least eight multimillion-dollar houses. Aresna Villanueva Lark’s rental application was as good as it gets: an excellent reference from his former Bondi landlord Charles Levy, a copy of his passport, a bank statement, a recent Origin Energy bill, and a reference from his manager at NovaData Consulting, Sandy Galvin. But it was all fake. There is no former landlord called Charles Levy, nor Sandy Galvin at NovaData Consulting; the passport had been doctored, as were the energy bill and bank statement, and there is unlikely to be any “excellent” reference from Lark’s former landlord in Bondi because he didn’t pay his rent.



That’s because Lark’s real name is Kim Anthony Sarkin, a serial rent fraudster who has defaulted on the rent he owes on at least eight multimillion-dollar houses across the eastern suburbs from Vaucluse to Bronte in the two years since he and his family moved to Sydney. All but one of Sarkin’s landlords have taken legal action through the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal in a bid to evict Sarkin and Hayley, their three children and two dogs from seven of those homes. In the process, they have revealed allegations of fake references and doctored receipts for purported rent and bond payments. Agents who have unwittingly handed over the keys of their top rentals to Sarkin say the backlog of cases before NCAT means Sarkin can live rent-free for three to four months before eviction orders are handed down. His unpaid rent bill has grown to more than $120,000. The four-bedroom house in Waverley that Sarkin applied to rent under his pseudonym Anthony Lark. Domain



Fortunately for agent Justine Kidnie, Lark’s application didn’t make it far before her suspicions were raised by a discrepancy on the payslip and Hayley Lark’s curious inability to recall her current address. “He didn’t actually get past first base with me, so I never worried about the fact his referee never responded. By that time I’d realised who he was,” said Kidnie. It wasn’t the first time Sarkin had allegedly lodged fraudulent documents in the name of his alter ego in a bid to rent yet another luxury residence in the beachside eastern suburbs. Anthony Lark’s name first appeared on a rental application in July, a few weeks after this masthead revealed Sarkin’s rental history. The application was for a four-bedroom house with a swimming pool in North Bondi on offer for $3500 a week. The North Bondi house that was listed for rent for $3500 a week when Anthony Lark applied to rent it. Domain



He wasn’t successful, but the doctored documents prompted leasing agent Henry Farage to take the matter to the police. A NSW Police spokesperson confirmed there was an investigation into alleged fraudulent activity, but no further action was taken. Sarkin, a data and AI governance specialist from South Africa, did not respond to questions. He has previously denied doctoring any bond payment receipts. Sarkin claimed this year that he intends to pay back the landlords once he gets his financial situation under control. “It’s not like I set out to create a problem. These things have happened, which is really unfortunate. There was never any intent to harm these people,” he said. Sarkin moved to Sydney from New Zealand in late 2024. At the time, his New Zealand business consultancy had been placed in receivership, and soon after ordered into liquidation by the Auckland High Court, owing almost $NZ1 million ($820,000) in unpaid taxes. He has since declared himself bankrupt in New Zealand.



Kim and Hayley Sarkin pictured in an Instagram post. Instagram The house in Auckland he claimed he owned as part of his rental application for the Waverley home is actually owned by his former landlord, Tony Wallace, who is still owed $NZ8000 in outstanding rent from Sarkin. Related Article Exclusive

Investigation The many multimillion-dollar homes of a ‘professional ratbag’ Corporate records show Sarkin recently set up a Sydney-based AI firm called NovaData Consultancy with an AI-generated website. The company is not to be confused with the Brisbane-based business intelligence and AI consultancy Nova Data, with which Sarkin has no relationship. The email address for the “manager” at the Sydney-based firm, Sandy Galvin, was registered this month by Kim Sarkin. World.title: Of all Melbourne’s sandwiches, these are the ones our critic happily drives an hour for
World.content:
Review Eating outBentleigh Of all Melbourne’s sandwiches, these are the ones our critic happily drives an hour for With Italian, Greek and Australian influences, Suburbia Deli’s sandwiches are “a perfect Melbourne story” between two slices of bread. And for Besha Rodell, they also take her straight back to New York’s delis. Besha Rodell October 27, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. 1 / 8 Suburbia Deli makes some of the most generous sandwiches going around. Pete Dillon 2 / 8 Suburbia Deli’s Bentleigh location was added this year. Pete Dillon 3 / 8 The No. 3: Roast beef, provolone cheese, rocket, semi-dried tomato and sauerkraut. Pete Dillon 4 / 8 The No. 6: Mortadella, leg ham, salami, provolone cheese, tomato and pickled chillies. Pete Dillon 5 / 8 The menu includes 10 sandwiches, plus a few savoury and sweet baked goods. Pete Dillon 6 / 8 A friend of the owners bakes the brownies and cookies. Pete Dillon 7 / 8 Spanakopita is made to a family recipe. Pete Dillon 8 / 8 Both the Mordialloc and Bentleigh locations sell quality pantry goods too. Pete Dillon Previous Slide Next Slide 13.5 / 20 Critics' Pick How we score Suburbia Deli Cafe$$$$ We are living in a golden age of sandwiches here in Melbourne, a boom that shows no signs of slowing. But where, among all of this focaccia and Turkish bread, are the New York deli sandwiches? We have New York pizza and New York bagels, so why not the sandwiches? I’m not talking about the huge Reubens you get at Katz’s and other Jewish delis. I’m talking about the more workaday hoagie, hero and grinder, bought from a deli (or bodega, depending on the neighbourhood and, honestly, the ethnicity of the proprietor). My love affair with these sandwiches began during my first week of grade 12 when I, at a new high school in Tarrytown outside of New York City, was taken to the North Tarrytown Deli by a girl named Jackie. She ordered a sandwich on a hoagie roll with smoked turkey, muenster cheese, lettuce, mayo and salt and pepper. This sandwich was such a revelation – the bread soft, the lettuce cut on the slicer so it was shredded and crunchy, the turkey sliced thin but stacked thick – that it remains my order in New York delis to this day.



Suburbia Deli’s Bentleigh location was added this year. Pete Dillon In other parts of America, I’ll order some kind of Italian sub or grinder, usually multiple kinds of meat on that same long roll. In Australia, the closest we tend to come is a conti or continental roll, most prevalent in Western Australia but gradually becoming more available in Melbourne, too. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up What’s more common is the far more Italian panini or focaccia sandwich, which many establishments are doing beautifully. But I find focaccia too sproingy, too much of a distraction, and the filling never seems to be hearty enough to overcome the personality of the bread. Which is why, on a whim, I found myself driving an hour from home towards Suburbia Deli in Bentleigh on a recent rainy Wednesday, lured by the photos I’d seen on social media of something very closely resembling a New York Italian deli sandwich. Suburbia Deli scratches an itch for me and my own nostalgia, but it will do the same for someone else with a very different background, which is part of its beauty. What I found was something akin to a hybrid, a sandwich influenced by Italy and Australia and, interestingly, the weekend sandwich traditions of one Melbourne Greek family. What I was not, was disappointed. Suburbia Deli is a fantastic addition to Melbourne’s sandwich landscape, and it’s already growing.



The first shop was opened in Mordialloc in June of last year, with a second location added in May in Bentleigh. The deli is a multi-generational family affair. Maria and Angelo Georgopoulos, who have been in hospitality for decades, co-own the shops with their son Nico and his wife Marissa. Nico remembers his parents bringing home cold cuts, cheese and bread each weekend after he and his siblings played team sports, the whole family making sandwiches together. For Suburbia, a family friend makes all the cookies and brownies, and Nico’s best man does the shop fit-outs. They’re growing quickly, and are in the midst of building a third location in Parkdale, which they hope will allow for more in-house production of sweets and non-sandwich savoury goods. The No. 6 sandwich, with its deli meats and pickled chillies, is similar to a New York hoagie. Pete Dillon The defining characteristic of Suburbia’s sandwiches is generosity: meats and toppings are piled on so that there is far more filling than bread. The secondary feature is that bread, which is a soft oblong roll developed especially for the Georgopouloses by Bakery Lievito in Carrum Downs. It is soft inside, with a medium-crunchy exterior, engineered to be appropriate for fresh or grilled sandwiches. I prefer most of these sandwiches fresh, but that may be my New York nostalgia talking. There’s no turkey and muenster, and no build-your-own option, but the No. 6 – which comes with mortadella, leg ham, salami, provolone cheese, tomato and pickled chillies – does a lot to satisfy the Italian grinder itch. And some of them do beg to be toasted, like the No. 3, a roast beef, provolone and sauerkraut number that gets all melty in the best ways when given some heat.



I’m excited for the Parkdale location, if only because it might bring more of the Georgopouloses’ home cooking to the fore. Right now, the spanakopita – made from grandma’s recipe, all dill- and lemon-forward in a melting filo casing – offers a delicious glimpse into what that might entail. Spanakopita is made to a family recipe. Pete Dillon We love sandwiches for all kinds of obvious reasons, but one is that we don’t need chefs or even particularly ambitious home cooks to do them extremely well. They are part of our home life, part of our cafe life and a beautiful example of the ways in which our various ethnic traditions collide between two slices of bread. Suburbia Deli scratches an itch for me and my own nostalgia, but it will do the same for someone else with a very different background, which is part of its beauty. Mostly, these are some of the best sandwiches around, made by one family for their wider community with huge amounts of love. What a perfect Melbourne story. The low-down Atmosphere: Bright, modern, cheerful Go-to dishes: No. 6 ($18); No. 3 ($18); spanakopita ($12) Drinks: Italian and regular soft drinks, coffee Cost: About $40 for two

World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament NSW Liberals abandon YIMBY truce as housing goes on the ballot Max Maddison October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Minns government’s planning reforms will be on the ballot in March as Liberal MPs break from a pro-YIMBY stance to criticise developments in their backyard and argue Labor’s push for more housing is unsupported by the necessary infrastructure. A year after then-opposition leader Mark Speakman declared the party was “unashamedly YIMBY”, Liberal MPs have become increasingly vocal in their criticism of Labor’s planning reforms, with one labelling the policies “destructive” and another saying some developments “lack social licence”. The NSW Liberals have broken a pro-YIMBY detente ahead of the election, attacking the government for failing to deliver infrastructure. Steven Siewer As the state grapples to materially lift the construction of housing and vocal community groups oppose developments in their neighbourhoods, bipartisan support for the government’s suite of housing policies appears to be on the verge of shattering as Liberal MPs draw battle lines over development in Sydney. A Labor strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity to speak freely, said that a year ago, they believed housing could have been a defining issue at the state election. Today, with One Nation in the ascendancy and migration an increasingly toxic issue, they no longer believed full-throated support for greater supply was a guaranteed vote winner.



Liberal MPs in inner Sydney electorates confirmed to this masthead they would run local campaigns against aspects of the Minns government’s planning reforms at the next election, arguing infrastructure commitments had not kept pace with increased housing supply. Planning Minister Paul Scully attacked the party’s argument as evidence of having “settled back into their anti-housing NIMBY tendencies” and returning to a default setting that housing growth solely belongs in western Sydney. Liberal MP Stephanie di Pasqua says the government’s vision displayed contempt for her marginal Sydney seat. Rhett Wyman “While the Young Liberals appear to still believe in the need to fix our housing challenges, their elected representatives are crab walking away from it and waiting for policy direction from One Nation,” he said. First-term Drummoyne MP Stephanie Di Pasqua earlier this month attacked the “massive and unprecedented” proposal to build 60,000 more homes in her electorate over 15 years, saying the government’s vision demonstrated “contempt” for her inner-west electorate.



“I want my community to know that if they vote Labor, they will get 50 storeys in almost every suburb. Labor’s planning policy is destructive,” she said. Held by 1285 votes, Drummoyne will be heavily targeted by Labor as it seeks to offset expected losses elsewhere and retain power. Matt Cross – whose safe Davidson electorate covers swaths of the north shore – used a speech in parliament in June to criticise the government’s transport-oriented development policy and use of state significant development pathways as “controversial”. “I repeat: those SSDs (state significant developments) lack social licence and community support because they were in Labor’s controversial TOD (transport oriented development) zone and not in the Ku-ring-gai housing strategy. Before people jump to give the community and me a label, I remind them that we live in a vibrant democracy,” he said.



Opposition planning spokesman Chris Rath accused the government of playing “postcode politics”, saying they only supported density “so long as it’s not in their backyard”. Editor's pick Sydney beyond 2026 Sydney’s booming population won’t kill the great Australian dream, but it will change it “For local communities to embrace new developments and to make a dent into the housing crisis, the government must provide the funding to address schools that are already overcrowded, roads that are gridlocked, and local hospitals under strain,” he said. The government’s planning policies would be one of the top-tier issues at the March election, frontbencher Tim James confirmed, saying his electorate felt shut out of planning decisions. “The Willoughby community is deeply concerned about the scale of development being imposed without proper consideration of the infrastructure and services needed to support it,” he said.



In the neighbouring seat of Lane Cove, veteran MP Anthony Roberts said the government’s planning policies would deliver a “sugar hit” of supply followed by an “awful crash” which would require significant taxpayer funds to remedy the lack of strategic planning. “You can’t put in massive unit towers with little parking with the expectation people use public transport when there’s no public transport,” he said. North Shore MP Felicity Wilson said development was the No.1 issue in her electorate, saying the government had shoehorned a 35 per cent increase in housing supply into one Mosman suburb without investing in infrastructure. Similarly, Hornsby MP James Wallace also criticised the proposed rezoning around the Cherrybrook Metro station, which is slated to deliver 10,000 homes. “There is no plan. No transparency on what infrastructure is actually required. No accountability to ensure it is delivered,” he said. The case against the government’s planning reforms comes a year after Speakman used a speech at a housing conference to define his party as being pro-development after an unconvincing attempt to straddle both sides. He acknowledged his support was largely driven by the party’s lack of appeal to younger voters, saying: “A way to reverse that, I think, is to be aggressively pro-housing.”



Related Article City life The developers, the courtrooms and the battle over what gets built in Sydney In November, the opposition supported the government’s reforms of the planning system. A Labor strategist said housing had become a “no win” issue for both sides, despite spending three years establishing the party’s pro-development bona fides. “It’s not the thing we’re battling on or wanting to battle on,” he said. “You have to acknowledge it is an issue you don’t win votes on. I don’t think this election will be defined on our or the Liberals’ position on housing.” A senior Labor source argued the Liberals’ inconsistency on planning policy would be exposed during the campaign, saying their criticism of the government’s planning policies would require them to articulate a realistic alternative plan. Travel newsTravel tips Demolished for apartments, major hotel returns to St Kilda at new site Julietta Jameson October 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the latter part of last century, Melbourne’s inner south was the epicentre of its youth culture and Fitzroy Street – with its grand old George Hotel, cafes, bars and late-night clubs of varying respectability – attracted a mix of bohemians, backpackers, sex workers, musicians and assorted characters. These days, the city’s cool crowd may have migrated north to Fitzroy, Collingwood and Brunswick, but St Kilda has never entirely surrendered its rock’n’roll soul. Artist’s impression of Novotel St Kilda’s foyer area. Fitzroy Street, though, had been off the boil for some years, given over to closed shopfronts and unsavoury elements. After closing in 2015, the legendary Esplanade Hotel (AKA The Espy, not quite on Fitzroy Street but just around the corner), reopened in 2018 after a spectacular transformation that, some might argue, filed away its rough edges.



In 2021, the street gained a significant cultural landmark when Australia’s first purpose-built LGBTQIA+ community hub, the Victorian Pride Centre, was established. 



The former Novotel St Kilda was demolished to make way for the luxury Saint Moritz apartments in 2019, but the brand’s new incarnation is a more intimate affair, with 80 rooms and a $15 million transformation. The hotel, previously operated as Rydges St Kilda, has undergone a comprehensive redesign with public spaces by Rebecca Trenorden of Versa and guestrooms and corridors by Dezign. Artist’s impression of the Novotel’s food and beverage space. At the heart of the hotel is a reworked internal garden atrium, which brings natural light into the building and connects its public spaces. The ground floor is designed to engage locals as well as visitors, with the new Urban Kitchen & Bar which can accommodate up to 120 diners and includes private dining spaces.



There’s also a flexible coworking area, while conference and event facilities cater for groups of up to 140. A rooftop event space adds a fresh-air dimension. Related Article ★★★★

Hotel reviews As a travel writer, here’s where I stay in Melbourne when I’m paying Post refurbishment, its developer Erdi has donated furniture and fittings from the old Saint Kilda Beach Hotel to the Sacred Heart Mission and written cheques for local charities. Some things about St Kilda remain constant: the beach, St Kilda Pier, the Palais Theatre, Luna Park and trams that connect the neighbourhood to central Melbourne. And whatever its changing fortunes, there’s still nowhere else in Melbourne quite like it. See novotelstkilda.com.au

World.title: Versatile Leicester Fainga'anuku named as loose forward in All Blacks' northern squad
World.content:
The increasingly versatile Leicester Fainga'anuku has been named in an All Blacks squad for the first time this year after returning from injury - and has officially been listed as a loose forward.

Fainga'anuku suffered a broken leg and high ankle sprain during the Crusaders' semifinal defeat to the Chiefs in July but returned for Tasman in the NPC.

Traditionally an outside back or midfielder during his 12 tests for the All Blacks, the 27-year-old has been named among six loose forwards in Dave Rennie's squad of 36 for next months' Nations Championship tests in the United Kingdom.

The others are Anton Segner, Ethan Blackadder, Wallace Sititi, Peter Lakai and Christian Lio-Willie, the latter also named in a first All Black squad of the year.

Fainga'anuku was a revelation in the No.7 jersey for the Crusaders this year with his ball carrying threat around the ruck and close to the tryline and is a potentially powerful replacement for injured skipper Ardie Savea, although Peter Lakai has been in outstanding form recently.

Fainga'anuku also has the potential to play on either wing - making him an ideal impact player. The door has been opened for his inclusion following Shannon Frizell's knee injury and Simon Parker's unavailability for personal reasons.

Codie Taylor has again been named tour captain in Savea's absence.

Fellow hooker George Bell and prop Saula Ma'u also join the squad, with Segner, Blackadder, Jordie Barrett, Richie Mo'unga, Anton Lienert-Brown, Quinn Tupaea, Asafo Aumua and Fehi Fineanganofo all returning from injury.

The returns of key midfielders Barrett and Tupaea will be gratefully received by Rennie, with Aumua's comeback also timely in the wake of Samisoni Taukei'aho's recent injury.

Jordie Barrett is back after missing the last All Blacks' test in Sydney. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Jamie Hannah, who played in Canterbury's NPC grand final victory over Northland on Monday, and Ma'u have been used as injury cover this year. Ma'u and Josh Jacomb are the only members of the squad yet to receive a test cap.

The Nations Championship Northern Series begins against Scotland in Edinburgh on 8 November 2026.

The All Blacks then play Wales in Cardiff, followed by England at Twickenham. Results from the series count towards the Nations Championship standings ahead of Finals Weekend from 28 to 30 November in London.

The three days of double-header fixtures will match teams from the Southern Hemisphere against their corresponding table-finishers from the Northern Hemisphere, culminating in the Championship decider on 30 November.

Rennie said the Northern Series was a great opportunity for the group to keep building on the work done during the Bledisloe Cup. The All Blacks retained the trophy with a big win at Eden Park and then beat the Wallabies in Sydney a week later in a similarly dominant victory.

"This is a really strong squad we have selected. It's great to officially welcome George, Saula, Leicester, Christian, Jamie and Chay back into the squad.

"They have all shown fantastic form during the NPC. We're also rapt to have eight players who have played a lot of footy for us this year return from injury. They bring a lot of quality and experience to the group.

"Playing Scotland, Wales and England on consecutive weekends is a tough assignment. These are all proud rugby nations with passionate home crowds. We will embrace the challenge and the opportunity to build on our Bledisloe Cup performances.

"We have enjoyed fantastic support at home and away this year and acknowledge the thousands of Kiwis who we know will be setting alarms to watch from the other side of the world," Rennie said.

The All Blacks squad assembles in Auckland on Tuesday morning ahead of departing for the United Kingdom on Thursday.
