World.title: Where are home loan rates heading now?
World.content:
Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2174268%2Fwhere-are-home-loan-rates-heading-now

The Reserve Bank will review the official cash rate this week and most economists expect a 25 basis-point increase - but what lies ahead for home loan rates?

Borrowers can currently lock in a one-year rate at 4.99 percent, while two-year rates vary between 5.29-5.45 percent at the big banks.

The cheaper one-year term has been popular with borrowers, but in its recent breakeven analysis, ANZ said shorter-term rates would not have to rise by a lot to make it cheaper to take a longer fix over time.

"Our sense is that there is nowhere to hide. Fixing for six months is cheapest, but will likely expose you to fixing at a higher rate, when you roll over in six months, so it's all about managing risks and, with our breakevens showing that rates like the one- and two-year don't have to rise by much to make fixing for 2-3 years cheaper in the long run, those tenors may appeal to borrowers, especially as the step-up from one-year or 18-months isn't that significant."

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said wholesale markets were now pricing in an OCR of 3.14 percent by the end of the year - or another one-and-a-half increases - and 4 percent by the end of next year.

He said rates longer than two years still looked expensive, ranging from 5.45-5.59 percent for three years and 5.45-5.79 percent for four, but he said a two-year rate of 5.35 percent could be better value than rolling two one-year rates.

"That's before you take into account the additional certainty that they offer from a borrower's perspective."

ASB senior economist Chris Tennent Brown expected home loan rates to rise through the rest of this year and into 2027.

"There is a bit more upward pressure on the outlook for interest rates, including mortgage rates, than there was a few months ago," he said. "We are concerned that inflation over 2027 could prove slow to recede.

"We have changed our OCR peak and now expect 75bps of hikes to a 3.5 percent OCR peak."

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones said the decision was balanced.

"It still comes down to whether households judge the additional certainty of fixing for longer terms to be worth the extra upfront costs."

He said there were reasons to think some of the shorter terms might increase.

"The fact the market is already pricing in the OCR rising to a peak near 4 percent is important context, because it will limit how far some of those particularly longer-term fixed mortgage rates rise as a higher OCR is actually delivered on. Our view is that additional increases in mortgage rates over the coming 6-9 months are more likely to be concentrated in the shorter-terms."

Squirrel chief executive David Cunnigham said the market had already priced in enough increases to the OCR that the decision this week would not make much difference.

It would push up floating home loan rates, but only about 10 percent of mortgages were floating.

He said he had previously wondered whether the Reserve Bank would be willing to increase the rate in an election campaign.

"I always thought that, in the back of their minds, they'd be considering that, but they're just returning to neutral interest rates as the storyline, so it's no big deal.

"You know, they're just lifting them to a level around 3-4 percent, maybe 3.5 is where they finish up, but that's already priced into fixed rates."

World.title: Private sector gets 80% of increase in public health funding - union report
World.content:
Eighty percent of the increase in public health funding from the government over the past three years has gone to the private sector, according to a new report.

The figure equates to $2.4 billion of a total $3b increase.

The report was produced by Public Futures Aotearoa, a coalition of healthcare worker unions, including the New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO), the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists (ASMS) and the Public Service Association (PSA), alongside the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (CICTAR).

It claims, in 2024/25, the private sector received almost half of all public health spending at 46.4 percent.

The PSA and NZNO are both campaigning for a change of government.

The report used data from Health NZ and ACC to show more public funding was now flowing to healthcare providers, which might be controlled by asset managers, pension funds, private equity funds and multinational corporations.

"There is a real concern that public health dollars are now being used to service financial obligations, such as debt repayments, investor yields, corporate acquisitions and portfolio growth," it said.

Report author and CICTAR researcher Edward Miller told RNZ the trend was a scaling-up of private-sector healthcare, while growth in public delivery had effectively stalled.

"There was a $3 billion increase [in ACC and Health NZ funding] and 80 percent of that went to the private sector," he explained.

That was compared to the increase for publicly delivered healthcare (through Health NZ and ACC) - $600 million, from $14 billion to $14.6 billion, in the same period.

"The pace of privatisation is no longer a creep - privatisation has bolted," Miller wrote.

General practice one of the biggest recipients of public funding

Doctors' practices were privately owned and, according to this report, public funding now accounted for 55 percent of general practice revenue, up from below 50 percent in the past two years.

According to a 2026 estimation, a quarter of all GPs were now owned by corporations, up from 14 percent in 2022.

Private hospitals also received a lot of public money

The report said more than a billion dollars went to private hospitals for publicly funded surgeries in 2024/25 - that's a 93 percent growth in the four years to 2025.

Public funding now made up an estimated 45 percent of private hospital revenue, up from 35 percent five years ago, and just three entities controlled 70 percent of private hospital beds, it said.

Large amounts of public money also went to diagnostics and imaging, where public funding accounted for about 65 percent of the sector's revenue, and aged residential care, where it accounted for an estimated 76 percent of revenue - some of which went offshore to international owners.

Home and community support services received nearly all their revenue from public sources, at 94 percent, according to the report.

Why is this a problem?

Miller told RNZ it showed the health system had to increasingly rely on the private sector to deliver care - the result of years of underinvestment.

"The problem with that... as Health New Zealand's internal advice shows, outsourcing is more expensive than insourcing," he explained. "It also means we end up using public dollars, taxpayer funding, to build up the capacity of the private sector rather than... the public sector."

Borrowing was also more expensive for the private sector than the government - a like-for-like hospital built by the private sector would cost more than one built by the public sector - and there also tended to be less transparency in private sector spending, he said.

A spokesperson for Health Minister Simeon Brown's office told RNZ he did not respond to reports commissioned by unions that were actively campaigning to change the government.

However, on background regarding elective surgeries, they pointed out Health NZ delivered 43,819 outsourced procedures in 2025/26 - many for patients who would otherwise still be waiting.

About 14,200 fewer people were waiting longer than four months for elective surgery than at the peak.

Health NZ had originally planned for 39,155 procedures as part of the Electives Boost, making it now 11.9 percent ahead of target.

World.title: Our Changing World: Saving Tara-iti shell by shell
World.content:
On an overcast winter's day at Bream Bay, about 20 people are doing something that, at first glance, seems a little odd.

They are shovelling shells into hessian sacks and moving them from one part of the beach to another. But the painstaking work has a purpose: creating safe places for tara-iti, New Zealand fairy tern, to nest.

Audio player for " Saving tara-iti, shell by shell " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/environment/2174090%2Four-changing-world-saving-tara-iti-shell-by-shell

Follow Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts

There are only about 45 of the birds left, making the subspecies one of New Zealand's rarest endemic breeding bird.

Department of Conservation (DOC) tara-iti programme lead Ayla Wiles told Our Changing World that the team was enhancing areas in the back dunes at Waipu to give breeding pairs more options.

"This just gives them nice safe options for nesting, so away from the tide, a bit of protection from storms and that sort of thing."

Department of Conservation tara-iti programme lead, Ayla Wiles, preps a possible nesting site. RNZ/Liz Garton

Tara-iti are mostly white with a black cap, orange bill and orange legs. They currently breed at Waipu Mangawhai, Pākiri Beach and Papakānui Spit at the southern end of the Kaipara.

The preferred habitat is an open sandy area with shell, with enough clear space for the birds to see potential predators. Bits of wood also provide places for chicks to hide from aerial predators.

Getting the recipe right

Creating a nesting site that tara-iti will actually use is not straightforward.

Waipu About-Tern volunteer Robyn Davies said one site created the previous year apparently had too much shell and getting the ratio right is important.

"They're quite fussy when it comes to their nesting site," she said, "If we don't get it right, they don't stay."

A possible New Zealand Fairy Tern nesting site in Bream Bay, north of Auckland RNZ/Liz Garton

The site at Waipu should be perfect, it's protected from high tides, storms and wind, while the nearby estuary gives young birds somewhere to learn to fish.

Signs of success

Wiles said there were signs the approach was paying off.

"Since we've been doing this sort of shell patch creation ourselves, we've seen nest success increase, so fewer nests lost because they are just away from those threats."

DOC has worked on tara-iti recovery since the 1980s, when the population was down to three or four breeding pairs.

Wiles said numbers had slowly increased as conservationists improved both protection in the wild and methods for raising birds in captivity.

One of the techniques involves collecting some of the first clutches laid in a breeding season and taking the eggs to Auckland Zoo, where chicks are hand-reared for their first few weeks. They are then transferred to a release pen, where they learn to fish before fledging.

Meanwhile, the breeding pair whose eggs were removed can lay another clutch.

"We've doubled the productivity for those pairs," Wiles said.

She said that had helped lift the number of fledglings from about six in a season to 12, and in one year as many as 18 or 19.

The team is hoping a milestone could be reached this breeding season: the first surviving female tara-iti raised in captivity may breed.

She had been prospecting at the northern end of Waipu the previous season but had not laid an egg.

"This year could be the year," Wiles said.

DOC workers and volunteers hard at work creating potential nesting sites for Tara-iti RNZ/Liz Garton

Tracking tara-iti's travels

GPS tracking of the birds has also revealed that some tara-iti roam much further than previously apparent.

The birds spend winter around Kaipara before returning to breeding sites, but some younger birds have travelled as far north as Te Paki and Hokianga Harbour. One travelled south to New Plymouth and another went to Pūkorokoro/Miranda on the Firth of Thames in Waikato.

Trackers were initially used on hand-reared birds, but wild males are also now being tagged.

Wiles said comparing the movements of wild and captive-reared birds could help researchers check whether they were behaving in the same ways and reveal previously unknown foraging areas or potential new breeding sites.

There is also hope that, as numbers grow, tara-iti could begin breeding beyond their four current sites.

Wiles said the team was considering a potential habitat north of Ruakākā.

Mangawhai remains the biggest breeding site, with up to eight or nine breeding pairs, compared with about two or three at Waipu. But the smaller sites are important too, she said, because they spread the risk across several locations.

Estuaries are an important source of food for Tara-iti / New Zealand Fairy Tern. RNZ/Liz Garton

'A messenger' between land and sea

For Ari Carrington, from Patuharakeke Te Taiao unit, the effort is about more than the recovery of one species.

He said tara-iti had not featured heavily in the pūrākau he grew up with, although some people remembered the birds in earlier times.

Working with them provided an opportunity to build and share knowledge within the hapū.

"Whatever's happening on the whenua is happening in the moana, and we must protect both of them," said Carrington.

"The tara-iti is like a messenger in between those."

Ari Carrington RNZ/Liz Garton

He said restoring tara-iti also meant thinking about the other species around them, including other manu, skinks and lizards.

"Sometimes we just focus on one species, one atua, one spot when we need to think wider sometimes. If they don't have any whānau, then just like us, they struggle."

Every nest matters

Protecting the birds requires much more than shifting shells.

Around 10 full-time site-based rangers work across the breeding season at nesting and captive-rearing sites. The transcript says nests are checked every day, while other work includes fencing nesting areas, predator control and educating people using the beaches.

Volunteers also help keep watch.

Waipu About-Tern volunteer Robin Davies pulls weeds as part of the preparation of this potential Tara-iti nesting site RNZ/Liz Garton

Davies has been monitoring tara-iti for about 16 years and said volunteers check that eggs and chicks are still present and being fed, as well as watching for predator tracks or signs a bird is unwell.

That long association also means getting to know individual birds.

"Each bird that you monitor, it has its own little thing, whether it's the cheeping of the female or the runaway chicks or the male that's very dominant," she said, "They've all got their own personalities."

The stakes remain high.

A third of eggs or newly hatched chicks were eaten by predators last breeding season, although with 11 chicks still fledging, the season was considered a success.

The tara-iti breeding season runs from September to January, with egg-laying expected to begin around the middle of November.

And after years in which the population remained below 40 birds, Wiles is allowing herself some cautious optimism.

"It's good to see the numbers creep up, and like this time next year we could be at 50 if, you know, all goes well."

Tara iti, or fairy terns, are fiercely protective parents. Supplied / Darren Markin

World.title: Work visas under India FTA worse deal than options already available, lawyer says
World.content:
New work visas under the India trade deal are "cosmetic at best" and completely undermine Winston Peters' warnings of "open slather immigration", an immigration lawyer says.

The two new pathways secured under the agreement opened last Tuesday, allowing up to 5000 skilled Indian professionals to work in New Zealand at any one time for up to three years.

Alastair McClymont told RNZ the newly published conditions showed the visas offered a worse deal than other options already available and would attract "very few, if any" extra migrants.

For example, workers had no right to bring their partners or children with them, and their work here would not count towards the experience needed to qualify to live in New Zealand permanently.

Alastair McClymont is an immigration lawyer. Supplied

McClymont said other work visas - which Indian citizens could still apply for - remain "significantly more attractive", offering both family rights and a route to settling here.

He accused New Zealand First of employing "incredibly dangerous" populism, and fuelling racism and abuse towards Indians through false warnings of mass migration and a "butter chicken tsunami".

"There's really nothing in here."

'Confusing' - NZ First leader Winston Peters

Asked for his response, Peters said the new work visa requirements actually proved him right on a different complaint - Indian workers would be treated worse than people coming here under similar trade deals.

"That was precisely my allegation," he told RNZ. "How can we justify that?"

In June, Peters dropped a bombshell in Parliament, accusing National of "covertly" changing course to adopt more "discriminatory" migration settings for Indians.

He also claimed officials wanted to keep the changes quiet for fear of India's reaction.

Peters told RNZ the whole situation had been "very, very confusing", with National Party ministers claiming one thing and Indian Prime Minister Narenda Modi claiming another.

"The only way to remove that misunderstanding is to release the documents," he said.

RNZ's initial request for documentation under the Official Information Act was refused on the basis the decision-making process was "ongoing". RNZ has lodged a fresh request now that the deal is in force.

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford told RNZ she had always been clear the new entry visas were extra options on top of all the other work visas Indian citizens could apply for.

"All work visas are designed for different purposes, and have different requirements and settings."

Asked why the rules differed from those in the China and South Korea trade deals, she said: "Each agreement is negotiated individually."

She said the immigration settings met New Zealand's commitments under the India trade deal.

'Storm in a teacup'

McClymont told RNZ his main concern was the number of people who believed claims the deal was opening the door to mass migration, and the racism and abuse toward the Indian community as a result.

He said the actual rules published on Tuesday showed claims otherwise were wrong, calling it a "storm in a teacup".

He said Indians applying under the Accredited Employer Work Visa, which had been around for a while, were able to use their work experience in New Zealand for a pathway to residency and bring their family into New Zealand while they worked.

"None of these things are being offered to the Indian citizens under these new visa categories announced as part of the Indian Free Trade Agreement and therefore are very unlikely to be attractive to many Indian citizens."

McClymont said he couldn't see the point of any of the provisions: "It's cosmetic at best."

World.title: Staff shortage leaves new Waitākere Hospital ICU ward empty
World.content:
A brand new intensive care unit at Auckland's Waitākere hospital sits empty, fully equipped, but with no money budgeted to run it yet.

No opening date has been scheduled, with no staff and no operating budget.

The unit was previously due for use by the end of this year.

The six-bed unit was heralded as West Auckland's first ICU, when it was announced as part of a $96 million, 30-bed urgent care ward building in 2021.

That Manaaki Hōhonu building officially opened last month, but only half the beds were used, because Health NZ had not employed enough nurses to staff every bed.

No staff were hired for the intensive care unit.

Manaaki Hōhonu officially opened last month, but only half the beds were used. Supplied/Health NZ

Health NZ advertised for a clinical lead - but on a one year, part-time (0.4 FTE) contract.

Waitākere Hospital operations director Brad Healey said more staff would be recruited, once the "model of care" was confirmed.

"Intensive care requires a highly specialised workforce, and detailed clinical and operational planning, before services can safely begin."

The union for senior doctors questioned why that recruitment was only happening now.

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton said there had been more than five years to prepare.

"There are clinicians and patients who are eagerly awaiting these improved facilities," she said. "They take years to plan and build.

"It is not like it's a surprise when they open."

The need for an intensive care unit for the area, which had a population of 250,000 people, had been discussed for years, before it was even announced, she said.

"It's just frustrating that, now it is open, there aren't the people to staff it."

Health NZ had a habit of building facilities, then not staffing them properly, such as the North Shore's Totara Haumaru surgical centre on the North Shore, she said.

Health NZ's Brad Healey said the new building provided the infrastructure to allow the delivery of more critical care services in a phased approach "over time".

The Manaaki Hōhonu project was announced in 2021. Supplied/Health NZ

A Ministry of Health audit of Manaaki Hōhonu in July noted that, when the intensive care unit eventually opened, two beds would have to close at the North Shore hospital ICU.

North Shore and Waitākere hospitals are both part of the Waitematā health district, which serviced a population of 650,000 - the biggest in the country.

The audit noted, when the wider, 30-bed ward first opened, it would only use 11 beds, and said, if all 30 beds were used, extra staff would have to relocate from other medical wards.

The practice, known as a 'lift and shift', meant there would be no extra capacity across the hospital by opening the extra 19 beds.

Health NZ said 15 beds were now used in the new ward and there would be 25 by 3 November.

West Auckland residents needing intensive care were normally either sent to North Shore or Auckland City hospitals.

Waitākere had 240,000 people and was expected to grow 25 percent in the next 15 years, a Health NZ document said.

World.title: Strong winds forecast to continue as firefighters tackle several bushfires
World.content:
Both sides of the Cook Strait continue to be lashed by wild weather as a front moves up the country.

While a heavy rain warning for the Grey and Buller districts expires at 6am Tuesday, another remains in place for the Tararua Ranges.

Strong wind warnings cover Marlborough until 8am, Wellington until 9am and Wairarapa through to 11am.

MetService meterologist Devlin Lynden is warning the temperature is also expected to drop for the top of the South and bottom of the North islands, with the northwest winds changing to the south.

Strong winds fan flames

A large smoke plume could be seen rising over the tussocky Central Plateau landscape near Waiouru, on 26 October, 2026. Supplied/ Sarah Moodie

The strong winds fanned the flames of multiple bushfires in separate parts of the country on Monday.

The Defence Force is warning a blaze in the Waiouru military zone could still take hours to be fully extinguished, and may not be out until Tuesday evening.

The large scrub fire was sparked during live fire training on Sunday and has burnt through more than 230 hectares.

It said the blaze, which took hold again on Monday, drew in nine firefighting crews and five helicopters alongside military personnel.

Fire and Emergency said crews were withdrawn from the fire ground overnight, but are expected back on site Tuesday morning.

Footage from motorists travelling on the Desert Road SH1 on Monday showed large plumes of smoke just north of the Waiouru township.

Meanwhile, firefighters down south continued to battle a blaze in the central Otago town of Roxburgh overnight.

Homes were evacuated on Ladysmith Road, east of Roxburgh township. Screenshot / Google Maps

Six households were evacuated and more 30 homes remain without power.

At least seven fire crews were working on the blaze - which is thought to have started in trees about 2.45pm Monday - with FENZ saying strong winds have added to the problem.

Crews are also being brought back to work on a scrub fire that has burnt through about 80 hectares in Southland.

The fire started on Sunday afternoon on high-country land in the Centre Hill area.

High winds prevented helicopters from reaching the fire on Monday, and the difficult terrain means ground crews were not able to get there either.

World.title: Dr Redmayne aims to lift Brisbane Heat's WBBL fortunes
World.content:
New Brisbane Heat captain Georgie Redmayne returned to work as a doctor this year and will now help improve the side's form after last season.

The wicketkeeper-batter takes over from all-rounder Jess Jonassen, who led the side for the past six WBBL seasons.

In 2025, the Heat finished last and did not win a match. The Queensland Fire, with many Heat players, then won the 2025-26 WNCL final with Redmayne captaining the 50-over side and scoring a century in the decider.

Strikers pip winless Heat The Adelaide Strikers pull off a tense WBBL victory over the struggling Brisbane Heat.

She said the form in the 20-over format was achievable for the Heat.

"If we win one game we are on the up," Redmayne said, grinning.

"To be more serious, pre-season has been really good and winning the WNCL was massive for us with a lot of the same core group, so we know we are still a winning team.

"We just have to tweak a few things to be successful in that T20 format. We have got our first game at home (on Friday night) against the Sixers, which is always a good rivalry.

"Last year we didn't really turn up in the high-pressure moments … but hopefully we go back to the winning ways which we were known for in the past"

Redmayne said she got a lot out of returning to work as a doctor after a few years where cricket took centre stage.

"I actually came back to it this year. It was really nice," she said.

"I did a bit of a stint in April and another stint in August/September this year at Greenslopes Private Hospital in Brisbane.

"It helps provide a great bit of grounding for me, especially when you go away playing cricket.

"You can think it is the be-all and end-all playing professional sport, but it is literally grounding seeing some real world problems."

Redmayne has been a great success at the top of the order for the Brisbane Heat and was the leading run scorer in three consecutive seasons from 2020-2022.

Grace Harris, her opening partner much of the time, topped the aggregates in 2023 and 2024. The Heat made the finals in all five of those years and were runners-up twice.

The Heat moved Redmayne down the order last season, but it did not work, so a return to opening with Harris would be a good place to start for the side to turn their form around.

"(Opening) is somewhere I really enjoy batting and where I would like to bat," Redmayne said.

"My favourite time playing cricket was always opening the batting with Grace. We had a couple of very successful seasons.

"Last year our order was very changeable. I started at number eight and ended up at number four.

"I don't mind where I bat, so long as we are winning games."

AAP

World.title: 'Tyranny of distance' weighs against big cycling call
World.content:
Cadel Evans is intrigued by the revolutionary idea of Australia hosting a Tour de France stage, especially given he's long retired as a pro cyclist.

The 2011 Tour champion, the only Australian to win cycling's most famous event, remains heavily involved in his sport as a race promoter and commentator.

Cycling's three-week Grand Tours, the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España, regularly start with stages outside their own borders.

Next year, the Tour's "Grand Depart" will be three stages through Scotland, England and Wales.

But it would be something else entirely to bring a Grand Tour start to the other side of the world.

Melbourne's NFL game is a battle of opposing jet lag strategies The San Francisco 49ers arrived a week in advance of their Melbourne NFL game, while the Rams will arrive the day before. A sleep expert says both strategies have merit, but one may have a slight edge.

The San Francisco 49ers and LA Rams faced massive logistical challenges last month to stage their NFL game at the MCG and they didn't have to play again until several days later.

"It would be possible — I wouldn't want to be the one telling the riders," Evans said on Monday.

"But it's never out of the question. There's been talk before … some Grand Tours are maybe considering stages in America.

"I'd be totally open to it, but I wouldn't want to ride it myself. Australia — as we all know, the tyranny of distance — it's pretty far."

Cadel Evans (centre) remains the only Australian to win the Tour de France. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

There was speculation last summer that the WA government was sounding out Giro organisers.

While a Grand Tour start remains at long odds, the likelihood of cycling superstar Tadej Pogačar returning to race in Australia may well be firming.

Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta in late August, ending his season early.

Tour Down Under race director Stuart O'Grady has been trying to lure Pogačar to Adelaide for several years. The project took a step forward this year when Pogačar's manager visited and spoke highly of the race.

If Pogačar returned to Adelaide, he would most likely also race at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race in Geelong the following weekend.

Pogacar competed at the two events in 2019 and last raced in Australia at the 2022 Wollongong world road championships.

Tadej Pogačar crashes out of La Vuelta a España Tadej Pogačar abandons the Vuelta a España after crashing during the eighth stage of the race.

"He wants to start his season early, apparently. If he would like to come back to our race, that would be amazing," Evans said.

"When you have the opportunity to see the greatest of all time in any sport, it's pretty unique for any sporting fan."

The Slovenian's stunning run of sustained success has invited comparisons with Belgian Eddy Merckx — until now, cycling's all-time greatest rider.

Evans gives the nod to Pogačar.

"It's unfair to compare periods, but it's a far more competitive environment that we race in now," he said.

"There are so many more specialists in our sport now and he's been an all-rounder, winning everywhere, It's just remarkable, and at such a young age as well [28].

"One thing that's so great about Pogačar, other than that he's just an amazing rider, is he wants to win everything."

Evans, at 174 centimetres, was standing alongside Max Gawn, at 209cm, to announce the Melbourne captain as an ambassador for the People's Ride, held on January 30 before the women's road race at Geelong.

"Particularly someone like Pogačar, he goes beyond our sport — and of course, that's having Max part of it [as well]," Evans said.

AAP

World.title: Three-game Bledisloe Cup series looms as new deal struck
World.content:
The Wallabies are set to play two Bledisloe Cup Tests at the MCG in a matter of years, fuelling hopes that one of rugby union's biggest rivalries could be permanently returning to a three-game series.

Rugby Australia struck a multi-year deal with the Victorian government which secures Melbourne to host the Wallabies and New Zealand in the Rugby Championship in 2027 and an additional Bledisloe Cup Test in 2029.

It comes as Lang Park in Brisbane is set to stage the first Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test next April, which sets up a three-match series between the bitter rivals for the first time since 2021.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

Whether a three-game series would persist beyond next year has been a hot question exercising pundits.

But Monday's announcement of an additional Test in Melbourne in 2029 will very much boost optimism that a permanent three-game Bledisloe Cup series could return.

That is because Brisbane has also secured the rights for the 2029 Anzac Day Test along with the 2031 instalment.

RA officials were coy on whether the announcement was a signal for a return to full-time three-Test series, and were unsure if 2028 would be similar to 2027 considering no Anzac Day Test has been announced.

An extra Bledisloe Cup Test would favour the Wallabies, who haven't held the trophy since 2002 and have been unable to win both Tests since it became a two-game duel in 2022.

In 2026, they were utterly humiliated by the All Blacks, conceding a mammoth 93 points across the two games, which dealt coach Les Kiss a harsh reality check ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallabies admit they 'faced the music' It was brutal and confronting, but the Wallabies knew they had to face the reality of Saturday night's defeat to the All Blacks sooner rather than later.

Regardless of the three-Test speculation, having a Bledisloe Cup Test at the MCG next July is set to be a stellar moment for the sport in Australia as it ramps up preparations for the World Cup.

The Wallabies last played the All Blacks at the MCG in 2023, where a crowd of 83,944 filled the historic ground, which was the largest rugby attendance in more than 20 years at the time.

Last year, 90,307 watched the Australians' second Test against the British & Irish Lions, breaking the Lions' all-time crowd record.

"The Melbourne Cricket Ground is one of the world's great stadiums — and a jewel in Australia's sporting crown — and the Wallabies are proud to be hosting the All Blacks at the iconic venue in 2027," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have played only four previous Test matches at the MCG, and this Bledisloe Cup encounter will mark 30 years since both teams took to the hallowed turf for the first time.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have won two Tests apiece at the 'G and another enthralling contest awaits next year."

Australia will also meet the All Blacks at least one more time in 2027 when they face off in their second Pool A match of the Rugby World Cup at Sydney's Olympic stadium.

AAP

World.title: RLWC quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
World.content:
The second week of the Rugby League World Cup was short on genuine contests as the tournament's haves and have-nots collided.

Aside from Australia's win over Fiji, where the gallant Bati gave the Kangaroos a hell of a scare, it was big scorelines across the board.

But with fans across three Australian states and two other counties voting with their feet, there are still plenty of quick hits from the second round of matches.

1. Tongan wall holds yet again

Tonga took care of business in their win over Lebanon. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

For the second week in a row, Tonga's opponent enjoyed plenty of field position and for the second week in a row Tonga's scrambling defence proved more than up to the challenge.

After holding England to 12 points last week, despite the English enjoying 34 tackles inside the red zone to Tonga's 18, they repeated the dose against Lebanon on Friday night.

Tonga down Lebanon in World Cup Tonga's win over Lebanon kicked off what's expected to be a lopsided weekend in the Rugby League World Cup but there's still something to be gained amid the blow-outs.

The Cedars came in with an offload-heavy game plan and had some success moving the ball up the field. By the end, they had 29 tackles inside the attacking 20 to Tonga's 30, but that was where they stalled.

Some of it was due to a lack of creativity but there were plenty of last-gasp Tongan efforts to deny Lebanese players who looked tryline bound, and it means Tonga carry a strong form line into Sunday's blockbuster against Samoa.

2. Samoa running riot over PNG is a sign of the times

Rarely will you see two halves of a single game more different than what Samoa and Papua New Guinea dished up in Port Moresby.

The Kumuls held the gloves up well through the opening 40, trailing just 14-6 at the break and could have been even closer had Robert Derby successfully grounded the ball for their second try.

But what followed was a procession: Samoa scored 50 unanswered points in the second half, as their size and athleticism totally overwhelmed PNG, who had just four sets in the entire stanza.

Of all the blowout results this weekend, this more than any other was a sign of the times. Rugby league's embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of the game makes it almost impossible for an underdog team to stay in the fight beyond a certain point and when things break they can break badly.

Samoa only had to make 36 tackles through the entire second and the Kumuls only got over halfway for two tackles.

They finished the game conceding six tries in 15 minutes against a side they had held their own against for the whole first half.

There were plenty of less-extreme examples of the same through this year's NRL season, most notably when a top eight side conceded the third-most points in a game ever, but it's been turned up to greater levels through this World Cup given the talent and fitness disparity and it stacks the deck even further against the underdogs.

3. France's woes continue in England smash-up

England ran out easy winners against a hapless France outfit. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

England beat the clock against their old rivals in Perth, running out 82-0 winners in a result that means France have conceded 160 points in as many minutes through their two matches.

It's hard to find any silver lining for Les Chanticleers and ahead of their tournament finale against Lebanon, the French game finds itself in a strange position.

The potential for growth or a return to the glory days when France were one of Test football's true powers is always the dream, and with two Super League clubs in Catalans Dragons and Toulouse — giving France more professional teams than New Zealand — they seemingly have the ingredients and infrastructure for improvement.

France just cannot seem to close the gap on their more illustrious rivals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

All but two of this year's squad were home-grown players and since 2020 they have won nine of the 16 Tests they have played, with all seven losses coming against England or Samoa.

Problem is, across those seven games they have been outscored by a cumulative total of 394-44, with this England loss the worst of them.

There's greater pathways to the top for French talent than ever before but they can't seem to close the gap between them and the big dogs.

If anything, the gap has become wider. Nine years ago, in the 2017 World Cup, they played England at the same ground and lost 36-6 a week after losing to Australia 52-6.

Those scorelines aren't exactly a good time, but they're not a point-a-minute for two straight weeks either.

The Southern Hemisphere racing ahead of the north is a wider issue for the sport, but France are the collateral damage and they don't have a contingent of heritage NRL players to paper over the cracks.

4. Christchurch puts its best foot forward

Despite the result, it was a healthy crowd in Christchurch. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

Despite Esom Ioka's first-half hat-trick that briefly gave the Cook Islands the lead, few would have ever expected the Aitu to trouble New Zealand for long in their match at Te Kaha in Christchurch.

That didn't stop a sell-out crowd of 26,800 coming through the gates, marking the fifth biggest Test attendance of the past century in New Zealand and the highest ever for a game outside of Auckland.

It was a strong week of crowds throughout the tournament — Tonga and Lebanon pulled in more than 25,000 and Australia topped 40,000 for the second week in a row despite taking on Fiji.

But with the NRL expansion race heating up as the league prepares to hand out a licence for a 20th team, Christchurch showing up in droves did their chances of winning the bid no harm at all.

5. Fiji take Australia to the brink

Australia are through to the semi-finals of the World Cup after their win over Fiji. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

Speaking of that Australian-Fiji crowd, the 41,108 punters who packed into Lang Park didn't just push the attendance past that of the 2017 World Cup final at the same venue, they were treated to easily the best clash of the weekend.

On the back of an inspired display by five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe and a hat-trick to Castleford winger Semi Valemei, Fiji pushed Australia all the way before a late Jacob Preston try wrapped up a 36-22 win for the green and golds.

Consider the previous margins between the two (42-8, 54-6 and 64-0 in their last three meetings) and it's a measure of how far the Bati have come and how this World Cup is more up for grabs than one might think.

A couple of contentious calls and some killer instinct in key moments got the Kangaroos home.

But on what they've shown through two weeks, Samoa, Tonga and New Zealand will all fancy their chances of springing an upset should they meet Australia, who have wrapped up a semi-final berth in surprisingly shaky fashion.

World.title: Antonelli is two points away from the F1 title, and can win it next week
World.content:
With his ninth grand prix win of the season on Monday morning (AEDT), Italian Kimi Antonelli put himself on the cusp of winning his maiden Formula 1 drivers' championship.

The 20-year-old Mercedes pilot has been a class above the rest in 2026, and could have sealed the championship with his victory in Texas on Monday, but other results meant he had to wait at least one more week before popping the champagne.

Next weekend's Mexican Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Antonelli needs just two more points

Heading into Monday's United States Grand Prix, there were still five drivers who could mathematically catch Kimi Antonelli in the race for the title.

Kimi Antonelli is in just his second season of Formula 1. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Simon Galloway)

But Antonelli's win reduced his challengers to teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

Drivers' championship standings

1: 365 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

2: 242 — George Russell, Mercedes (-123)

3: 241 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari (-124)

With just five grands prix left to run, there is a maximum of 125 points a driver can achieve by winning every race.

Antonelli has 365 points, 123 ahead of Russell and 124 over Hamilton.

The maximum total Russell and Hamilton can end the season with is 367 and 366 points, respectively.

That means Antonelli needs to win just one more point to eliminate Hamilton from the title race, and two points to eliminate Russell.

Antonelli can achieve that in Mexico City by finishing ninth or higher.

He would also win the title if neither Russell or Hamilton win the race.

Even if Russell or Hamilton finish exactly 100 points adrift of Antonelli at the end of the race in Mexico, with 100 points still available, the Italian would be crowned champion, as his nine grand prix wins cannot be topped by either rival.

'Very excited' Antonelli wants to win in style

Antonelli has held the lead of the drivers' championship since his victory at the Japanese Grand Prix in round three.

Despite leading since March, Antonelli has dismissed any and all notions of thinking about winning the drivers' championship in just his second season.

But with the championship all but won, he has finally been able to acknowledge that only the most calamitous set of circumstances would deny him becoming champion.

Speaking after his tremendous win in Texas, Antonelli said his mindset for the rest of the 2026 season was to continue pushing and scoring as many points as possible.

"I am very excited. We would love to clinch the title in style with a great result," Antonelli said about his impending title win.

"That's always the mindset, and that is going to be the mindset from now until the end of the season.

"Just going to try and enjoy every moment, because these we'll always remember."

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the F1 Mexican Grand Prix on Monday, November 2, with the race beginning at 7am AEDT.

World.title: Youth boxing program fights off negativity, provides positive role models
World.content:
Encouraging young boys to put on gloves and fight each other inside a boxing ring may not seem like the most obvious way to keep them out of trouble at first glance.

But those behind this weekend's amateur Gloves of Hope challenge in Darwin would argue the sport is helping do just that, and much more, for young people in the Northern Territory.

The event is an initiative of local grassroots organisation Hoops 4 Health — an Aboriginal-led service behind several sport programs designed to support struggling youth, including some inside NT detention centres.

The sold-out event saw boxers from across the region compete at Marrara Stadium. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

The free Gloves of Hope program aims to give young men and women a chance to learn boxing skills from professional coaches while building resilience, discipline and a support network in their community.

"We try to improve their mental health, but also guide them with integrity about how they live their lives," social impact director Matthew Bonson said.

Mr Bonson said the program was based on evidence-backed models of therapy which use patterned, rhythmic exercise to help trauma-affected youth regulate their emotions.

Matthew Bonson says the patterned, rhythmic exercise has been shown to help with emotional regulation. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Through sport and the structures around good coaches, you can help these young men stay cool longer and also help young women get more confidence about who they are," he said.

As the NT grapples with some of the highest youth incarceration rates in the country, particularly among First Nations boys aged 10 to 14, Mr Bonson said providing young people with positive role models was a key part of the program's success.

While the program is "not a magic-wand solution", Mr Bonson says it exposes the young boxers to positive role models. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Particularly with young men, if you put the right older men in front of them — who they know are trying to help them — they do want to listen," Mr Bonson said.

" It's not a magic-wand solution, but we're trying our best to give [young people] positive examples. "

Territory boxing talent on show

On Saturday, Gloves of Hope teamed up with Boxing NT to host one of Darwin's biggest amateur boxing events of the last decade.

The sold-out event at Marrara Stadium brought together boxing clubs from across Darwin and Alice Springs, with one team even travelling from Kununurra in Western Australia.

Declan Unwin-Walker was one of the fighters competing for the title belt on Saturday and said he was "keen, excited, nervous — but ready to go".

Declan Unwin-Walker says Gloves of Hope is all about supporting each other and encouraging fellow boxers to continue showing up. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Mr Unwin-Walker trained with Gloves of Hope for more than a year in the lead-up to the event and said the sport had been rewarding, physically and mentally.

"We all push each other and show up every day and its definitely about pushing each other and just yeah — keep showing up," he said.

Jerrel O'Riley from the Kununurra Warriors Boxing Club said it was exciting to compete on a big stage.

Jerrel O'Riley and his team were visiting from Kununurra in Western Australia, with plenty of representation from rural Darwin clubs in attendance too. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"I was pretty surprised to hear there was 1,000 people coming," he told the ABC ahead of the sold-out event.

" That's the main thing I'm worried about, getting knocked out in front of 1,000 people. "

Richard Garling, who has coached the sport for more than four decades, was there on behalf of the Humpty Doo Boxing Club.

Mr Garling said pathways into boxing that helped kids from rural areas compete were essential to fostering NT talent.

Mr Garling hopes events like this will encourage young boxers to continue on their journey, going on to compete in even bigger competitions over time. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"There's a lot of potential in the Territory," he said.

" Hopefully all these kids tonight can continue their journey somewhere higher — state titles, national titles or Golden Gloves. "

The event also featured a half-time performance by NT music star Yung Milla, fresh from his triumph on reality music competition show The Voice Australia.

The funds raised from ticket sales were donated to help the Gloves of Hope initiative, with organisers hopeful the event will return next year.

World.title: Fowler's City draw to end winning start
World.content:
Manchester United striker Elisabeth Terland scored a late equaliser to knock visitors Manchester City off top spot in the Women's Super League table on Sunday evening as a hotly contested derby finished 1-1 at the Leigh Sports Ground.

Matildas star Mary Fowler slid the ball to Bunny Shaw to open the scoring for the champions in the 66th minute.

Making her 100th WSL appearance, Shaw brushed off the challenge of Dominique Janssen and powered a shot into the far corner to break the deadlock and silence the home fans, who booed and heckled her throughout.

However, Norway international Terland was on hand to blast the ball into the net to grab a point for her side in the 89th minute of the game.

It was the first time that City has dropped points this season, allowing Ellie Carpenter's Chelsea to go top on goal difference after it came back from a goal down to beat Crystal Palace 3-1 earlier in the day.

Ellie Carpenter had to battle hard for Chelsea. (Getty Images: WSL/Tom Dulat)

Chelsea and City both have 19 points, with London City Lionesses third on 16 and Manchester United fourth on 11.

On Merseyside, Liverpool's Jana Fernandez Velasco struck deep into stoppage time to snatch a 2-2 draw at home to London City.

Aston Villa raced out to a 3-0 lead over Everton by the 50th minute with Amalie Vangsgaard scoring twice, but the home side scored twice late on to ensure a nervous finish as Villa held on for a 3-2 win.

Charlton Athletic's miserable run continued as it slumped to its seventh straight defeat.

Substitute Wilma Leidhammar scored the only goal of the game for Birmingham City in the 68th minute to leave Charlton, who counts Matildas veteran Emily van Egmond among its ranks, still firmly rooted to the bottom of the table and searching for its first point of the season.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: England 'gutted' after second extraordinary ODI defeat in as many games
World.content:
Shadab Khan hit an epic ODI century, and England suffered a second extraordinary defeat in as many games as Pakistan snatched a one-wicket victory on Sunday to secure its place in the cricket tri-series final.

Pakistan's chase looked doomed at 9-154 before a defiant 89-run, last-wicket stand between Shadab and number 11 Haris Rauf secured Pakistan a dazzling win. Shadab smashed his first one-day ton to take Pakistan to 9-243 in 47.1 overs.

Even within that 10th-wicket stand, Pakistan seemed to have been beaten when Gus Atkinson won an LBW decision against Shadab with 21 runs still required.

Shadab threw his bat down and started congratulating England's players before asking for a speculative review, which showed the faintest inside edge, leaving Shadab screaming with joy at the reprieve.

"The boys are absolutely gutted," England coach Brendon McCullum told the BBC.

"Today they fought incredibly hard … we were in a pretty good position, well, a very good position and then obviously we weren't able to get across the line.

"The last game was, the boys were gutted after that, and you look in the dressing room now, they're also extremely gutted now."

England, which scored 429 and still lost in its last game against Sri Lanka, was earlier all out for 241 in 46.4 overs.

Playing his first game in the tournament, Shadab scored 113 not out off 96 balls and farmed most of the strike. Rauf (7 not out in 19 balls) hit the winning boundary as Pakistan enjoyed its third successive win.

It was the biggest last-wicket partnership in a successful chase in ODIs.

The 10th-wicket partnership was the largest ever to win a game in ODI cricket. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali)

Left-handed opener Ben Duckett scored 105 for England — his fifth ODI century and first against Pakistan — after Shaheen Shah Afridi won his first toss in the tournament and elected to field after successfully defending 300-plus scores in the first two games.

It was England's third successive defeat in the tournament after losing to Pakistan by 87 runs and seeing Sri Lanka pull off the second-highest successful run chase in ODI history despite captain Harry Brook scoring a blistering 114-ball double century.

Pakistan will take on Sri Lanka in their last league game on Tuesday after beating the Sri Lankans by 37 runs in the opening game.

Rauf joined Shadab at 9-154 in the 34th over and launched a partnership neither side will quickly forget. While Shadab outsmarted England pace with his brilliant batting, Rauf gave him ample support by sensibly not going for expansive shots.

Shadab protected Rauf well by keeping the strike to himself and counterpunching the bowlers by hitting boundaries early in the over, completing his century by playing a late cut off Atkinson for his 12th boundary before hitting the fast bowler over long off for a six to reduce the target to three runs off the final three overs.

Rauf drilled debutant fast bowler Henry Crocombe for a straight boundary to cap a remarkable recovery for Pakistan.

Earlier, Jamie Overton (3-43) took two smart slip catches to remove both struggling opening batters Fakhar Zaman (10) and Saim Ayub (6) and Babar Azam will continue his search for a big innings after Atkinson pegged back his off stump as Pakistan slumped to 3-31 inside the first seven overs.

Brook then turned to Overton soon after the batting power play, and the fast bowler responded immediately in his first over when 19-year-old Saad Baig (32) cut straight to Will Jacks at point.

Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson (2-30) and Jacks (1-18) then bowled tidily and raised England's hopes of their first win.

Duckett revived England from a precarious 4-52 with a 93-run stand with Sam Curran, who made 42 off 52 balls.

Afridi picked up 4-46 and England lost four of the five top batters for single digits. That included the run-out of Brook, who went for a second run but fell short of his crease to an electrifying throw from debutant Razaullah.

England lost quick wickets and slipped to 9-201 after Afridi removed Curran in his return spell when he holed out to fine leg off a mistimed pull. Razaullah took 2-38, grabbing the wickets of Jacks and Dawson.

Duckett, who hit 10 fours and two sixes in his 111-ball knock, fell in the 37th over when he top-edged a sweep to fine leg against left-arm spinner Arafat Minhas before Atkinson (36 not out) shared a 40-run last-wicket stand with Crocombe.
