Tech.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer.

After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.

But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.

An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

Tech.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it’s aware of “an issue impacting the inner display” on a “small number of iPhone Duo units.” If your iPhone Duo is affected, Apple says to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Shortly after launch, iPhone Duo users started reporting similar issues where the hinge would tighten, and opening the device caused a crack and the distinctive bright lines on the display. One user in Australia said that an Apple Store replaced their unit “on the spot.”

This weekend, iFixit published its teardown of the phone and gave its perspective on why some phones might be cracking. Where the damage has been happening, iFixit shows how the foldable screen might be pushing against a center bar.

The Verge has contacted Apple about the reports, but has not received an on-the-record response about the issues with these new phones. They’re some of the first devices to launch after new CEO John Ternus took over from Tim Cook.

Tech.title: Nothing’s eye-catching Ear 3A earbuds are matching their best price to date
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a lot of features for the price, and they’re an even better value now that all four colors are on sale at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy for $79 ($20 off), matching their all-time low price.

The Ear 3A deliver great performance for the price, with extensive EQ options that let you fine-tune the sound to your liking. My colleague John Higgins found the default sound a little too bass-heavy, but appreciated how easy it was to adjust — which is great, since that level of customization is unusual for earbuds at this price. While they won’t completely drown out chatter of your local coffee shop, the ANC does a good job of quieting low drones, including air conditioners and airplane cabin noise. We did encounter some bugs in testing, however, including abrupt changes in noise cancellation levels when using adaptive ANC, as well as occasional issues with voice calls in noisy environments.

Still, they’re relatively minor drawbacks given what you get for the price. The Ear 3A also come in some fun colors — including a striking pink shade — and each pair includes extra-small ear tips for a more comfortable fit. They even offer a shortcut to access ChatGPT and include 32MB of built-in storage, letting you record up to two hours of a phone call and transfer the recording through the companion app.

Tech.title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.

At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass:

It pays to be an Amodei

Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale, but it is still a tidy sum.

And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.

The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.

Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors

Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. Anthropic’s is no exception. But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too.

For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company.

It’s hungry for compute

It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.

Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.

It has a really weird corporate structure

Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.

Anthropic names only two rivals

There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google. Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world.

Tech.title: Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
Tech.content:
Last week, I sank into my living room couch and watched a bedraggled, nihilistic Matthew McConaughey take a drag of a cigarette in season 1 of True Detective. “You know, someone once told me time is a flat circle. Everything we’ve done, or will do, we’re gonna do over and over and over again.” I assume most people aren’t thinking about fitness trackers or gadgets while watching that scene. But in that moment, I couldn’t help but think about the Fitbit Edge on my wrist.

The $179.99 Edge is a modernized version of the 2014-to-2020 era of fitness bands — your Charges, your Altas, your Inspires. If you’ve ever owned one, you already know the vast majority of what the Edge is like. It’s lightweight. You swipe on a small display that shows you basic health and fitness metrics. It lasts for about a week on a charge — though that shrunk down to about a day and a half with the always-on display enabled. It’s a device that isn’t trying to be much more than what it is.

The difference is that the Edge feels more refined on the wrist. Where the Fitbit Charge 6’s display felt boxy, the Edge is fully rounded, giving it a softer vibe. The straps are interchangeable, but with an easier button-release system. The metal link bracelet gives it a more jewelry-like feel, though it costs almost as much as the Edge itself at $150. I’m partial to the $60 magnetic strap, which mimics leather despite being made of silicone. The widgets borrow heavily from the Pixel Watch’s Material 3 Expressive redesign. Though to be clear, this is a proprietary Fitbit OS, not Wear OS. Some of the new watchfaces are elegant, though others highlight the Edge’s big black bezels. (Some things truly never change.)

Functionally, it’s also a step above the Fitbit Air. There’s built-in GPS for tracking walks and runs without your phone. You can have alarms, view notifications, and control music. You can’t take calls on the wrist — there are no microphones or speakers. Contactless payments are also a no-go. Andy Abramson, head of product at Google Health, says that’s because “less than one percent [of Charge 6 owners] used the feature” and that Google instead prioritized a “sleek design, altimeter, and weeklong battery.” That walks back some of the advancements that have come to the Charge lineup over the years, but if you want to put a silver lining on that, it narrows the Edge’s focus. This is a fitness tracker. There’s some glanceable information, but there’s absolutely no smartwatch creep here.

The metal links look nice, but do they look $150 extra nice?? I’m more partial to the magnetic strap. The rounded face gives a sleeker look and feel on the wrist compared to the Charge 6.

The big software change is the demise of the Fitbit app as we knew it. It’s Google Health now, with an AI coach if you pony up for the yearly subscription. (You get three months free with purchase; otherwise it’s $10 monthly.) I’ve written about the overall experience in my Fitbit Air review. The broad strokes are the same, though in the months since, Google has spent a lot of time tinkering with and iterating on it. Most notably, the company has beefed up automatic activity tracking.

To test this, I tracked a handful of runs on the Edge without officially starting an activity. I then compared that to one tracked by an Apple Watch Ultra 4 and my iPhone’s Runna app. I was surprised, but noticed limitations. For example, on a 2.4-mile run with a five-minute warmup walk and cooldown, the Edge correctly identified the exact moment my warmup transitioned into a legit run and then back into a walk. The estimated distance was also pretty decent at 2.55 miles. It wasn’t quite as good at gauging my running speed. It logged me as running a 10’49” mile pace, whereas my actual pace according to the Apple Watch and my phone was 11’38”. This pattern was fairly typical across my testing, so it’s more that this is a nifty way to still “get credit” if you forget to track an activity.

Otherwise, the AI coach is still a Chatty Cathy and requires some weekly hand-holding to get the most out of it. I’ll say it again: The Google Health app can feel cluttered, and I get tripped up looking for information that used to be easy to find, like past workouts. However, if you’re new to fitness and want guidance in creating and sticking to a custom AI-generated routine, this is still the best experience I’ve had so far. The bar is in hell, though, and beware what you initially share with the coach. I regret ever telling it I used to have shin splints, as it remains convinced my perfectly fine shins are in danger of disintegrating with every run.

It’s still such a Chatty Cathy.

I wish I could tell you about the Health Guardian features, which should let Fitbit Edge users see noninvasive insulin resistance and blood pressure trends. Alas, the way my testing schedule worked out, I have to wait until November 1st to get my initial results.

All in all, I enjoyed the Fitbit Edge as a low-key tracker. This will appeal to folks who just want the basics, but aren’t willing to commit to the screenless life. I’m thinking of the Vergecast listeners who occasionally write in, wondering what happened to simple fitness bands, tired of the smartwatch agenda that took over the past few years. The only gripe I really have is $179.99 feels a tad expensive for what you’re getting. Especially since the Fitbit Air is only $99, and for iPhone users, the Apple Watch SE 3 starts at $249. Brands like Xiaomi and Amazfit also offer much cheaper trackers with displays, even if they’re not quite as sleek on the wrist.

You have to admit: It’s kind of funny that in 2026 we’ve gone full circle and come back to this particular form factor. For the past two weeks of testing, I felt like I’d been blasted back to what I thought was a bygone era in my career. My bet is still on smartwatches being the dominant wrist-based wearable in the years to come. However, this renewed yearning for simpler trackers feels significant at a time when AI health and fitness coaches demand more data in increasingly invasive ways. There’s a growing weariness that can’t be ignored — and yet for many of us, it’s not fully practical to truly log off with a screenless device. So if that’s you, the Edge is here because hey — time truly is a flat circle.

Agree to Continue: Google Fitbit Edge Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Google Fitbit Edge, you must pair it with an iPhone or Android smartphone. That includes the phone’s Terms of Service, privacy policy, and any other permissions you grant. The same goes for any third-party health integrations with other services. For example, if you choose to upload your medical records, you’re agreeing to use CLEAR for identity verification — meaning you’d be agreeing to CLEAR’s terms of service and privacy policies too. There are several optional permissions for things such as location, Bluetooth, camera, background app refresh, notifications, and cellular data. By setting up the Fitbit Edge, you’re agreeing to: Fitbit Terms of Service

Google Health Additional Terms of Service

Google Health Data and Privacy Policy (formerly Fitbit) If you’re concerned about your health data being used to train Google’s AI, that option is turned off by default and must be opted in to. Similarly, the terms and conditions for Google’s acquisition of Fitbit require that your health data be stored separately and not used for Google’s targeted ad business. Final Tally: three mandatory agreements, several optional permissions

Tech.title: The Sony WH-1000XM4C bring back a beloved headphone design
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

When Sony announced the WH-1000XM4C headphones, I was perplexed. A product revamp usually includes at least one or two significant improvements. Or if it’s a nostalgia play, it’s from a decades-old product and not one that came out in 2020. Beyond a few minor tweaks, though, the XM4C are remarkably similar to their six-year-old namesake, the beloved WH-1000XM4. They even use the same processor for active noise cancellation (ANC).

And while I went into this review questioning the XM4C’s existence, after spending some time with them, I get it. The Sony XM4C aren’t the cutting edge of headphone technology, but they are great headphones that I love using. They still sound great, the design is classic, and they get you pretty close to the performance of Sony’s current-gen flagship, the WH-1000XM6, for a lot less money.

What I, and many others, loved about the original XM4 is still at the heart of the XM4C. They fold up into a compact size and come with a hard-shell zippered case (which now has its loop on the zipper instead of the edge) that’s easy for travel. The faux-leather ear cups are squishy and comfortable — I wore them for hours at a time during testing without issue. Codec support is also the same as the XM4, with SBC, AAC, and LDAC for high-res wireless audio with supported devices.

The similarities continue with the XM4C’s 40mm driver and, by extension, their sound. Bass is on the heavier side as it is with the XM4, but it isn’t overpowering and instead supports everything above it. Kick drum and tom hits have good oomph and definition. Low-end loving tracks like “bad guy” by Billie Eilish really drive forward. The midrange — like the attack of the acoustic guitar in Tracy Chapman’s “Fast Car” or the bite of Robert Plant’s vocals — can sound slightly covered or muted. It’s not something I hear on my original XM4s, although the difference isn’t drastic. There’s a 10-band EQ in the Sony Sound Connect app (up from five bands on the original XM4) and after boosting the frequencies between 1kHz and 4kHz, the midrange opened up. But even without that small EQ change, the XM4C sound great.

In a world that’s continuing to move away from 3.5mm connections, the XM4C still have one, which works in both powered mode (to use the ANC) or with the headphones off if the battery is low. Like the XM4 (and the XM5 and even last year’s XM6), the XM4C only support wired listening over 3.5mm, though, and not USB-C. The XM4C headphones also only include a 3.5mm cable. You’ll need to provide your own USB-C cable for charging.

The XM4C (in white) are remarkably similar to the original XM4 (in black), and that’s not a bad thing.

As with the XM4, the XM4C use four mics with Sony’s older QN1 chip for noise canceling, and because of that the ANC performance is basically the same. Going back and forth between the two, the XM4C blocks out a little more of the low end from air conditioners and big trucks driving by outside. But that difference could come from the XM4C’s ear pads, which are six years newer than the worn ones on my XM4.

Not that the XM4C’s ANC is bad, but it’s where their six-year-old tech shows the most. ANC has improved a lot over the past few years, and there are headphones that offer comparable performance for half the price, like the Anker Soundcore Space 2. And it doesn’t compare to the more expensive headphones in Sony’s XM series. Both the XM5 (which also has the QN1 chip, although with eight mics) and XM6 (12 total mics with the more advanced QN3) are better at isolation across the frequency range, especially at the lower end. The slightly more expensive second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones block lower frequencies a bit better than the XM4C, too. Still, the performance is solid, and I never felt distracted by outside noise when it was active.

While recent headphones have been eschewing the 3.5mm jack, the XM4C include one for wired listening.

It’s the same with call quality. The XM4C block ambient sound on calls well, and my voice is clear and understandable, but sometimes louder noises break through or cause my voice to sound a bit compressed. They get the job done; they’re just not top tier like the XM6 (which cost $160 more).

One of the selling points of the XM4C is their replaceable battery — required by upcoming EU regulations for Sony to sell them in Europe. The replacement battery is not for sale in North America, and there’s no indication from Sony when (or if) it might be available here. At the moment, there also aren’t any instructions on how to do the replacement yourself. The ear cups are definitely easier to remove than before — I was able to pop them off and on with my hands instead of prying them up with an extra tool. But once they’re off, there’s no easy way to figure out which screws to remove to get to the battery. (Removing just the four visibly obvious silver screws with arrows pointing to them doesn’t do it.) Now, this isn’t a huge deal on brand-new headphones with batteries that should last you a few years, but it’s also not encouraging for American customers expecting the extra longevity that a user-replaceable battery provides.

The change to a removable battery has also slightly affected battery life on the XM4C, down to 27 hours with ANC on from the 30 hours with the XM4. It’s still more than enough to get through a few days, though.

One disappointing omission is Bluetooth LE, and therefore Auracast support. With the move to Bluetooth 6.0, and the fact the XM5 and XM6 both support it, I was hoping these would, too. It doesn’t mean they might not eventually get Auracast through a firmware update. (That’s what happened with the XM5.) It’s just a shame they don’t have it at release.

The XM4C can fold into a compact size.

The XM4C also keep the capacitive touch controls apart from the power and ANC buttons, like in the XM series. A sensor on the right ear cup allows for track and volume controls. Holding your palm over it activates transparency mode until you move it away for quick moments when you need to hear someone. The controls work decently, but I’ve always preferred physical buttons.

The release of the XM4C was a surprise, but it’s a welcome one. Even with only minor improvements on a six-year-old design, the XM4C are still great headphones. I enjoy how they sound, the ANC works well, and they’re incredibly comfortable. Is $300 a bit more than I’d expect for headphones based on a model from 2020? Yeah, a little. But those looking for an XM4 replacement will be incredibly happy with them. The Sony XM4C prove that even though a design is old, it doesn’t mean it should be forgotten.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

Tech.title: Instagram chases YouTube with a push for longer, widescreen videos
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Instagram is announcing a big push into longform horizontal video, which the platform is calling “Features.”

Instagram boss Adam Mosseri has been against doing longform video on the platform “for a long time,” he says in a six-and-a-half-minute video (here’s the widescreen version) with VP of product Tessa Lyons, saying that “one of my concerns has been, how do we make sure that we keep Instagram not just about entertainment, but about connecting with friends. If you watch a longform video, that’s “it’s a lot of Reels, photos, and carousels that you might not have sent to a friend,” meaning less likes and shares.

Now, though, the team is working on making shortform and longform video “symbiotic,” according to Mosseri, like podcasts or comedy specials that can be both long videos and broken up into shorter ones.

The announcement of this widescreen video push also follows the launch of Instagram’s TV app late last year. That app launched first as a Reels-focused experience and as a pilot for Amazon Fire TV devices in the US, but it’s since expanded to Google TVs, Samsung TVs and Apple TV, and Instagram launched new features like the ability to watch Stories earlier this year.

Mosseri also talked about the updates with creators Samir Chaudry and Colin Rosenblum, and their video includes some clips of how longform video will show up on the platform.

Today, Features are expanding to the US in a small test and is in testing with some creators in Brazil, according to Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley. Instagram is testing a few other video-focused features as well, including clips pointing to a long video, a way for creators to create a “series” of Reels, and improvements for live video discovery.

Tech.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees
Tech.content:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to up to 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India. In a message to employees, Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman writes that this gives staff members “the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources” as the company looks to trim staff without another round of layoffs.

Sources familiar with the situation tell The Verge that staffers across Microsoft are eligible for the voluntary exit offers, including those in its AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance, and human resources teams. Microsoft’s cloud + AI, MicrosoftAI teams, and corporate, external, and legal affairs are partially participating, the sources say. Meanwhile, employees on Microsoft’s marketing, commercial business, discovery and quantum, and security teams aren’t participating.

The voluntary exit offers come just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees, a move that primarily impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is also planning new rounds of layoffs, according to a report from Fortune.

This voluntary exit offer doesn’t target Microsoft’s commercial sales teams, and it’s also very different to the previous voluntary retirement program that the company offered long-serving employees earlier this year. That previous offer was only available to around 9,000 employees, for US employees at a certain employee level whose combined years of service added to their age totaled 70 or more.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman writes in a memo to employees. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”

In a note posted to Microsoft’s internal HRweb site, seen by The Verge, the company says today’s offer isn’t based on age, length of service, or performance. Microsoft also says it may consider a future voluntary exit offer “where there is a business and workforce need.”

Tech.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
Tech.content:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, reads.

As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upwards of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.

Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.

Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.

“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides, but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers, and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20 times as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”

Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”

The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

Customer concentration is another risk.

“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers…could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Tech.title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
Tech.content:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday. SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” in a statement.

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business. SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s Oct. 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Tech.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees, reports say
Tech.content:
In Brief

Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees, according to reports from Business Insider and Bloomberg. The move marks Microsoft’s latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce for AI.

Employees at the vice president level and below on select teams in the U.S., Canada, India, and the U.K. will be eligible, the reports say. Some employees, including those working in data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.

Microsoft’s Chief People Officer Amy Coleman sent a note to employees on Monday about the buyouts.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” the note reads. “This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support.”

Employees who choose the offer will receive benefits similar to those offered in a standard severance package, the reports say. Earlier this year, Microsoft offered buyouts to retirement-age employees, with more than 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible workers accepting.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
Tech.content:
After weeks of leaked S-1s, Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.

That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”

The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.

As previously reported, Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.

Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission, will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

Tech.title: Apple unveils new iPad mini with OLED display and faster A20 Pro chip
Tech.content:
Apple on Monday announced a new iPad mini with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display. The tablet features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor and is powered by an A20 Pro chip. The new iPad mini starts at $699 for the Wi-Fi model and $849 for the Wi-Fi and cellular model. The tech giant revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday.

The new iPad mini is 5.4 mm in thickness, and available in two colors.

The device delivers peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits, more than twice that of the previous-generation device, along with full screen brightness of 600 nits for SDR and HDR content and a 2 million:1 contrast ratio. Apple says the iPad mini is ideal for dim-light environments.

Image Credits:Apple

The iPad mini also comes with a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare in bright environments, a feature already available on the iPad Pro. The updated tablet now also features a 12-megapixel center stage front camera, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support.

The Super Retina XDR display uses OLED technology for pixel-level lighting control, delivering deeper blacks, richer contrast, and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vibrant colors.

It also features an “Acoustic Display” that Apple says enhances the audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company.

Image Credits:Apple

The new iPad mini launches with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions, and understand what’s on their screen.

Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple. The A20 Pro also features a 6-core CPU, delivering up to 60% faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks such as photo editing and multitasking across apps.

The device can be preordered on October 28, with availability beginning November 6.

Tech.title: Matiks raises $10M to expand its math and puzzle gaming platform
Tech.content:
Over the past decade, head-to-head brain games like QuizUp rocketed in popularity, reaching at one point millions of users. After that, battle royale games like Fortnite and PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds had their moment in the spotlight. Lately, growth of mobile games has slowed down amid a barrage of AI content across platforms. Now, the India-based gaming company Matiks wants to steer people away from AI-riddled timelines with its math, logic, and brain-game puzzle platform.

The namesake app has been around for two years, but has seen real traction this year. The startup said that its daily users have grown from 22,000 earlier in the year to over 300,000 by September. The app also saw 2.2 million monthly active users in that month, with the company’s growth attracting fresh investor interest.

The startup said Monday that it has raised $10 million in pre-Series A funding led by General Catalyst, with participation from Indian entrepreneur Ronnie Screwvala and existing investors InfoEdge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners, and Untitled Ventures. With this round, the company has raised over $13.5 million to date.

Matiks was founded by Sudhanshu Bhatia, Mohan Kumar, and Sushant Timmapur, who were college friends. Bhatia, who has a background in competitive mental math, said that he started working on the idea while he was working at American Express on an anti-money laundering strategy.

“For the last 10 years, the platforms have made entertainment consumption easy, but much of it is brain slop. We started exploring how we can make math-related games fun and entertaining like the other content,” Bhatia told TechCrunch over a call.

“Since I’ve had this background in mental math, I knew that a competitive ecosystem exists there. We got to know that the same exists for puzzles and memory. We wanted to make our app as entertaining as physical sports, so we opted for a dual format,” said Bhatia.

In the app, users can choose from Math, Puzzle, Memory, and Logic categories and play different games against bots to practice, and then against real players. Users can also play challenges and quests to earn points, maintain streaks, and unlock new games.

I have been playing the games for more than a week, and they are a good distraction for me, as I like games I can finish in a few minutes. The app hasn’t pushed me much toward purchasing more in-game items or shown distasteful ad pop-ups that would prompt me to uninstall the app completely.

Until now, Matiks has been focusing on user growth and just started testing a subscription this month, which unlocks game analysis, tips and tricks, practice, and additional features. The startup also allows for in-game purchases to skip certain challenges, maintain a streak, and boost XP points.

Bhatia said that while the majority of the game’s players are based in India, the startup has seen traction from other markets like the U.S., South Korea, and Japan. The startup plans to bring in localization to grow the latter two markets.

While Matiks is battling against AI slop, it isn’t entirely rejecting AI. The company has debuted an experimental game-creation platform called Jelo, which lets users make their own games and lets others play them. There is a ton of competition in this area, including Google’s new platform called Playground.

The startup, with 41 full-time employees, wants to use the funding to scale this platform by expanding into newer markets.

Rahul Humayun, a partner at General Catalyst, told TechCrunch in an email that the product’s pace of iteration and user engagement have given the firm encouraging signs.

“We found the Matiks vision, product, and most importantly the community to be truly N of 1. The team’s product taste and pace of iteration made it a no-brainer,” said Humayun. The exceptional product love and power user behaviour are clear signs that the team is onto something special. We believe these are strong leading indicators for monetisation, with early results looking promising. The depth of engagement across surface areas like duels, social, Snac, and now creation only helps.”

Tech.title: Tesla turns to Turo to boost adoption of Full Self-Driving (Supervised)
Tech.content:
Car rental giant Turo will start advertising which Teslas on its marketplace are outfitted with the automaker’s advanced driver assistance system, Full Self-Driving (Supervised) — or FSD, a collaboration that could boost further adoption of the driving software.

Eligible Turo “hosts” who rent their cars on the platform will also receive a free one-month trial of FSD. Turo said it is working with Tesla to directly access the automaker’s API to verify which cars have FSD enabled.

The announcement comes just a few days after Tesla offered updated figures that show the carmaker is finally getting more customers to pay for the software, which can handle most driving tasks but still requires human supervision.

Last week, Tesla revealed that around 1.7 million customers have paid for FSD globally, out of more than 10 million cars built and sold to date. The company said more than 75% of customers who took delivery of a car in North America during the third-quarter paid for an FSD subscription. That was a roughly 20% increase from the second quarter, though the company’s U.S. sales have been in decline.

Tesla has spent much of the last year re-working some of its showrooms to focus more on FSD as a selling point. In a post last week, the company’s chief executive Elon Musk said the effort is working.

“People are buying FSD with a car attached, not the other way around,” wrote Musk.

“Customers are now coming in and saying: ‘Can we get into an FSD drive?’ They’re not asking for [Model] 3, [Model] Y, or Cybertruck,” Tesla’s finance chief Vaibhav Taneja said on last week’s earnings call.

For Turo, the addition of FSD rentals gives the company a chance to boost what are already some of its most heavily rented vehicles. Turo said Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y are the third- and fourth-most popular vehicles on its platform this year. “[T]his integration further increases host earning opportunities as interest in self-driving technology grows,” said Turo.

“This industry-first integration with Tesla is another example of how Turo is redefining what car rental and access can look like,” Turo chief executive Andre Haddad said in a statement. “Most travelers have had limited opportunity to experience driver’s assistance technology, but the demand is clear. Our own research shows that 55% of Americans are interested in driverless technology for travel, growing to 71% for Gen Z. Turo’s marketplace model is uniquely positioned to close the gap between consumer curiosity and hands-on access.”

Customers who rent an FSD-enabled Tesla through Turo will be served cautionary language that requires drivers to monitor the software, and be ready to take over at any moment. Drivers will also have the option to view a Tesla-created tutorial.

“When enabled, your vehicle will drive you almost anywhere with your active supervision, requiring minimal intervention,” a screenshot of the Turo app reads.

The listings themselves, meanwhile, allow owners to promote their cars as “Self-Driving,” according to another screenshot provided by Turo.

Tech.title: The best apps for tracking your reading and discovering new books
Tech.content:
From discovering new books and organizing your reading list to tracking your reading goal and sharing recommendations, book apps make it easier to maintain reading as a hobby. There are numerous apps on the market that promise to do just that, so we’ve compiled a list of some of the best ones to help you pick the right one for you. Whether you’re an occasional reader or a dedicated bookworm, these apps can help you make the most of your reading journey.

Some of the apps on this list are somewhat new, while others have been around for a few years. Amazon-owned Goodreads, which is arguably the most popular book-related app, isn’t included in this list because we’re focusing on newer, lesser-known platforms.

Fable

Image Credits:Fable /

Fable is a reading app that combines book tracking with a social platform. It lets you organize reading lists, set reading goals, track streaks, write reviews, and join virtual book clubs. You also get personalized book recommendations and the chance to discuss what you’re reading with other readers.

The app differs from others on this list because it puts reading and community at the forefront of the platform, which makes it a great option for people who like staying motivated to read by being part of a community and discussing their reads.

Fable is free to download on iOS and Android, but also offers a Fable Plus subscription tier that unlocks additional features like custom goals and advanced analytics for a monthly fee of $5.99.

Bookshelf

Image Credits:Bookshelf /

Bookshelf is a reading app designed to help people organize their libraries, discover new books, and remember more of what they read. The app positions itself as an alternative to Goodreads, and combines traditional reading logs with AI-powered recommendations and tools.

You can create custom shelves, set reading goals, receive reminders, save favorite quotes, and access AI-generated book summaries, key insights, and thematic analyses to recall the books you’ve read and get a deeper understanding of them.

Bookshelf is free to download on iOS, but offers a $6.99 monthly fee to unlock premium features like unlimited collections and enhanced analytics.

Pagebound

Image Credits:Pagebound /

Pagebound is a book app that lets readers track their books, create lists, set goals, and discuss individual titles in dedicated forums. Instead of having to join an actual book club group, users can post reactions and thoughts to connect with others reading the same title.

You don’t have to worry about spoilers for the end of the book, as conversations are organized based on reading progress, allowing readers to share theories and thoughts as they read. The app is a great option for people who want to discuss their reads with others without having to commit to a scheduled book club.

Pagebound is free to download on iOS and Android and offers a $9.99 monthly subscription for added features like profile customization.

StoryGraph

Image Credits:Storygraph /

StoryGraph is a reading app that lets users track their reading, discover new books, and access detailed reading statistics and personalized recommendations. Users can set reading goals, join reading challenges, and find new titles based on their preferred moods, themes, genres, and pacing.

The app is ideal for readers who want to better understand their reading habits and discover books that match their current interests. Its recommendation system doesn’t solely rely on what’s popular or trending, and instead caters to exactly what readers are looking for.

StoryGraph is free to use on iOS and Android, but also offers a paid subscription called StoryGraph Plus that costs $4.99 per month and unlocks custom charts, additional statistics, and more.

Margins

Image Credits:Margins /

Margins is a great option for mood readers, as it offers mood-based discovery alongside a more focused reading experience. It helps users find their next read based on how they feel in the moment by searching for specific vibes, such as “books like 1920s Paris.” Users can also track their reading goals.

The app also lets users customize their virtual library by choosing book covers that match their aesthetic and organizing their shelves in different ways, including by color. For users who enjoy a more immersive experience, Margins offers a built-in “Reading Time” meditation timer that blocks social media apps.

Margins is free to download on iOS and Android.

Tech.title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
Tech.content:
Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.

While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.

“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)

Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.

The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Reveals What’s Under the Hood
Tech.content:
Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.

According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.

“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”

The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.

Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.

While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”

Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.

It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.

Tech.title: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
Tech.content:
Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.

Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.

The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”

Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”

Tech.title: Some iPhone Duo Models Are Breaking. iFixit’s Teardown Might Explain Why
Tech.content:
The first batch of Apple’s first folding phone may already have some screen issues.

The iPhone Duo is a strong first foldable from the company, but multiple Reddit reports say the phone’s inner screen cracks when customers open the device. Some apparently happen very soon, like during device setup. (Others might be from influencers trying to break the thing, like YouTuber JerryRigEverything.) People are already calling this “crackgate.”

It’s unclear how widespread the problem is or whether it only affects a small number of units. (WIRED’s review unit hasn’t had any issues after more than two weeks of daily use.) Apple did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

This is familiar territory for foldable phones. A hinge means strain on the screen and the components inside. It’s also a place for dust to seep in and break the phone, as with Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold in 2019, forcing the company to pause sales and fix the issue. Some devices handle it better than others, and as the product category has grown, those issues have largely diminished. But fewer problems don’t mean easier fixes.

Tech.title: The Hottest New Side Hustle Is Stripping Copper Wire and Posting About It
Tech.content:
A woman wearing blue overalls and a pink tank top sits on a bench in a workshop lined with tools. Holding a broken copper wire in one hand and a small mechanical tool in the other, she looks at the camera and smiles. “Let’s make money stripping …” she says, pausing for effect. “Wire!”

This play on words is common in a specific corner of TikTok where users document the process of stripping copper wire in order to sell it for extra cash. Most of these creators don't appear to collaborate or use a common hashtag, and they haven’t coined a new term ending in -maxxing. But many of their videos have a similar, visually striking setup: A complex appliance is broken down into bits, or an industrial wire is split like ropes of licorice, and in the end, what’s left is a bundle of glistening amber.

The participants are diverse: Some are hobbyists or electricians looking for extra income. There are also people who claim to be saving for a big purchase, and others who appear to be cash-strapped teenagers. They speak a wide range of languages, including English, French, Spanish, German, and Romanian. At least one has an Etsy shop for selling hand-cast copper bricks, also known as ingots, which are made by pouring molten metal into molds.

Selling scrap copper is nothing new. The metal is relatively scarce, a strong electrical conductor, and fully recyclable—qualities that have made it a particularly valuable scrap metal for centuries. But copper prices reached an all-time high this year, making it an opportune moment for scrappers. In September, according to International Monetary Fund data, copper was worth about $14,473 per metric ton, or about $7.23 per pound, more than double what it was worth in September 2020.

While there’s no reliable data on how often people sell scrap copper, rates of copper theft—often involving metal taken from vehicles, plumbing, building roofs—may offer some clues. Craig Depken II, chair and professor of economics at the University of North Carolina, Charlotte, who has studied the phenomenon, says it tends to increase under two conditions.

The first is when the price of copper is increasing, much like it is now. The second is when people’s level of “economic distress” is high enough to make them believe the potential monetary benefits of stealing copper outweigh the risks of getting caught. (It’s legal to sell lawfully obtained copper everywhere in the US except Minnesota, which requires a state-issued license.)

Tech.title: LG B6 OLED TV Review (2026)
Tech.content:
The B6 comes with two legs that are easy to install (two screws each), though I generally prefer a single pedestal stand design. The 65-inch model I tested fit comfortably on two 38-inch IKEA SPIKSMED TV benches set side by side that measure 76 inches long.

Like all LG TVs, setup involves LG’s own WebOS interface or ThinQ app, not built-in Google TV or Fire TV. It was easy to complete the setup using the LG ThinQ app on my iPhone—in minutes, I was loading my usual assortment of apps like Prime Video, Disney+ and Apple TV+.

The B6 is packed with features too. A few of my favorites include a gaming mode that helps improve low latency gaming, AI picture enhancements that actually work and make a discernible difference, an artwork mode called LG Gallery+ that costs $5 per month, and an LG music app in case you don’t like Spotify or other music apps. It also has settings for audio dialogue sync, similar to what you can do with powered speakers like the Klipsch The Fives II. A desktop mode means you can mirror your laptop screen and even run a Gmail app.

Photograph: John Brandon

I have mixed feelings about WebOS, though. My main gripe is that you cannot disable the pointer on the LG remote, and it jumps around a lot. When you press the center dial on the remote, it turns off temporarily as though LG user interface designers are admitting it isn’t that great. I also have mixed feelings about the remote—it’s hard to use in the dark by feel. The Home button is offset so it’s hard to find, and shortcuts for Netflix and other apps are situated at the bottom, but not backlit.

OLED Strengths, OLED Weaknesses

Based on the pricing, it’s obvious LG has positioned the B6 as the entry-level OLED in their line-up. That became crystal clear once I started testing movies and TV shows.

In the official specs, LG only lists “wide color gamut” and not a percentage for the specific BT.2020 spec, nor a specific brightness rating. This is where the benchmark testing comes in handy, and what I tested right away.

Tech.title: Lykyn Review: A Mushroom Garden Worth Showing Off
Tech.content:
If your online algorithm detects your having even the slightest interest in growing mushrooms, you will, at some point, probably see an ad for the Lykyn. It looks like something out of a science fiction movie—a clear box with theatrical lighting, fog, and a giant mushroom displayed like an otherworldly specimen.

After trying the Lykyn myself for a month, I can confirm that it really does look like that in real life, and as someone who has tried many different mushroom-growing methods, I was impressed by how well the Lykyn worked as a legitimate fruiting chamber. The thing you’ll have to decide for yourself is whether it’s worth $300 to showcase a process that lasts only a week or two.

Photograph: Kat Merck

Some Assembly, Some Fog

Even though the company is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, Lykyn manufactures all fruiting chambers in Turkey and ships them straight from Istanbul for free. I worried about a delay, but my unit arrived in just 11 days, with none of the duty fees or other customs weirdness that seem to plague many overseas shipments these days. The speed was even more impressive given that I had the custom wood handle engraving add-on ($15), which puts your own text on the handle instead of “Lykyn.” (Mine had my name.)

Video: Kat Merck

The 13 x 13 x 15-inch unit, available in white or black plastic, arrives mostly disassembled—you will need to peel the protective film off both sides of each acrylic panel, slide them into plastic tracks on the base, add the corner posts, and fill the unit with distilled water. One panel doubles as a sliding door, and installing it was fiddly on my unit; I had to open and close it a few times to loosen it, and even now it still takes two hands to wrench it open. The Lykyn must be connected to 2.5-GHz Wi-Fi and a power source with its 5-volt USB-C cable (there is no provided brick), and the light—a little LED pad that sits on top—plugs into the base.

The only troubleshooting I had to do was with the ultrasonic humidifier, which emits an occasional cloud of fog (and is audible, but no louder than a typical humidifier), with extra humidity being pulled out by a fan. Despite my following directions, the mister produced no mist, and I kept getting notifications from the Lykyn app that the unit was out of water, despite the reservoir being visibly full. I eventually had to push the preinstalled wick farther down into its slot and “prime” the membrane on top with a little bit of water. (I later verified the Lykyn app’s humidity reading against my own hygrometer; the readings were similar within a couple of percentage points.) Other than refilling the water reservoir, the Lykyn needs no maintenance.

Brief but Spectacular Blooms

The Lykyn is a “smart” fruiting chamber, which means the humidity, airflow, and light schedules are controlled by settings for your specific species in the easy-to-use Lykyn app. There are also options to control these variables manually. (Note also that though the app shows the temperature, the Lykyn is not able to heat or cool.) While you can use any brand of fruiting block in the Lykyn up to 6 pounds, I tested my unit with the brand’s own 5-pound shiitake and pink oyster blocks, which came separately—no fruiting block is included with your Lykyn purchase. There are also no instructions on or with the blocks themselves, so be sure to check online for how yours needs to be prepared—some, like the shiitake, need to be taken totally out of their packaging, while others simply need an X cut into the side of the bag.

Having the block in versus out of the bag had a dramatic effect on the overall aesthetic of the Lykyn, which sat front and center in my dining room during the test. The bare shiitake block looked like a moon rock or quirky scientific specimen under the colorful lighting (which is customizable, but the default indicates the mushroom's “emotions," from green for “happy and thriving” to red for “stressed and worried”), while the black-bagged oyster mushroom block looked like … well, a black plastic bag. With the precisely controlled lighting and humidity, both mushroom blocks fruited within several days, compared with several weeks with other methods I’ve tried. This is especially impressive for shiitake, which are notoriously fussy in their requirements.

Tech.title: The Tragedy of Having a Wikipedia Page—and Then Losing It
Tech.content:
What do you need to know—need to know—about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff?

All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies—of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer—are purged from the world’s free encyclopedia.

It’s not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn’t have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav’s three singles is better spent—the logic goes—by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. “We’re not really looking for what’s true,” Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. “We’re looking for what’s verifiable.”

WIRED Ghost Stories Five hauntings from the other side of technology. Have a ghost story of your own? Share it in the comments below.

Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim. One person who recently lost her Wikipedia biography on notability grounds is Kimberly Small, the CEO of a Nevada nonprofit that supports survivors of sexual assault. The debate occurred in a public page on Wikipedia itself; it’s in that space that the really tricky decisions about what is and what isn’t good enough for the encyclopedia are made. One editor raised a question: “How should we judge not-for-profit executives? By the nature of their job, the focus is, as it should be, on the organization and the work the organization does, not them.” Another editor replied: “I don’t think there is anything wrong with not-for-profit executives being less often individually notable. Wikipedia coverage is not a prize.”

Is it not? “Having an article says something,” Gustafson admitted. “It implies something.” For six weeks over April and May, I reached out to hundreds of people who were about to lose their Wikipedia page, almost all of whom were learning that information from me. “If you want to write something to save the page, I would appreciate it,” a Spanish filmmaker told me. A biography on Wikipedia might not be intended as a prize, but nobody knows its value like the people who’ve had one and then lost it.

Martina Dimoska is a scientist, originally from North Macedonia, who works at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Specifically, Dimoska is an “analog astronaut”—she takes part in missions that simulate a space environment—and a “science communicator.” She posts often about her work in the can-do, aspirational register that is de rigueur on LinkedIn, where she cites her “recognition by … Forbes, Bloomberg, the United Nations … and global innovation networks.” A Facebook reel of hers, filmed during the crew announcement of NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission, shows Dimoska alongside the text, “When you work hard so you belong in rooms where history gets proactively written.” On TikTok, she’s had paid partnerships with a makeup brand whose products are tested for effectiveness during spaceflight.
