Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Just Passed 55,000 in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?
Tech.content:
Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched Friday and was met with long lines and product sellouts. We braved three hours at the Apple Store on Friday to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

Now the big question? How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 9:45 a.m. ET on Monday, we’ve just passed 55,000 folds.

The goal is simple. On Friday afternoon, my team and I loaded the iPhone Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube on Monday from 1-5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and ask questions about our iPhone Duo testing process.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

Tech.title: Meta Muse Makes Marketplace Better. How I Set It Up to Help Me Shop Online
Tech.content:
I have a to-buy list that I never seem to tackle. It’s got the kinds of “adult” items that aren’t necessarily fun to shop for, unlike clothes. Things like furniture, appliances and office equipment. But there are three items I need right now: an ottoman, an air purifier and a humidifier.

Our old ottoman broke, but I’m happy about it. It was dragged along from two previous apartments, and I’ve been wanting to replace it. The air purifier is also necessary, given we’re on the fifth floor and dust tends to cling to everything. With the radiators burning old dust, we’re constantly sneezing. I also promised myself I’d buy a humidifier last winter, so that’s also on the list.

In an effort to snag all three items second-hand, and given that Facebook Marketplace is basically a sport in my area, I put Meta Muse up to the task. I’ve used Muse for shopping and tech support before, but ran into roadblocks with payment and account verification. I had higher hopes using Muse for Marketplace, given it’s a Meta product.

More from CNET

Getting Muse set up

I’d previously used Muse from the chat interface, but this time I went to Ideas in the sidebar and clicked on the specific Marketplace prompt. It’s a recurring task rather than a one-off search.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

First, I gave it some parameters around what I was looking for, how far I could travel and what I wanted to pay: “I’m looking for three items: an ottoman, an air purifier and a humidifier. Ideally, in Montclair, NJ, but happy to travel to Manhattan for the air purifier or humidifier if needed. Price-wise, I’d like to pay around $150 for the ottoman, $50 for an air purifier and $50 for a humidifier.”

It immediately surfaced a few options, all within the price range, then noted that it would sweep Facebook Marketplace every 4 hours for new options, which is genuinely helpful.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

It even found the air purifier brand I had in mind, and surfaced one that was listed the day before by a five-star seller. For the humidifier, Muse found one in a town that’s hard to get to, so I gave it clearer geographical preferences.

The chat function was helpful, as I was able to ask Muse which brands and models were most expensive and what they retail for, with links to cross-check. What was also cool was Muse’s seller notes. It found a good humidifier in Manhattan, but warned that the seller is new.

I replied by instructing the agent to keep scanning locally as I wasn’t in a rush to buy the humidifier.

I told Muse I was ready to buy the air purifier, and it drafted a message to send to the seller. I made a few edit requests, connected my Messenger to the AI agent, and then Muse took over. I opened Messenger and saw that it had sent the message. Muse checks in every 30 minutes to see if the seller has replied, then notifies me.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

While I was waiting, I gave Muse more context around the ottoman. I was after a midcentury style, about the height of a standard lounge and large enough for two people to rest their feet on.

Muse surfaced plenty of options, but this search was less straightforward as it concerned a style choice, too. I pulled one example from the search that I liked and asked Muse for more options like it.

I quickly got through all of the inventory within a 5-mile radius, so I asked Muse to keep monitoring. It would notify me, or I could check in on the Goals tab or click on the Muse avatar and “Upcoming,” which lists every scheduled task.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I assigned Muse to do one more search – to see if my town had any affordable espresso machines or plastic-free coffee brewers. I have my eye on a model, but it’s $400, so I wanted to see what Muse could find.

I loved being able to follow up every find with “Tell me more about this product.” I instructed Muse to send another seller message with the coffee machine it found.

I was on a roll at this point. One last search: an air fryer, but non-toxic. Within minutes, I found one I liked, and Muse messaged them, too.

The verdict on Muse in Marketplace

I was pleasantly surprised by Muse’s Marketplace sweep. It was a much more dynamic experience, being able to narrow the search via the chat function, versus an endless scroll in Marketplace.

Muse scans active searches every 4 hours, which means I’m not missing listings. If a product sells or the seller doesn’t respond, it automatically searches for alternatives. To have this running in the background is super helpful.

It checks before replying to a seller, but I’d rather those messages be in my own voice anyway, and avoid sharing sensitive information with Muse (like my phone number or address). Muse did inform me of some price drops, but it wasn’t for the products I liked.

I saw a seller reply before Muse told me they did (as the agent scans every 30 minutes), so I took over the conversation manually from there. I was able to arrange a pickup — and my list of boring things to buy at last had one checkmark thanks largely to using Muse on Marketplace.

Tech.title: Canva Chases AI Domination With a New AI Image Model for Designers
Tech.content:
Canva is going deeper down the AI rabbit hole with the release of its first proprietary AI image model, called Canva Craft. It’s now available globally to all Canva users and is made specifically for designers.

This isn’t the first time Canva has added AI, to be sure. The beginner-friendly design program has been adding AI tools and third-party AI models for years. Its first take on creative AI, Magic Media, debuted in 2023. But Canva’s head of AI research, Stefano Corazza, told CNET that the company’s acquisition of Leonardo.Ai and internal ramp-up of AI research helped bolster its efforts to create its own AI image model, one made specifically for designers. Keeping all the AI tech in-house also helps the company keep cloud costs down and inference time quicker, Corazza said.

Canva Craft is meant for designers, and a big part of that is how the model actually works. The model has a two-stage architecture, the company said in a blog post. That means the model, combined with Canva’s behind-the-scenes prompt-improvement tools, can “reason” before generating a design. The model is trained on Canva’s library, licensed and public databases, and data from Canva users who opted in to training, Corazza said. The result is, ideally, more complex and comprehensive designs.

More from CNET

“[The AI] can actually create a whole plan for how the image is going to look like, all the layout. If you think about designers, that’s exactly what they do right when they create a design,” said Corazza. Designers carefully place elements to create a story. “Our model does basically the exact same thing. So we are mimicking exactly the design process.”

Early benchmarking results are positive. On DesignArena, Canva Craft is in fourth place overall for image models, trailing only OpenAI’s ChatGPT Images and beating bigwigs like Google’s Nano Banana and Microsoft’s MAI-Image models. Canva also ranks highly for generating portraits and product-focused imagery, though it trails in the marketing subcategory, which is where a lot of people use Canva.

The ability to edit AI outputs is a priority for Canva, and it’s an important one for anyone who uses AI tools. Often, no matter how perfect your AI prompt is, an image or video generator will spit out a result that is almost, but not quite, right. Canva has been tackling this problem with tools like its Magic Layers, which let you break down an AI design into its most basic elements and adjust them, a technologically complex process that solves a big problem for AI enthusiasts. Canva Craft builds on that foundation and lets you edit results.

Creative controversy

Creative AI tools are controversial, to put it mildly. Photographers, illustrators and artists have been calling out concerns for years about how AI is allegedly trained on their work in violation of copyright protections, used to create abusive material and being offered up to executives as a replacement for real artists. Creative companies from Adobe to Canva have maintained that AI is just a tool they want to offer their creators.

In an apt analogy of the current state of generative media, Eric Wittman, CEO of the popular photo editing and sharing platform VSCO, replied to Canva CEO Melanie Perkins’ LinkedIn post about Canva Craft and said that real photographers, not AI, will always rank No. 1 for portraits.

While executives argue over the best way to incorporate AI, photographers have to deal with AI headaches on every design platform, including VSCO. As AI models improve, it’s also forcing real creators to consistently verify their work as human-made, not AI-generated. But digital verification methods are sporadic, creating an even more complex web for creators to navigate.

Tech.title: As iPhone Duo Cracked Screen Reports Surface, a New Teardown Shows a Possible Culprit
Tech.content:
With reviews out in the world and real people getting their hands on it, you might assume there’s little left to say about the iPhone Duo that hasn’t already been said. But this is a long-awaited Apple product we’re talking about, and ongoing scrutiny of this show-stealer of a device is not just desirable; it’s pretty much mandatory.

This is because, while we’ve loved using the device so far and think Apple’s first attempt at a foldable is admirable, some early iPhone Duo owners have reported problems with the screen.

We’re currently conducting our own testing on the screen, folding the iPhone Duo 900 times per hour with a custom-made machine to see how long its hinge will last. At the time of writing, it had passed 55,000 folds without issue, but other people with a Duo haven’t been so lucky. Most commonly, people have reported issues with display cracks and lines of faulty pixels appearing along the hinge, according to MacRumors and Reddit.

More from CNET

As quickly as the faults have come to light, repairability experts at iFixit think they might already have discovered the culprit. Using teardown footage, patents and CT scans it collected while breaking down the iPhone Duo to ascertain its repairability score, iFixit built a 3D hinge model to identify where things could be going wrong.

What it found was that the breaks seemed to be occurring in the same place: just below the cable that connects the two screens, in a spot where a bunch of different connectors all meet.

“All those edges meeting in this spot mean lots of possible culprits,” iFixit’s Elizabeth Chamberlain wrote in a lengthy blog post. “That center pivot looks different from the rest of the hinge. Could it be getting stuck? Could something else be getting stuck?

“Here’s one possible answer. In our closing simulation … the center support bar fails to drop far enough. The screen’s curved fold comes down onto it, creating a small stress hotspot near the reported break location.”

iFixit has created an interactive CT scan that allows you to play around with the Duo and see how the hinge supports, cable and nearby components fit beneath the display.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the faults, but anyone experiencing issues with their iPhone Duo should be protected under warranty at this stage. Apple will charge $999 for inner screen replacement at a later date — whether that makes an AppleCare subscription a worthwhile investment is a choice only you can make.

The ‘most repairable foldable’

Any reports of screen problems are obviously bad news for Apple, but the company does also have reason to be proud of itself.

iFixit has declared the iPhone Duo “the most repairable foldable smartphone we’ve ever taken apart.” The phone has scored a 5/10 repairability rating, which might not be as impressive as the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max’s scores of 7/10, but still makes Apple the industry leader in terms of foldable repairability.

In its teardown, iFixit called out the trim surrounding the Duo’s screen as being particularly easy to pull away in contrast to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8’s trim, which “crumbled” as it was removed. The flat layout of the Duo’s components also garnered praise from iFixit. Being able to access components like the cameras and logic board without taking the whole device apart makes repairs simpler if any of those components require replacement.

iFixit praised the flat layout of the Duo’s internal components. iFixit/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

iFixit also praised Apple’s electrically releasable adhesive, which can be used to easily remove the battery by passing a low voltage through it. This is an innovative repair technology that Apple pioneered and is also used across its other devices. It allows the cells to be removed without any bending or prying that could result in a puncture risk to the battery.

Finally, a key part of making tech more repairable is ensuring that the companies making the products also make instruction manuals and official parts accessible to people — whether they’re doing the repairs themselves at home, or taking them to a third-party repair shop. iFixit is still awaiting official parts from Apple, but it praised the company for publishing its repair manual so quickly.

Major points were deducted for the hinge and inner display — both of which would be difficult and time-consuming to repair.

“For a first attempt, Apple has done well,” Chamberlain wrote. “The easy battery removal alone is something we’d like to see on every foldable. But of course we’ll hold Apple accountable for making replacement parts available, and here’s hoping that the next generation of the Duo features a more affordable inner display and a more accessible hinge repair.”

Tech.title: Here’s What Happens to Bacon When You Add Water While Cooking
Tech.content:
Charred and crisp, softer with a chewy middle: no matter how you cook your pork belly, bacon rules the roost among craveable breakfast meats. A handful of ways exist to make the salty strips, but a TikTok cooking hack that calls for a few ounces of water while cooking is making the rounds. The claim is that it even cooks the bacon, prevents dangerous oil splatters and keeps the meat from burning beyond recognition.

But does it work?

Though I’m a fan of the quick, easy, CNET-approved oven-baking technique and even speedier air fryer method, the water-cooked method allegedly renders the bacon’s fat slowly and consistently, resulting in uniform cooking, fewer splatters and even reduced sodium.

More from CNET

Not one to take social media’s word for it, I put the viral bacon hack to the test.

The water-cooked bacon trick

The technique couldn’t be simpler. Joey Skladany/CNET

The stovetop process is simple:

Place bacon slices in an oversized skillet so they lie flat. Add ¼ cup of water to the skillet and cook over medium heat. Allow the water to steam and evaporate. Once the water is gone, lower the heat to medium-low and cook the bacon until it reaches your desired crispiness. Remove the cooked bacon from the skillet and place on a paper towel to soak up excess oil.

I assumed the water would cause grease bombs, but it did the opposite. Joey Skladany/CNET

Ultimately, the water is said to suppress hot grease from popping violently and landing on stovetops or, more importantly, your skin. It also lets the meat cook low and slow before it fries in its own grease, rather than crisping immediately as the skillet heats up.

Water can also draw out some of the bacon’s sodium, which is ideal for those who find it too salty.

The results

The bacon turned out crisp with a slight chew. Joey Skladany/CNET

Color me shocked by the results: This cooking tip was executed flawlessly and lived up to the hype. The bacon strips were chewy yet crispy, with no bitter char, and cleanup took mere seconds with a quick wipe with a sponge and towel. (Pro tip: Reserve the leftover bacon grease to cook everything, from vegetables to rice, for added flavor.)

My only gripe was that it took a few minutes longer than using an oven or cast-iron skillet. And, frankly, the cleanup of pesky splatters would far surpass the time it takes to cook with water, at least with the latter tool.

TikTok cooking tips are a mixed bag, but this bacon hack proved itself a winner. Joey Skladany/CNET

In an industry full of gimmicks and unverifiable shortcuts, it’s nice to sift through the culinary fluff and find something that actually works, especially with an ingredient as universally beloved as bacon. The fact that this trick has trended on TikTok is just a footnote and proof that social media sometimes gets it right.

Hungry for more tips? Here’s how to recycle frying oil, plus a neat trick for degreasing a frying pan before washing.

Tech.title: Apple’s New iPad Mini Gets OLED and Water Resistance
Tech.content:
The new iPhone Duo, unfolded, almost feels like an iPad Mini. But if you want the real thing, Apple also has a new iPad Mini coming on Nov. 6. The upgrade, which starts at $699, adds a larger OLED screen and water resistance for the first time.

The new iPad Mini has been expected for months, and it was announced two days ahead of an expected showcase of new Macs on Wednesday. It has a number of updates this time around, making it look, on paper, like a killer upgrade for anyone who’s been waiting for one. Unfortunately, it’s also more expensive than before.

One of the two new iPad Mini colors, midnight. Apple

The $699 starting price comes with 128GB of storage, with 256 and 512GB options that are $799 and $999. Compared to the last iPad Mini, which came out two years ago, the new one has an A20 processor (upgraded from A17), but also has a larger display (8.5 inches compared to the older one’s 8.3) that’s also OLED for the first time. The front-facing camera’s also been shifted to the landscape edge, matching the other iPads and making it more centered for video chats if you’re standing it on a table in a case.

More from CNET

It’s thinner and lighter than before, but also is the first iPad that’s water-resistant (IP67), which means it could survive pool, ocean or tub dunks. There’s a through-screen speaker system on this model, too, which I’m curious to try. It’s called Acoustic Display.

The Mini’s available to order on Oct. 28, and is going on sale Nov. 6. We’ll have more thoughts when I eventually get to review one, but for anyone who’s wanted a new Mini and didn’t want to spring for a Duo this iPad looks like good news.
